source: IoT Security - Ch1
question: IoT (Internet of Things)
answer: Network of physical objects embedded with sensors, software, and connectivity enabling data exchange over internet. Three layers: Perception (sensors), Network (connectivity), Application (processing). IoT devices constrained in power, memory, and processing.

source: IoT Security - IoT Protocols
question: MQTT (Message Queue Telemetry Transport)
answer: Lightweight publish/subscribe messaging protocol for IoT (ISO 20922). Uses broker architecture, TCP port 1883. QoS levels: 0 (at most once), 1 (at least once), 2 (exactly once). Minimal packet overhead (2-byte header). Ideal for constrained devices.

source: IoT Security - IoT Protocols
question: CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol)
answer: RESTful protocol for constrained IoT devices (RFC 7252). UDP-based with reliability via CON/NON messages. Four message types: CON (confirmable), NON (non-confirmable), ACK (acknowledgment), RST (reset). Uses GET/PUT/POST/DELETE like HTTP. Supports observation and resource discovery.

source: IoT Security - IoT Protocols
question: 6LoWPAN (IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks)
answer: Adaptation layer enabling IPv6 over IEEE 802.15.4 (RFC 4944). Fragmentation: 1280-byte IPv6 packet over 127-byte MAC frames. Header compression (HC1, IPHC) reduces IPv6/UDP headers from 48 to ~7 bytes. Supports mesh networking.

source: IoT Security - IoT Protocols
question: RPL (IPv6 Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks)
answer: Distance-vector routing protocol for LLNs (RFC 6550). Builds DODAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) using objective functions. Supports multipoint-to-point, point-to-multipoint, point-to-point traffic. Uses trickle timer for control message suppression.

source: IoT Security - IoT Protocols
question: IEEE 802.15.4
answer: Standard for low-rate wireless personal area networks (LR-WPANs). Defines PHY/MAC layers. Data rates: 20-250 kbps. Range: 10-100m. 16-bit/64-bit addressing. Superframe structure with beacon mode. Used by ZigBee, 6LoWPAN, Thread, Zigbee IP.

source: IoT Security - LPWAN
question: LPWAN (Low-Power Wide-Area Network)
answer: Wireless technology for long-range, low-power IoT. Range: 2-15 km (urban), 15-40 km (rural). Battery life: 10+ years. Data rate: 0.3-50 kbps. Technologies: LoRaWAN (unlicensed ISM bands), NB-IoT (licensed LTE bands), Sigfox (ultra-narrowband). Ideal for smart city sensors.

source: IoT Security - LPWAN
question: LoRaWAN
answer: MAC layer protocol for LoRA (Long Range) physical layer. Star-of-stars topology: end devices → gateways → network server. Device classes: A (lowest power, bidirectional), B (scheduled receive slots), C (continuous receive, highest power). AES-128 encryption (NwkSKey, AppSKey).

source: IoT Security - Ch2/3/4
question: Sybil Attack
answer: Malicious node creates multiple fake identities to subvert network. Impacts: voting systems, reputation systems, routing protocols, resource allocation. Detection: radio resource testing, identity verification, position verification. In vehicular networks: can simulate multiple vehicles to cause traffic disruption.

source: IoT Security - IoT Attacks
question: Black Hole Attack
answer: Malicious node drops all received packets instead of forwarding. Disrupts network routing. In IoT/RPL: node advertises low rank to attract traffic, then drops packets. Detection: sequence number monitoring, ACK analysis, watchdog nodes.

source: IoT Security - IoT Attacks
question: Wormhole Attack
answer: Two colluding attackers tunnel packets between distant network regions. Makes nodes believe they are neighbors when they are not. Disrupts routing topology. Impractical for localized detection due to private tunnel. Defense: packet leashes (geographic/temporal), directional antennas.

source: IoT Security - IoT Attacks
question: Hello Flood Attack
answer: Attacker broadcasts high-power HELLO messages to convince all nodes it's their neighbor. Nodes attempt to route through attacker causing data loss or eavesdropping. Common in WSN routing protocols using HELLO for neighbor discovery. Defense: bidirectional link verification, geographic routing.

source: IoT Security - Ch4: Malware
question: IoT Malware Propagation Models
answer: Epidemiological models adapted for IoT. SI (Susceptible-Infected): basic propagation. SIR (Susceptible-Infected-Recovered): includes recovery. SIS: reinfection possible. SEIR: includes exposed (latent) phase. Factors: patch rate, infection rate, network topology. Mirai botnet used SIP-based propagation.

source: IoT Security - Ch4: Malware
question: Mirai Botnet
answer: IoT malware (2016) that infected hundreds of thousands of devices (DVRs, cameras, routers). Scanned for telnet/SSH with default credentials. Used for massive DDoS attacks (620 Gbps against Krebs, 1.1 Tbps against Dyn). Source code released publicly leading to many variants.

source: IoT Security - Ch4: Malware
question: IoT Malware Defense Strategies
answer: Network segmentation: isolate IoT devices from critical systems. Firmware updates: automatic patching via OTA. Anomaly detection: ML-based traffic analysis. Device authentication: certificate-based identity. Least privilege: minimize device permissions. Honeypots: decoy IoT devices to detect scanning.

source: IoT Security - Ch5: Smart Home
question: Smart Home Attack Vectors
answer: Attack surfaces in smart homes: 1) Cloud interface (weak authentication, API vulnerabilities), 2) Mobile app (insecure storage, reverse engineering), 3) Device firmware (unencrypted, unsigned updates), 4) Network traffic (lack of encryption, MQTT without TLS), 5) Physical access (debug ports, JTAG). Defense: defense-in-depth, regular updates.

source: IoT Security - Ch5: Smart Home
question: ZigBee Security
answer: Wireless protocol for home automation (IEEE 802.15.4). Security: 128-bit AES-CCM at MAC layer. Key types: master key (pre-shared), link key (device-to-device), network key (broadcast). ZigBee 3.0: mandatory security, centralized key management. Vulnerabilities: sniffing (if key extracted), physical attacks.

source: IoT Security - Ch10: Trust Models
question: Trust Models for IoT
answer: Frameworks for establishing trust between IoT entities. Direct trust: based on past interactions. Indirect trust: recommendations from other nodes. Types: centralized (trust authority), distributed (peer-to-peer), hybrid. Metrics: honesty, cooperativeness, energy level, data consistency. Subjective logic: opinions with belief/disbelief/uncertainty.

source: IoT Security - Ch10: Trust Models
question: Bayesian Trust Model
answer: Probabilistic trust model using Beta distribution. Represents reputation as Beta(α, β) where α = successful interactions + 1, β = failed interactions + 1. Expected trust = α/(α+β). Updates dynamically with each interaction. Forgetting factor: older interactions weighted less. Suitable for IoT due to low computational cost.

source: IoT Security - Ch9: WBSN
question: Lightweight Cryptography for IoT
answer: Cryptographic algorithms optimized for constrained devices (low power, memory, gates). PRESENT: 64-bit block, 80/128-bit key, 31 rounds (2500 GE). SPECK/SIMON: NSA-designed, extremely lightweight (SIMON: 1234 GE). CHAM: Korean standard for IoT. TWINE: 64-bit block. Applications: RFID tags, sensor nodes, medical implants.

source: IoT Security - Ch9: WBSN
question: Physical Unclonable Function (PUF)
answer: Hardware security primitive generating unique device fingerprint from manufacturing variations. Challenge-response pairs (CRP): device-specific output for each input. Types: SRAM PUF (power-on state of SRAM cells), Arbiter PUF (path delay difference), Ring Oscillator PUF (oscillation frequency variation). Applications: device authentication, key generation, anti-counterfeiting.

source: IoT Security - Ch13: Authentication
question: IoT Authentication Mechanisms
answer: Methods to verify IoT device/user identity. Types: 1) Certificate-based (X.509 PKI — high overhead), 2) Pre-shared key (PSK — simple, scalable), 3) PUF-based (hardware fingerprint), 4) Biometric (for human users), 5) Multi-factor. DTLS handshake overhead problematic for constrained devices. ECC-based certificates preferred for IoT.

source: IoT Security - Ch13: Authentication
question: DTLS (Datagram Transport Layer Security)
answer: TLS variant for UDP-based IoT protocols (CoAP, MQTT-SN). Provides encryption, authentication, integrity over unreliable transport. Handshake: 3-4 round trips (high overhead for constrained devices). Solutions: session resumption, cached information extension, pre-shared key cipher suites. DTLS 1.3 (RFC 9147): reduced latency, 1-RTT handshake.

source: IoT Security - Ch6/15: Privacy
question: Differential Privacy
answer: Privacy framework ensuring output of analysis does not reveal individual data. Adds calibrated noise (Laplace/Gaussian mechanism) to query results. Epsilon (ε): privacy budget — lower ε = stronger privacy. In IoT: aggregate sensor data without revealing individual readings. Trade-off: privacy vs accuracy.

source: IoT Security - Ch6/15: Privacy
question: Homomorphic Encryption
answer: Encryption scheme allowing computation on ciphertext without decryption. Result encrypted, decrypt matches computation on plaintext. Types: Partially HE (either addition OR multiplication), Somewhat HE (limited operations), Fully HE (arbitrary computation — slow). In IoT: privacy-preserving data aggregation without exposing individual readings.

source: IoT Security - Ch12: Access Control
question: IoT Access Control Models
answer: Frameworks controlling who can access sensor data and actuate devices. RBAC: role-based (admin, user, viewer). ABAC: attribute-based (time, location, device type). Capability-based: token granting specific access rights. Usage Control (UCON): decision based on mutable attributes (e.g., remaining credit). OAuth 2.0: delegated authorization framework for IoT APIs.

source: IoT Security - Ch3: Vehicular
question: Vehicular Network Security Requirements
answer: V2V/V2I communication security needs: 1) Authentication — verify vehicle identity (PKI-based, IEEE 1609.2), 2) Message integrity — prevent tampering (ECDSA signatures), 3) Non-repudiation — sender can't deny (digital signatures), 4) Privacy — pseudonyms to prevent tracking, 5) Low latency — <100ms for safety messages. DSRC/WAVE (802.11p) vs C-V2X (LTE/5G).

source: IoT Security - Ch18: Governance
question: Decentralized IoT Trust Management
answer: Blockchain/DLT-based trust for IoT without central authority. Smart contracts automate trust decisions. Identity: self-sovereign identity (SSI) on blockchain. Attribute verification: zero-knowledge proofs. Use cases: supply chain, smart grid, multi-domain IoT. Challenges: transaction throughput (blockchain limits), energy consumption (PoW), storage overhead.

source: IoT Security - Ch18: Governance
question: Fog Computing for IoT
answer: Decentralized computing infrastructure between cloud and IoT devices. Reduces latency, bandwidth usage, and cloud dependency. Security functions at fog node: local authentication, data filtering, anomaly detection, policy enforcement. Fog node: edge router, gateway, or dedicated server. Three-layer architecture: IoT → Fog → Cloud.

question: k-Anonymity
answer: Privacy model: each record in anonymized dataset indistinguishable from at least k-1 other records. Quasi-identifiers (age, zip, gender) generalized until each combination appears ≥ k times. Weaknesses: homogeneity attack (all k records have same value), background knowledge attack. Extensions: l-diversity (diverse sensitive values), t-closeness (distribution close to overall).

source: IoT Security - Ch6
question: l-Diversity
answer: Extension of k-anonymity ensuring each equivalence class has at least l well-represented values for each sensitive attribute. Types: distinct l-diversity (l distinct values), entropy l-diversity (entropy ≥ log(l)), recursive (c,l)-diversity (most frequent value not too frequent). Prevents homogeneity and background knowledge attacks. Limitation: may be hard to achieve with skewed distributions.

question: t-Closeness
answer: Privacy model requiring distribution of sensitive attribute in each equivalence class close to its global distribution (difference ≤ threshold t). Uses Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to measure distribution dissimilarity. Numerical attributes: EMD based on distance between values. Categorical: EMD based on hierarchical distance. Stronger than k-anonymity and l-diversity against attribute disclosure.

question: Beta Distribution Trust Update
answer: Trust represented as Beta(α, β). Update rule on positive interaction: α' = α + 1 + λ (weight). Update on negative interaction: β' = β + 1 + λ. Forgetting factor: α ← α·φ, β ← β·φ (0 < φ < 1, older interactions weighted less). Expected trust E = α/(α+β). Variance V = αβ/[(α+β)²(α+β+1)] — high variance = high uncertainty.

question: Attribute-Based Encryption (ABE) for IoT
answer: Encryption scheme where ciphertext/keys are associated with attributes (role, time, location, device type). CP-ABE (Ciphertext-Policy): data encrypted with access policy (e.g., 'role:doctor AND location:hospital'). User key has attributes — decrypt if attributes satisfy policy. KP-ABE (Key-Policy): attributes on ciphertext, policy in user key. IoT benefit: one-to-many encrypted data sharing without re-encryption per user.

source: IoT Security - Ch12
question: Usage Control (UCON)
answer: Extended access control model with mutable attributes and continuity decisions (ISO/IEC 22600). UCONABC: Authorizations (pre-decision), oBligations (post-decision), Conditions (contextual), mutable Attributes (updated during access). Example: view medical record only if patient has remaining data allowance, decremented per access. Application: IoT metered data services, time-limited emergency access.

source: IoT Security - Ch12
question: OAuth 2.0 for IoT Device Authorization
answer: Authorization framework adapted for IoT. Device Authorization Grant (RFC 8628): device shows code on-screen → user authorizes via browser → device polls for token. OAuth 2.0 Device Flow: no browser on device needed. Token scopes limit device access. Client credentials grant for device-to-cloud. ACE (Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments — RFC 9200): DTLS-based OAuth for CoAP.

source: IoT Security - Ch12
question: Sensor Data Access Policy Enforcement
answer: Policy enforcement mechanisms for IoT access control. PEP (Policy Enforcement Point): intercepts access requests. PDP (Policy Decision Point): evaluates access policy. PAP (Policy Administration Point): policy management. PIP (Policy Information Point): attribute data sources. XACML (eXtensible Access Control Markup Language) for policy specification. Lightweight XACML profiles for IoT.

source: IoT Security - Ch12
question: Capability Token Revocation
answer: Methods to revoke capabilities before expiry: 1) Token blacklist — resource checks list (requires connectivity). 2) Token validity period — short-lived tokens (reduced revocation latency). 3) Onion tokens — recursive revocation (revoke parent invalidates children). 4) Capability recursion — node can delegate sub-capabilities. 5) Blockchain — revocation recorded on-chain.

source: IoT Security - Ch13
question: Fundamentals of Authentication
answer: Three factors: 1) Knowledge (password, PIN, passphrase). 2) Possession (token, smart card, phone). 3) Inherence (fingerprint, iris, voice). Multi-factor authentication (MFA): use ≥2 factors. IoT challenges: limited input (no keyboard), limited processing (slow hash). Approaches: lightweight protocols, hardware-backed (PUF, TPM), certificate chain verification optimization.

source: IoT Security - Ch13
question: Kerberos-based IoT Authentication
answer: Adaptation of Kerberos for IoT. KDC (Key Distribution Center) issues tickets. IoT client requests TGT (Ticket-Granting Ticket) with pre-shared key. Uses ticket for service access without re-authentication. Advantages: single sign-on, mutual authentication. Challenges: KDC availability (needs always-online AS), clock synchronization requirement, ticket overhead for constrained devices.

source: IoT Security - Ch13
question: PKI-based IoT Authentication
answer: X.509 certificate chain. CA (Certificate Authority) issues device certificates. Device presents certificate to authenticator. Path validation: certificate chain → trusted root. Certificate types: IEC 62351 (smart grid), IEEE 1609.2 (vehicular — compressed certificates). Challenges: revocation (CRL/OCSP overhead), certificate storage (constrained flash), handshake latency (TLS full handshake >10KB). Solutions: raw public key (RFC 7250), cached certs, session tickets.

source: IoT Security - Ch13
question: PUF-based Authentication Protocol
answer: Challenge-Response Authentication using PUF. Enrollment phase: server collects CRPs (Challenge-Response Pairs) from each device. Authentication phase: server sends random challenge → device computes PUF(C) → server verifies against stored response. Properties: unique (manufacturing variation), unclonable (cannot duplicate from design data), tamper-evident. Attack: ML modeling (if CRPs linear, can be predicted). Countermeasure: CRP obfuscation, hashing.

source: IoT Security - Ch13
question: Two-Factor Authentication for IoT
answer: Combinations: 1) Device factor + User factor — require device cert + user password/biometric. 2) Device factor + Location factor — require device cert + GPS proximity. 3) Time-based OTP + PSK — TOTP (RFC 6238) on second device. 4) PUF + PIN — first use PUF response as key derivation then verify PIN. Implementation: constrained devices may offload second factor verification to gateway.

source: IoT Security - Ch13
question: Group Authentication in IoT
answer: Authenticate multiple IoT devices simultaneously. Batch verification: verify n signatures with < n cost (ECDSA batch verification: about 2× faster per additional signature). Group signatures: any group member can sign on group's behalf. Ring signatures: signer anonymous within group. Threshold signatures: t-of-n group members must sign. Use cases: firmware update authenticity (group attestation), consensus-based decisions.

source: IoT Security - Ch13
question: Mutual Authentication for IoT
answer: Both parties verify each other's identity. Device verifies server (cloud/gateway) before sending data. Server verifies device before granting access. DTLS with certificates (both sides): mutual auth via CertificateRequest/CertificateVerify. PSK-based: both sides prove knowledge of same PSK. Lightweight mutual auth: one message (combined identity proof + freshness nonce). Prevents MITM during initial handshake.

source: IoT Security - Ch14
question: Computational Security for IoT
answer: Security based on computational hardness assumptions (not information-theoretic security). Adversary limited to polynomial-time computation. Security parameter λ determines key sizes. IoT implications: lightweight primitives match computational budget. Trade-off: security level vs. device resources. Quantifiable security: bit security (2^k operations required for break).

source: IoT Security - Ch14
question: Lattice-Based Cryptography for IoT
answer: Post-quantum cryptography based on lattice problems (Learning With Errors — LWE, Ring-LWE). Advantages: resistant to quantum attacks (Shor's algorithm), efficient operations (polynomial multiplication), parallelizable. NIST PQC standardization: CRYSTALS-Kyber (KEM), CRYSTALS-Dilithium (signatures). Key sizes: ~1KB (Kyber-512) — larger than ECC but small enough for many IoT devices.

source: IoT Security - Ch14
question: Hash-Based Signatures (HBS) for IoT
answer: Post-quantum signature scheme using hash functions (no number-theoretic assumptions). LMS (Leighton-Micali, RFC 8554): stateful, one-time signature chains. XMSS (eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme, RFC 8391): hash trees for multi-signature. Advantages: quantum-resistant, simple operations (only hash function needed). Limitation: stateful (must track used keys). Suitable for firmware signing.

source: IoT Security - Ch14
question: Physical Layer Security (PLS)
answer: Security exploiting physical layer characteristics (no cryptographic computation). Channel-based key generation: RSSI (Received Signal Strength) variation → shared secret bits between two devices. Secret key rate: bits/second extracted from channel fluctuations. Eavesdropper at different location sees uncorrelated channel. Confidentiality: beamforming (direct signal to intended receiver). Authentication: RF fingerprint (distinct transmitter hardware characteristics).

source: IoT Security - Ch14
question: Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) for IoT
answer: Hardware-isolated secure environment on main processor. ARM TrustZone: secure world (TEE) and normal world (OS). Trusted apps run in secure world, can't be accessed from normal world. IoT use cases: secure key storage, secure boot, attestation, secure firmware update. TEE vs SE (Secure Element): TEE uses main CPU (lower cost), SE dedicated chip (higher security). GlobalPlatform TEE standards.

source: IoT Security - Ch14
question: Side-Channel Attack Countermeasures
answer: Side-channel attacks exploiting physical emanations: 1) Power analysis — monitor power consumption (simple SPA, differential DPA). Countermeasures: constant-time operations, power-balancing (dual-rail logic), dummy operations. 2) Timing — data-dependent execution time. Countermeasure: constant-time code (no secret-dependent branches). 3) EM emanations — electromagnetic radiation. Countermeasure: EM shielding, randomized clock.

source: IoT Security - Ch15
question: Privacy-Preserving Time Series Aggregation
answer: Aggregating time-series IoT data (smart meters, temperature sensors) without exposing individual readings. Sliding window aggregation: sum/avg over time window. Privacy: Paillier homomorphic encryption (additive). Each sensor encrypts reading: c_i = E(m_i). Aggregator computes E(Σ m_i) = Π c_i without decrypting. Only final aggregate decrypted by authorized entity.

source: IoT Security - Ch15
question: Additive Homomorphic Encryption (Paillier)
answer: Public-key cryptosystem with additive homomorphism: E(m1)·E(m2) = E(m1+m2). Encryption: c = g^m · r^n mod n². n = p·q (RSA modulus). Security: decisional composite residuosity assumption. IoT use: smart meter aggregation. Limitation: ciphertext expansion (2× plaintext size). Performance: expensive exponentiation on constrained devices.

source: IoT Security - Ch15
question: Concealed Data Aggregation (CDA)
answer: End-to-end encryption in WSN where aggregator computes on encrypted data. Sensors encrypt readings with homomorphic scheme. Aggregator computes sum/average on ciphertext (without knowing sensor keys). Base station decrypts only aggregate. Advantages: privacy even if aggregator compromised. Extensions: C-MAC (Concealed Message Authentication Code) verifies aggregate integrity.

source: IoT Security - Ch15
question: Differential Privacy for IoT Aggregation
answer: Privacy-preserving aggregation with noise addition. Laplace mechanism: add Lap(Δf/ε) noise to query result. Δf = sensitivity (max change from one record). ε = privacy budget (lower = stronger privacy). Concentrated DP (zCDP): tighter bounds for iterative queries. Composition: multiple queries consume ε budget (sequential composition: Σ εi). IoT: adding noise to aggregated power readings before sending to grid operator.

source: IoT Security - Ch15
question: Slicing and Mixing Privacy
answer: Data obfuscation by slicing and shuffling. Each sensor splits reading into s slices (secret addition). Slices shuffled with slices from other sensors. Recipient reconstructs by summing slices: Σ m_i = Σ slices. Without knowledge of slice-sensor mapping, individual readings concealed. Slice size: smaller → more mixing partners → stronger privacy. Slice overhead grows linearly.

source: IoT Security - Ch16
question: Green IoT Security
answer: Energy-efficient security mechanisms for sustainable IoT. Goals: minimize security computation energy while maintaining protection. Metrics: mJ per authenticated bit, security energy overhead %. Techniques: 1) Adaptive security (adjust crypto strength by context). 2) Energy-harvesting powered security (harvest energy for crypto operations). 3) Duty-cycled security (sleep during idle, wake for critical events).

source: IoT Security - Ch16
question: Secure Path Generation for Green IoT
answer: Routing path selection considering both energy efficiency and security. Path metrics: residual energy, link quality, security level. Multi-objective optimization: minimize energy consumption AND maximize path security. Security level: encryption strength, authentication overhead, trust score of intermediate nodes. Dynamic adaptation: adjust path when energy low or attack detected.

source: IoT Security - Ch16
question: Energy-Efficient Cryptographic Hardware
answer: Cryptographic hardware optimized for low energy. ASIC (Application-Specific IC): highest efficiency, fixed function (0.5-2 µJ per AES operation). FPGA (Field-Programmable Gate Array): reconfigurable, moderate efficiency (1-5 µJ). MCU with crypto accelerator: AES-NI instruction set (0.2 µJ per AES operation on Cortex-M). Dynamic voltage/frequency scaling (DVFS): reduce energy by 40% at lower voltage.

source: IoT Security - Ch16
question: Energy Harvesting Security Constraints
answer: Energy harvesting devices (solar, vibration, thermal) have intermittent power. Computation may be interrupted mid-operation (state must be saved). Security operations must be atomic (encrypt/decrypt cannot be interrupted without data corruption). Power-failure-resistant crypto: save intermediate state to non-volatile memory before power loss. Checkpoint-aware crypto design.

source: IoT Security - Ch16
question: Green IoT Protocol Stack
answer: Energy-aware security across IoT stack. PHY: adaptive modulation (lower rate = lower energy). MAC: duty cycle (99% sleep), secure preamble (Schweitzer protocol). NET: energy-aware routing (RPL with ETX metric). APP: CoAP observe (server pushes, reduces polling). Security: DTLS 1.3 session resumption (0-RTT reduces handshake energy). Cross-layer optimization: security parameters shared between layers.

source: IoT Security - Ch16
question: Energy Attack (Battery Depletion)
answer: Attack draining IoT device battery to disrupt availability. Methods: 1) Sleep deprivation — keep device awake by repeated requests. 2) Jamming — force repeated transmissions. 3) Complex handshake — initiate expensive DTLS handshakes repeatedly. 4) Amplified computation — send work (e.g., hash calculations) to device. Defense: rate limiting, energy budget per source, lightweight authentication before accepting work.

source: IoT Security - Ch17
question: IoT Access Network Security
answer: Security technologies connecting IoT devices to access networks (LTE, 5G, WiFi, LoRa). LTE-M (Cat-M1): 1.4 MHz bandwidth, mobility support, VoLTE. NB-IoT: 200 kHz, ultra-low power, massive connections. 5G NR in mMTC (massive Machine-Type Communication): 1 million devices/km², <10µs synchronization, network slicing for security isolation.

source: IoT Security - Ch17
question: 5G Network Slicing for IoT Security
answer: Virtual network slices isolated for different IoT services. eMBB (enhanced Mobile Broadband): high bandwidth (video surveillance). URLLC (Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency): <1ms latency (industrial control). mMTC (massive Machine-Type): massive connections (sensors). Security isolation: slice-specific encryption, authentication, firewall policies. Inter-slice communication: controlled via NSSF (Network Slice Selection Function).

source: IoT Security - Ch17
question: EPS-AKA (Evolved Packet System Authentication and Key Agreement)
answer: LTE authentication protocol (3GPP TS 33.401). UE (device) ↔ HSS (Home Subscriber Server) authentication. Vectors: RAND (random challenge), AUTN (authentication token), XRES (expected response), KASME (derived key). Mutual authentication: UE verifies AUTN (validates network), network verifies RES matches XRES. Key hierarchy: K → CK/IK → KASME → NAS/AS keys. IoT concern: signaling overhead (frequent authentication drains battery).

source: IoT Security - Ch17
question: 5G-AKA vs EPS-AKA
answer: 5G authentication (5G-AKA, 3GPP TS 33.501) improvements: 1) SUPI (Subscription Permanent Identifier) encrypted as SUCI (Subscription Concealed Identifier) — prevents IMSI catching. 2) HN (Home Network) key confirmation — prevents fake base station attacks. 3) Extended Master Session Key (EMS-K) segmentation — separate keys for different network slices. 4) Secondary authentication — EAP-based for enterprise IoT.

source: IoT Security - Ch17
question: WiFi IoT Security (WPA3)
answer: WiFi Protected Access 3 for IoT devices (IEEE 802.11-2016 amendment). SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals — Dragonfly handshake): replaces WPA2-PSK (4-way handshake) with password-authenticated key exchange (resists offline dictionary attacks). OWE (Opportunistic Wireless Encryption, RFC 8110): encrypted open networks. 192-bit security mode for enterprise. IoT constraint: SAE computation heavy for low-end devices (fractional SAE possible).

source: IoT Security - Ch17
question: LoRaWAN Security
answer: LoRaWAN (Long Range Wide Area Network) security architecture (LoRa Alliance). Two layers: 1) Network security (NwkSKey) — MIC verification, frame counters. 2) Application security (AppSKey) — payload encryption (AES-128 CTR). Join procedure: OTAA (Over-The-Air Activation) — device sends Join-Request → network server verifies AppKey → sends Join-Accept with session keys. ABP (Activation By Personalization) — pre-configured keys (less secure).

source: IoT Security - Ch18
question: User-Centric Decentralised Governance Framework
answer: Privacy and trust management where user controls their IoT data. Components: 1) Identity management — self-sovereign identity (SSI). 2) Policy manager — user-defined data sharing rules. 3) Consent manager — explicit consent per data use. 4) Audit log — transparent data access logging. 5) Enforcement — automated policy enforcement (smart contracts). Architecture: blockchain-anchored distributed governance nodes.

source: IoT Security - Ch18
question: Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) for IoT
answer: Decentralized identity model where user/device owns identity without central issuer. DIDs (Decentralized Identifiers, W3C): DID method (e.g., did:iot:0x1234). DID Document: public keys, service endpoints. Verifiable Credentials (VCs): attestations from issuers (manufacturer certifies device type). Holder (device) presents VC, verifier checks issuer signature + revocation status (no central registry needed).

source: IoT Security - Ch18
question: Smart Contract for IoT Trust Management
answer: Blockchain-based smart contracts automating trust decisions. Functions: 1) Device registration — store device identity and attestation. 2) Trust scoring — update reputation based on interactions. 3) Access control — enforce data sharing policies. 4) Dispute resolution — adjudicate SLA violations. 5) Reward/punish — token incentives for honest behavior. Ethereum/IOTA/Hyperledger. Challenge: transaction cost (gas) for frequent updates.

source: IoT Security - Ch18
question: Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKP) for IoT Privacy
answer: Proof that statement is true without revealing evidence. ZKP types: 1) zk-SNARK (Succinct Non-interactive Argument of Knowledge) — short proof, fast verification, trusted setup required. 2) zk-STARK (Scalable Transparent ARgument of Knowledge) — no trusted setup, larger proof. IoT use: prove device firmware is authentic (without revealing firmware hash). Prove sensor reading is in valid range without revealing value.

source: IoT Security - Ch18
question: Blockchain Scalability for IoT
answer: Challenges of blockchain for massive IoT: 1) TPS throughput — Bitcoin 7 TPS, Ethereum 15-30 TPS vs millions of devices. 2)Transaction latency — 10 min+ (Bitcoin) vs real-time requirement. 3) Storage — full node >500 GB vs constrained devices. 4) Energy — PoW >300TWh/year vs green IoT. Solutions: IOTA Tangle (DAG-based, no fees, scalable), Hyperledger Fabric (permissioned, high TPS), sharding, rollups.

source: IoT Security - Ch18
question: Accountability and Audit in IoT
answer: Mechanisms for holding entities responsible for actions. Logging: immutable audit trail (blockchain-anchored). Provenance: track data origin and transformations. Chain of custody: documenting data handling through IoT pipeline. Non-repudiation: digital signatures prevent denial. Forensic readiness: sufficient logging for post-incident investigation. Data protection impact assessment (DPIA) for GDPR compliance.

source: IoT Security - Ch19
question: Informed Consent in IoT
answer: Process of obtaining explicit user permission for data collection and processing. GDPR requirements: 1) Specific — purpose clearly stated. 2) Informed — what data, who processes, retention. 3) Unambiguous — clear affirmative action (not pre-ticked boxes). 4) Withdrawable — easy to revoke. IoT challenge: how to present consent on headless device (no screen). Solutions: companion app, QR code to web form, audio consent.

source: IoT Security - Ch19
question: Policy-Based Consent Management
answer: Formal policy language for expressing data sharing consent. XACML profile for consent: subject (user), action (collect/process/share), resource (sensor data type), conditions (time, location, purpose). ODRL (Open Digital Rights Language, W3C): standard for expressing permissions and obligations. Example: 'Allow temperature sensor data collection for heating optimization only during winter months, revocable anytime.'

source: IoT Security - Ch19
question: Consent Lifecycle Management
answer: Stages of consent: 1) Collection — obtain consent record (who, what, when, how). 2) Storage — immutable consent log (blockchain for integrity). 3) Enforcement — verify consent before processing data. 4) Review — user can view current consents. 5) Update — user changes preferences. 6) Withdrawal — revoke consent, stop processing (delete data). 7) Expiry — time-limited consent auto-exit.

source: IoT Security - Ch19
question: Consent Receipt
answer: Standardized record of granted consent (Kantara Initiative Consent Receipt Specification V1.1). Fields: consent receipt ID, jurisdiction, collection method, PII controller (contact info), purpose category, PII categories, DPAs (Data Processing Agreements), sensitivity, consent timestamp, expiry, status. IoT receipt: stored on device/cloud, user can retrieve anytime. Proof of valid data collection for regulatory compliance.

source: IoT Security - Ch19
question: Purpose-Based Access Control (PBAC)
answer: Access control where permission is tied to data processing purpose. Policy: user can access only if purpose matches consent. Purpose categories: research, billing, personalization, compliance, emergency. IoT example: smart meter data for billing (aggregate consumption) vs for research (individual interval data). Purpose binding: data tagged at collection with allowed purposes.

source: IoT Security - Ch19
question: Data Processing Agreement (DPA) for IoT
answer: Legal contract between data controller (cloud provider) and data processor (device manufacturer). Specifies: types of personal data, processing purposes, security measures, sub-processors, data retention/deletion, breach notification, audit rights. IoT controllers must ensure all devices and cloud services comply. Joint controllers: multiple parties determine processing purposes (smart home: device manufacturer + service provider).

source: IoT Security - Ch20
question: IoT Impact on Mobile Network Security
answer: Massive IoT device connections strain mobile network security infrastructure. Challenges: 1) Signaling storm — each device generates attach/detach/tracking area update signaling (HSS overload). 2) DDoS amplification — mobile IoT botnets using SMS flooding, signaling storms. 3) Small data efficiency — inefficient whole-security-context per tiny transaction. 4) Roaming security — inter-PLMN authentication for global IoT.

source: IoT Security - Ch20
question: Signaling Storm Attack on Mobile IoT
answer: Attack using many IoT devices to overwhelm mobile core network signaling. Devices repeatedly attach/detach, send TAU (Tracking Area Update), PDP context activation. Impact: MME (Mobility Management Entity) overload, HSS (Home Subscriber Server) overload, failed service for legitimate users. Defense: MME throttling, congestion awareness (NAS level backoff timer, access control barring), device categorization.

source: IoT Security - Ch20
question: Mobile IoT Botnet Threats
answer: IoT botnets using cellular connectivity. Unique aspects: 1) SMS C2 channel — hard to block (vs TCP traffic). 2) Geographic diversity — global cellular coverage distributes bots. 3) Always-connected — no WiFi proximity limitation. 4) Network-level detection harder — traffic encrypted at NAS layer. 5) Over-the-top services (WhatsApp, Telegram) as C2. Defense: network-based anomaly detection (DPI only on user plane), SMS filtering.

source: IoT Security - Ch20
question: LTE/5G IoT Device Authentication Challenges
answer: Authentication challenges for massive IoT: 1) IMSI catching — attacker forces UE to send IMSI in clear (mitigated by SUCI in 5G). 2) AKA amplification — expensive authentication vectors per device (mitigation: group authentication). 3) EPS fallback — 5G to LTE fallback resets to less secure EPS-AKA. 4) Null cipher — emergency calls use no encryption. 5) Paging abuse — attacker pages devices to trigger wake-up (battery drain).

source: IoT Security - Ch20
question: Network-Based IoT Security (3GPP SA3)
answer: 3GPP SA3 security group standards for IoT. 3GPP TS 33.187 — Machine-Type Communication (MTC) security features: 1) SCEF (Service Capability Exposure Function) security — API authentication for IoT service providers. 2) Group message delivery security — secure broadcast to device groups. 3) Small data transmission security — CIP (Control Plane CIoT EPS Optimization) security. 4) Monitoring enhancement — tamper detection notification.

source: IoT Security - Ch20
question: CIoT EPS Optimizations Security
answer: Cellular IoT (CIoT) optimization security (3GPP Rel-13/14). Control Plane CIoT EPS Optimization: data in NAS messages (no DRB setup — saves signaling). User Plane CIoT EPS Optimization: RRC Suspend/Resume (skip full RRC setup). Security: NAS encryption (if data in control plane). Extended DRX (eDRX) security: longer sleep cycles mean delayed authentication updates (key refresh). Power Saving Mode (PSM): device unreachable during sleep (security event reporting delayed).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch1
question: Internet Security Truisms
answer: 1) There is no such thing as absolute security. 2) Security is a process, not a product. 3) The cost of security must be balanced against the value of what's being protected. 4) The most secure system is one that's powered off and buried in concrete — but also unusable. 5) Humans are the weakest link in any security system.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch1
question: Security Trade-off: Cost vs Risk
answer: Security measures have direct costs (hardware, software, personnel) and indirect costs (usability reduction, performance impact, user frustration). Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Impact. Optimal security level is where marginal cost of additional security = marginal reduction in expected loss. Over-investment wastes resources; under-investment leaves unacceptable exposure.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch1
question: Security Policy
answer: Formal document defining: 1) What is being protected (assets). 2) From whom (threat actors). 3) What constitutes acceptable use. 4) Rules for access control, authentication, and accountability. 5) Incident response procedures. 6) Enforcement mechanisms and consequences. Policy must be approved by management, reviewed regularly, and enforced consistently.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch1
question: Network Perimeter
answer: Boundary between trusted internal network and untrusted external networks (Internet). Security mechanisms at perimeter: firewalls, intrusion detection/prevention systems, VPN gateways, proxy servers, network access control (NAC). Defense-in-depth: multiple layers at perimeter plus internal controls. Zero Trust: remove concept of trusted perimeter entirely — verify every access regardless of source.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch1
question: Attack Surface
answer: Sum of all points where an attacker can enter or extract data from a system. Components: network ports (TCP/UDP), services (daemons), user input fields, APIs, physical interfaces (USB, console), wireless (WiFi, Bluetooth), social engineering vectors. Reduction strategies: disable unnecessary services, firewall rules (default deny), input validation, physical access controls, security awareness training.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch2
question: Defense in Depth (Layered Security)
answer: Multiple independent security layers so that if one fails, others still provide protection. Layers: 1) Perimeter firewall — first line of defense. 2) Internal segmentation — separate servers from workstations. 3) Host hardening — secure OS configuration. 4) Application security — secure coding, input validation. 5) Data encryption — protect data at rest and in transit. 6) Monitoring and logging — detect breaches. 7) User education — prevent social engineering.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch2
question: Principle of Least Privilege
answer: Every entity (user, process, device) should have the minimum permissions necessary to perform its function. Implementation: 1) Default-deny access control. 2) Role-based access control (RBAC) with minimal roles. 3) Time-limited privileges (just-in-time access). 4) Regular privilege audits. 5) Separation of duties — no single entity has complete control. Violation example: running web server as root.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch2
question: Default-Deny vs Default-Permit
answer: Default-permit: all traffic allowed unless explicitly blocked (default firewall attitude for early Internet). Default-deny: all traffic blocked unless explicitly permitted. Security best practice: default-deny with explicit allow rules for required traffic. Default-permit is dangerous because new vulnerabilities in any permitted protocol become immediately exploitable. Migration: start with default-deny, test, whitelist needed traffic.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch2
question: Choke Point
answer: Single point where all traffic in/out of a network must pass, enabling concentrated security monitoring and enforcement. Implementation: place firewall at single gateway between internal network and Internet. Variations: dual choke points (redundancy), tiered choke points (separate DMZ, internal, management networks). Risk: if choke point compromised, all traffic exposed. Mitigation: hardened bastion hosts at choke point.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3
question: IP Spoofing
answer: Forging source IP address in packet headers to impersonate a trusted host. Attack types: blind spoofing (attacker cannot see replies — used in SYN floods), non-blind spoofing (attacker on same subnet can see replies). Defenses: 1) Ingress filtering (RFC 2827) — ISP drops packets with source IP not from their network. 2) egress filtering — organization drops outgoing packets with internal source IPs. 3) IPsec — authenticate all packets. 4) TCP sequence number randomization.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3
question: TCP SYN Flood
answer: Denial-of-service attack exploiting TCP three-way handshake. Attacker sends many SYN packets with spoofed source IPs. Server allocates TCB (Transmission Control Block) for each half-open connection. Connection table fills up → new legitimate connections rejected. Mitigations: 1) SYN cookies (encode connection state in SYN-ACK sequence number, no TCB allocation until ACK received). 2) Reduce SYN-RECEIVED timeout. 3) Increase backlog queue. 4) Firewall rate-limiting.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3
question: TCP Sequence Number Prediction
answer: Attack where attacker guesses the ISN (Initial Sequence Number) of a TCP connection to inject spoofed packets. Early TCP implementations used predictable ISN generation (e.g., linear increment based on time). Blind hijacking: attacker predicts ISN, sends spoofed RST to close connection or spoofed data. Defense: RFC 6528 — ISN calculated as hash of (local IP, remote IP, local port, remote port, secret key), making prediction infeasible.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3
question: Source Routing Attack
answer: Attacker uses IP source routing options (Loose Source Route, Strict Source Route) to force packets through a specific path, bypassing security controls. The reply follows reverse path, allowing attacker to see traffic. Mitigations: 1) Configure routers to drop source-routed packets. 2) Firewall rules blocking IP options. 3) Modern OS kernels disable source routing by default (sysctl net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route=0 on Linux).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3
question: IP Fragmentation Attack
answer: Attack exploiting IP fragmentation mechanisms. Teardrop attack: overlapping fragments cause kernel crash (old Linux/Windows). Tiny fragment attack: split TCP header headers across multiple fragments so firewall cannot inspect complete header. Fragment overlap: second fragment overwrites data in first fragment byte range. Defenses: 1) Fragment reassembly before firewall inspection. 2) Drop overlapping fragments. 3) Fragment rate limiting. 4) Minimum fragment size enforcement.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3
question: ICMP Attacks
answer: Abuse of ICMP protocol for attacks. Types: 1) ICMP Redirect — attacker sends fake redirect packet to alter victim's routing table. 2) ICMP Destination Unreachable — attacker sends false unreachable messages to kill connections. 3) ICMP unreachable flooding — bandwidth attack (Smurf attack uses ICMP echo to broadcast address). 4) ICMP tunneling — encapsulate data in ICMP echo packets to bypass firewalls. Defenses: 1) Filter ICMP types at perimeter. 2) Ignore ICMP redirects (sysctl). 3) Rate-limit ICMP.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3
question: UDP Attacks
answer: UDP is connectionless with no built-in authentication or sequencing, making it vulnerable. UDP flood: attacker sends many UDP packets to random ports → server responds with ICMP Unreachable → resource exhaustion. DNS amplification: attacker sends small DNS query with spoofed source IP → authoritative DNS sends large response to victim (amplification factor up to 54×). UDP hijacking: attacker sends fake UDP packets to data stream. Defenses: 1) Rate-limit UDP. 2) Block UDP except for known services. 3) Use DNS over TCP for zone transfers.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3
question: DNS Cache Poisoning
answer: Attack where attacker inserts forged DNS records into a resolver's cache. When user queries example.com, resolver returns attacker's IP. Variants: 1) Kaminsky attack (2008) — attacker floods resolver with queries for non-existent subdomains, sends forged responses with additional records poisoning unrelated domains. 2) Bailiwick checking bypass. Defenses: 1) DNSSEC (RRSIG/NSEC/DS records). 2) Source port randomization (RFC 5452). 3) Query ID entropy. 4) Rate limiting per domain.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3
question: BGP Security Issues
answer: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) has no built-in authentication in its original design. Threats: 1) Route hijacking — AS announces prefixes it doesn't own (traffic redirected). 2) Route leak — AS announces learned routes to wrong peers (traffic detoured). 3) AS path forgery — AS advertises fake AS_PATH to influence routing decisions. Defenses: 1) BGP TCP MD5 signature (RFC 2385) — TCP option 19. 2) RPKI — cryptographic verification of prefix ownership. 3) BGPsec — AS_PATH signatures. 4) Prefix filtering — accept only legitimate prefixes from peers.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3
question: RIP (Routing Information Protocol) Security
answer: RIP uses UDP for route advertisement with no authentication by default. Attackers can inject fake routes to redirect traffic. RIP v1: no authentication at all. RIP v2: supports plaintext password authentication (MD5 in later implementations). Mitigations: 1) Use RIP v2 with MD5 authentication. 2) Passive interfaces — only listen, don't advertise. 3) Distribute-list filtering — only accept/announce specific routes. 4) Use OSPF/EIGRP with stronger authentication instead.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3
question: OSPF Security
answer: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) supports authentication: Type 0 (none), Type 1 (plaintext password), Type 2 (cryptographic MD5/SHA). OSPF neighbor authentication prevents fake LSAs. Area Border Router (ABR) filtering — only inject permitted routes between areas. Virtual link authentication — protect cross-area adjacencies. LSDB (Link-State Database) overflow protection — limit number of LSAs. OSPFv3 (IPv6) uses IPsec AH for authentication instead of OSPF-specific auth.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3
question: DNS Zone Transfer
answer: DNS secondary servers request full zone data from primary via AXFR (full zone transfer) or IXFR (incremental). Risk: anyone can enumerate all hosts in a domain if zone transfer is unrestricted. Attackers use this for reconnaissance. Mitigations: 1) Restrict AXFR to authorized secondary DNS servers only (allow-transfer directive in BIND). 2) TSIG (Transaction Signatures, RFC 2845) — shared secret HMAC authentication for zone transfers. 3) Split DNS — internal and external views.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3
question: TCP Wrappers (hosts.allow/hosts.deny)
answer: Host-based access control for Unix services (tcpd wrapper). /etc/hosts.deny: ALL: ALL (default deny). /etc/hosts.allow: service: client_pattern. Example: sshd: 192.168.1.0/255.255.255.0. Uses libwrap to intercept connection before service daemon. Logs attempted connections via syslog. Limitations: only works with services compiled against libwrap, does not encrypt traffic. Superseded by firewall rules and host-based firewalls (iptables, pf).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch4
question: HTTP Security Issues
answer: HTTP is plaintext — all data (URLs, headers, cookies, body) visible to anyone on the network path. Risks: 1) Session hijacking via cookie theft. 2) Man-in-the-middle reading/modifying traffic. 3) Cache poisoning (intermediary proxies caching sensitive data). 4) Referer header leakage (previous URL sent to next site). Mitigations: 1) HTTPS/TLS for all communications. 2) Secure and HttpOnly cookie flags. 3) Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store for sensitive pages. 4) Referrer-Policy header.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch4
question: CGI (Common Gateway Interface) Security
answer: CGI scripts executed by web server with server privileges — a major attack vector when CGI programs have bugs. Risks: 1) Shell injection via unsanitized parameters. 2) Path traversal (../../etc/passwd). 3) Buffer overflows in compiled CGI. 4) Resource exhaustion (fork bomb, disk fill). Best practices: 1) Do not write setuid CGI scripts. 2) Validate all input against whitelist. 3) Run CGI as least-privileged user (nobody). 4) chroot CGI environment. 5) suEXEC (Apache) or equivalent.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch4
question: SSL/TLS Stripping
answer: Attack where attacker converts HTTPS links to HTTP, intercepting the unprotected connection. Tools like sslstrip (Moxie Marlinspike, 2009) proxy the victim connection: victim → HTTP (attacker) → HTTPS (server). Victim sees HTTP; attacker decrypts and re-encrypts. Defenses: 1) HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) — browser remembers HTTPS-only policy. 2) HSTS preload list. 3) Secure cookies (Secure flag prevents sending over HTTP). 4) Browser HTTPS-only mode.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5
question: Password Theft Methods
answer: Techniques attackers use to obtain passwords: 1) Shoulder surfing — watching user type password. 2) Dumpster diving — finding written passwords in trash. 3) Keylogging — hardware/software capturing keystrokes. 4) Phishing — fake login page. 5) Credential stuffing — using leaked passwords from other sites. 6) Password spraying — trying common passwords against many accounts. 7) Hash cracking — offline brute force against password hashes (John the Ripper, Hashcat). 8) Network sniffing (unencrypted protocols — FTP, Telnet, HTTP).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5
question: Social Engineering
answer: Psychological manipulation of humans to divulge confidential information or perform actions. Techniques: 1) Pretexting — fabricating scenario to obtain information. 2) Baiting — leaving infected USB drives where target will find them. 3) Tailgating — following authorized person through secure door. 4) Quid pro quo — offering fake service in exchange for information. 5) Phishing/vishing/smishing — fraudulent communication impersonating trusted entity. Mitigations: 1) Security awareness training. 2) Multi-factor authentication. 3) Clear procedures for verifying identity.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5
question: Buffer Overflow
answer: Program writes more data to a buffer than it can hold, overwriting adjacent memory. Stack overflow: overwrites return address → attacker controls execution flow → shellcode execution. Heap overflow: overwrites heap metadata → arbitrary write primitive. Defenses: 1) W^X (write XOR execute) — no memory page is both writable and executable. 2) ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization) — randomize memory addresses. 3) Stack canaries — detect stack corruption before return. 4) Safe languages (Rust, Go, Java). 5) Compiler flags: -fstack-protector, -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5
question: Denial-of-Service (DoS) Attack Types
answer: Overwhelming a system's resources to deny service. Resource categories: 1) Bandwidth — saturate network link (amplification attacks: DNS, NTP, SSDP). 2) CPU — hash collision attacks (slow HTTP headers), SSL renegotiation. 3) Memory — SYN flood (half-open connections), hash table collisions. 4) File descriptors — HTTP keep-alive hold open connections. 5) Disk — fill logs with spurious requests. Distributed DoS (DDoS): multiple compromised hosts (botnet) coordinate attack. Defenses: rate limiting, load balancing, CDN, anycast.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5
question: Smurf Attack
answer: DDoS attack using ICMP echo request (ping) to broadcast address. Attacker sends ICMP echo request with spoofed source IP (victim) to network broadcast address. All hosts on network respond to victim, amplifying traffic by number of hosts. Cisco routers: 'no ip directed-broadcast' prevents forwarding broadcast to LAN. Modern networks: 1) Directed broadcast disabled by default. 2) Ingress filtering drops spoofed packets. 3) Hosts don't respond to broadcast echo requests (RFC 1122 was advisory, now default deny).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5
question: Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) Attack
answer: Attacker secretly intercepts and relays communication between two parties. Methods: 1) ARP spoofing — fake ARP replies map attacker MAC to gateway IP. 2) DNS spoofing — fake DNS responses redirect to attacker. 3) Rogue DHCP — attacker DHCP server gives attacker as gateway. 4) BGP hijack — redirect traffic through attacker AS. 5) Proxy attack — transparent proxy intercepts traffic. Detection: certificate warnings (TLS), ARP table monitoring, asymmetric latency. Prevention: mutual authentication, TLS, IPsec, SSH.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch6
question: Network Scanning Tools
answer: Tools for discovering hosts and services: 1) Nmap — port scanning (SYN, TCP connect, FIN, Xmas, Null), OS fingerprinting, service version detection. 2) Zmap — internet-wide scanning (send raw packets, 1.3M pkt/s). 3) Masscan — similar to Zmap, asynchronous. 4) Netcat (nc) — TCP/UDP read/write, port scanning. 5) Unicornscan — asynchronous TCP scanning. 6) Hping3 — custom packet crafting, firewall testing, OS fingerprinting. Defenses: rate limiting, port knocking, knocking + single-packet auth.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch6
question: Footprinting (Reconnaissance)
answer: Phase 1 of hacking methodology — gathering information about target. Passive footprinting: no direct interaction with target. WHOIS lookups, DNS enumeration (nslookup, dig), search engines (Google dorking), social media, job postings, public documents (SEC filings). Active footprinting: direct interaction with target systems. Ping sweeps, port scans, OS fingerprinting, service banner grabbing, traceroute, zone transfers. Goal: map network topology, identify hosts, services, OS versions.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch6
question: Rootkits
answer: Software designed to hide attacker presence by subverting normal system monitoring. Types: 1) User-mode (ring 3) — replace system executables (ls, ps, netstat, find) with trojan versions. 2) Kernel-mode (ring 0) — loadable kernel module (LKM) intercepts system calls. 3) Bootkit (ring -1) — infect MBR/UEFI bootloader, loaded before OS. 4) Hypervisor (ring -2) — Blue Pill type, run target OS inside VM. Detection: offline analysis (boot from clean media), behavioral detection, integrity checking (Tripwire, AIDE).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch7
question: S/Key One-Time Password System
answer: Lamport's hash chain OTP scheme (RFC 2289). User chooses secret passphrase. Server computes hash chain: w_0 = passphrase, w_1 = H(w_0), w_2 = H(w_1), ..., w_n = H(w_{n-1}). Server stores w_n. Login N: user provides w_{n-N}. Server computes H(w_{n-N}) and compares to stored w_{n-N+1}. After verification, server stores w_{n-N} as new expected. Each password used once only. Resistant to replay attacks. Limitation: finite chain length, requires reinitialization.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch7
question: Kerberos Authentication
answer: Network authentication protocol (MIT, RFC 4120) using tickets and symmetric cryptography. Components: KDC (Key Distribution Center) — AS (Authentication Server) + TGS (Ticket Granting Server). Process: 1) Client→AS: request TGT (Ticket-Granting Ticket). 2) AS→Client: TGT encrypted with client's password hash + session key. 3) Client→TGS: TGT + authenticator + request for service ticket. 4) TGS→Client: service ticket encrypted with server's key. 5) Client→Server: service ticket + authenticator. Mutual authentication. Single sign-on.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch7
question: PAP (Password Authentication Protocol)
answer: PPP authentication where password sent in cleartext. Two packets: Authenticate-Request (username+password), Authenticate-Ack/Nack. No encryption, no replay protection, no mutual authentication. Attacker can sniff credentials. Obsolete; replaced by CHAP, EAP, and MS-CHAP. Still used in some legacy RADIUS configurations. CHAP (Challenge Handshake Auth Protocol): server sends random challenge, client responds with MD5(challenge+password), iterative challenge.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch7
question: TACACS+ (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus)
answer: Cisco AAA protocol (RFC 1492 evolved). TCP-based (port 49). Encrypts entire packet body (not just password) — RADIUS encrypts only password. Separates authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA) into distinct processes. Supports multiple authentication types. More granular command authorization than RADIUS (per-command ACLs). Typically used for device administration (router/switch access). vs RADIUS: TACACS+ encrypts full packet, uses TCP, separates AAA functions.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch7
question: Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM)
answer: Flexible authentication framework (Sun, now Linux/Unix standard). /etc/pam.d/service files define auth stack. Four management groups: auth (verify identity), account (authorization — time, access), password (password update), session (logging, environment). Control flags: required, requisite, sufficient, optional. Modules: pam_unix.so (Unix passwords), pam_ldap.so (LDAP), pam_radius.so (RADIUS), pam_google_authenticator.so (TOTP). Stack ordering enables MFA (e.g., Unix password + TOTP).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch7
question: Biometric Authentication
answer: Authentication based on physical/behavioral characteristics. Types: fingerprint (reader), iris scanning, facial recognition, voice recognition, gait analysis, keystroke dynamics, signature verification. Error rates: FAR (False Acceptance Rate), FRR (False Rejection Rate), CER (Crossover Error Rate — FAR=FRR). Limitations: 1) Biometrics are not secrets — fingerprints left everywhere. 2) Cannot be changed if compromised. 3) Privacy concerns (tracking, surveillance). 4) Spoofing — replay attacks on sensor. Use as second factor only (not primary).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch8
question: Email Spoofing
answer: Forging email From/Sender header to impersonate someone. Attackers send email appearing to come from trusted source (CEO, bank, colleague). Mechanisms: 1) SMTP has no mandatory sender authentication — MAIL FROM can be any value. 2) Display name spoofing — display name set to trusted name, actual address different. Defenses: 1) SPF (Sender Policy Framework) — DNS TXT record lists authorized mail servers. 2) DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) — cryptographic signature on email. 3) DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting & Conformance) — policy for unauthenticated mail.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch8
question: Sendmail Security
answer: Sendmail MTA (Mail Transfer Agent) has historically been a major security concern due to its complexity and setuid root operation. Risks: 1) Buffer overflows in header processing. 2) Pipe executions via .forward files (user can pipe email to any command). 3) Writable aliases file allows redirecting mail. 4) Debug mode (sendmail -d) can be exploited. Best practices: 1) Run sendmail with least privilege. 2) Use restricted shell for .forward pipes (smrsh). 3) Keep updated. 4) Consider alternatives: Postfix, Exim, OpenSMTPD.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch9
question: FTP Security Issues
answer: FTP (File Transfer Protocol, RFC 959) has fundamental security problems: 1) Passwords transmitted in cleartext. 2) Two connections (control port 21, data port 20). Active FTP: server connects back to client (PORT command) — blocked by NAT/firewalls. Passive FTP (PASV): client connects to server-allocated port — needs wide firewall range. 3) Anonymous FTP writable directories for malware distribution. 4) Bounce attack — FTP server used to send arbitrary TCP traffic. Replacement: SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol), FTPS (FTP over TLS/SSL).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch9
question: NFS (Network File System) Security
answer: NFS allows remote file access over network. Security concerns: 1) NFSv3 uses AUTH_UNIX (UID/GID based) — all NFS requests claim a user ID, server trusts it. 2) Root squashing — root UID (0) mapped to nobody (65534) for NFS access (prevents root filesystem modification). 3) portmapper/rpcbind — register RPC services (exploitable for DDoS amplification). 4) NFS export misconfiguration — entire filesystem exported world-readable. NFSv4 improvements: Kerberos (RPCSEC_GSS), compound operations, stateful. Best practice: use VPN + NFSv4 + Kerberos.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch9
question: SMB/CIFS Security
answer: SMB (Server Message Block) / CIFS — Windows file sharing protocol. Ports: TCP 445 (direct SMB), TCP 139 (NetBIOS session service). Risks: 1) SMBv1 is inherently insecure — uses pre-session authentication, allows MITM. 2) EternalBlue (MS17-010) — buffer overflow in SMBv1 used by WannaCry (2017). 3) Null session — anonymous access to NetBIOS providing user/enumeration. Defenses: 1) Disable SMBv1. 2) Use SMBv3 (encryption + signing, AES-128/256). 3) Block SMB at firewall (TCP 139, 445 from Internet). 4) Network segmentation (separate file servers from user networks).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch10
question: Application Proxy Firewall
answer: Firewall that terminates the connection at the application layer. Client connects to proxy; proxy establishes separate connection to server. Proxy understands the application protocol (HTTP, FTP, SMTP) and can inspect, filter, or modify content. Examples: HTTP proxy (Squid), SOCKS proxy. Advantages: deep packet inspection, protocol validation, can authenticate users, content filtering (block malware URLs, inappropriate content). Disadvantages: higher latency, requires proxy-aware clients or explicit configuration, resource intensive. Each protocol needs its own proxy.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch10
question: Circuit-Level Proxy (SOCKS)
answer: Firewall operating at Layer 5 (session layer). SOCKS proxy (RFC 1928): SOCKS4 (TCP only, no auth), SOCKS5 (UDP, TCP, GSS-API/auth). Client connects to SOCKS proxy and requests connection to target. Proxy establishes connection and relays data. No application-layer inspection — proxy just forwards bytes once connection established. Advantages: works with any TCP application (no protocol-specific proxy needed), moderate security. Used by SSH dynamic forwarding (-D), Tor SOCKS. Disadvantage: no content filtering.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch10
question: Bastion Host
answer: Hardened computer specifically designed to withstand attacks, positioned at network perimeter. Properties: 1) Runs minimal services — only those needed for firewall/proxy function. 2) No user accounts except administrators. 3) All unnecessary software removed. 4) Extensive logging and monitoring. 5) Connected to screened subnet (DMZ). 6) Typically a dual-homed host (two network interfaces) bridging DMZ and internal networks. 7) Regularly patched. 8) Configuration management (no unauthorized changes). Common OS: hardened Linux/BSD.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch10
question: Screened Subnet (DMZ)
answer: Demilitarized Zone — network segment between internal and external firewalls (three-legged firewall architecture). Public-facing servers placed in DMZ (web, mail, DNS). External firewall: Internet → DMZ (80/443, SMTP, DNS). Internal firewall: DMZ → internal network (specific protocols only). If DMZ host compromised, attacker still must penetrate internal firewall. Alternatives: 1) Single firewall DMZ (three interfaces: outside, DMZ, inside). 2) Two-firewall DMZ (external + internal firewall). 3) Multitier DMZ (web/app/db segments).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch10
question: Dual-Homed Host
answer: Host with two network interfaces acting as a firewall/gateway between two networks. IP forwarding typically disabled in OS kernel — traffic cannot pass directly. Applications on host proxy services between networks. Security: no packets traverse the host (IP forwarding disabled), so host must be compromised to breach network separation. vs screened subnet: dual-homed host is simpler but single point of failure. Bastion host commonly deployed as dual-homed host. Risk: if host compromised via allowed service (e.g., web proxy), attacker controls both networks.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch11
question: Firewall Ruleset Design Principles
answer: Rules: 1) Default-deny policy — last rule drops all traffic. 2) Most specific rules first (improves performance). 3) Rules symmetric (allow inbound response for outbound request). 4) Minimize rule count — combine where possible. 5) Document each rule (purpose, date, owner). 6) Regular audit — remove stale rules. 7) Change control — formal process for rule modifications. 8) Order matters — first match wins. Testing: tcpdump/tshark to verify expected traffic passes and malicious is blocked. Tools: iptables -L -v, pfctl -sr.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch11
question: Firewall Testing
answer: Methods to verify firewall effectiveness: 1) Port scanning from outside (nmap -sS, -sT, -sV) — verify only allowed ports open. 2) Protocol-specific tests — verify application proxies correctly filter protocol commands. 3) Fragmentation tests — verify fragment reassembly before inspection. 4) Source port manipulation — test if rules using source port (e.g., DNS port 53) can be bypassed. 5) Tunnel over allowed protocol (e.g., SSH tunnel through HTTP proxy). 6) Penetration testing — simulate attacker exploitation through firewall. 7) Log review — verify all blocked and allowed traffic logged appropriately.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch11
question: Firewall Configuration Change Management
answer: Process for modifying firewall rules. Procedure: 1) Request — submit change request with justification, risk assessment. 2) Review — security team reviews impact. 3) Test — apply in lab/test environment first. 4) Approve — management approval for production change. 5) Implement — apply change during maintenance window. 6) Verify — test connectivity and security. 7) Document — update ruleset documentation and rule metadata. 8) Audit — regular ruleset review for orphaned/ineffective rules.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch12
question: VPN Technologies Comparison
answer: IPsec: most secure, complex configuration, OS-integrated. SSL/TLS VPN: easier client deployment (browser-based), application-specific access. PPTP (obsolete): MPPE encryption, MS-CHAPv2 auth — broken security. L2TP/IPsec: L2TP tunnels PPP, IPsec provides encryption. WireGuard: modern protocol (kernel-integrated), Curve25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305, minimal config (single config file). OpenVPN: SSL/TLS-based, flexible (TCP/UDP, port obfuscation), open-source. Choose based on: security requirements, client compatibility, ease of management.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch12
question: VPN Split Tunneling
answer: VPN configuration where only traffic destined for corporate network goes through VPN; Internet traffic goes directly. Advantages: Internet access remains full speed, corporate bandwidth conserved, user can access local resources simultaneously. Disadvantages: 1) Malware on user machine can attack corporate network over VPN. 2) Internet traffic not inspected by corporate security. 3) Split tunneling may bypass corporate content filtering. 4) Risk of DNS leakage (corporate DNS queries travel over Internet). Full tunnel (all traffic through VPN): more secure but higher bandwidth consumption and latency.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch12
question: NAT Traversal (NAT-T)
answer: Technique for IPsec ESP through NAT devices. Problem: ESP protocol 50 does not have port numbers, so NAT cannot track sessions. Solution: UDP encapsulation of ESP (RFC 3948) — wrap ESP packet in UDP (port 4500). IKE uses UDP 500, switches to 4500 when NAT detected (detection via NAT-D payloads in IKE). Additionally allows IPsec through firewalls that only allow UDP. MOBIKE (IKEv2, RFC 4555): supports changing IP addresses without re-establishing tunnel — useful for mobile VPN users.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch13
question: Screened Host Architecture
answer: Single firewall device connecting internal network directly to Internet. All traffic flows through firewall — it is the only point of contact. Bastion host on internal network provides proxy services. Simpler than screened subnet but: if firewall compromised, entire internal network exposed. Also: no DMZ for public servers — often placed between firewall and bastion. Less secure than screened subnet, more secure than no firewall. Suitable for small organizations with limited security requirements.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch13
question: Intranet Routing Security
answer: Internal network routing protocols must be secured to prevent internal attacks. RISKS: 1) Rogue DHCP server providing false gateway. 2) ARP spoofing redirecting traffic through attacker host. 3) Rogue router advertising false routes. 4) Spanning tree attack (network loops). Defenses: 1) DHCP snooping — only trusted DHCP servers can respond. 2) Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) — validate ARP packets against DHCP snooping binding. 3) IP Source Guard — filter traffic based on DHCP binding (IP+MAC+port+interface). 4) BPDU Guard — disable port if BPDU received (prevent rogue switch). 5) Port Security — limit MAC addresses per port.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch13
question: Virtual LAN (VLAN) Security
answer: VLANs logically segment networks on same physical switch. Security concerns: 1) VLAN hopping — attacker frames tagged with different VLAN ID (switchport mode trunk → talk to any VLAN). 2) Double tagging — attacker adds two 802.1Q tags, outer stripped first switch, inner processed by second switch (attacks cross native VLAN). Defenses: 1) Disable DTP (Dynamic Trunking Protocol) — set switchport mode access, no trunk negotiation. 2) Use dedicated VLAN ID for native VLAN (not default VLAN 1). 3) Prune unused VLANs from trunks. 4) Private VLANs — isolate ports within same VLAN.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch14
question: Host Hardening Checklist
answer: Steps to secure a host: 1) Install minimal OS — no unnecessary packages/services. 2) Remove setuid binaries that are unneeded (chmod u-s /usr/bin/lppasswd). 3) Disable unused services (inetd entries, rc scripts, systemd services). 4) Configure firewall (host-based: iptables, pf, Windows Firewall). 5) Apply security patches (automated updates). 6) Enable auditing/logging (syslog, auditd, Windows Event Log). 7) Strong password policy + account lockout. 8) File integrity monitoring (Tripwire, AIDE). 9) Regular vulnerability scanning. 10) Backup and recovery plan.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch14
question: Field-Stripping a Host
answer: Removing all components not required for the host's function to minimize attack surface. 1) Remove compilers, interpreters, development tools. 2) Remove manual pages, documentation. 3) Remove unnecessary user accounts and groups. 4) Remove sample configuration files and scripts. 5) Remove unnecessary kernel modules. 6) Remove X Window System (if not needed). 7) Remove font files, wallpapers, screensavers. 8) Set filesystem read-only where possible (mount -o ro). 9) Remove unused libraries. 10) Remove SETUID/SETGID binaries except those required.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch14
question: chroot Jail
answer: Unix mechanism to restrict process filesystem access to a specific directory. Process cannot see files outside chroot directory. Common for security-sensitive daemons (DNS BIND, FTP server, web server). Creation: 1) Create chroot directory structure (/var/chroot/named/). 2) Copy required binaries, libraries, config files into chroot. 3) Run daemon with chroot() syscall. Limitations: 1) Root user inside chroot can escape via various methods (freebsd jail more secure). 2) Cannot restrict network access, process table, or kernel resources. More robust: containers (Docker), jails (FreeBSD), zones (Solaris).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch14
question: Tripwire (File Integrity Monitoring)
answer: Security tool that checks for unauthorized file changes. Phase 1 (initialization): compute cryptographic hash (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256) of all tracked files and store as signature database. Phase 2 (monitoring): recompute hashes and compare to database. Reports added/deleted/changed files. Policy file (twpol.txt) specifies what files to monitor and how strictly (permissions, ownership, size, inode, hash). Typical use: monitor /etc, /bin, /sbin, /usr/bin, /usr/sbin, /lib, system startup files. Run from cron daily. Alternative: AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch15
question: NIDS vs HIDS
answer: Network Intrusion Detection System (NIDS): monitors network traffic passively (sniffer). Analyzes packets against signatures and anomalies. Examples: Snort, Suricata, Zeek (formerly Bro). Placement: behind firewall, on DMZ segment, at network choke point. Host Intrusion Detection System (HIDS): monitors events on individual host. Analyzes system logs, file changes, process activity. Examples: OSSEC, Wazuh, Tripwire (file integrity), auditd. Advantages: NIDS sees all network traffic; HIDS sees encrypted traffic after decryption. Combined for defense in depth.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch15
question: Signature-Based vs Anomaly-Based Detection
answer: Signature-based: match traffic/events against known attack patterns (signatures). Advantages: low false positive rate, proven detection of known attacks. Disadvantages: cannot detect zero-day attacks, requires signature database updates. Anomaly-based: establish baseline of normal behavior, alert on deviations. Methods: statistical (mean/stddev), machine learning (clustering, neural nets), protocol conformance (protocol RFC validation). Advantages: detect zero-day and novel attacks. Disadvantages: high false positive rate (prone to false alarms from legitimate changes), requires training period.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch15
question: Snort IDS
answer: Open-source NIDS (Sourcefire/Martin Roesch, 1998). Three modes: sniffer (packet display), packet logger (save to disk), NIDS (analyze). Rule format: action protocol src_ip src_port -> dst_ip dst_port (options). Example: alert tcp $EXTERNAL_NET any -> $HOME_NET 80 (msg:'SQL Injection'; content:'union select'; nocase;). Preprocessors: HTTP Inspect, Frag3 (fragmentation reassembly), Stream5 (TCP state tracking). Output: syslog, unified2 (Barnyard2), database (MySQL, PostgreSQL). Community rules: Emerging Threats (ET).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch16
question: Incident Response Process
answer: Structured approach to handling security incidents. NIST SP 800-61: 1) Preparation — create IR plan, assemble team, acquire tools. 2) Detection & Analysis — identify incident via monitoring, alerts, user reports. 3) Containment, Eradication & Recovery — short-term containment (isolate host, block IP), long-term containment (patch, rebuild), eradicate (remove malware, backup restore), recover (restore to normal operations). 4) Post-Incident Activity — lessons learned, evidence retention, report to management. Chain of custody for legal proceedings.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Appendix A
question: Symmetric vs Asymmetric Cryptography
answer: Symmetric: same key for encryption and decryption. Fast, efficient for bulk data. Algorithms: AES (128/192/256), ChaCha20, 3DES (obsolete). Key distribution problem — both parties must securely share key. Asymmetric (public key): mathematically related key pair — public key encrypts, private key decrypts. Algorithms: RSA (2048+ bits), ECC (Elliptic Curve — 256-bit ECC ≈ 3072-bit RSA), Ed25519. Key agreement: Diffie-Hellman (DH), ECDH. Digital signatures: RSA, ECDSA, EdDSA. Hybrid cryptosystems: use asymmetric for key exchange, symmetric for data encryption (PGP, TLS, IPsec).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Appendix A
question: RSA Cryptosystem
answer: Public-key cryptosystem (Rivest, Shamir, Adleman, 1977). Key generation: 1) Choose large primes p, q. 2) Compute n = p*q. 3) Compute φ(n) = (p-1)(q-1). 4) Choose e (public exponent, 65537 common). 5) Compute d = e^(-1) mod φ(n) (private exponent).
