OSSEC: host-based IDS (not just file integrity), log analysis, rootkit detection, active response (block IP). Samhain: centralized file integrity monitoring. All detect changes to monitored files; should be initialized immediately after OS installation (baseline). Database stored on read-only medium (CD, offline) to prevent tampering.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: BSD Securelevels
answer: FreeBSD/OpenBSD security level mechanism. sysctl kern.securelevel: -1 (permanently insecure — default, can be raised), 0 (secure mode — immutable file flags honored, cannot be lowered), 1 (secure — /dev/mem and /dev/kmem read-only, raw disk read-only for mounted filesystems), 2 (highly secure — disk write-only, cannot set securelevel lower, modules disabled). Network operations restricted at level 1+. Setting to level 1+ prevents modification of firewall rules, loading kernel modules, writing to raw disk devices. Used by bastion hosts — once set, cannot be lowered without reboot. Useful for read-only firewall systems.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: OpenBSD Security Focus
answer: OpenBSD: security-focused BSD variant. Known for: 1) Proactive auditing — complete system source code review for bugs/security holes (six-year effort). 2) Claims: 'Only one remote hole in default install in over 20 years'. 3) Security features: W^X (non-executable stack/heap), ASLR, ProPolice/StackGuard (stack protection), arc4random (secure random), strlcpy/strlcat (bounds-checked string functions). 4) pf (packet filter) — stateful firewall developed on OpenBSD. 5) OpenSSH, OpenNTPD, OpenSMTPD, httpd — security-focused implementations of common services. 6) LibreSSL — fork of OpenSSL after Heartbleed, CVE reductions.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: Logging Strategies
answer: Centralized logging: all hosts send logs to central syslog server. Syslog priority: facility.level (auth.info, kern.warning). UDP 514 (default, no reliability), TCP 514 (RFC 3195 — reliable), RELP (Reliable Event Logging Protocol). Syslog-ng/rsyslog: advanced filtering, database output, TLS encryption. Security logging: 1) Authentication failures (SSH, sudo, su). 2) Firewall denied connections. 3) File modification alerts. 4) Privilege escalation. 5) Process execution. 6) Network connections. Log rotation: compress, archive, retention policy (weeks/months/years depending on regulation). Log integrity: sign logs (syslog-sign), write-once media, remote append-only storage. Never store logs only locally — attacker deletes evidence after compromise.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: Zeek (formerly Bro) IDS
answer: Network analysis framework (different from Snort — not signature-based). Event-driven: generates typed events for network activity (connection, HTTP request, DNS query, SSL certificate, file extraction). Zeek scripts define event handlers. Capabilities: 1) Protocol analysis — deep decode 40+ protocols (HTTP, DNS, SMTP, FTP, SSL, SSH, IRC, DHCP, NFS, SMB, Kerberos). 2) File extraction — reconstruct files from network streams (HTTP downloads, email attachments). 3) SSL certificate validation — detect invalid/mismatched certs. 4) Threat intelligence integration — MISP, STIX/TAXII. Output: conn.log (connection summary), http.log, dns.log, ssl.log, files.log, notice.log (warnings).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: Suricata vs Snort
answer: Suricata: modern IDS/IPS engine (OISF). Multi-threaded (Snort single-threaded). GPU acceleration (CUDA). Protocol detection (auto-detect HTTP, TLS, SMB on non-standard ports). File extraction, MD5/SHA256 hash. Lua scripting for custom rules. IPv6 support (full). App-layer parsing: HTTP2, TLS 1.3, SMTP, SMB v2/3, Kerberos, DNSSEC. Suricata can replace Snort rules (same rule syntax). Performance: typically 2-5× throughput vs Snort (multi-core). Compatible with Snort ruleset (Emerging Threats, VRT). Both: NFQUEUE integration (inline IPS). Both: can use Hyperscan (Intel) for fast pattern matching.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: IDS Evasion Techniques
answer: Techniques attackers use to evade network IDS: 1) Fragmentation — split attack signature across multiple IP fragments (IDS must reassemble). 2) TCP segmentation — split data across small segments (IDS must TCP reassemble). 3) Unicode obfuscation — encode URL path in different Unicode encodings (IDS must normalize). 4) Polymorphic shellcode — encrypt/encode payload with variable decryption stub. 5) Split across multiple connections — slow data delivery. 6) Whitespace insertion — add spaces/alternate commands. 7) Protocol confusion — use HTTP over non-standard ports. 8) Encryption — TLS hides payload from NIDS. Defense: normalizer before IDS, application proxy firewall, TLS interception (MITM proxy).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: Shannon's Maxim
answer: 'The enemy knows the system.' (Claude Shannon, 1949 — 'Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems'). Also known as Kerckhoffs's Principle (1883): 'The system must not require secrecy — it should be safe even if it falls into enemy hands.' Modern interpretation: security depends on key secrecy, not algorithm secrecy. Relying on algorithm secrecy (security through obscurity) provides no real security. All widely-used cryptographic algorithms (AES, RSA, SHA-256, ChaCha20) are fully public and extensively analyzed.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: Entropy Sources for Cryptographic Keys
answer: Cryptographic keys require high-quality random numbers. Entropy sources: 1) Hardware RNG — dedicated CPU instruction (Intel RDRAND/RDSEED, via CPU thermal noise). 2) Kernel entropy pool — Linux /dev/random (blocks if entropy low), /dev/urandom (non-blocking, CSPRNG). 3) Mouse/trackpad movements. 4) Keyboard timings. 5) Disk seek latency. 6) Network packet timings. 7) Microphone ambient noise. Insufficient entropy at boot time can produce predictable keys (Debian OpenSSL bug 2006 — predictable keys due to valgrind removing entropy source, affected SSL keys generated for 2 years). Embedded devices (routers, IoT) often have low entropy — use hardware RNG.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: pfctl -ss
answer: BSD pf: Show current state table — all active connections tracked by firewall. Each entry: protocol, src IP:port -> dst IP:port, state flags, packets/bytes.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: pfctl -si
answer: BSD pf: Show interface statistics — packets passed/blocked per interface, byte counts, error counters. Used for firewall monitoring and capacity planning.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: iptables -L -v -n --line-numbers
answer: List iptables rules with verbose statistics (packets/bytes matched per rule), numeric output (no name resolution), and line numbers for rule insertion/deletion.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -m recent --name web --set
answer: Use iptables recent module to track connections. Can rate-limit: --hitcount 20 --seconds 60 --name web --update then DROP. Mitigation against HTTP flood attacks.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: ip link set eth0 txqueuelen 10000
answer: Increase transmit queue length. Useful for firewall handling burst traffic (default 1000). Reduces packet drop at high throughput at cost of more memory.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-rst) != 0'
answer: Capture only TCP SYN and RST packets — useful for detecting port scans (SYN flood) and connection resets (RST attacks).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: ip xfrm state list
answer: Linux: List all IPsec SA states in kernel SAD (Security Association Database). Shows SPI, crypto algorithms (enc/auth), key IDs, lifetime. Also: ip xfrm policy list (SPD).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: openvpn --genkey --secret /etc/openvpn/static.key
answer: Generate pre-shared static key for OpenVPN in pre-shared key mode (not recommended — TLS mode with certificates is more secure). Key used for HMAC + encryption.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: dig +short txt _dmarc.example.com
answer: Query DMARC TXT record — shows email authentication policy (p=reject/quarantine/none, rua report-to addresses). Missing DMARC means anyone can spoof your domain.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: host -t ns example.com
answer: Query name server records for domain. Useful for DNS investigation: find authoritative nameservers, then check zone transfer vulnerability with host -l.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -a 100
answer: Generate Ed25519 SSH key (modern, 128-bit security, small key/fast). -a 100 sets KDF rounds (increases brute-force cost on passphrase). Preferred over RSA for SSH since OpenSSH 6.5+.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: ssh-keygen -R hostname.example.com
answer: Remove host key from known_hosts file. Used when a server is rebuilt and host key changes (man-in-the-middle warning). Alternative: ssh-keygen -F hostname to search, -H to hash.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: Order the path a packet takes through Linux iptables/netfilter:
steps: Packet arrives on network interface (e.g., eth0)
PREROUTING chain (raw table — connection tracking) — packet before routing decision
Routing decision: if destination is local → INPUT; if forwarding → FORWARD
INPUT chain (filter table) — for locally destined packets
Process delivered to local application (e.g., web server listening on port 80)
OUTPUT chain (filter table) — for packets generated locally
POSTROUTING chain (nat table — SNAT/MASQUERADE) — routing decision completed
Packet leaves on outgoing interface

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - P2
question: Site-to-site IPsec VPN between two firewalls: tunnel establishes (Phase 1 complete) but traffic does not pass through. Troubleshoot:
answer: 1) Check Phase 2 (IPsec SA) — is it established? 'ipsec status' or 'show crypto ipsec sa'. If not, check proxy-IDs (local/remote subnet definitions) mismatch. 2) Verify interesting traffic — a packet must match ACL to trigger IPsec. Send test traffic: ping from behind-SiteA to behind-SiteB. 3) Check firewall rules — traffic may be allowed by IPsec tunnel but blocked by firewall ACL. 4) Check routing — both sides need route to remote subnet pointing to tunnel interface (or policy-based routing if not using VTI). 5) Check NAT — if both sites use RFC 1918 addresses, ensure no NAT interfering with IPsec (NAT before encryption breaks IPsec). Exempt IPsec traffic from NAT with 'nat (inside,outside) source static ... destination static ... no-proxy-arp'. 6) Check MTU — IPsec adds headers (50-60 bytes). If original MTU 1500 → 1540-1560 bytes exceeds link MTU → fragmentation issues. Set TCP MSS to 1350 on IPsec interface or reduce tunnel MTU. 7) Check DPD (Dead Peer Detection): ensure both sides have DPD configured, else zombie SAs persist. 8) Check logs: 'show logging', 'debug crypto ipsec 255' (careful — production). 9) Packet capture on both sides to confirm ESP packets arriving with correct SPI.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Windows User Account Control (UAC)
answer: UAC runs all applications in standard user mode — even if logged in as administrator. Admin approvals: consent.exe prompts for elevation (Yes/No). Four levels: (0) Never notify (disabled — insecure), (1) Notify only for non-Microsoft binaries, (2) Notify only when app makes changes (default — no desktop dim), (3) Always notify (dim desktop — highest, recommended). Secure desktop: dimmed background prevents other apps from modifying the prompt. Auto-elevation: Windows components may auto-elevate if signed by Microsoft (exploitable by DLL hijacking). Best practice: enable level 3 (always notify), avoid running as admin daily.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Windows Credential Guard
answer: Virtualization-based security feature (Windows 10 Enterprise/Education). Uses Hyper-V to create isolated LSA process that protects Kerberos tickets, NTLM hashes, and credentials. Even SYSTEM-level processes cannot read protected credentials. Prevents: Pass-the-Hash (PtH), Pass-the-Ticket (PtT), credential dumping (Mimikatz). Requirements: UEFI Secure Boot, virtualization enabled in BIOS, SLAT-capable CPU. Enable via Group Policy: Computer Config > Admin Templates > System > Device Guard > 'Turn On Virtualization Based Security' > 'Enable with UEFI lock'.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Windows Defender Application Guard (WDAG)
answer: Hyper-V sandbox for Microsoft Edge. Untrusted sites run in isolated container — separate kernel, separate memory. If compromised, the malware cannot access host OS, files, or enterprise network. Data persistence: cookies and favorites survive container restart. Data exfiltration: copy/paste is blocked by default. Enterprise mode: enterprise-trusted sites run normally, untrusted in container. Hardware requirements: 8GB+ RAM, SSD, VT-x/AMD-V, SLAT. Available: Windows 10 Pro/Enterprise, Windows 11.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Windows Sandbox
answer: Lightweight VM for running untrusted applications. Uses Windows 10 Pro/Enterprise 1903+. Features: 1) Clean state every boot — no persistence. 2) Host isolation — sandbox runs separate Windows instance. 3) Integrated with Windows (no separate Hyper-V/VirtualBox). 4) Clipboard sharing (configurable). 5) Network access (can be disabled). Use: test suspicious attachments, run unknown executables, browse risky sites. Configuration: .wsb file (XML format) controls vGPU, networking, mapped folders. Limitation: does not prevent malware from using guest-side exploits that escape VMs (VM escape).

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: AppLocker vs Software Restriction Policies (SRP)
answer: SRP (Windows XP+): enables/disables applications based on path, hash, certificate, zone (Internet/Intranet). GPO-based but limited control. AppLocker (Windows 7 Enterprise/Ultimate+, Windows 10 Enterprise): advanced whitelisting. Rules: Publisher (signed binary), Path (file/folder), Hash (SHA256 file hash). Enforcement: Audit only (log, no block), Enforce rules (block unapproved). Default rules allow Windows system files and Program Files. Best practice: enable AppLocker with default rules + organization-specific allow rules. Blocks ransomware, unauthorized software, script-based attacks. Windows 10 1903+: AppLocker for Windows 10 Pro via MDM.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Windows Defender Exploit Guard (WDEG)
answer: Suite of host intrusion prevention capabilities. Components: 1) Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules — block common malware behaviors (Office macro execution, script downloads, ransomware-like file operations, credential theft from LSASS). 2) Network Protection — block outbound connections to malicious IP/domains. 3) Controlled Folder Access — ransomware protection (allow only approved apps to modify protected folders: Documents, Pictures, Desktop). 4) Exploit Protection — system-wide exploit mitigations (DEP, ASLR, CFG, SEHOP, ForceRandomization for images). Configure via GPO, PowerShell (Set-ProcessMitigation), Intune, or Microsoft Defender Security Center.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Windows Defender System Guard
answer: Hardware-rooted security starting from boot. Secure Boot: UEFI verifies bootloader signature (validates against Microsoft certificate). Trusted Boot: Windows bootloader verifies kernel, drivers, startup files. Measured Boot: firmware records boot measurements in TPM (PCR registers) — can be remotely attested (Device Health Attestation). Kernel DMA Protection: block DMA attacks via Thunderbolt 3 ports. Memory integrity (Hypervisor-protected Code Integrity — HVCI): run kernel-mode drivers in VSM isolation — vulnerable drivers cannot modify kernel. System Guard Secure Launch: measured launch of hypervisor (Intel TXT / AMD SVM) — protects even if firmware compromised.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Windows Hello for Business
answer: Passwordless authentication using biometric (face, fingerprint) or PIN backed by TPM 2.0. Keys: asymmetric keypair generated and stored in TPM (private key never leaves hardware). PIN is tied to specific device — cannot be used on another device (even if PIN stolen, attacker needs physical device). Biometric: on-device matching (no face/fingerprint data sent to server). Enterprise: integrates with PKI — certificate enrollment for domain users. Cloud: Microsoft account-based, FIDO2/WebAuthn for Azure AD. Multi-factor: PIN + biometric = two factors (possession + inherence).

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE)
answer: Enterprise EDR platform. Capabilities: 1) Endpoint detection and response — real-time behavioral monitoring, automated investigation, remediation. 2) Threat & Vulnerability Management (TVM) — discover vulnerabilities, prioritize by risk. 3) Attack Surface Reduction — ASR rules, network protection, web protection. 4) Automated Investigation and Remediation (AIR) — AI-driven incident response (isolate machine, kill process, remove file). 5) Microsoft Threat Experts — managed hunting service. 6) Microsoft 365 Defender integration — correlates endpoint, email, identity, cloud app signals. Stack rank in industry: Gartner MQ Leader, Forrester Top.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Windows Event Log IDs for Security
answer: Key Event IDs: 4624 = successful logon (includes logon type: 2=interactive, 3=network, 4=batch, 5=service, 7=unlock, 10=remote interactive-RDP). 4625 = failed logon. 4648 = explicit credential logon (runas). 4672 = special privileges assigned to new logon (admin). 4688 = new process created (command line included). 4698 = scheduled task created. 4700/4701 = Windows Filtering Platform block. 4776 = credential validation (NTLM). 5140 = file share accessed. 5156 = Windows Firewall connection allowed. 5157 = blocked. 1102 = audit log cleared (suspicious). 7036 = service started/stopped. Enable command line logging via GPO: 'Include command line in process creation events'.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Android Security Model
answer: Application sandbox: each app runs as separate Linux user (UID), in its own process. Permissions model: install-time (Android <6.0) vs runtime (Android 6.0+). Groups: CAMERA, RECORD_AUDIO, READ_CONTACTS, ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, SEND_SMS, READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE. Dangerous vs normal permissions. Sideloading: install APKs from outside Google Play — 'Unknown sources' (Android 8+: 'Install unknown apps' per-app). Google Play Protect: built-in malware scanning (on-device + cloud). Android Enterprise: work profile separates personal/work apps (Android for Work). Verified Boot: dm-verity — block device integrity, detect system partition modification. SafetyNet/Play Integrity: hardware attestation for device integrity checking.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: iOS Security Model
answer: Sandbox: each app runs in its own directory (container), cannot access other app data without explicit sharing (UIDocumentPickerViewController). App Store review: all apps reviewed by Apple (code analysis, not comprehensive). No sideloading by default (enterprise: MDM certificate, developer: local signing). Secure Enclave: hardware security coprocessor (A7+ chips) — separate OS (SEPOS), handles Touch ID, Face ID data, cryptographic keys. Data Protection: file-level encryption based on class (Complete — NSFileProtectionComplete: accessible only when unlocked, Protected Unless Open, Protected Until First User Authentication). iOS 15+: on-device processing for Siri, Photos, keyboard.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: SIM Swapping Attack
answer: Attacker contacts mobile carrier, impersonates victim, requests SIM transfer to attacker-controlled SIM. Once activated: 1) Victim's phone loses service (no calls/SMS/data). 2) Attacker receives SMS verification codes → can reset passwords for email, bank, social media. 3) Attacker takes over accounts. Motivations: cryptocurrency theft, social media handle theft, bank account takeover. Defenses: 1) Use mobile carrier PIN/password for account changes. 2) Use authenticator app (TOTP) not SMS for 2FA. 3) Use hardware security key (FIDO2). 4) Enable Google/Facebook account recovery protections. 5) Don't link phone number to sensitive accounts if avoidable. 6) Prepaid carriers often more vulnerable (less identity verification).

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Mobile Device Management (MDM) vs Mobile Application Management (MAM)
answer: MDM: full device management — enroll device, configure policies (PIN policy, encryption, WiFi/VPN config, remote wipe). Device must be enrolled (BYOD concerns — privacy). MAM: manage applications only — no device enrollment. Protect corporate data in apps (copy/paste restrictions, app PIN, encrypted data, selective wipe). Microsoft Intune: supports both MDM and MAM. Android Enterprise: work profile (MAM-like separation without full MDM). Apple: MDM protocol (iOS 7+), Managed Open In, Per-App VPN. Best practice: MAM for BYOD (respect privacy), MDM for corporate-owned devices.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: App Permissions Audit
answer: Check app permissions regularly. Android: Settings → Apps → App → Permissions. Risky: SMS (read/send — premium SMS, intercept 2FA), Accessibility Service (read all on-screen data, control device — abused by banking trojans), Location (background + foreground), Contacts, Call Log. iOS: Settings → Privacy → each service. Micro-permissions: 'Allow Once' (iOS 15+), 'Ask Next Time', 'While Using the App'. Principle: grant minimum permissions needed for function (camera app doesn't need contacts). Revoke unused permissions. Watch for apps with Accessibility Service enabled that don't need it.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Cloud Storage Encryption Options
answer: Client-side encryption: encrypt files before upload (Cryptomator, Veracrypt container, Boxcryptor). Provider cannot read your data. Keys stored client-side. Server-side encryption: provider encrypts data at rest. AES-256 key typically managed by provider (transparent encryption). Bring Your Own Key (BYOK): customer generates and manages encryption key, provider uses it for data encryption. Hold Your Own Key (HYOK): customer holds key, provider sends data to customer for encrypt/decrypt. End-to-end: Microsoft 365 Message Encryption, Proton Drive, Tresorit. Best: client-side + zero-knowledge provider (cannot access keys).

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Data Privacy Laws Comparison
answer: GDPR (EU, 2018): applies to any org processing EU resident data. Rights: access, rectification, erasure (right-to-be-forgotten), portability, objection. Fines: up to 4% global revenue or €20M. Breach notification: 72 hours. CCPA (California, 2020): right to know what personal info collected, right to delete, right to opt-out of sale. LGPD (Brazil, 2020): modeled on GDPR. PIPEDA (Canada, 2000): consent-based, meaningful purpose. APPI (Japan, 2003): amended 2020. Impact on security: mandatory breach notification drives improved detection/response. Encryption serves as safe harbor (no breach notification if data encrypted).

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Zero Trust Architecture
answer: Security model: no implicit trust based on network location. 'Never trust, always verify.' Principles: 1) Verify explicitly — authenticate and authorize every access (device + user + data). 2) Least privilege — minimal access with Just-In-Time and Just-Enough-Access (JIT/JEA). 3) Assume breach — segment access, encrypt end-to-end, analytics for visibility. NIST SP 800-207: Zero Trust pillars — Identity, Device, Network, Application, Data. BeyondCorp (Google): access based on device/user context, not network IP. Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA): replaces VPN with per-app, context-aware access (Zscaler, Cloudflare Access, Tailscale).

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Multi-Cloud Security Challenges
answer: Complexities of using multiple cloud providers. Challenges: 1) Consistent IAM policies across AWS/Azure/GCP (different RBAC models). 2) Network segmentation: VPC (AWS), VNet (Azure), VPC (GCP) — interconnected with cloud WAN. 3) Key management across KMS providers (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP Cloud KMS). 4) Log aggregation/audit — CloudTrail (AWS), Activity Log (Azure), Cloud Audit (GCP) → SIEM. 5) Compliance boundaries — data across jurisdictions. 6) Cost management + Shadow IT. Tools: HashiCorp Terraform (IaC), Vault (secrets), Crossplane. CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker): monitor/control cloud usage.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Fileless Malware
answer: Malware that does not write files to disk — lives only in memory. Execution: 1) PowerShell/Python/JavaScript script runs in-memory (no .exe written). 2) Regsvr32 — execute code from .sct file (scriptlet). 3) WMI — persistence via WMI event subscription. 4) MSHTA — execute HTA application. 5) VBScript/JScript launched from Office macro. Defense: 1) AMSI (Anti-Malware Scan Interface) — script content scanned before execution. 2) Constrained Language Mode (PowerShell) — restrict cmdlets, COM objects. 3) Windows Defender ASR rules: 'Block JavaScript/VBScript from launching downloaded executable content'. 4) AppLocker/Windows Defender Application Control. 5) Enable PowerShell script block logging and transcription.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Supply Chain Attacks
answer: Attacker compromises software at source, before reaching end-user. Types: 1) Compromised development tools — SolarWinds Orion (2020): attackers inserted backdoor into legitimate Orion update, deployed to 18K customers (including US govt). 2) Compromised dependency — dependency confusion (npm, PyPI, Maven, RubyGems) — attacker publishes package with same name as internal private package. 3) Compromised CI/CD pipeline — attack build servers to inject malicious code. 4) Hardware supply chain — compromised firmware on motherboard NIC (LoJack). Defense: 1) SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) — track all dependencies. 2) Signed commits (GPG). 3) Pin dependency versions. 4) SLSA (Supply chain Levels for Software Artifacts). 5) Vendor security assessments. 6) Code signing verification.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Living Off the Land (LotL) Binaries
answer: Attackers use built-in OS tools (LOLBins) for malicious activity — reduces forensic evidence as tools are legitimate. Windows: certutil (download file), bitsadmin (download), wmic (process execution), powershell (everything), mshta (execute HTA), cscript/wscript (run scripts), schtasks (persistence), regsvr32 (execute COM). Linux: curl/wget (download), bash (reverse shell), python/perl/ruby (code exec), netcat (C2), cron (persistence), chkrootkit (if modded). Detection: monitor command-line arguments (process creation Event 4688 enable command line), correlate with known good (baseline), restrict execution policy, disable unnecessary tools, AMSI scanning, Sysmon (Event 1 process creation).

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: DLL Hijacking / Side-loading
answer: Windows search order exploit: application loads DLL without full path - Windows searches CWD, System32, PATH. Attacker places malicious DLL earlier in search order (writeable directory). Types: 1) Missing DLL - app tries to load DLL that does not exist. 2) DLL phantom - replace DLL in CWD that app loads. 3) DLL search-order - exploit search path precedence. 4) WinSxS / side-by-side - manifest-based DLL resolution bypass. Detection: Process Monitor (procmon) filter on CreateFile operations for DLL files, look for missing DLL or user-writeable paths. Defense: Safe DLL Search Mode (default in modern Windows), disable loading from remote UNC (webdav), application manifests with absolute paths.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Process Injection Techniques
answer: Code injection into running process to evade detection. Techniques: 1) Classic DLL injection — CreateRemoteThread + LoadLibrary (easy to detect). 2) Reflective DLL injection — implement LoadLibrary in-memory (no LoadLibrary call). 3) Process hollowing — legitimate process created in suspended state, its memory unmapped, malicious code written, resumed (ReplaceSection/WriteProcessMemory). 4) APC injection — QueueUserAPC to thread (run code in context of existing thread). 5) Thread execution hijacking — suspend thread, overwrite context with shellcode address. 6) AtomBombing — global atom table used to transfer shellcode. Detection: EDR monitors CreateRemoteThread, WriteProcessMemory, SetThreadContext API calls. Memory scanning detects injected sections.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Mimikatz
answer: Post-exploitation tool for credential extraction from Windows (Benjamin Delpy, 2011). Capabilities: 1) sekurlsa::logonpasswords — extract plaintext passwords from LSASS (wdigest, kerberos, tspkg, SSP). 2) sekurlsa::ekeys — extract Kerberos encryption keys. 3) kerberos::golden — create Golden Ticket (forge TGT using KRBTGT hash). 4) kerberos::silver — create Silver Ticket (service ticket for specific SPN). 5) lsadump::dcsync — replicate AD to extract all password hashes (DCSync attack). 6) sekurlsa::pth — pass-the-hash (NTLM hash for authentication without password). Defenses: 1) LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) — restricts access to LSASS. 2) Credential Guard (VBS isolation). 3) Disable WDigest (plaintext fallback). 4) Protected Users security group. 5) Limit debug privilege (SeDebugPrivilege). 6) Event ID 4663 for LSASS access. 7) Windows Defender ASR rule: 'Block credential stealing from Windows LSASS'.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: PowerShell Security — Constrained Language Mode
answer: PowerShell security restrictions. Full Language: all cmdlets, .NET access, COM, WMI. Constrained Language Mode: limits to specific types (no [System.Runtime.InteropServices], no [Microsoft.Win32.RegistryKey], no Win32 API calls via Add-Type -MemberDefinition). System-wide: $ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode = 'ConstrainedLanguage'. Enforce via GPO: 'Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging', 'Set PowerShell Execution Policy'. AMSI integration: Windows Defender scans PowerShell script content before execution. Script block logging: logs full script content (not just invocation). Defense: execute PowerShell via ConstrainedLanguage, block ConstrainedLanguage break (Registry key), enable Module Logging, Transcription.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Tor (The Onion Router) Network
answer: Anonymity network: traffic routed through three relay nodes (entry, middle, exit). Each layer decrypts one layer of encryption — knows only previous/next hop (not full path). Onion encryption: TLS between client and entry, TLS overlay encryption between each relay. Entry guard: first node — selected for months (prevent profiling by attacker controlling many nodes). Exit node: last node — decrypts final layer, communicates with destination. Risks: exit node sees plaintext traffic (use HTTPS always). Blocking: some services block Tor exit nodes (use cloud provider IP lists). Hidden services (.onion): client and server anonymous — rendezvous point without exposing IP. Alternatives: I2P (anonymous within I2P network), Freenet (censorship-resistant publishing).

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Signal Messenger Protocol Details
answer: Signal Protocol (formerly TextSecure/Axolotl). Double Ratchet: provides forward secrecy (compromise of current key does not expose past messages) + future secrecy (compromise of current key does not expose future messages after ratchet step). X3DH (Extended Triple Diffie-Hellman): initial key agreement — asynchronous, does not require both parties online. Public keys registered on Signal server (identity key, signed pre-key, one-time pre-keys). Server: ephemeral message storage (deleted after delivery). Minimal metadata: only stores account creation date + last connection timestamp. Encryption: AES-256-CBC + HMAC-SHA256 for message body. Voice/video: ZRTP (SRTP with ephemeral DH key exchange for per-call key). Open-source: client (GPLv3), server (AGPLv3). Audit: NCC Group, Cure53.

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Metadata and Its Privacy Implications
answer: Data about data — not content but context. Email: From, To, Subject, Date, routing headers (Received: lines show mailserver path). Phone: calling party, called party, duration, timestamp, cell tower location. Internet: IP addresses, DNS queries, connection timestamps, bandwidth usage, visited domains (even over HTTPS — SNI, DNS). Email metadata is visible in transit (not encrypted). Phone metadata collected by carriers (US §215 Patriot Act, now FISA Amendments Act). Analysis: phone metadata reveals relationships, locations, movements, sleep patterns (classified research: metadata analysis as effective as content surveillance). Protection: use Tor (obfuscates IP, DNS), VPN (hides IP from destination but VPN provider sees metadata), Signal (minimal metadata), email: use encrypted subject (PGP), anonymous remailers (Mixmaster).

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: Secure Deletion / File Shredding
answer: Regular delete marks file space as available — data remains until overwritten (recoverable with forensic tools). Secure deletion: overwrite data before marking free. Windows: cipher /w:C: overwrites free space. Linux: shred -f -n 3 filename (3 passes), wipe, srm. Single file: overwrite with 0xFF, 0x00, random data (most SSDs: TRIM command renders overwrite useless — SSD firmware may remap blocks). Full disk: DBAN (Darik's Boot and Nuke), Parted Magic. SSD secure erase: ATA Secure Erase command (firmware-level, erases all NAND blocks, including overprovisioning area). iPhone: Settings → General → Reset → Erase All Content and Settings (triggers Data Protection key escrow deletion + ATA Secure Erase). Cloud: delete all versions, empty recycle bin. Physical destruction: degauss (magnetic), shredder (physical), incineration (burn).

source: Complete Internet Security Manual - P2
question: DNS Privacy: DoH, DoT, DNSCrypt
answer: Standard DNS queries (UDP/53): plaintext — ISP, WiFi provider, any network observer sees all websites visited. DoT (DNS over TLS, RFC 7858): TCP/853, encrypted DNS between client and resolver. DoH (DNS over HTTPS, RFC 8484): TCP/443, DNS queries encapsulated in HTTPS (looks like normal web traffic — harder to block). DNSCrypt: encrypts + authenticates DNS (not standard, but widely used: OpenDNS, SimpleDNSCrypt). OS support: Android 9+ (DoT), Windows 10 2021+ (DoH configurable), iOS 14+ (DoH/DoT configuration profile), Firefox/Chrome (DoH built-in). Resolvers: Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 (DoH/DoT), Quad9 9.9.9.9 (blocks malicious domains, DoH/DoT), Comcast, Google 8.8.8.8 (DoH/DoT). Privacy: DoH/DoT moves DNS query visibility from ISP to DNS provider — trust the resolver.

question: reg save HKLM\SAM sam.save && reg save HKLM\SYSTEM system.save
