source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What do the Python libraries grpcio and grpcio-tools do?
answer: They are used to autogenerate the Python gRPC bindings from the protobuf definition. A gRPC insecure channel establishes a TCP connection without certificate validation.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is the small set of gRPC operations defined by gNMI?
answer: CapabilityRequest, GetRequest, SetRequest, and SubscribeRequest. These are defined in the gnmi.proto file, part of the OpenConfig project.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: How do gNMI operations map to NETCONF operations?
answer: CapabilityRequest maps to hello; GetRequest maps to get/get-config; SetRequest maps to edit-config; SubscribeRequest maps to establish-subscription.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Why has gNMI gained popularity in the observability realm?
answer: Because it provided the first implementation of dial-in streaming telemetry.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is gNMIc?
answer: An open source CLI client for exploring gNMI, adopted under the OpenConfig umbrella. It can be installed via a bash script (bash -c "$(curl -sL https://get-gnmic.openconfig.net)") or run as a Docker container.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Is there a standard TCP port for gNMI, and what is the Arista default?
answer: No standard TCP port exists; you must double-check the TCP port used. The default port for Arista is TCP/6030, but it can be changed.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: gnmic -a eos-spine1:6030 -u ntc -p ntc123 --insecure capabilities
answer: Sends a CapabilityRequest (equivalent to the NETCONF hello) to the device, listing the supported data models (e.g., openconfig-network-instance-types, iana-if-type, arista-vlan-deviations) and supported encodings (JSON, JSON_IETF, ASCII).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: gnmic -a eos-spine1:6030 -u ntc -p ntc123 --insecure --gzip get --path '/interfaces/interface/config'
answer: Performs a gNMI GetRequest to retrieve the configuration state from the running configuration, targeting the config container in an OpenConfig data model.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: gnmic -a eos-spine1:6030 -u ntc -p ntc123 --insecure --gzip set --update-path '/interfaces/interface[name=Management0]/config/description' --update-value 'New Description'
answer: Performs a gNMI SetRequest using update-path and update-value, using XPath filtering to target a specific interface's description leaf and set its value.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: gnmic -a eos-spine1:6030 -u ntc -p ntc123 --insecure subscribe --path "/interfaces/interface/state/counters"
answer: Performs a gNMI Subscribe operation to subscribe to interface counters, keeping a session established to get updates on the data model.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question:
Complete the gNMIc command that checks which data models are supported (equivalent to NETCONF hello):
gnmic -a eos-spine1:6030 -u ntc -p ntc123 --insecure ___

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What do the supported data models and supported encoding in gNMI capabilities tell you?
answer: Supported data models define what can be changed/retrieved from the device (from standards bodies IANA/IETF, OpenConfig, and the vendor). Supported encoding is the encoding of the payload (not the transport encoding, which is protobuf): JSON and JSON_IETF allow structured data, and ASCII is used for semistructured CLI configuration.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What syntax do gNMI paths use?
answer: gNMI paths are a simplified variant of the XPath syntax (e.g., /interfaces/interface/config or /interfaces/interface[name=Management0]/config). Paths can be obtained by observing YANG data models or using tools like Cisco YANG Suite.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: How do OpenConfig and IETF differ in data model organization for intended vs operational state?
answer: In OpenConfig, a model node has two containers, config and state, representing the intended and operational state respectively. The IETF proposed to split both configurations into different data stores.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is returned when targeting the state container instead of the config container in a gNMI Get?
answer: Besides the interface configuration (with default values), the interface stats are returned, including counters, admin-status, oper-status, ifindex, and last-change.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What two Set operation modes does gNMI support?
answer: update and replace, which are similar to a PATCH versus PUT in REST APIs.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
symptoms: A gNMI SetRequest to update the mtu leaf on an Arista switch fails with 'rpc error: code = Aborted ... Unavailable command (not supported on this hardware platform)'.
root_cause: Not all attributes are configurable because of dependencies on the platform. The error also reveals that the device translates the YANG data model changes into CLI commands (e.g., 'l2 mtu 1400'), which are invalid on this hardware.
troubleshooting_steps: Check which leaves are actually writable in the platform's gNMI backend/data model.
Review the error message, which shows the CLI commands executed behind the scenes, to understand why the translation failed.
Update only attributes the platform supports, or use a different data model/encoding.
resolution: Do not attempt to set read-only or unsupported leaves such as mtu on this platform; the YANG-to-CLI translation fails because the command is not supported on the hardware.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: How does gNMI Subscribe work?
answer: It keeps a session established from the client to get updates on a data model (e.g., interface counters, operational status, or BGP session establishment). Updates can be sampled periodically or triggered when the value changes, so you get notified only when something happens.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What was the first data-model interface to support data-model-driven (dial-in) telemetry?
answer: gNMI, with its subscribe operation.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Which statement correctly describes the data encoding of the three data-model interfaces?

choices.label: NETCONF uses XML, RESTCONF uses JSON or XML, and gNMI uses protobuf or JSON
NETCONF and gNMI both use XML
gNMI only supports JSON encoding
RESTCONF only supports XML like NETCONF

explanation: Table 10-6: NETCONF uses XML, RESTCONF uses JSON or XML, and gNMI uses protobuf or JSON. gNMI chose protobuf because binary encoding reduces payload size, important for streaming operational data.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Which statement correctly describes the transports of the data-model interfaces?

choices.label: NETCONF uses SSH, RESTCONF uses HTTP/TLS, and gNMI uses gRPC over HTTP/2
All three use SSH as their transport
gNMI uses SSH while NETCONF uses gRPC
RESTCONF uses only FTP transport

explanation: NETCONF's de facto transport is SSH, RESTCONF leverages HTTP/TLS to become a REST API, and gNMI adopted gRPC over HTTP/2 to support protobuf encoding.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Which statement correctly describes the transaction scope of the three data-model interfaces?

choices.label: NETCONF is network-wide, RESTCONF is single-target single-shot, and gNMI is single-target single-shot sequenced
All three support network-wide transactions
RESTCONF supports network-wide transactions but gNMI does not
gNMI supports network-wide transactions through the subscribe operation

explanation: NETCONF came from operator best practices supporting network-wide transactions; RESTCONF adheres to REST principles, dealing with only one target at a time without relevant operation sequence; gNMI assumes a specific order of all its operations (sequenced).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Why did gNMI choose protobuf encoding?
answer: Because this binary encoding reduced the payload when compared to XML, and streaming operational data was an important use case that creates a lot of network traffic.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What was the historical progression of NETCONF, OpenConfig/gNMI, and RESTCONF?
answer: NETCONF (first RFC 2006) addressed SNMP's limitations for configuration management. Around 2014 the OpenConfig consortium was founded (led by Google), focused on streaming telemetry and gNMI (open source project, first commit 2017). Around 2017 the IETF created RESTCONF, combining the NETCONF approach with the simpler RESTful API paradigm.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: How do IETF and OpenConfig differ in their development lifecycle?
answer: IETF develops technical recommendations via an open process with volunteers and rough consensus (mission defined in RFC 3936); its process of proposal, approval, and implementation usually takes longer. OpenConfig is a working group of operators and vendors operating as an open source project with direct contributions, leading to a faster release cycle.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Give an example of a successful nonstandard solution later adopted by IETF.
answer: NetFlow and IPFIX (Internet Protocol Flow Information Export). Successful nonstandard solutions have been adopted multiple times, showing that IETF standards and OpenConfig-style projects can coexist.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What operational limitations of SNMP led to model-driven telemetry?
answer: SNMP retrieves data via a poll method, with the management server asking for data every time, adding delay and extra processing to get data continuously. These performance limitations plus data-model management adoption led to the push-based model.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is dial-in telemetry?
answer: A dynamic model where an external application opens a session to the network device and establishes one or more subscriptions (to different parts of the data store) over the same session. The network devices send operation data for as long as the session stays up.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is dial-out telemetry?
answer: A configured model where subscriptions are configured on the network device in advance using any of the available interfaces, and it's up to the device to open a telemetry session to the receiver. If this session goes down, the network device will open a new one.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Which statement correctly distinguishes dial-in from dial-out telemetry?

choices.label: Dial-in: an external app opens a session to the device and subscribes; Dial-out: the device is configured in advance and opens the session to the receiver
Dial-in: the device opens the session; Dial-out: the collector subscribes
Dial-in sends data over UDP only
Both models require the collector to maintain persistent sessions to devices

explanation: Dial-in is dynamic: the external application opens a session to the device and establishes subscriptions. Dial-out is configured: subscriptions are configured on the device in advance, and the device opens the telemetry session to the receiver.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What benefits does the dial-out model add?
answer: (1) Reduces a network device's exposure to external threats as the connection is initiated from the device itself, avoiding firewall configurations to let access in. (2) Collectors can be stateless; they only listen and store collected data. The control is on the configuration management system that created the subscription.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Which interfaces support the dial-in model, and how is dial-out configured?
answer: Both NETCONF and gNMI support the dial-in model. Dial-out mode is simply a configuration setting that can be done via any configuration interface (including CLI), and the data is exported over a transport protocol (TCP or UDP).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Why has telemetry prioritized TCP over UDP?
answer: TCP provides more reliable data transfer and nonrepudiation (UDP is used by SNMP). However, UDP support provides benefits in highly intense event traffic, such as in sampling mode when TCP benefits are not mandatory.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is CBOR?
answer: Concise Binary Object Representation, standardized in RFC 8949, a binary data format based on JSON that supports schema definition directly with the YANG language.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is YANG Push?
answer: IETF standards grouped as YANG Push, which support more use cases (e.g., more encoding options like JSON and CBOR) and UDP and HTTPS/TCP transport options. It comes from a standardization body (IETF), important for some network industry actors such as service providers.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What are the five libraries/packages used for automation in this chapter?
answer: Python Requests (HTTP-based APIs), Go net/http (HTTP-based APIs, especially RESTCONF), Python ncclient (NETCONF), Go OpenConfig gNMIc (gNMI), and Python Netmiko (SSH-based automation).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs

question: In the Requests library, what do the arguments passed to requests.get() represent?

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What does the status_code attribute of a Requests response provide?
answer: The HTTP response code as an integer (e.g., print(response.status_code) gives 200).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What does the json() method of a Requests response do?
answer: Returns the response content as a dict (or list), decoding the JSON contained in the text attribute (which stores the actual response string).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is the difference between a Python dictionary and a JSON string when sending HTTP request bodies?
answer: You work with dictionaries in Python to construct the required body, but it is sent over the wire as a JSON string. To convert the dictionary to a well-formed JSON string, use json.dumps() from the json module and assign it to the data key of the request.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What does the HTTPBasicAuth class from Requests provide?
answer: A Requests class used to create the basic authentication header (Base64 encoding of user:password), passed via the auth parameter, e.g., HTTPBasicAuth('ntc', 'ntc123').

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Why is using an http:// endpoint not recommended for production, and how are warnings handled?
answer: Traffic is not encrypted. If you use a self-signed certificate or unverified HTTPS connection (adding verify=False), you will receive a warning, which can be disabled with requests.packages.urllib3.disable_warnings().

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: In the eAPI response with format: "json", what does the result key contain?
answer: The output of the commands executed - a list of dictionaries, with one list element for each command executed (e.g., a dict with a vlans key for show vlan brief).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is the purpose of the issue_request(device, commands) helper function in the eAPI LLDP example?
answer: It wraps the API request so you can pass different target devices and different commands to obtain the response (already converted from JSON to a Python object). It demonstrates the Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY) software development principle.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: In the eAPI LLDP autoconfiguration example, what does get_lldp_neighbors() extract and how?
answer: It issues the 'show lldp neighbors' command via issue_request() and returns response['result'][0]['lldpNeighbors'], a list of dictionaries each containing ttl, neighborDevice, neighborPort, and port.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What does configure_interfaces(device, neighbors) do in the LLDP example?
answer: It builds a command_list starting with 'enable' and 'configure', then for each neighbor with a local interface starting with 'Eth' it appends 'interface <port>' and 'description Connects to interface <neighborPort> on neighbor <neighborDevice>' commands, then sends them in a single API call per device via issue_request().

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What two useful approaches to code readability does the LLDP example demonstrate?
answer: (1) Self-descriptive naming (e.g., get_lldp_neighbors clearly defines its intent). (2) Leveraging function docstrings to explain the function's purpose, such as the format of the response.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is the correct order to autoconfigure interface descriptions based on LLDP neighbors using eAPI?
correct_sequence: Get the LLDP neighbors with issue_request(device, ['show lldp neighbors']) and extract response['result'][0]['lldpNeighbors']
Build a command_list starting with 'enable' and 'configure' and append 'interface <port>' and 'description ...' commands for each Ethernet interface
Send the whole command_list in a single API call per device via issue_request()
Repeat for each device in the devices list and print a confirmation message
distractor_sequences: Send configuration commands first, then query LLDP neighbors
Query LLDP neighbors and configure interfaces in separate sessions without reusing the request function
Build the description from the local interface name instead of the neighbor's port and device
explanation: The workflow first gathers LLDP data, then builds the configuration commands for each Ethernet interface, and finally sends them in a single API call per device, looping over all devices.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is an API SDK?
answer: A software package that abstracts access to an API by using functions, methods, and/or classes. It allows faster development because all common conventions are implemented, making code simpler and more readable, but may introduce constraints from non-implemented features or add library dependencies increasing the application's footprint.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs

answer: Cisco Meraki SDK (meraki.DashboardAPI) and Arista eAPI SDK.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is an advantage of using the Meraki API SDK over the Requests library?
answer: You get the same output without having to know about API conventions, such as the custom authentication header the API expects. This improves maintainability because if the header key changes, you don't need to update your code.

question: Which statement correctly describes an API SDK trade-off?

choices.label: It speeds up development with common conventions implemented but may add constraints and library dependencies
It always covers every feature of the underlying API
It removes the need for API documentation entirely
It only works with non-RESTful APIs

explanation: An SDK comes with all common conventions implemented (faster, simpler, more readable code), but it could introduce constraints due to non-implemented features or add library dependencies increasing the footprint of the application.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What does the basicAuth(username, password string) string helper function in the Go example do?
answer: It constructs the expected format of the basic authentication string by concatenating username:password and encoding it with base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString. The result is placed in the Authorization header as "Basic " + basicAuth(...).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What does http.NewRequest do in the Go RESTCONF example?
answer: It creates a new HTTP request with a method, URL, and optional body (nil for GET). Headers are then set via request.Header.Set (e.g., Accept: application/yang-data+json and the Authorization header).

answer: client.Do() performs the HTTP request; ioutil.ReadAll() reads the body content from the response; result.Body.Close() closes the response body.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: How do you narrow a RESTCONF GET in Go to a specific interface?
answer: Use URI-encoded path expressions, e.g., restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces/interface=GigabitEthernet1. The expression matches the identifier field (name) of the interface in the YANG model and returns only that interface's configuration.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What does the TLSClientConfig: &tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: true} transport configuration do in the Go example?
answer: It creates an http.Transport that ignores expired/self-signed SSL certificates so the HTTP client can connect to devices that don't have valid certificates.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Why does the chapter recommend starting with PATCH and gradually migrating to PUT for RESTCONF configuration management?
answer: Because PUT declaratively replaces the entire targeted section, so a small change sent via PUT can have catastrophic consequences (e.g., eliminating all other routing protocol configs). PATCH makes small additions safely.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Which statement correctly describes the danger of a PUT targeting the router key in RESTCONF?

choices.label: It would replace everything under the router key, technically eliminating all other routing protocol configurations
It would only append the new routing config to the existing one
It is identical to PATCH in its behavior
It only works over gRPC transport

explanation: PUT replaces the whole targeted hierarchy. Targeting the router key would replace all routing protocol configurations under it, which shows the power and potential danger if PUT is not used and understood properly.

question: What does the ncclient manager.connect() function do?
answer: It establishes a persistent connection to the device. Since NETCONF runs over SSH, this connection is stateful and persistent (as compared to RESTful APIs being stateless). It returns a Manager object exposing methods for NETCONF RPC operations.

question: Why are all Junos vMX filters in this chapter subtree filters?
answer: Because that platform doesn't support XPath for get operations. The ncclient supports XPath filters, but support depends on the NETCONF capabilities of the platform.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What types of filter objects can you pass to ncclient's get()?
answer: XML strings or native XML objects (lxml etree objects). Strings are more human-readable and easier to use when getting started; use etree objects if you need to dynamically build a filter object.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is stored in the data attribute of the ncclient reply, and how is it converted to a string?

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What does the find() method of an lxml.etree object do, and what expression syntax does it use?
answer: It provides a simple way to search a full XML object for a given XML tag using the expression denoted by .// (e.g., nc_get_reply.data.find('.//address')).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: When XML namespaces are used, how must the tag name be specified in an lxml find() call?
answer: The tag name must include the namespace concatenated, in other words {namespace}tag, e.g., {http://yang.juniper.net/junos/conf/interfaces}address. Alternatively, if an XML namespace alias is defined, it can be used as alias:tag.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
symptoms: nc_get_reply.data.find('.//address') fails to find the XML element even though the tag exists in the response.
root_cause: When XML namespaces are used, the tag name must include the namespace concatenated as {namespace}tag; searching for 'address' without the namespace fails because the default namespace is overridden in the hierarchy.
troubleshooting_steps: Determine which namespace the target element belongs to by printing one child object at a time.
Use the fully qualified name, e.g., .//{http://yang.juniper.net/junos/conf/interfaces}address.
Then extract the inner <name> tag the same way and read its .text attribute.
resolution: Concatenate the namespace with the tag name as {namespace}tag in the find() expression, or strip namespaces from the XML object before parsing.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is the default edit operation in NETCONF edit-config, and how is the delete operation specified in ncclient?
answer: The default edit operation is merge. To delete, set the operation attribute on the element, e.g., <community operation="delete">, where only the <name> tag is required to identify the object.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: In NETCONF, what is the replace operation equivalent to in RESTCONF, and what is the caution?
answer: The replace operation is the same as doing a PUT with RESTCONF: you define the replace operation (<snmp operation="replace">) and the desired configuration. Placing operation="delete" or "replace" at the wrong place in the XML hierarchy can have a catastrophic effect (e.g., replacing the <snmp> tag replaces the full SNMP configuration).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Which statement correctly describes NETCONF merge versus replace operations?

choices.label: merge manages configuration from its current state (add/update), while replace implements a declarative approach that only needs the final state
merge deletes all existing configuration, while replace adds to it
replace is the default operation, while merge must be explicitly specified
merge requires the full configuration, while replace only needs a partial one

explanation: merge is the default and enables adding or updating configuration from the current state; replace defines the desired final state declaratively, like RESTCONF PUT, and automatically removes anything not in the replacement.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What are the ncclient methods for vendor-specific and standard NETCONF operations?
answer: Standard ones include edit_config(), get(), commit(), copy_config(), delete_config(), lock(), and unlock(). commit() commits a candidate configuration to the active running configuration; copy_config() and delete_config() create/replace and delete an entire configuration data store; lock() and unlock() prevent/allow other systems from making changes during a session.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: How do you use vendor-specific ncclient operations?
answer: You need to specify the correct platform in the device_params parameter when instantiating a device object, e.g., device_params={"name": "junos"}. Every example in the chapter used device_params={} because it used industry-standard operations.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What vendor-specific ncclient operations does Juniper provide?
answer: Custom methods such as get_configuration(), load_configuration(), compare_configuration(), and command(). With device_params={"name": "junos"}, device._vendor_operations includes keys like rpc, get_configuration, load_configuration, compare_configuration, command, reboot, halt, commit, and rollback.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Why should you lock the configuration data store in a production environment?
answer: So that no other person or system can make changes during your NETCONF session; when complete, you unlock the configuration.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is the OpenConfig gNMIc Go package?

question: What is the most popular Python library for gNMI management?

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: In the gNMIc subscribe example, what are the subscription modes and list modes?
answer: SubscriptionMode can be sample, on_change, or target_defined. SubscriptionListMode selects stream instead of poll. sample mode uses a SampleInterval; on-change only sends data when there is a change in the data source.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: How is the gNMI subscription managed in the Go example?
answer: tg.Subscribe(ctx, subReq, "sub1") runs in a new goroutine; a second goroutine stops the subscription after 30 seconds via tg.StopSubscription("sub1"); the main process reads responses and errors via two Go channels (tg.ReadSubscriptions()) in an infinite loop until the subscription is stopped.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is Netmiko?
answer: A popular open source network-first SSH client for Python whose purpose is to simplify SSH device management specifically for network devices. It supports dozens of device types (Arista, Brocade, Cisco, Dell, HPE, Juniper, Palo Alto Networks, Linux, and more).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Why is SSH automation with Python still important?
answer: (1) Not all devices support a programmatic API. (2) You may want to automate the turning on of the API. (3) Even if automating a device with an API, it's good to have a backup plan, and not all operations of a device may be supported with the API.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is one of the great things about Netmiko's usage across vendors?
answer: The overall usage is common across vendors - only the commands used are specific to each platform.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs

question: What is the send_command_expect() method in Netmiko?
answer: Used for long-running commands that may take a while to process (show run on a larger chassis, show tech, etc.). By default, it waits for the same prompt string to return before completing; optionally you can pass the new expected prompt string via expect_string.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is the send_command_timing() method in Netmiko?
answer: Used for short-running commands; it is timing based and does not check the prompt string.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is the send_command() method in Netmiko?
answer: An older method in Netmiko that now acts as a wrapper for calling send_command_expect(); thus send_command() and send_command_expect() perform the same operation.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Which statement correctly distinguishes send_command_expect() from send_command_timing()?

choices.label: send_command_expect() waits for a prompt string while send_command_timing() is timing based and does not check the prompt
send_command_timing() is for long-running commands and waits for a prompt string
send_command_expect() never supports an expect_string parameter
Both methods require the expect_string parameter to work

explanation: send_command_expect() is for long-running commands and by default waits for the same prompt string (optionally a new prompt via expect_string); send_command_timing() is timing based and does not check the prompt string.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question:
Complete the Python code that sends a command changing the prompt and specifies the new expected prompt:
output = device.send_command_expect('end', ___='nxos-spine1#')

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What does the send_config_set() method do in Netmiko?
answer: It sends several commands at once (the parameter must be iterable, e.g., a Python list or set). It checks whether you're already in configuration mode; if not, it goes into config mode, executes the commands, and by default exits configuration mode.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question:
Complete the Python code that sends a set of configuration commands with Netmiko:
commands = [
  'interface Ethernet1/1',
  'description configured by netmiko',
  'shutdown'
]
output = device.send_config_set(___=commands)

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question:
Complete the Python code that sends CLI commands from a file with Netmiko:
output = device.___(filename)

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What workflow does send_config_from_file() enable?
answer: Create a Jinja template, render it with variable data, write the data to a file, and then execute those commands from the file with Netmiko's send_config_from_file(). Afterwards, use show commands to verify the change succeeded.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question:
Complete the Python code that gracefully disconnects from the device with Netmiko:
device.___()

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: How can Netmiko be used as a context manager?
answer: Netmiko provides netmiko.ConnectHandler as a context manager, which establishes the SSH session at the beginning and tears it down when exiting, so you don't leave open SSH connections: with netmiko.ConnectHandler(**device_config) as device: device.send_command("show run").

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
symptoms: device.send_command_expect('end') raises OSError: 'Search pattern never detected in send_command: nxos-spine1(config)#' after leaving config mode.
root_cause: send_command_expect() expects to see the same prompt string by default. While in config mode the prompt is nxos-spine1(config)#, but typing 'end' changes the prompt to nxos-spine1#, so the expected pattern is never detected.
troubleshooting_steps: Use the expect_string parameter to define the new expected prompt: send_command_expect('end', expect_string='nxos-spine1#').
Alternatively, use send_command_timing('end'), which is timing based and does not expect a particular prompt string.
resolution: Pass the new prompt via expect_string or use send_command_timing() for commands that change the prompt.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is TextFSM?
answer: An open source project built by Google that converts semiformatted text (the CLI output) to structured data, using templates. For each CLI output you need to provide a specific template.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is NTC Templates?
answer: An open source project sponsored by Network to Code that provides a large collection of TextFSM templates for many network vendors. It is a dependency of Netmiko, so it is already installed with it.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What are the two steps to transform Netmiko raw CLI output into structured data?
answer: (1) Get raw CLI output from Netmiko and store it as a string. (2) Use the NTC Templates parser to transform the raw output into structured data.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question:
Complete the Python code that parses raw CLI output with NTC Templates:
from ntc_templates.parse import parse_output
show_interfaces_parsed =  parse_output(
    platform="cisco_nxos",
    command="show int brief",
    data=show_interfaces_raw,
)

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: How can Netmiko use NTC Templates directly since its 2.0.0 release?
answer: Using the use_textfsm argument: device.send_command('show int brief', use_textfsm=True). This combines the two manual steps into one.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question:
Complete the Python code that gets structured output directly from Netmiko:
show_interfaces_parsed_directly = device.send_command(
    'show int brief',
    ___=True,
)

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is NAPALM, and how does it relate to Netmiko?
answer: NAPALM is a robust and multivendor network Python library for configuring devices and retrieving data. Netmiko is used as the primary SSH driver for devices within NAPALM. NAPALM is covered in Chapter 12.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: Why is the unstructured data of CLI output a drawback in the automation journey?
answer: SSH output is text viewable by a human; it does not use structured encoded data such as XML or JSON over the wire. Helpers like TextFSM and NTC Templates convert it into structured data.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is the correct order to make a configuration change via NETCONF with a candidate configuration?
correct_sequence: Establish the NETCONF session and exchange capabilities (server hello, then client hello)
Issue a get request to learn the structure of the configuration object you want to change
Send an edit-config targeting the candidate data store with the desired config
Execute a commit operation to write the candidate configuration to the running configuration
distractor_sequences: Commit first, then send the edit-config
Send the edit-config to the running data store and commit afterwards
Skip the capabilities exchange and immediately send edit-config
explanation: You must exchange capabilities first, learn the object structure via a get, load changes into the candidate data store with edit-config, and then commit to activate them.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is the correct order to add OSPF network statements via RESTCONF on Cisco IOS XE?
correct_sequence: Discover the RESTCONF path via /.well-known/host-meta if unknown
Perform a GET on the configuration section to check the expected data model structure (e.g., the router/router-ospf section)
Send a PATCH request targeting the router-ospf leaf with the new networks using the same process-id
Verify the change by repeating the GET and confirming the new networks appear
distractor_sequences: Send a PUT request to a router key to add two networks
PATCH the whole native config without knowing the data model structure
Use GET to add the networks to the configuration
explanation: You first need to know the data model structure (from a GET), then PATCH appends the new networks to the existing process-id, and you verify with a GET afterwards.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is the correct order to explore and manage a device via gNMI with gNMIc?
correct_sequence: Verify the TCP port for gNMI and run the capabilities operation to see supported data models and encodings
Use get with the desired path (e.g., /interfaces/interface/config) to retrieve configuration
Use set with update-path and update-value to change a leaf such as description
Use subscribe to receive streaming updates (e.g., interface counters)
distractor_sequences: Subscribe first, then run capabilities
Use set before checking the data model structure
Run capabilities after configuring the device
explanation: Capabilities tell you what the interface supports first; then get retrieves current state, set changes it, and subscribe streams updates.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What is the big shared challenge slowing the adoption of data-model interfaces?
answer: The translation between standard or community data models and the device models does not always cover all features or may not be fully supported. Text-based configurations remain the main interface for many network devices for this reason.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch10: Working with Network APIs
question: What determines which network interface you should use for automation?
answer: It depends on the device you are trying to automate - including the interfaces it supports and the capabilities you need to use - and the tooling you prefer.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is source control?
answer: Source control is a way of tracking files and the changes made to those files over time. It is also known as version control or revision control.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What does it mean for a source control tool to 'track' files?
answer: The source control tool keeps a record of the files, the changes made to the files over time, and who made each set of changes. If a change breaks something, you can revert, or roll back, to a previous version to get back to a known good state.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What are the three main use cases for source control described in the chapter?
answer: 1) A developer tracking code written as part of a larger software development project; 2) A team of administrators tracking network device configuration files; 3) Tracking documentation for an organization's IT infrastructure.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is the 'change tracking' benefit of source control?
answer: You can track the changes to the files stored in the source control tool over time, see the state of the files at any given point, and see exactly what changed between versions. Most tools also let you add metadata about the change, such as why it was made or a reference back to an issue or trouble ticket.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is the 'accountability' benefit of source control?
answer: Source control tools track who made the changes; every change is logged with who made that particular change, so in a team environment you never again have to ask 'Who made this change?'

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is the 'process and workflow' benefit of source control?
answer: Source control helps enforce a healthy process and workflow, such as requiring all changes to be logged in source control before being pushed to production. This gives a linear history of changes plus a log of who is responsible, and enables enforcing things like review and automated testing.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: Name networking-specific benefits of using source control.
answer: Python scripts that interact with network devices can be versioned; network device configurations can be stored so their state can be seen at any point in time; changes between config versions can be highlighted to verify only desired changes; configuration templates and network documentation can be tracked; and all changes are captured along with the responsible person.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is RANCID?
answer: A well-known tool that uses a source-control-style approach for storing network device configuration backups, so you can see the state of a network device configuration at any point in time.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: Who launched Git and when, and why?
answer: Git was launched by Linus Torvalds, the creator of the Linux kernel, in early April 2005 in response to a disagreement between the Linux kernel developer community and the proprietary system they were using at the time, a system called BitKeeper.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What were Torvalds' five key design goals for Git?
answer: Speed (rapidly apply patches to the Linux source code); Simplicity (design as simple as possible); Strong support for nonlinear development (rapid branching and merging with lightweight branches); Support for fully distributed operation (every developer gets a full copy of the entire source code and its history); and Scalability (able to handle large projects like the Linux kernel).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What does 'self-hosted' mean in the context of Git's development?
answer: Within a few days of its launch, Git was self-hosted, meaning that the source code for Git was being managed by Git itself.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: Which popular online source control services are based on Git?
answer: GitHub, Bitbucket, and GitLab. Some of these services also offer on-premises implementations.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is a 'project' in Git terminology?
answer: An arbitrary grouping of files for a particular purpose or effort. The repository stores all the files and information associated with the project.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is the working directory in Git?
answer: The directory where you, as the user of Git, will modify the files contained in the repository. The working directory is not the same as the repository; it specifically refers to the directory where the .git repository is stored (the parent directory of the .git directory).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is the index in Git?
answer: The index describes the repository's directory structure and content at a point in time. It is a dynamic binary file maintained by Git and modified as you stage changes and commit them to the repository.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is a commit in Git?
answer: An entry in the Git repository recording metadata for each change introduced to the repository, including the author, the date of the commit, and a commit message. A commit also captures the state of the entire repository at the time the commit was performed. Multiple changes to multiple files can be lumped together as a single commit.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: Where is the Git repository data stored by default?
answer: In a directory named .git in the root of the working directory. The working directory is the parent directory of the .git directory.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What components are found within the .git directory?
answer: The index at .git/index; content-addressable objects stored in subdirectories in .git/objects; repository-specific configuration in .git/config; and metadata about the repository, changes, and objects in .git/logs.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is a blob in Git?
answer: A binary large object that represents a file's content. Blobs are content-addressable objects identified by the SHA-1 hash of their contents.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is a tree object in Git?
answer: An object that represents the files and their directory structure in the repository. Tree objects reference the blobs that contain the file contents.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is a commit object in Git?
answer: An object added when you commit changes. It references the tree objects, which in turn reference the blobs, giving you a point-in-time reference to the entire state of the repository.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is a parent commit?
answer: Every commit except the very first has a pointer to its parent commit, which lets you follow the chain of commits all the way back to the initial one. A merge commit is a special commit object that has two parents, one for each branch brought together in the merge.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: How does Git address objects in the repository?
answer: Git uses SHA-1 hashes to create content-addressable objects. Objects are immutable; changes to an object result in the creation of a new object addressed by the SHA-1 hash of the object's content. Identical content produces identical hashes.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: How many characters of a SHA-1 hash do you usually need to supply to Git commands?
answer: Git often uses just the first seven characters of a SHA-1 hash, and will automatically use more characters as needed to keep the hashes unique.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is HEAD in Git?
answer: A pointer referencing the last commit you made (or the last commit you checked out into the working directory). Every time you commit, Git updates HEAD to point to the latest commit. When you check out a branch, HEAD moves to point to that branch's reference.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What does 'HEAD~1' refer to?
answer: The commit just before HEAD. HEAD~2 refers to the commit two places back from HEAD, HEAD~3 three commits back, and so on.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is a tracked file vs an untracked file in Git?
answer: A tracked file is a file about which Git already knows and is tracking. An untracked file is a file not previously added to the repository; Git detects it in the working directory but isn't tracking its content or changes.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What are the recommendations for committing changes to a repository?
answer: Commit frequently (you can only view the state of the repository at the time of a commit); commit at logical points (don't commit halfway through a change); and use helpful, straightforward commit messages.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is a branch in Git?
answer: A branch is a pointer to a commit. Because branches are so lightweight (just a reference to a commit), you are strongly encouraged to use multiple branches. Branches isolate new changes from other branches.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is the name of the default branch and how is it configured?
answer: By default every Git repository starts out with a single branch named master (this is configurable). Many services now use 'main' instead. You can set the name with git config --global init.defaultBranch <name>.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: Why is a branch described as 'lightweight' in Git?
answer: Because a branch is just a reference (pointer) to a commit, so creating branches is fast and cheap, which is what enables strong support for nonlinear development and parallel branching.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What happens to uncommitted changes when you switch branches?
answer: For untracked files, the changes are left in the working directory (and the file remains untracked in either branch). For tracked files, uncommitted changes are saved into a temporary area called a stash, and the contents of the tracked file are restored to what's stored in the commit referenced by the branch you switched to.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is stashing in Git?
answer: Stashing places uncommitted changes into a temporary storage area so you can recall them later. It's useful for switching branches or moving uncommitted changes from one branch to another.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is a fast-forward merge?
answer: A merge where it was possible to merge the branches by simply replaying the same set of changes to the target branch as was performed on the branch being merged. In a simple fast-forward merge, no additional merge commit is created.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is a merge commit?
answer: A new commit object created when merging two branches that have diverged (both branches have changes that need reconciling). A merge commit has two parents, each representing one of the branches brought together. This maintains the link back to previous commits so you can roll back to previous versions.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is rebasing in Git?
answer: Rebasing is taking changes committed on one branch and replaying (applying) them onto another branch. This can allow you to use a fast-forward merge and avoid a merge commit, keeping a 'cleaner' commit history.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is a lightweight tag in Git?
answer: A tag that is only a pointer to a commit. Lightweight tags are primarily intended for temporary object labels and don't require a tag message.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is an annotated tag in Git?
answer: A tag that is a full object in the repository with its own metadata (such as a tag message and the tagger). Annotated tags should be used for any long-term purposes, such as version/release management, and can even be cryptographically signed using GnuPG.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is a Git remote?
answer: A Git remote is a lightweight reference to another repository, specified by a location. A remote has two attributes: a name (purely symbolic) and the location of the remote repository.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What special significance does the remote named 'origin' have in Git?
answer: origin is the default remote name. When you have multiple remotes and run a git fetch without specifying a remote, Git will default to origin. Otherwise no special attributes are given to the remote named origin.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is a bare repository?
answer: A Git repository without a working directory. In a non-bare repository, the actual repository is in the .git subdirectory; in a bare repository the Git repository sits directly at the root of the specified directory. It is strongly recommended that you push only to a bare repository.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: Why are you strongly recommended against pushing to a nonbare repository?
answer: Because a push doesn't reset the working directory. Changes pushed to a nonbare repository won't appear in its working directory until you run git reset --hard HEAD, which throws away changes in the working directory. A bare repository eliminates these problems but eliminates the ability to interactively work with the repository.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
answer: git fetch retrieves (fetches) changes from a remote repository but does not make them part of the current repository; you then merge them with git merge. git pull combines git fetch and git merge into a single operation.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is the difference between git stash pop and git stash apply?
answer: Both take changes from a stash and apply them against the working directory of the checked-out branch, but git stash pop drops the stash afterward (assuming no conflicts), while git stash apply does not—you must use git stash drop manually.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: Why is copying a Git repository with a tool like cp able to produce an intact repository?
answer: Because Git uses SHA-1 hashes to identify all content, identical content produces identical hashes, and the contents of the Git repository are immutable. The combination of these attributes means a simple copy preserves all data and metadata intact.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What transport protocols does Git support for communicating between systems?
answer: SSH, HTTPS, and Git's own native protocol. Git's native protocol uses TCP port 9418 and is unauthenticated, used for anonymous (generally read-only) access. The ssh:// syntax tunnels Git over SSH for authenticated access, and HTTP/HTTPS variants exist as well.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is forking a GitHub repository?
answer: Forking is essentially the same as cloning a Git repository, but it happens on GitHub's servers: GitHub clones the repository into your user account as a full and complete copy, including all content and commit history. Links are maintained back to the original project, much like a Git remote. Forking does not create a local copy.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is a pull request?
answer: A notification to the authors of the original repository that you have changes you'd like them to consider including in their repository. It's created after you push changes into a branch in your forked repository. GitLab may call it a merge request; the basic idea and workflow are the same.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is the purpose of an 'upstream' remote when forking on GitHub?
answer: Adding a second remote named upstream that points to the original (upstream) repository lets you keep your fork in sync with the original project. origin points to your forked repository; upstream points to the original.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What is a .gitignore file?
answer: A file stored in the repository (in the working directory) that lists filenames or filename patterns, one on each line, that Git should exclude from being tracked. It must be staged and committed like any other content, and it gets distributed as part of the repository, which is useful for teams.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: How do you exclude files from a Git repository globally for all repositories on a computer?
answer: Create a .gitignore_global file in your home directory and add exclusions to it, then configure Git to use it with: git config --global core.excludesfile /path/to/.gitignore_global (typically ~/.gitignore_global).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What guidance does the chapter give about putting secrets (passwords, SSH keys) in a Git repository?
answer: It depends on how the repository is used. For a strictly private repository where per-user secrets aren't needed, including secrets is probably fine. For repositories where per-user secrets should be used, or repositories that may be shared publicly, you'll likely want to exclude secrets using mechanisms like .gitignore.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What does the git config command do and how are its scopes controlled?
answer: git config sets Git configuration options. The --global option sets a user-specific value (stored in .gitconfig in the home directory); omitting --global sets a repository-specific value (stored in .git/config of the current repository, and you must be in an active repository's working directory or Git reports an error).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: How does git diff represent differences in its output?
answer: The lines just after the index line show that dashes represent file a (--- a/...) and pluses represent file b (+++ b/...). Lines that exist only in file a are preceded by a dash, lines that exist only in file b are preceded by a plus, and lines that are the same in both files are preceded by a space.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: What does git commit --amend do?
answer: It amends (modifies) the last commit. Under the hood Git creates new objects, but in the repository's history you'll see only the amended commit, not the original, resulting in a 'cleaner' history. Amending commits already sent to a shared repository is generally a bad idea unless using Gerrit.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: Why might you want to split changes to multiple files into separate commits instead of using git commit -a?
answer: To limit the scope of changes in a single commit so it's less impactful to revert to an earlier version, so others can review your changes more easily, and because when collaborating it's considered best practice to limit commits to a single logical change.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git init
answer: Initializes, or creates, a new Git repository. It creates the .git directory and all its subdirectories and contents, and sets up the initial branch.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git init --bare shared-repo.git
answer: Creates a new bare repository (a repository without a working directory), where the Git repository sits directly at the root of the specified directory instead of in a .git subdirectory.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git config --global user.name "John Smith"
answer: Sets the user name as a user-specific (--global) configuration value, stored in the .gitconfig file in the home directory, so Git can track who made each set of changes.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git config --global user.email "john.smith@example.com"
answer: Sets the user email address as a user-specific (--global) configuration value stored in the home directory's .gitconfig file.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git config --global init.defaultBranch <name>
answer: Configures the name Git uses for the initial branch in all new repositories (commonly set to main instead of master), which suppresses the initial branch-name hint.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git config --global core.excludesfile /path/to/.gitignore_global
answer: Configures Git to use a global excludes file (such as ~/.gitignore_global) for excluding files from all repositories on the computer.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git config pull.rebase false
answer: Sets the Git configuration so that git pull uses merge (the default strategy) rather than rebase when reconciling divergent branches; it also silences the pull hint about divergent branches.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git config --global user.name "John Smith" (without --global)
answer: Sets the user name as a repository-specific value stored in the current repository's .git/config file. You must be in the working directory of an active repository first, or Git reports an error.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git status
answer: Shows the current status of the repository, including the current branch, staged changes, unstaged modifications, and untracked files.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git add sw1.txt
answer: Stages (adds) the specified file from the working directory into the index, putting the index in sync with the working directory and marking the file as ready to commit.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git add sw*.txt
answer: Uses shell globbing to stage multiple files at the same time—in this example, all files beginning with 'sw' and ending with '.txt'.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git add sw{1,2,3}.txt
answer: Uses bash brace expansion to stage multiple files with a single command—in this case sw1.txt, sw2.txt, and sw3.txt.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git add .
answer: Stages everything in the current directory, such as staging and committing a newly added .gitignore file into the repository.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git rm --cached <file>
answer: Removes a file from the index to unstage it (as suggested in git status output), leaving the file in the working directory untracked.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git restore <file>
answer: Discards changes in the working directory, restoring the file to the content referenced by HEAD.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git restore --staged <file>
answer: Unstages a file, removing it from the index so the working directory and index are no longer synchronized (the file is restored from HEAD by default).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git reset HEAD <file>
answer: The earlier-version command for unstaging a file: it makes the index look like the content referenced by HEAD, undoing changes to the index made by git add. git restore --staged does the same thing.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git commit -m "First commit to new repository"
answer: Commits the staged changes to the repository with a commit message supplied on the command line via the -m option, creating a point-in-time reference (a commit object) to the state of the repository.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git commit -a
answer: Tells Git to add all changes from all known (tracked) files and commit them in a single step, avoiding the need to run git add first. Only works for changes to files Git already knows about.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git commit -am "Committing all changes to tracked files"
answer: Combines the -a option (add all changes from tracked files) with the -m option (commit message on the command line) in a single command.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git commit (without -m)
answer: Launches the default text editor so you can provide a commit message (commit messages are required). The editor Git launches is configurable via git config or by editing .gitconfig.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git commit --amend
answer: Amends (modifies) the last commit. You follow the normal commit steps (make changes, stage them), then run git commit --amend to commit the changes as an amendment of the previous commit, producing a cleaner history.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git log
answer: Shows the various commits (checkpoints) created over the lifetime of the repository, up to HEAD, including each commit's SHA-1 hash, author, date, and commit message.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git log --oneline
answer: Shows the commit history in abbreviated form: the (abbreviated) SHA-1 hash and just the commit message for each commit. Useful as a starting point before drilling into a specific commit.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git --no-pager log --oneline
answer: Runs git log --oneline with Git's default behavior of piping output through a pager disabled, making it possible to find things by piping the output to grep.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git log dcddb60..045c1aa
answer: Shows more details on a range of commits, from the start SHA to the end SHA (the syntax is git log startSHA..endSHA).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git log HEAD~1..HEAD
answer: Uses symbolic references to show the commits in a range—here, the commit just before HEAD through HEAD (equivalent to the last one or two commits, depending on the repository).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git cat-file -p <sha>
answer: Shows the 'contents' of a commit (or other object) as a file on screen, with the -p option formatting the output based on the type of file. For a commit, it shows the tree SHA-1, parent commit SHA-1, author, committer, and commit message.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git ls-tree <sha>
answer: Lists the files (and their blob SHA-1 hashes and modes) that were in the repository at the time of a given commit, showing what the tree object references.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git diff 8d18465..f3a00e6 sw1.txt
answer: Shows the differences between two versions of a file (the file at two points in time) identified by two commits. Adding the filename limits the diff to just that file; omitting it shows a diff for all files changed between the commits.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git diff
answer: Shows the differences between the working tree and the index—that is, the changes that have not yet been staged for the next commit.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git diff --cached
answer: Shows the differences between the index and HEAD (the last commit)—in other words, the differences between the staged changes and the last commit.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git difftool
answer: The command to use instead of git diff when you want to use a third-party (including graphical) diff tool, since Git supports integration with third-party diff tools.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git tag golive d40fe74
answer: Creates a lightweight tag named 'golive' pointing to the specified commit. If the commit hash is omitted, the tag is added to the latest commit (HEAD).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git tag -a v1.0 d268c37 -m "Version 1.0 release"
answer: Creates an annotated tag (full object with its own metadata) named v1.0 on the specified commit, with a tag message supplied via -m.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git tag
answer: Lists all the tags found in a Git repository (git tag --list works the same way). Any tag listed can be used in place of a commit hash in commands like git diff.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git tag -d <tag-name>
answer: Deletes a tag from the repository.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git show golive
answer: Shows the details of a commit referenced by a tag (or by a commit hash). For an annotated tag it also displays the tag message and tagger information.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git branch
answer: Outputs the list of branches in the repository. The active (checked-out) branch has an asterisk before it.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git branch testing
answer: Creates a new branch named 'testing'. A branch is just a reference to a commit, so the new branch points to the commit referenced by HEAD at creation time.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git branch -m old_name new_name
answer: Renames a branch (for example, renaming the default branch from master to main). Can be used to rename any branch; renaming gets more complicated once Git remotes are involved.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git checkout testing
answer: Checks out the specified branch, making it the active branch—the branch whose contents will be available in the working directory for you to edit or modify.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git checkout -b sw5-updates
answer: Creates a new branch and checks it out at the same time, so it becomes the active branch in a single step.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git checkout --track -b add-sw-tmpl origin/add-sw-tmpl
answer: Creates a new local branch that tracks a remote tracking branch (origin/add-sw-tmpl), setting up the local branch to track that remote branch, so you can review changes from a collaborator's pushed branch.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git branch -d add-sw-tmpl
answer: Deletes a branch that has been merged (Git will prompt you if you try to delete a branch that hasn't been merged). Once merged, its changes are safely stored in another branch, so it's safe to delete.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git branch -D <branch>
answer: Force-deletes a branch that hasn't been merged. In such situations you will lose the changes in that branch, so tread carefully.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git branch -a
answer: Shows all branches, including remote tracking branches, which aren't listed by default.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git branch -r
answer: Shows remote tracking branches only (for example, origin/main or laptop/main).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git merge testing
answer: Merges the specified branch into the currently checked-out branch. In a simple case the merge is a fast-forward (changes replayed onto the target branch, no merge commit); for divergent branches Git creates a merge commit with two parents.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git merge first/main
answer: Merges the remote tracking branch first/main into the current branch, bringing changes retrieved from the remote repository into the local branch.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git rebase main
answer: Rebases the current branch onto the specified upstream branch, replaying (applying) the changes committed on the current branch on top of the upstream branch. This can enable a fast-forward merge and avoid a merge commit.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git stash push -m "Updated changes for sw5"
answer: Pushes uncommitted changes onto the stash (the -m adds a stash-specific message), restoring the working directory to match HEAD. Without -m, the last commit message is used as the description.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git stash list
answer: Lists the stashed changes, showing the syntax Git uses to refer to each stash (such as stash@{0}).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git stash show stash@{0}
answer: Shows the changes in a specific stash as a diff (similar to git diff), between the stashed contents and the commit when the stash entry was first created.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git stash pop stash@{0}
answer: Takes the changes from a specified stash, applies them to the checked-out branch, and then drops the stash (assuming no conflicts were encountered).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git stash apply
answer: Takes changes from a stash and applies them against the working directory of the checked-out branch, but does not drop the stash afterward; you must use git stash drop manually.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git stash drop
answer: Drops (removes) a stash from the list of stashes after git stash apply, or as needed.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git remote
answer: Lists any existing remotes for the repository.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git remote add first ~/net-auto
answer: Adds a remote with a symbolic name ('first') and a location (~/net-auto, here a filesystem path). The name is purely symbolic; the location can be a filesystem path or a network URL.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git remote add -f name location
answer: Adds a remote and fetches information from the remote repository in a single step, instead of the two-step git remote add followed by git remote update.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git remote update first
answer: Updates (fetches) information from the specified remote repository only. Without a remote name it updates all remotes for the repository.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git remote -v
answer: Shows remotes with more verbose output, including the full location of each remote repository for both fetch and push.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git remote rename origin desktop
answer: Renames a remote from its default name (origin) to a more descriptive name ('desktop').

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git fetch first
answer: Updates (fetches) information from the specified remote repository. git fetch is considered the conventional way of retrieving information from a remote. It retrieves the changes but does not merge them into your working branch.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git fetch --prune origin
answer: Fetches from the remote and deletes any remote tracking branches that no longer exist on the remote (for example, origin/add-sw-tmpl after the branch was deleted remotely).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git pull first
answer: Fetches changes from the specified remote and merges them into the current branch in a single operation. git pull is simply the git fetch and git merge operations combined.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git pull origin main
answer: Fetches changes from the main branch of the origin remote and merges them into the current branch in one step. Newer Git versions may prompt you to reconcile divergent branches unless a pull strategy is configured.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git push origin add-sw-tmpl
answer: Pushes changes from the local branch add-sw-tmpl to the branch of the same name on the origin remote. The general syntax is git push remote branch. The remote repository should be a bare repository.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git push origin --delete add-sw-tmpl
answer: Deletes a branch on the remote repository (in this case, the add-sw-tmpl branch on origin) by pushing a branch deletion.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git clone ~/net-auto na-clone
answer: Clones a repository into the specified directory, making a copy of the repository with all data and metadata intact. It automatically creates a remote named origin pointing back to the original repository and creates remote tracking branches.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git clone ssh://ubuntu/~/net-auto net-auto
answer: Clones a repository over SSH from a remote system (ubuntu) into the specified directory, creating a remote named origin and remote tracking branches.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git clone --bare net-auto na-shared.git
answer: Clones an existing repository into a new bare repository. Git does not add any remotes or remote tracking branches when cloning with --bare, because with a bare repository you aren't interacting directly; a clone on another system will have the remotes and remote tracking branches.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: git help commit
answer: Opens the man page for that part of Git's documentation (the syntax is git help <command>). You can also use man git-commit (putting a dash into the git command).

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: man git-commit
answer: Shows the man page for git commit by putting a dash into the git command; the same documentation is available via git help commit.

source: NPA 2nd Ed - Ch11: Source Control with Git
question: touch .gitignore
answer: Creates an empty .gitignore file in the working directory, which you then edit to add filenames or filename patterns for Git to ignore.
