source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -P INPUT ACCEPT
answer: Sets the default policy of the INPUT chain to ACCEPT (done before flushing when working remotely to avoid being locked out).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -P OUTPUT ACCEPT
answer: Sets the default policy of the OUTPUT chain to ACCEPT.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -P FORWARD ACCEPT
answer: Sets the default policy of the FORWARD chain to ACCEPT.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -F
answer: Flushes all existing firewall rules so you start with a clean configuration.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
answer: Appends a rule to the INPUT chain accepting TCP packets destined for port 22 (ssh).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT
answer: Appends a rule to the INPUT chain accepting TCP packets destined for port 80 (HTTP).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp -j ACCEPT
answer: Appends a rule to the OUTPUT chain allowing all outgoing TCP traffic (needed so replies to ssh/http clients can go out).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -I INPUT 1 -i lo -j ACCEPT
answer: Inserts a rule at the first position of the INPUT chain accepting all packets bound for the loopback (lo) interface.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -A OUTPUT -p udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT
answer: Allows outgoing UDP DNS queries (destination port 53).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -A INPUT -p udp --sport 53 -j ACCEPT
answer: Allows incoming UDP packets whose source port is 53 (DNS replies from a local or remote DNS server).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -A OUTPUT -p udp --sport 53 -j ACCEPT
answer: Allows outgoing UDP packets whose source port is 53 (DNS replies sent by a local DNS server).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -A INPUT -p udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT
answer: Allows incoming UDP DNS queries destined for port 53 (received by a local DNS server).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -P INPUT DROP
answer: Sets the INPUT default policy to DROP so only packets matching explicit rules enter the machine.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -P OUTPUT DROP
answer: Sets the OUTPUT default policy to DROP.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -P FORWARD DROP
answer: Sets the FORWARD default policy to DROP.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -L
answer: Lists all current firewall rules and chain policies (INPUT, FORWARD, OUTPUT).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -t mangle -A PREROUTING -j TTL --ttl-inc 5
answer: Adds a mangle-table rule on PREROUTING that increases the TTL of all packets by 5.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -A OUTPUT -m owner --uid-owner 1000 -j DROP
answer: Drops all packets generated by processes run by the user with UID 1000 (uses the owner extension on the OUTPUT chain).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
answer: Allows only outgoing TCP packets that belong to an established (or related) connection, blocking new outbound connections like telnet.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo iptables -D INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
answer: Deletes the matching rule from the INPUT chain (cleanup of individual rules).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo insmod telnetFilter.ko
answer: Loads the telnet-filter kernel module into the running kernel.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: sudo rmmod telnetFilter
answer: Removes the telnet-filter module, restoring normal telnet functionality.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: lsmod | grep kMod
answer: Lists loaded kernel modules and filters for kMod to verify the module is inserted.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: dmesg
answer: Shows the kernel log buffer, e.g. 'Registering a Telnet filter' and 'Dropping telnet packet to 10.0.2.5'.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: telnet 10.0.2.5
answer: Attempts a telnet connection to 10.0.2.5; fails when the telnet-filter module or firewall blocks port 23, succeeds after it is removed.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: telnet 10.0.2.6
answer: Tests the simple firewall: blocked because the firewall only allows ports 22 and 80.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: wget 10.0.2.6
answer: Downloads the default page over HTTP (port 80), succeeding because the firewall allows port 80.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: su bob
answer: Switches to user bob, used to verify the owner-module rule only affects user seed.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: ssh -L 8000:work:23 seed@apollo
answer: Establishes a static SSH tunnel: forwards local port 8000 to port 23 (telnet) on machine 'work' through apollo, evading the ingress firewall.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: ssh -L 8000:www.facebook.com:80 seed@home
answer: Establishes an SSH tunnel from inside the company to 'home', forwarding local port 8000 to Facebook's port 80 to evade egress filtering.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: ssh -D 9000 -C seed@home
answer: Creates a dynamic SOCKS proxy tunnel on local port 9000 to 'home' with compression (-C); the browser is configured to use localhost:9000 as a SOCKS proxy.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: ssh -R 8000:web-server:80 seed@home
answer: Creates a reverse SSH tunnel from an inside machine: requests to port 8000 on 'home' are forwarded to port 80 of the internal 'web-server', letting outsiders reach the internal website.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: telnet localhost 8000
answer: Connects to the local SSH tunnel endpoint (port 8000) so the telnet traffic travels through the tunnel to the real destination.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the three types of firewalls?

choices.label: Packet filter inspects each packet in isolation; stateful firewall tracks connection states; application firewall inspects up to the application layer via a proxy
All three types inspect up to the application layer
A stateful firewall keeps no information about previous packets
An application firewall is faster than a packet filter

explanation: Packet filters are stateless (per-packet header decisions, fast); stateful firewalls track connection state in a connection state table; application/proxy firewalls terminate connections and inspect application-layer data (slowest but most secure).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: Which statement correctly describes the firewall actions?

choices.label: Rejected is like Denied but sends an ICMP packet to inform the source
Denied and Rejected are exactly the same behavior
Accepted means the packet is silently dropped
Rejected sends a TCP RST packet to the source

explanation: Accepted lets the packet in; Denied drops it without informing the source; Rejected also drops it but sends a specially crafted ICMP packet to notify the source.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: Which statement correctly describes ingress versus egress filtering?

choices.label: Ingress filtering inspects incoming traffic to protect the internal network; egress filtering inspects outgoing traffic to restrict what internal users send out
Ingress filtering inspects outgoing traffic
Egress filtering protects against outside attacks
Both only inspect the application layer

explanation: Ingress filtering protects an internal network from outside attacks by inspecting inbound traffic; egress filtering restricts what internal users can reach/send, e.g. the Great Firewall of China.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: Which statement correctly distinguishes NF_DROP from NF_STOLEN?

choices.label: NF_DROP discards the packet; NF_STOLEN makes netfilter forget the packet while the module takes over its processing
NF_DROP sends the packet to user space
NF_STOLEN discards the packet permanently
NF_DROP asks the module to be called again

explanation: NF_DROP discards the packet so it cannot continue; NF_STOLEN passes responsibility to the module (used e.g. to store fragmented packets), and the packet remains valid in kernel tables.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: Which statement correctly distinguishes NEW from ESTABLISHED conntrack states?

choices.label: NEW means the connection is starting with traffic seen in only one direction; ESTABLISHED means two-way communication has already happened
NEW means two-way traffic has been exchanged
ESTABLISHED means the packet is starting a connection
NEW only applies to TCP connections

explanation: NEW marks the initialization of a connection (one-directional traffic seen); ESTABLISHED means two-way communication has occurred. Both apply to TCP, UDP, and ICMP flows.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: Which statement correctly describes the RELATED state?

choices.label: It links a secondary connection (e.g. FTP data on a high port) to an existing primary connection (FTP control on port 21)
It means the connection has not sent any packets yet
It applies only to the initial TCP handshake
It means the packet does not belong to any connection

explanation: RELATED establishes a relationship between connections; in FTP the control traffic on port 21 is ESTABLISHED while the data-transfer traffic on a high port is RELATED. INVALID marks packets that do not follow expected behavior.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: Which statement correctly describes the iptables tables?

choices.label: filter is for packet filtering, nat for changing source/destination addresses, mangle for packet content modification
nat is used for packet filtering
mangle contains only the INPUT and OUTPUT chains
filter contains the PREROUTING and POSTROUTING chains

explanation: filter (INPUT/FORWARD/OUTPUT) filters packets; nat (PREROUTING/INPUT/OUTPUT/POSTROUTING) modifies network addresses; mangle has all five chains and modifies packet content.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: Which statement correctly describes iptables versus netfilter?

choices.label: Netfilter provides kernel hooks; iptables (user-space) configures rules enforced at those hooks via the kernel's Xtables
iptables is the kernel framework and netfilter is the user-space tool
Netfilter is a hardware firewall
iptables does not rely on netfilter hooks

explanation: Netfilter supplies the kernel packet hooks; the built-in firewall is configured by the iptables user-space program and implemented in the kernel by Xtables, which registers callbacks on the netfilter hooks.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: Which statement correctly distinguishes static and dynamic SSH port forwarding?

choices.label: Static forwarding fixes the final destination at setup (ssh -L); dynamic forwarding lets the client supply the destination at connect time via SOCKS (ssh -D)
Dynamic forwarding fixes the destination at setup
Static forwarding requires a SOCKS proxy in the browser
ssh -R is an example of static local forwarding

explanation: ssh -L fixes the destination when the tunnel is created; ssh -D creates a SOCKS proxy so the destination is decided per-request by the client. ssh -R is reverse (remote) forwarding.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: Which statement correctly describes SOCKS versus a web proxy?

choices.label: SOCKS works at the session layer and is protocol-independent; a web proxy works at the application layer and only handles web traffic
A web proxy works at the session layer
SOCKS only forwards HTTP traffic
SOCKS needs no handshake from the client

explanation: SOCKS (RFC 1928) operates at the session layer, requiring a handshake to learn the destination and native client support, making it generic; web proxies (e.g. Squid) work at the application layer and only proxy web traffic.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: What is the correct order to build and test a kernel module?
correct_sequence: 1. Write the module source (kMod.c) with module_init/module_exit and MODULE_LICENSE
2. Build it with make (obj-m += kMod.o)
3. Insert it with sudo insmod kMod.ko
4. Verify with lsmod | grep kMod and check dmesg
5. Remove it with sudo rmmod kMod
distractor_sequences: 1. Insert the module before compiling it
1. Run rmmod before insmod
1. Skip MODULE_LICENSE so the kernel rejects it
explanation: Modules are written, compiled, inserted with insmod, verified via lsmod/dmesg, and removed with rmmod; removing the telnet filter restores normal telnet behavior.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: What is the correct order to build the simple iptables firewall?
correct_sequence: 1. Set all default policies to ACCEPT (sudo iptables -P INPUT ACCEPT, etc.)
2. Flush existing rules with sudo iptables -F
3. Allow TCP ports 22 and 80 on INPUT and all outgoing TCP on OUTPUT
4. Insert the loopback rule: sudo iptables -I INPUT 1 -i lo -j ACCEPT
5. Add the four DNS (UDP 53) rules
6. Set default policies back to DROP
distractor_sequences: 1. Set default policy to DROP before adding allow rules
1. Flush the rules after setting the default policy to DROP
1. Skip the loopback and DNS rules
explanation: You start clean (policies ACCEPT, flush), open the needed ports, add loopback and DNS rules, and finally set the default policy to DROP so only matching traffic passes. When remote, keep the default at ACCEPT until all allow rules are in place.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: What is the correct order of steps in the cleanup script after a firewall experiment?
correct_sequence: 1. Set the INPUT default policy to ACCEPT
2. Set the OUTPUT default policy to ACCEPT
3. Set the FORWARD default policy to ACCEPT
4. Flush all rules with iptables -F
distractor_sequences: 1. Flush the rules before setting policies to ACCEPT
1. Set only the INPUT policy to ACCEPT
1. Leave the default policy at DROP
explanation: The cleanup script (cleanup.sh) first sets all default policies to ACCEPT, then flushes rules with iptables -F so later experiments are not affected.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: What is the correct chain traversal order for a packet that is forwarded to another host?
correct_sequence: 1. PREROUTING (mangle, then nat)
2. Routing decision (packet is for another host)
3. FORWARD (mangle, then filter)
4. POSTROUTING (mangle, then nat)
distractor_sequences: 1. INPUT then OUTPUT then FORWARD
1. POSTROUTING before FORWARD
1. Skip the routing decision
explanation: Forwarded packets enter through PREROUTING, get a routing decision, traverse the FORWARD chain, and leave through POSTROUTING; locally destined packets instead traverse INPUT, and locally generated packets traverse OUTPUT.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: What is the correct netfilter hook order for a packet destined to the local host?
correct_sequence: 1. NF_IP_PRE_ROUTING (before routing)
2. Routing decision: destination is the local machine
3. NF_IP_LOCAL_IN
4. Delivered to the network stack / local application
distractor_sequences: 1. NF_IP_LOCAL_IN before NF_IP_PRE_ROUTING
1. NF_IP_FORWARD for a locally destined packet
1. NF_IP_POST_ROUTING before NF_IP_LOCAL_IN
explanation: Incoming packets hit PRE_ROUTING first; after routing decides the packet is for the host itself, it traverses LOCAL_IN; packets for other hosts go to FORWARD instead.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: What is the correct order to reach machine 'work' from home through an ingress firewall using an SSH tunnel?
correct_sequence: 1. On home, establish the tunnel: ssh -L 8000:work:23 seed@apollo
2. Run the telnet client on home targeting the local tunnel endpoint: telnet localhost 8000
3. SSH forwards the TCP data from port 8000 through the encrypted tunnel to apollo
4. From apollo the data is put in a new TCP packet sent to port 23 on work
distractor_sequences: 1. Telnet directly to work's IP from home
1. Use ssh -D instead of ssh -L to fix the destination
1. Telnet to apollo's port 23 directly
explanation: The tunnel receives telnet data at local port 8000, carries it to apollo, which re-encapsulates and forwards it to port 23 of work; the firewall only sees encrypted ssh traffic.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: What is the correct order of connection states for a TCP connection as seen by conntrack?
correct_sequence: 1. First SYN packet: NEW
2. Handshake completes and two-way traffic flows: ESTABLISHED
3. Related secondary flows (if any): RELATED
4. Packets that violate expected behavior: INVALID
distractor_sequences: 1. The first SYN is marked ESTABLISHED
1. RELATED comes before NEW
1. INVALID is the initial state of every connection
explanation: conntrack marks the first packet of a flow NEW, marks it ESTABLISHED after two-way communication, uses RELATED for associated secondary connections, and INVALID for packets that break expected behavior.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: After loading telnetFilter.ko, telnet to any machine fails.
symptoms: telnet prints 'Trying 10.0.2.5...' then 'Unable to connect'; dmesg shows 'Dropping telnet packet to 10.0.2.5'.
root_cause: The netfilter kernel module deliberately drops all outgoing packets destined for TCP port 23 (telnet).
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Run dmesg to confirm 'Dropping telnet packet' messages
2. Remove the module with sudo rmmod telnetFilter
3. Retry telnet — it should succeed once removed
resolution: Unload the telnet filter module after the experiment so later experiments are not affected.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: While configuring a firewall over SSH, the connection drops and you cannot reconnect.
symptoms: SSH session freezes after running iptables commands; subsequent SSH attempts time out.
root_cause: The default policy of iptables is DROP; flushing all rules (iptables -F) while working remotely removed the allow rules, so your remote access is now blocked.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. On a remote machine, set the default policy to ACCEPT before flushing (iptables -P INPUT ACCEPT)
2. Add all allow rules first
3. Set the default policy to DROP only at the very end
resolution: When working remotely, keep the default policy ACCEPT and only flush after it is set, so you are not locked out.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: DNS lookups fail after applying the simple firewall.
symptoms: Websites do not resolve; nslookup/dig time out; the browser cannot reach any domain.
root_cause: The firewall has no rules allowing DNS traffic; on the SEED VM the DNS server runs locally on 127.0.1.1, so both directions on both chains are needed.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Add iptables -A OUTPUT -p udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT
2. Add iptables -A INPUT -p udp --sport 53 -j ACCEPT
3. Add iptables -A OUTPUT -p udp --sport 53 -j ACCEPT and iptables -A INPUT -p udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT
4. Retry DNS resolution
resolution: Add the four DNS (UDP 53) rules covering sport/dport on both INPUT and OUTPUT chains.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: Programs on the same machine cannot communicate with each other after the firewall is enabled.
symptoms: Local services (e.g. program A connecting to program B on port 5050 of 127.0.0.1) fail.
root_cause: The firewall has no rule allowing loopback (lo) traffic.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Add sudo iptables -I INPUT 1 -i lo -j ACCEPT
2. Retry the local communication
resolution: Allow loopback traffic with a rule on the loopback interface so local inter-process communication works.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: User seed cannot telnet out, but user bob can.
symptoms: telnet from seed hangs after 'Trying 10.0.2.5...'; switching to bob with su bob makes telnet work.
root_cause: An owner-module rule drops packets created by seed's processes: iptables -A OUTPUT -m owner --uid-owner seed -j DROP.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Check the rules with sudo iptables -L
2. Identify the --uid-owner rule on OUTPUT
3. Delete it with sudo iptables -D OUTPUT -m owner --uid-owner seed -j DROP
resolution: Remove or adjust the owner-based rule so the affected user can send packets.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: With the stateful OUTPUT rule (conntrack ESTABLISHED,RELATED), outbound telnet produces no packets on Wireshark.
symptoms: telnet attempts fail and Wireshark shows no TCP packets related to the telnet leaving the machine.
root_cause: New outbound connections are in the NEW state, but the rule only allows ESTABLISHED,RELATED, so the initial telnet packets are blocked by design.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify the rule is iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
2. Understand this blocks data exfiltration via new outbound TCP connections
3. To allow new connections, also allow --ctstate NEW for permitted services
resolution: The stateful rule intentionally blocks new outbound connections to prevent data exfiltration; only existing ssh/http connections can continue.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: From another machine, telnet fails but wget succeeds against the firewall host.
symptoms: telnet 10.0.2.6 says 'Unable to connect'; wget 10.0.2.6 returns HTTP 200.
root_cause: The simple firewall only allows incoming TCP to ports 22 (ssh) and 80 (http); telnet uses port 23, which is dropped by the default DROP policy.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Confirm the INPUT rules allow only --dport 22 and 80
2. Verify the default policy is DROP (iptables -L)
3. Check that the connection to port 80 (wget) succeeds as expected
resolution: This behavior is correct: the firewall blocks all ports except 22 and 80; telnet (23) is intentionally blocked.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch17: Firewall
question: make fails to build the kernel module.
symptoms: make reports missing build files or cannot find the kernel build directory.
root_cause: The kernel headers/build environment are missing; the Makefile needs /lib/modules/$(shell uname -r)/build with configuration and header files (usually installed under /usr/src).
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/build exists
2. Install the matching kernel headers for the running kernel
3. Re-run make (which invokes make -C .../build M=$(PWD) modules)
resolution: Install the kernel headers/source that match the running kernel so the module can be built.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the primary task of the Domain Name System (DNS)?
answer: Translating hostnames to IP addresses (and vice versa). Computers need IP addresses to communicate, and DNS resolves names like www.google.com to the corresponding IP address; without DNS the Internet cannot function.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the ROOT domain in the DNS hierarchy?
answer: The root of the DNS hierarchy tree, denoted by the dot symbol '.'. It is the highest level; the next level below it consists of Top-Level Domains (TLDs).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is a Top-Level Domain (TLD)?
answer: The last label of a domain name (e.g., com in www.example.com). Initially there were few TLDs such as com, net, edu, org; more have been created since, including country-code TLDs and special-purpose TLDs. The official list is maintained by IANA.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is a country-code Top-Level Domain (ccTLD)?
answer: A top-level domain generally used or reserved for a country, such as .us, .uk, .fr. For ccTLDs, second-level domains are usually equivalent to the generic TLDs but only for their specific countries.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is IANA and what role does it play in DNS?
answer: The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority. It maintains the official list of all top-level domains and oversees the approval process for new proposed TLDs. As of March 31st 2019 the root domain contained 1532 top-level domains.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is a registry in DNS?
answer: The designated manager that each TLD is delegated to by IANA. Examples: VeriSign manages com and net; EDUCAUSE manages edu. Registries are responsible for maintaining information about second-level domains in their registry databases.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is a domain registrar?
answer: An entity that contracts with a TLD's registries to provide registration services to the public, e.g., GoDaddy, eNom, Tucows, Melbourne IT. When an end user buys a domain name, the registrar adds the info to the registry databases.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is a second-level domain?
answer: The level below the TLD in the DNS hierarchy. For generic TLDs, second-level domains are usually assigned to specific entities such as companies, organizations, schools, and individuals.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is a DNS zone?
answer: A grouping of contiguous domains and sub-domains on the domain tree, to which management authority is assigned to an entity. Each zone is managed by an authority, while a domain does not indicate any authority information. A domain can be divided into multiple zones.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: How do a DNS zone and a domain differ?
answer: A DNS zone contains only a portion of the DNS data for a domain. If a domain is not divided into sub-domains (or its sub-domain data stays in one zone), zone and domain are essentially the same; they differ only when sub-domains have their own zones.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is an authoritative nameserver?
answer: A DNS server that publishes information about a zone and provides original and definitive answers to DNS queries, as opposed to obtaining the answers from other DNS servers. Each DNS zone has at least one.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is a master (primary) nameserver?
answer: An authoritative nameserver that stores the original (master) copies of all zone records. A slave (secondary) server uses an automatic updating mechanism to maintain an identical copy of the master records.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is a slave (secondary) nameserver?
answer: An authoritative nameserver that maintains an identical copy of the master records using an automatic updating mechanism. For redundancy, each zone should provide multiple authoritative nameservers.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the ROOT zone and how many authoritative nameservers does it have?
answer: The root of the DNS zone tree, maintained by IANA. There are 13 authoritative nameservers called DNS root servers, named a.root-servers.net through m.root-servers.net.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: How do DNS resolvers bootstrap queries?
answer: The IP addresses of the 13 root servers are given to DNS resolvers through a file typically provided by operating systems or DNS resolver software. Every name resolution either starts with a query to one of these root servers, or uses information once obtained from the root servers.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the /etc/hosts file in Linux?
answer: A file used to store static IP addresses for some hostnames. Before contacting its local DNS server, a machine first looks in this file. It is a simple text file associating IP addresses with hostnames, one line per IP address (Windows path: %SystemRoot%\System32\drivers\etc\hosts).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the /etc/resolv.conf file?
answer: The file that provides the DNS resolver with the IP address of the local DNS server. If a machine uses DHCP, the DNS server IP is provided by DHCP and stored here; DHCP clients overwrite the file, so manual changes get overwritten.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is a local DNS server?
answer: The helper that a machine's DNS resolver sends queries to when the answer is not in its own data. Although called local, it does not need to be on the local network (e.g., Google Public DNS). It performs an iterative process to resolve hostnames.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the iterative query process?
answer: The process a local DNS server uses to resolve a hostname: it queries the ROOT server, which points to the TLD nameservers; it queries a TLD server, which points to the zone nameservers; it queries the zone nameserver, which returns the final answer.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What are the four sections of a DNS response?
answer: Question section (describes the question to the nameserver), answer section (records that answer the question), authority section (records that point toward authoritative nameservers), and additional section (records related to the query but not strictly answers).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is DNS cache and what is a TTL?
answer: When a local DNS server gets information from other DNS servers it caches it so it does not ask again. Each cached piece of information has a time-to-live (TTL) value, so it eventually times out and is removed, because DNS information is dynamic and changes frequently.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the transaction ID field in the DNS header?
answer: A field that matches a query to its response. The ID in the response must be the same as that in the query, or the response will be discarded. It is a random 16-bit number.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What does the qr flag in the DNS header indicate?
answer: A one-bit field that specifies whether the message is a query (0) or a response (1).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What does the aa flag in the DNS header indicate?
answer: The authoritative answer flag; it specifies whether the answer is authoritative or not.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What does the rd flag in the DNS header indicate?
answer: The recursion desired flag, meaningful only for queries; it specifies whether recursion is desired.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What are the count fields in the DNS header?
answer: qdcount (number of question records), ancount (number of answer records), nscount (number of authority records), and arcount (number of additional records). A packet can have zero to multiple records per section.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: Why does BIND 9 use a random source port for DNS queries?
answer: For security, BIND 9 uses a random 16-bit source port number in its UDP packets. This makes attacks harder because a forged DNS reply must use the same source port number in its UDP header.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is BIND?
answer: The Berkeley Internet Name Domain, the most widely used DNS server software, originally designed at UC Berkeley in the early 1980s. The latest version is BIND 9, first released in 2000.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the dump-file option in BIND?
answer: An option in the named.conf options block specifying where the cache content is dumped when BIND is asked to dump its cache. If not specified, BIND dumps to a default file called /var/cache/bind/named_dump.db.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What are the two typical types of attacks against DNS?
answer: (1) Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks that make DNS servers unresponsive, cutting off communication; (2) DNS spoofing attacks whose primary goal is to provide a fraudulent IP address to victims, tricking them into communicating with a different machine.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is DNS spoofing?
answer: An attack that provides a fraudulent IP address to victims. For example, if a user intends to visit a bank web site but the DNS process returns the attacker machine instead, the user may be tricked into providing credentials to the attacker web server.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is DNS cache poisoning?
answer: An attack on a local DNS server in which spoofed replies that arrive before legitimate ones are accepted and cached. Because the forged data stays in the cache, the damage lasts for a long period of time.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the attack surface of compromising local DNS files?
answer: Attackers with root privilege modify /etc/resolv.conf to point the victim to a malicious DNS server, or modify /etc/hosts to hard-code IP addresses for selected domains. The victim gets answers from the file without sending any DNS query.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the attack surface of attacks on the user machine?
answer: When the user machine sends a DNS query to its local DNS server, the attacker immediately sends a spoofed reply using the local DNS server IP as source, putting an arbitrary IP in the reply. Damage is limited because the user machine does not cache results.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the attack surface of attacks on the local DNS server (cache poisoning)?
answer: When the local DNS server sends iterative queries, attackers send spoofed replies; as long as the spoofed replies arrive earlier than legitimate ones they are accepted and cached, so damage lasts a long time. Local attackers can sniff the query; remote attacks use the Kaminsky technique.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the attack surface of attacks from a malicious DNS server?
answer: When a user queries a malicious authoritative nameserver (e.g., attacker32.com), in addition to the answer section the server can place fraudulent information in the authority and additional sections, which may be cached if no restriction is placed on them.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: Why does attacking the authority section amplify a DNS cache poisoning attack?
answer: If a fake NS record for a target domain is cached, then whenever the victim DNS server tries to resolve any hostname in that domain it queries the malicious nameserver. Such an attack affects ALL hostnames in the target domain, not just one.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the cache effect in remote DNS poisoning?
answer: If a spoofing attempt fails, the real reply arrives and is cached; to try again the attacker must wait for the server to send another query for the same name, which will not happen until the cache times out (hours or days). This made remote cache poisoning unrealistic before Kaminsky.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the Kaminsky attack?
answer: An elegant technique by Dan Kaminsky to defeat the cache effect in remote DNS cache poisoning. The attacker triggers the victim DNS server to query random non-cached hostnames in the target domain and floods spoofed replies (each with different transaction ID/port) that include a fake NS record in the authority section.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: In the Kaminsky attack, why must the queried hostname be random?
answer: Because if the spoofed reply fails, the attacker repeats the attack with a different hostname. Since the victim cache does not contain the new hostname, it sends out another query, giving the attacker another chance and defeating the cache effect.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: In the Kaminsky attack, what must the attacker guess to make a spoofed reply accepted?
answer: The 16-bit UDP source port number and the 16-bit transaction ID, plus which of the possible authoritative nameserver IPs was used as the destination. A reply must contain the correct transaction ID and UDP port and arrive before the legitimate reply.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: How are names encoded in DNS resource records?
answer: Each section of the name (separated by dots) starts with a one-octet length followed by the string; a 0x00 value marks the end of the name. For example, example.com is encoded as \x07example\x03com\x00. Real DNS uses pointer compression, but the book handcrafted packets do not.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What names in a spoofed reply must match the query?
answer: The names in the question and answer records must match exactly with the name in the query packet, or the response will not be accepted.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: Why must the name in an authority record be related to the query?
answer: The name in the authority record must be within the zone of the query, or it is considered out-of-zone data and discarded for security reasons. E.g., if bank32.com is in the authority record for an example.com query, the record is ignored.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: How does Scapy represent DNS records?
answer: Scapy defines class DNS for the DNS packet, DNSQR for question records, and DNSRR for answer and authority records. The answer and additional sections both use DNSRR; the rdata element of DNSRR maps to the data field of a record.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the sniff-and-spoof technique used in the DNS labs?
answer: A sniffer program (Scapy sniff) monitors network traffic; when it sees a DNS query matching the target, it immediately sends a spoofed DNS reply. This is used for local cache poisoning, for emulating malicious DNS servers, and for emulating DNS rebinding.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What happens if a malicious nameserver puts fake A records in the additional section?
answer: If accepted, the local DNS server cache would be poisoned with fraudulent IP addresses for unrelated popular domains. However, the experiment shows additional-section data is cached but NOT used: BIND does not trust second-hand IP addresses from the additional section and re-queries.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What happens if a malicious nameserver puts a fake NS record for an out-of-zone domain in the authority section?
answer: The record is discarded. The resolver uses the queried zone to decide whether authority-section data is inside the zone. For example, an NS record claiming facebook.com is served by ns.attacker32.com when answering an attacker32.com query is out-of-zone and ignored.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: Why were additional-section records (www.attacker32.com and facebook.com A records) not used even though they were cached?
answer: BIND caches data from the additional section but does not trust it, because it is second-hand information. The answer-section data is first-hand and more trustworthy, so BIND sends out new queries to resolve those hostnames itself.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: Can a domain authoritative nameserver be outside the domain zone?
answer: Yes. A domain authoritative nameservers do not necessarily need to be a name inside the domain; e.g., the actual nameserver for example.net is a.iana-servers.net, which is outside the example.net zone.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the danger of fake answers in reverse DNS lookups?
answer: A malicious nameserver can lie and map an IP address to a different domain (e.g., claim 192.168.0.101 is www.facebook.com instead of www.example.net). If machines use reverse-lookup domain names for security decisions (e.g., firewall filtering), attackers can bypass restrictions. Mitigation: do a forward lookup and compare the IP.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: How does a reverse DNS lookup work?
answer: Given an IP such as 128.230.171.184, the resolver constructs the fake name 184.171.230.128.in-addr.arpa and performs an iterative lookup starting from the ROOT server to the in-addr.arpa servers, eventually reaching the nameserver hosting the zone that answers with a PTR record.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the DNS rebinding attack?
answer: An attack where an attacker who owns a domain and its nameserver maps a hostname first to the attacker real IP (to serve a malicious page) and later to the IP of an internal target server, rebinding the name to defeat the Same Origin Policy so JavaScript can interact with the internal server.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the Same Origin Policy (SOP)?
answer: The browser sandbox policy enforced on Ajax: code inside a web page can only interact with the same server (origin) the page came from. SOP does not prevent Ajax from SENDING requests, but prevents it from GETTING the reply data from other servers.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: Why is SOP enforced based on the server name rather than IP address?
answer: Because enforcement uses the hostname in the URL, and the mapping from name to IP is done via DNS, which the attacker controls. By remapping the name, the attacker Ajax code can communicate with any server, defeating SOP.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: In DNS rebinding, why is a very small TTL (e.g., 3 seconds) used in the first DNS answer?
answer: So the first answer (mapping the name to the attacker real IP) is not cached for long. After the TTL expires, the JavaScript code next request triggers a fresh DNS query that can be answered with the target server IP.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the purpose of the password in the IoT device set-temperature API?
answer: The password is not for authentication; it is used to defeat Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks. To set the temperature a user first gets the password via the getpassword API, then includes it in the settemperature request.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: How can DNS rebinding be defended?
answer: (1) Stronger authentication on the IoT device itself; (2) browser-side solutions such as pinning the IP address so rebinding becomes hard; (3) hardening DNS resolvers to prevent external names from resolving to internal addresses.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is DNSSEC?
answer: Domain Name System Security Extensions, a set of DNS extensions providing authentication and integrity checking on DNS data, defined in RFC 4033/4034/4035. All answers from DNSSEC-protected zones are digitally signed; checking signatures defeats cache poisoning because fake data fails signature checking.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What are the RRSIG, DNSKEY, and DS records in DNSSEC?
answer: RRSIG contains the digital signature for a record set, verifiable using the public key in the DNSKEY record. The DS record contains the one-way hash of a child zone public key, provided by the parent zone to establish trust.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: How does the DNSSEC chain of trust work?
answer: The public key of a child zone is signed by its parent zone (via the DS record). In an iterative query, the parent is queried before the child, so the resolver already holds the hash of the child public key before reaching the child. Trust ultimately falls upon the root zone (trust anchors).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the fundamental problem with DNS that DNSSEC and TLS/SSL address?
answer: The lack of authenticity checking on DNS responses. When a DNS resolver receives a response there is no way to verify its authenticity; the entire packet can be spoofed and its data fake. The DNS protocol does not provide an authentication mechanism.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: How does TLS/SSL defend against DNS spoofing?
answer: After getting an IP via DNS, the client asks the server to prove it owns the domain by presenting a public-key certificate signed by a trusted entity (e.g., VeriSign) and demonstrating knowledge of the corresponding private key. A fake server cannot obtain such a certificate, so even with a poisoned IP the attack fails.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: How do DNSSEC and TLS/SSL chains of trust differ?
answer: DNSSEC builds its chain of trust using the DNS zone hierarchy, where parent-zone nameservers vouch for child-zone nameservers. TLS/SSL relies on the Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) with many Certificate Authorities (CAs) that vouch for other computers.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: Why is a DoS attack on DNS so damaging?
answer: Computers depend on local DNS servers and authoritative nameservers; if they do not respond, computers cannot find IP addresses for the machines they need, essentially cutting off communication even though the Internet itself is still connected.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is anycast and how is it used by root nameservers?
answer: A technology where many servers in different locations carry the same IP address; BGP simultaneously announces the same destination IP from many places and routers pick one (usually the nearest). It is used by 10 root servers (A,C,E,F,G,I,J,K,L,M) and is mainly for connectionless services like UDP-based DNS.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: Why are attacks on root servers unlikely to bring down the Internet?
answer: (1) Root servers are mostly queried to get TLD nameserver info, which is cached by local DNS servers for up to 48 hours; (2) there are 13 root server names, each typically a server farm of redundant computers; (3) 10 of them use anycast with servers on multiple continents.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What was the Dyn attack of October 2016?
answer: Multiple distributed DoS attacks against the Dyn network, a major DNS provider for BBC, CNN, HBO, PayPal, Netflix, and Twitter, causing major services to be unavailable in Europe and North America. It is believed to have been launched through a botnet of IoT devices (IP cameras, baby monitors, printers).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What happened in the DNSPod / Baofeng incident of May 2009?
answer: DNSPod DNS servers were hit by a DDoS attack targeting one customer. When cached responses timed out, Baofeng media player (due to a bug) continuously sent DNS queries at a very fast rate instead of waiting; the massive query flood congested China Telecom network, affecting users in more than 20 provinces.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: Why was the Aug 25 2013 attack on .cn nameservers significant?
answer: Denial-of-service attacks were launched on the .cn (China country-code TLD) nameservers and likely shut them down for two to four hours. ccTLDs are common DoS targets because bringing one down can bring down the Internet of the targeted country.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What was the UltraDNS attack?
answer: On December 24, 2009 a DoS attack was launched against UltraDNS, a DNS provider for major e-commerce companies (Amazon, Walmart, Expedia), causing an hour-long outage felt by thousands of online shoppers in Northern California. Authoritative nameservers of second-level domains are easier to attack than root/TLD servers.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What does the dig command do?
answer: A DNS lookup utility that sends DNS queries and prints the response sections (question, answer, authority, additional). Without an @server option the query goes to the local DNS server, which performs the iterative process.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What does the @server option of dig do?
answer: Specifies which DNS server the query should be sent to directly (e.g., dig @a.root-servers.net www.example.net), letting the user emulate the iterative query process by hand.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What does the -x option of dig do?
answer: Performs a reverse DNS lookup: given an IP address it finds the corresponding hostname (e.g., dig -x 192.168.0.101).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What does the -p option of dig do?
answer: Specifies a nonstandard UDP port number to send the query to (e.g., dig @10.0.2.69 -p 1053 www.example.com).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What does the @ symbol mean in a BIND zone file?
answer: A special notation representing the origin specified in named.conf (the string after zone). For example, in the zone bank32.com, @ stands for bank32.com.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What resource records were in the bank32.com zone file?
answer: 7 resource records: one SOA (Start Of Authority), one NS (Name Server), one MX (Mail eXchanger), and four A (host Address) records (for www, mail, ns, and a wildcard *.bank32.com).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is a PTR record?
answer: The resource record used in reverse lookup zone files to map an IP address (via in-addr.arpa names) to a hostname.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What does $TTL do in a zone file?
answer: Sets the default expiration time (time-to-live) of all resource records that do not have their own TTL value.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What three VMs are used in the DNS experiment environment and their IPs?
answer: User machine (10.0.2.68), local DNS server (10.0.2.69), and attacker machine (10.0.2.70), all Ubuntu 16.04 VMs on the same network.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: Why use /etc/resolvconf/resolv.conf.d/head to set the DNS server?
answer: Because DHCP clients overwrite /etc/resolv.conf with DHCP-provided info. The content of the head file is copied into resolv.conf when DHCP modifies it, so putting nameserver 10.0.2.69 in the head file persists the setting.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: Why did the lab turn off DNSSEC and fix the source port in BIND?
answer: To show how DNS attacks work without protections. DNSSEC is turned off (dnssec-enable no) so spoofing works; the source port is fixed (query-source port 33333) so the remote attacker does not have to guess the random UDP source port.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: Why disable Firefox DNS cache in the rebinding experiment?
answer: Firefox caches DNS results for 60 seconds by default, which would force the rebinding attack to wait at least 60 seconds. Setting network.dnsCacheExpiration to 0 disables the cache so the attack works quickly.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: Why is an external DNS server (8.8.8.8) used on the User machine in the rebinding experiment?
answer: The emulation technique uses DNS spoofing; using localhost (127.0.1.1) as the DNS server makes DNS queries too fast for the emulation to intercept, so an outside DNS server is used instead.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What two APIs does the emulated IoT device web server provide?
answer: getpassword (returns the secret password) and settemperature (sets the room temperature if the password in the query matches). It runs on port 8000 at 10.0.2.69.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: Why did the IoT device in the rebinding experiment have weak security?
answer: IoT devices are typically protected by a firewall and cannot be accessed directly from outside, so many do not implement strong authentication. The password only defends against CSRF, not against attackers who can interact directly.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What lesson does the FactCheck.com story illustrate?
answer: Domain names that look alike can be very different; Cheney directed viewers to FactCheck.com instead of FactCheck.org, and the owner of FactCheck.com forwarded the traffic to GeorgeSoros.com. Users should be careful with similar-looking domain names.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: Why did the book recommend a hybrid Scapy + C approach for the Kaminsky attack?
answer: Scapy is convenient for constructing DNS packets but too slow (too few packets per second) for the flood; C is fast but tedious. The hybrid: create the spoofed packet template with Scapy, save it to a file (ip.bin), then load it in C and modify a few fields before sending via raw sockets.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is sr1() in Scapy?
answer: A Scapy function that sends a packet and waits for a reply (used in send_dns_query.py to send a DNS query and receive the response).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What does the ls() command do in Scapy?
answer: Lists the elements (fields) of a Scapy class with their data types and default values, e.g., ls(DNS), ls(DNSRR), ls(DNSQR).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: Why must a spoofed reply IP/UDP source/destination be the reverse of the query?
answer: In the response packet, the source field should be the same as the destination field of the query packet and vice versa. The spoofed reply for a query from the local DNS server to an upstream server uses src=upstream server and dst=local DNS server, with UDP sport=53.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: In the Kaminsky attack, which IP addresses might the victim query target, and how do attackers handle it?
answer: The query for a hostname in example.com can go to a ROOT server, a .COM server, or one of example.com nameservers. After the first query, the nameserver is cached, so later queries go directly to one of the two example.com nameservers (199.43.133.53 or 199.43.135.53). Without sniffing, attackers take a chance or send two replies (one for each IP).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What value does the Flags field take in the forged Kaminsky reply and what does it mean?
answer: 0x8400, indicating the packet is a DNS response and the answer is authoritative.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: Why not provide the IP address of ns.attacker32.com in the additional section of the spoofed reply?
answer: Because BIND does not trust (use) IP addresses obtained from the additional section - they are second-hand information. Even if cached, the server re-queries to get the IP itself, so the trick does not work.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: In the local cache poisoning attack, why is damage to the user machine limited?
answer: The user machine does not store DNS results; every time it needs an IP address it sends out a query again. Attacking the local DNS server is more damaging because it caches the forged reply (the cache becomes poisoned).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: How many bits must a remote attacker guess in the naive DNS poisoning attack, and why is that hard?
answer: The 16-bit source port and 16-bit transaction ID (2^32 total). Even at 1000 spoofed queries/second it takes about 50 days to try 2^32 times (or about 1.2 hours with a 1000-host botnet), and the cache effect makes repeat attempts impossible until the cache times out.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: What is the timing window in the DNS rebinding experiment and why?
answer: The attacker must rerun the DNS spoofing program with the IoT device IP within 10 seconds of the victim fetching index.html, because the JavaScript waits 10 seconds before requesting www.attacker32.com. Within that window the hostname must be remapped to the IoT IP so the request goes to the target.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: dig @a.root-servers.net www.example.net
answer: Sends a DNS query directly to a root server to emulate step 1 of the iterative process; the root server replies with the .NET zone nameservers (NS) and their IPs (A) in the authority/additional sections.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: dig @m.gtld-servers.net www.example.net
answer: Sends the same query to a .NET gTLD server; it does not know the answer but returns the authoritative nameservers of the example.net zone (a.iana-servers.net and b.iana-servers.net).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: dig @a.iana-servers.net www.example.net
answer: Sends the query to the example.net authoritative nameserver, which returns the final answer: www.example.net A 93.184.216.34.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: dig www.bank32.com
answer: Queries the local DNS server for www.bank32.com; returns the zone configured answer 192.168.0.101 with the authority record ns.bank32.com.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: dig -x 192.168.0.101
answer: Performs a DNS reverse lookup of 192.168.0.101 using the reverse zone (0.168.192.in-addr.arpa), returning the PTR record.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: dig @10.0.2.69 -p 1053 www.example.com
answer: Sends a DNS query to server 10.0.2.69 on the nonstandard UDP port 1053, the port the simple dns_server.py program is bound to.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: sudo resolvconf -u
answer: Updates the resolv.conf file, applying changes made to /etc/resolvconf/resolv.conf.d/head so the new nameserver setting takes effect.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: sudo apt-get install bind9
answer: Installs the BIND 9 DNS server software (already installed in the pre-built SEED VM).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: sudo rndc dumpdb -cache
answer: Tells BIND to dump the content of its DNS cache to the file specified by the dump-file option (e.g., /var/cache/bind/dump.db), used to verify that the cache has been poisoned.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: sudo rndc flush
answer: Flushes (clears) the DNS cache, so the local DNS server must send out new queries instead of using stale cached answers.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: sudo service bind9 restart
answer: Starts or restarts the BIND 9 DNS server; must be run every time the DNS configuration is modified.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: sudo iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -i enp0s3 -p udp --dport 53 -j REDIRECT --to-port 1053
answer: Sets up port forwarding from the standard DNS port 53 to port 1053, so the simple dns_server.py program can receive queries without stopping the BIND server that already uses port 53.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: sudo iptables -t nat -F
answer: Flushes all the NAT table rules (cleanup of the port-forwarding rule after the experiment is done).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: dig @a.root-servers.net -x 128.230.171.184
answer: Emulates reverse-lookup step 1: asks a root server for the PTR of 184.171.230.128.in-addr.arpa; gets the in-addr.arpa zone nameservers.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: dig @f.in-addr-servers.arpa -x 128.230.171.184
answer: Emulates reverse-lookup step 2: asks an in-addr.arpa nameserver, getting the 128.in-addr.arpa nameservers (r.arin.net, u.arin.net).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: dig @r.arin.net -x 128.230.171.184
answer: Emulates reverse-lookup step 3: asks a 128.in-addr.arpa nameserver, getting the 230.128.in-addr.arpa nameservers (ns1.syr.edu, ns2.syr.edu).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: dig @ns2.syr.edu -x 128.230.171.184
answer: Emulates reverse-lookup step 4: asks the authoritative nameserver, which returns the final PTR answer (syr.edu).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: python3 (then: from scapy.all import * / ls(DNS))
answer: Starts a Python interpreter, imports Scapy, and lists the DNS class fields (id, qr, opcode, aa, tc, rd, ra, z, ad, cd, rcode, qdcount, ancount, nscount, arcount, qd, an, ns, ar).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: sudo ./send_dns_query.py
answer: Runs the Scapy program that constructs and sends a DNS query for www.syracuse.edu to 8.8.8.8 and prints the reply (requires root).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: dig www.example.net (during local cache poisoning attack)
answer: Triggers the user machine to query the local DNS server for www.example.net; the forged reply is received, showing www.example.net A 1.2.3.4 and the authority record example.net NS ns.attacker32.com.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: dig abc.example.net
answer: After hijacking the example.net zone, queries the local DNS server for any hostname in the domain; shows the domain is completely hijacked (answer 1.2.3.6, NS ns.attacker32.com, A 10.0.2.70).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: dig abc.attacker32.com
answer: Triggers a query that the malicious nameserver (or sniff-and-spoof emulation) answers; used to test what fake records in the additional/authority sections get accepted and cached.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: sudo ./dns_rebinding.py 10.0.2.70
answer: Runs the DNS rebinding spoofing program with the attacker server IP as the answer; provides the truthful mapping of www.attacker32.com to the attacker web server during the first phase of the attack.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch18: DNS and Attacks
question: sudo ./dns_rebinding.py 10.0.2.69
answer: Reruns the DNS rebinding spoofing program with the target IoT device IP as the answer, remapping www.attacker32.com to 10.0.2.69 within the 10-second window so the JavaScript request hits the IoT device.
