source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
symptoms: Feeding %s%s%s%s%s%s%s%s to the vulnerable program causes a segmentation fault
root_cause: printf() dereferences each fetched value as a string pointer; values on the stack beyond the real arguments are zeros, protected memory, or unmapped addresses, so dereferencing crashes.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Confirm the program accepts format strings as input
2. Increase the number of %s specifiers if no crash happens on the first try
3. Use fewer %x specifiers instead if the goal is only to leak data
resolution: The crash is the intended Attack 1 (denial of service); to leak memory instead, use %x/%s carefully, and to prevent it, pass user input as data: printf("%s", input).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
symptoms: The %n attack ran but the target variable was not modified
root_cause: The va_list pointer did not reach the placed address when %n executed, or the address was not on the stack at the expected position.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify the target address bytes were placed at the start of the input (little-endian)
2. Count how many %x are printed before the address value appears
3. Adjust the number of %x so %n lands on the address (e.g., 5 %x then %n in Attack 3)
resolution: Use trial-and-error or a %.8x probe to determine the exact offset from the va_list start to the placed address, then put %n at that position.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
symptoms: The variable was modified but only some of its bytes changed (e.g., changed from 0x11223344 to 0x11223305)
root_cause: The wrong length modifier was used: %hhn only writes the least significant byte, %hn only the least two bytes; %n writes all four.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Check which length modifier is in the format string
2. Use %n to overwrite all 4 bytes, or combine %hn writes to set each half precisely
3. Verify with the test program using a, b, c variables
resolution: Pick the length modifier matching how many bytes you intend to write: %n=4 bytes, %hn=2 bytes, %hhn=1 byte.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
symptoms: Using a single %n to write 0x66887799 would take about an hour to finish
root_cause: %n writes the count of printed characters; reaching 0x66887799 (~1.72 billion) requires printing that many characters, which is extremely slow.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Break the target into two 16-bit halves
2. Use two %hn specifiers with addresses 0xBFFFF306 and 0xBFFFF304
3. Use precision modifiers (%.26204x, %.4369x) to reach the smaller intermediate totals quickly
resolution: Use the %hn (two-write) approach, which completes in under a second instead of an hour.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
symptoms: After the attack, the printed return address is unchanged (still the original 0x080485c4) and no root shell appears
root_cause: %n/%hn wrote to the wrong address, i.e., the va_list did not reach the placed target addresses, or the format specifier count/padding was miscalculated.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Compare the printed return address before and after printf() as a debug check
2. Feed %.8x probes to find the exact position of the two placed addresses
3. Recompute small = 0xbfff - 12 - 19*8 and large = 0xeca4 - 0xbfff and rebuild badfile
resolution: If the after-value equals the before-value, the write missed the return address field; adjust the number of %.8x/padding specifiers so %hn hits both 0xbfffebee and 0xbfffebec.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
symptoms: Compilation of vul.c shows: warning: format not a string literal and no format arguments [-Wformat-security]
root_cause: gcc detects that printf(input) uses a non-literal format string with no arguments - a sign of a potential format string vulnerability.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Recognize this is the countermeasure warning discussed in the chapter
2. For the lab, the warning can be ignored
3. For production code, fix it by using printf("%s", input)
resolution: The warning is only a reminder; the program still compiles. The real fix is never passing user input as the format string.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
symptoms: The %x dump prints only a few values then stops / the wrong addresses appear
root_cause: The format string may be too short to reach the target, or the va_list advanced by an unexpected amount (e.g., double types consume 8 bytes, and @@@@ separators shift positions).
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Use a series of %.8x: probes and observe which position prints the first placed address
2. Account for every consumed argument slot, including the @@@@ integer between two addresses
3. Adjust the number of %x before each %hn/%n
resolution: Determine the required va_list advances empirically and encode them in the format string (e.g., 20 %x to the first address; one more %x to the second).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
symptoms: The shell runs but is a normal shell, not a root shell, even though the code injection worked
root_cause: bash/dash drop privileges when invoked inside a Set-UID process, so the spawned /bin/sh has no root privilege.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Add setuid(0) instructions (bytes \x31\xc0\x31\xdb\xb0\xd5\xcd\x80) at the start of the shellcode
2. Regenerate badfile and re-run
3. Verify the returned address became 0xbfffeca4
resolution: Include a setuid(0) prefix in the shellcode so real and effective user IDs become 0 before launching /bin/sh.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
symptoms: With ASLR enabled the crafted addresses (e.g., 0xbfffebec) are wrong on the next run
root_cause: Randomizing the stack/address space moves the target addresses between executions, invalidating the hard-coded values in the format string.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Turn off randomization with sudo sysctl -w kernel.randomize_va_space=0 for the lab
2. Re-collect the printed addresses (input array, frame pointer, return address)
3. Rebuild badfile with the new addresses
resolution: Disable ASLR for the experiment, or rely on the program printing its own addresses to derive them dynamically.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
symptoms: The format string length is limited and 20 %x specifiers do not fit in the buffer
root_cause: Advancing the va_list one argument at a time consumes many characters; when space is tight this is impractical.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Use the parameter field %k$ to jump directly to the k-th argument (e.g., %21$hn, %22$hn)
2. Drop the @@@@ separator because the pointer can jump between the two addresses
3. Use a single %.Nx to print the needed characters before the first %hn
resolution: Use the k$ parameter field form to select arguments directly, drastically shrinking the format string.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: What is the correct order to leak a secret value from the stack (Attack 2)?
correct_sequence: 1. Feed a series of %x format specifiers
2. printf() prints each fetched integer and advances the va_list pointer by 4 bytes
3. Observe that the secret var value (0x11223344) appears at the 5th %x
4. Adjust the number of %x to control which stack slot is leaked
distractor_sequences: 1. feed %n, 2. read a file, 3. print var
1. feed %s, 2. write to memory, 3. crash
explanation: %x prints integers from where va_list points; each one advances the pointer 4 bytes, revealing successive stack positions including secret data.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: What is the correct order to change a program's data to a specific value using %hn (Attack 4 fast)?
correct_sequence: 1. Break the target value into two 2-byte halves (0x6688 high, 0x7799 low)
2. Put both target addresses (0xBFFFF306 then 0xBFFFF304) on the stack, separated by @@@@
3. Advance va_list to the first address (5 %x) and print 0x6688 chars total (%.26204x) then %hn
4. Print the @@@@ as an integer (%.4369x) to raise the count to 0x7799, then the second %hn
distractor_sequences: 1. write low half first, 2. high half second
1. use one %n for all 4 bytes, 2. print 1.7 billion chars
explanation: Because %n values are accumulative, writing the higher value first (0x6688) then adding the difference (4369 = 0x7799 - 0x6688) hits the lower value without printing billions of characters.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: What is the correct order to launch the format string code injection attack?
correct_sequence: 1. Inject shellcode (with setuid(0)) and NOPs at the end of the format string buffer
2. Compute the entry address A (buffer address + 144) and the return address location B (framep + 4)
3. Place the two write addresses (0xbfffebee and 0xbfffebec) at the start of the format string
4. Use %.8x*, %hn specifiers to write 0xbfff and 0xeca4 into the return address field
5. Run fmtvul to redirect execution into the shellcode and get a root shell
distractor_sequences: 1. write addresses, 2. inject code, 3. compute A
1. run, 2. compute addresses, 3. inject
explanation: Code must be in place and its address known before writing that address into the return address field; then running the program triggers the redirect.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: What is the correct order to build the format string that writes two 16-bit values with %hn?
correct_sequence: 1. Calculate the smaller value 0xbfff and the larger 0xeca4
2. Convert 0xbfff to a print count: 0xbfff - 164 = 48987 more characters after 12+19*8 already printed
3. Build the specifier chain: 19 %.8x, then %.48987x, %hn, then %.11429x, %hn
4. Prepend the two little-endian addresses separated by @@@@
5. Append NOPs and shellcode, then write to badfile
distractor_sequences: 1. write 0xeca4 first, 2. then 0xbfff
1. prepend shellcode, 2. append addresses
explanation: The accumulative count starts from 0xbfff (the higher half) and increases by 0x11429 = 0xeca4 - 0xbfff to reach 0xeca4 for the second write.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: What is the correct order to determine how many %x are needed to reach a placed address?
correct_sequence: 1. Put the address bytes at the start of the input
2. Feed a series of %.8x: format specifiers
3. Read the output and find which position prints the address
4. Use that position count (e.g., 21st -> 20 %x) in the exploit
distractor_sequences: 1. guess the count, 2. run once, 3. hope
1. feed %n first, 2. count the numbers, 3. no probe needed
explanation: Empirically probing with %.8x: reveals exactly how many arguments separate the va_list start from the placed address on this stack layout.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: What is the correct order to set up the fmtvul.c code injection lab?
correct_sequence: 1. Compile with gcc -z execstack -o fmtvul fmtvul.c
2. Turn it into a root-owned Set-UID program: sudo chown root fmtvul and sudo chmod 4755 fmtvul
3. Create badfile (touch badfile) and run fmtvul to collect the printed addresses
4. Run fmtexploit.py to generate badfile and attack
distractor_sequences: 1. chmod first, 2. compile after
1. disable ASLR, 2. skip execstack
explanation: Compilation with an executable stack is required for injected code, the Set-UID root ownership gives the payload root privilege, and the printed addresses drive the attack.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: What is the correct order of the stdarg operations inside a variadic function?
correct_sequence: 1. Declare a va_list pointer
2. Call va_start(ap, last_named_arg) to position it after the last named argument
3. Loop with va_arg(ap, type) to fetch values, advancing the pointer
4. Call va_end(ap) to finish
distractor_sequences: 1. va_end first, 2. va_arg, 3. va_start
1. va_arg, 2. declare, 3. va_start
explanation: The pointer must be initialized with va_start before va_arg can fetch anything, and va_end is the final cleanup (a no-op in GNU C).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch5: Return-to-libc Attack and ROP
question: Why is the spacing Y-X = 0x20 (32 bytes) chosen between chained stack frames?
answer: 32 bytes of space is enough to hold the next-ebp, return address, and up to (32-8)/4 = 6 arguments per frame. If more arguments are needed, the distance can be increased; the exact value also lets attackers avoid zero bytes.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch5: Return-to-libc Attack and ROP
question: What argument does chain_witharg.py pass to the chained baz() calls?

source: Hands-on Security - Ch5: Return-to-libc Attack and ROP
question: Why is the program compiled with -g to measure the ebp-to-buffer distance?
answer: The -g option adds debug information so gdb can resolve symbols and variables; with it we can set a breakpoint at foo, print $ebp and &buffer, and compute the distance (108 bytes).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch5: Return-to-libc Attack and ROP
question: What does the initial padding in the exploit scripts (bytearray(0xaa for i in range(112))) represent?
answer: It fills the first 112 bytes (the buffer plus locals up to the return address field) with a non-zero filler so strcpy() copies the whole payload and the overwritten fields land at the correct offsets.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch5: Return-to-libc Attack and ROP
question: In the register-tracking table, what does the prologue instruction 'push ebp' do to esp and ebp?
answer: esp decreases by 4 (it pushes the old ebp value); ebp is unchanged. The instruction saves the caller's frame pointer so it can be restored at the end of the function.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch5: Return-to-libc Attack and ROP
question: What result demonstrates that chaining 20 printf() calls worked in chain_printf.py?

source: Hands-on Security - Ch5: Return-to-libc Attack and ROP
question: What are the three tasks of the basic return-to-libc attack?

source: Hands-on Security - Ch5: Return-to-libc Attack and ROP
question: In the basic attack, why are two functions' frames only 4 bytes apart when chaining without leaveret?
answer: When A() returns to B()'s entry, B()'s prologue sets ebp = esp, which is only 4 bytes above A()'s frame pointer (Observation 5.1 gives X+4). That 4-byte gap holds only the return address, leaving no room for arguments.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch5: Return-to-libc Attack and ROP
question: What is the purpose of exit() in the basic layout beyond graceful termination?
answer: It also provides a clean target for system()'s return address field (offset 116); without a valid address there, the program would jump to a random location after the shell command finishes and likely crash.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch5: Return-to-libc Attack and ROP
question: Which statement about the register-tracking table is correct?

choices.label: push ebp: esp -4; ret: esp +4; pop ebp: ebp = *(esp)
push ebp: esp +4; ret: esp -4
ret does not change esp
pop ebp does not change ebp

explanation: push decreases esp by 4, pop increases it by 4 and sets the register from the stack, and ret pops the return address (esp +4) and jumps to it.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch5: Return-to-libc Attack and ROP
question: What is the correct order of esp/ebp changes as foo() returns and system()'s prologue runs?
correct_sequence: 1. mov ebp,esp: esp = X (foo's frame pointer value)
2. pop ebp: esp = X+4, ebp = *(X)
3. ret: esp = X+8, jump to the stored return address (system)
4. push ebp: esp = X+4
5. mov esp,ebp: ebp = X+4
distractor_sequences: 1. ret first, 2. push, 3. mov
1. mov, 2. push, 3. pop
explanation: After foo's epilogue (mov/pop/ret) and system's prologue (push/mov), ebp ends at X+4, so system()'s first argument at ebp+8 is at X+12 = buffer offset 120.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch5: Return-to-libc Attack and ROP
question: Why must the distance Y-X be chosen so the frame values contain no zero byte?

choices.label: A zero byte in the payload terminates strcpy(), truncating the overflowed data
Zero bytes make the chain execute slower
Zero bytes trigger ASLR
Zero bytes are interpreted as function addresses

explanation: strcpy() copies until the first null byte. Any 0x00 in the constructed frames would stop the copy and leave the rest of the chain off the stack.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch5: Return-to-libc Attack and ROP
Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: What happens when printf() continues calling va_arg() past the last real argument?
answer: There is no boundary marker on the stack, so va_arg() keeps fetching values from beyond printf()'s stack frame. With %s those values are dereferenced as pointers (crashing); with %x they are printed; with %n they are used as write addresses.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: What is the role of the @@@@ separator between the two target addresses in the %hn attack?
answer: It occupies 4 bytes (0x40404040) between the two addresses on the stack. After the first %hn, a %x consumes this value as an integer, advancing the va_list pointer to the second address and printing extra characters toward the next %n total.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: What value is written by the slow Attack 4 and why?
answer: %.10000000x prints 10,000,000 characters; combined with 36 already printed (4 address bytes + four %.8x), the total 10,000,036 = 0x9896a4 is written to var by %n. To reach 0x66887799 with %n would need about an hour.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: In the code injection attack, what is the entry point address A and where is it written?
answer: A = 0xbfffec14 + 144 = 0xbfffeca4 (input array address plus offset 144, inside the NOP area). It is split into 0xbfff and 0xeca4 and written to 0xbfffebee and 0xbfffebec (the return address field at framep + 4).

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: What does the example printf("%3$.20x%6$n", 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, &var) demonstrate?
answer: It prints the third optional argument (3) with width 20 (18 leading zeros) and then writes the character count 20 into var via %6$n, changing var from 1000 to 20. This shows the k$ parameter field.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: What is the correct, safe version of printf(user_input)?
answer: printf("%s", user_input). The user input is passed as data, and the format string is a literal with no attacker-controlled specifiers.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: Why can a format string attack in a privileged (root Set-UID) program lead to a root shell?
answer: The format string attack can overwrite a function's return address to jump to injected shellcode; if the vulnerable program runs with root privileges, the shellcode executes with those privileges, yielding a root shell.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: How can a format string attack defeat the non-executable stack countermeasure?
answer: Use the return-to-libc technique: modify two memory locations with one format string - the return address field (set it to system()) and the memory 4 bytes above it (set to the '/bin/sh' address) - so system('/bin/sh') runs.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: What is the difference between %5$x and %x%x%x%x%x?
answer: %5$x directly selects and prints the 5th optional argument using the parameter field. The five %x specifiers each consume and advance the va_list pointer one step to reach the 5th value, printing all the intermediate values too.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: Why is the fmtstr() return address stored at framep + 1 (four bytes above ebp)?
answer: The stack layout at ebp is: [saved frame pointer][return address][arguments]. Since framep is the saved ebp value, framep + 4 (i.e., +1 unsigned int) is the return address slot.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability

question: Which statement correctly describes how the two halves are written in the code injection attack?

choices.label: 0xbfff is written to 0xbfffebee and 0xeca4 is written to 0xbfffebec, jointly forming 0xbfffeca4
0xeca4 is written to 0xbfffebee and 0xbfff to 0xbfffebec

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
symptoms: The var value becomes 0x2c (44) instead of a chosen value in Attack 3
root_cause: %n writes the current character count, which is 44 (the number of characters printed before %n); to write a specific value you must control the printed count with precision/width modifiers.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Count the characters printed before %n
2. Use precision modifiers (e.g., %.8x, %.10000000x) to tune the total
3. For exact arbitrary values, switch to the two-%hn approach
resolution: 0x2c is the expected result of the default format string; precise values are achieved by adding width/precision padding or by writing two halves with %hn.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
symptoms: After the code injection attack the return address prints the same value before and after printf() (0x080485c4)
root_cause: The %hn writes did not land on the return address field; the va_list count, padding totals, or address byte order were wrong, so the target memory was never modified.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Use the before/after return-address printout as a debug check
2. Verify 0xbfffebee/0xbfffebec bytes appear little-endian at the start of badfile
3. Probe with %.8x: to confirm the addresses are the 21st/22nd stack values
4. Recheck small = 0xbfff - 12 - 19*8 and large = 0xeca4 - 0xbfff
resolution: If before == after, the write missed; correct the position count/padding so %21$hn and %22$hn (or 20/21 %x) reach both target addresses.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
symptoms: The format string itself gets truncated in the buffer, so later specifiers are lost
root_cause: The format string (with many %.8x and %.Nx specifiers) plus NOPs plus shellcode exceeds the available 200-byte buffer, or the string contains a null byte that ends the copy.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Switch to the parameter field form (%k$) to remove the 20 %x specifiers and @@@@
2. Avoid non-printable bytes except the leading addresses
3. Keep the shellcode compact and reduce padding
resolution: Use fmtexploit_revised.py with %21$hn/%22$hn to fit the whole format string within the buffer.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: What is the correct order to modify var using %n (Attack 3)?
correct_sequence: 1. Determine var's address (0xBFFFF304)
2. Place the little-endian address at the start of the input so it is on the stack
3. Advance the va_list to the address with %x specifiers (5 %x)
4. Write the character count with %n
distractor_sequences: 1. use %n first, 2. then %x
1. place address at the end of the string
explanation: The target address must be reachable on the stack, then %x advances va_list to it, then %n writes the printed-character count to it.

source: Hands-on Security - Ch6: Format String Vulnerability
question: What is the correct order to build the Attack 4 fast input with two %hn writes?
correct_sequence: 1. Compute the two half addresses 0xBFFFF306 and 0xBFFFF304
2. Put 0xBFFFF306, @@@@, 0xBFFFF304 at the start of the format string
3. Use 4 %.8x + %.26204x so the count reaches 0x6688, then %hn
distractor_sequences: 1. write low half first, then high half
1. single %n for the whole value
explanation: Writing the larger half value first and adding the difference keeps printed totals small, and %n is accumulative, so the second %hn writes 0x6688 + 0x1111 = 0x7799.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What is Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP)?
answer: A Cisco proprietary Layer 2 protocol that is media and protocol independent and runs on all Cisco-manufactured equipment including routers, bridges, access servers, and switches.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What is CDP primarily used for?
answer: To obtain the protocol addresses of neighboring devices and discover the platform of those devices. CDP can also be used to display information about the interfaces that your device uses.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: Is CDP enabled or disabled by default on Cisco devices?
answer: CDP is enabled on all Cisco devices by default.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What is Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)?
answer: An industry-standard alternative to CDP (IEEE 802.1AB). It is a neighbor discovery protocol used for network devices to advertise information about themselves to other devices on the network.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What layer does LLDP run over?
answer: The data link layer (Layer 2), which allows two systems running different network layer protocols to learn about each other.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: On which interface types does LLDP work?
answer: LLDP works on Ethernet type interfaces only.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: How does LLDP treat a switch stack?
answer: A switch stack appears as a single switch in the network, so LLDP discovers the switch stack, not the individual stack members.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What is the default LLDP holdtime value and its range?
answer: The default holdtime is 120 seconds. The range is 0 to 65,535 seconds. It is the amount of time a receiving device should hold the information sent by another device before discarding it.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What is the default LLDP timer value and its range?
answer: The default transmission frequency of LLDP updates is 30 seconds. The range is 5 to 65,534 seconds.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What is the default LLDP reinit value and its range?
answer: The default delay time for LLDP to initialize on any interface is 2 seconds. The range is 2 to 5 seconds.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)

answer: When CDP is not required at all, or when the device is located in an insecure environment. Use the no cdp run command.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)

answer: When management is not being performed, when the switch interface is a nontrunk interface, or when the interface is connected to a nontrusted network. Use the no cdp enable command.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
symptoms: show cdp neighbors returns no neighbor information on a Cisco router.
root_cause: CDP is disabled globally (no cdp run) or on the interfaces (no cdp enable), or the neighbor device is not a Cisco device running CDP.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify CDP is running globally with show cdp.
2. Verify CDP is enabled on the relevant interfaces with show cdp interface.
3. Re-enable with cdp run (global) and cdp enable (interface).
4. Confirm the neighbor is a Cisco device with CDP enabled.
resolution: Router(config)# cdp run; Router(config-if)# cdp enable; recheck with show cdp neighbors.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
symptoms: show lldp neighbors on a switch shows no LLDP neighbors.
root_cause: LLDP is disabled globally (no lldp run) or lldp transmit/lldp receive is disabled on the interface; LLDP only works on Ethernet type interfaces.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify global LLDP with show lldp.
2. Verify LLDP on the interface with show lldp interface.
3. Enable with lldp run globally and lldp transmit/lldp receive on the interface.
4. Confirm the interface is an Ethernet type interface and the neighbor also runs LLDP.
resolution: Switch(config)# lldp run; Switch(config-if)# lldp transmit; Switch(config-if)# lldp receive.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
symptoms: show lldp traffic reports a high number of unrecognized TLV fields.
root_cause: Neighbor devices are sending LLDP Type Length Value (TLV) fields this device does not recognize, often vendor-specific extensions.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Note the unrecognized TLV count in show lldp traffic.
2. Identify the neighbors involved with show lldp neighbors.
3. Investigate vendor-specific TLV usage of the neighbor device.
resolution: Monitor with debug lldp packets and show lldp traffic.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What is the correct order to configure LLDP to send and receive on a single interface?
correct_sequence: 1. Enable LLDP globally with Switch(config)# lldp run
2. Enter interface configuration mode with Switch(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
3. Enable sending with Switch(config-if)# lldp transmit
4. Enable receiving with Switch(config-if)# lldp receive
distractor_sequences: 1. Switch(config-if)# lldp transmit 2. Switch(config-if)# lldp receive 3. Switch(config)# lldp run
1. Switch(config)# no lldp run 2. Switch(config-if)# lldp transmit
1. Switch(config)# lldp timer 60 2. Switch(config)# lldp run
explanation: LLDP must be enabled globally with lldp run first; then the interface must be selected and both lldp transmit and lldp receive must be enabled to send and receive.

1. RouterOrSwitch(config)# no lldp run 2. RouterOrSwitch(config)# interface fastethernet 0/1
explanation: To disable CDP on a single interface, enter the interface configuration mode and use no cdp enable. Use no cdp run to disable CDP globally.

answer: 5 to 65,534 seconds; the default is 30 seconds.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What is the range for the LLDP reinit command?
answer: 2 to 5 seconds; the default is 2 seconds.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: Which two commands are used to disable CDP?
answer: no cdp run (disables CDP globally) and no cdp enable (disables CDP on a specific interface).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What does the chapter caution about CDP and management?
answer: Although CDP is necessary for some management applications, CDP should still be disabled in some instances, such as when it is not required or when the device is in an insecure environment.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: RouterOrSwitch(config-if)# no cdp enable
answer: Disables CDP on a specific interface, for example after entering interface fastethernet 0/1 for a nontrusted network.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What information does show cdp neighbors detail display?
answer: More detail about neighbor devices compared to show cdp neighbors.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What does show lldp neighbors [detail] display?
answer: Information about neighbors, including device type, interface type and number, holdtime settings, capabilities, and port ID.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What does the clear cdp counters command do?
answer: Resets the CDP traffic counters to 0.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What does the clear cdp table command do?
answer: Deletes the CDP table.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What does show cdp traffic display?
answer: CDP traffic information (packets in/out and version).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What does debug cdp packets monitor?
answer: CDP packet-related information.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What does debug cdp adjacency monitor?
answer: CDP neighbor information.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What does debug cdp ip monitor?
answer: CDP events specifically for IP.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What does show lldp display?
answer: Global LLDP information, such as the frequency of transmissions, the holdtime for packets being sent, and the delay time for LLDP to initialize on an interface.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What does show lldp traffic display?
answer: LLDP counters, including the number of packets sent and received, packets discarded, and unrecognized Type Length Value (TLV) fields.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What is the command to see which interfaces have CDP running?
answer: show cdp interface.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What are the reasons given to disable CDP on an interface?
answer: Management is not being performed, the switch interface is a nontrunk interface, or the interface is connected to a nontrusted network.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What do the lldp transmit and lldp receive interface commands do?
answer: lldp transmit enables the interface to send LLDP packets; lldp receive enables the interface to receive LLDP packets.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch13: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)
question: What is the main difference between CDP and LLDP?
answer: CDP is a Cisco proprietary protocol, while LLDP is an industry-standard (IEEE 802.1AB) alternative used for neighbor discovery.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What does the Router> prompt indicate?
answer: User EXEC mode: limited viewing of configuration; you cannot make changes in this mode.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What does the Router(config)# prompt indicate?
answer: Global configuration mode: this prompt indicates you can start making changes.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What does the Router(config-if)# prompt indicate?
answer: Interface mode.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What does the Router(config-subif)# prompt indicate?
answer: Subinterface mode.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What does the Router(config-line)# prompt indicate?
answer: Line mode.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What does the Router(config-router)# prompt indicate?
answer: Router configuration mode.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Why must you be careful about which router mode you are in?
answer: Not all commands work in all modes. If you type a correct command like show running-config and get an error, make sure you are in the correct mode.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router> enable
answer: Moves from user EXEC mode to privileged EXEC mode.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# configure terminal
answer: Moves from privileged EXEC mode to global configuration mode.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# hostname Cisco
answer: Sets the router name to Cisco. The name should start with a letter and contain no spaces. Works on both routers and switches.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# enable password cisco
answer: Sets the enable password to cisco (clear text, not encrypted by default).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# enable secret class
answer: Sets the enable secret password to class (encrypted by default).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# line console 0
answer: Enters console line mode.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-line)# password console
answer: Sets the console line mode password to console.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-line)# login
answer: Enables password checking at login.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# line vty 0 4
answer: Enters vty line mode for all five vty lines (0 through 4).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-line)# password telnet
answer: Sets the vty password to telnet.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# line aux 0
answer: Enters auxiliary line mode. This is not available on Cisco switches.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-line)# password backdoor
answer: Sets the auxiliary line mode password to backdoor.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What is the difference between enable secret and enable password regarding encryption?
answer: The enable secret password is encrypted by default; the enable password is not.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What is the recommended practice for enable passwords?
answer: Never use the enable password command; use only the enable secret password command in a router or switch configuration.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Can you set both enable secret and enable password to the same password?
answer: No. Setting both to the same password defeats the use of encryption.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# service password-encryption
answer: Clear text passwords will be hidden using a weak encryption algorithm.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# no service password-encryption
answer: Turns off password encryption.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: If you turn on service password-encryption, use it, and then turn it off, what happens to existing passwords?
answer: Any passwords that you have already encrypted stay encrypted. New passwords remain unencrypted.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: router# show ip interface brief
answer: Displays a summary of all interfaces, including status and IP address assigned. Use this to see which interfaces are installed on a particular router.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What is an on-board port?
answer: A fixed port that is built directly into the motherboard.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What is a slot?
answer: A slot is used to expand the port density of a device by inserting a module that plugs into the motherboard. A module may contain several ports.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What are the interface names on a Cisco 2501 router?
answer: On board Ethernet: ethernet0 (e0); on board Serial: serial0 (s0) and serial1 (s1). Uses interface-type number notation.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What are the interface names on a Cisco 1841 router?
answer: On board Fast Ethernet: fa0/0 and fa0/1; Slot 0 (HWIC/WIC/VWIC): s0/0/0 and s0/0/1. Uses interface-type 0/slot/port notation.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What is special about Gi0/0/0 on the 4221/4321 routers?
answer: Only one of the RJ45 Gi0/0/0 or SFP (fiber-optic) Gi0/0/0 can be used because they share the same interface name.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-if)# exit
answer: Returns to global configuration mode from interface configuration mode.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What happens when you move directly from one interface mode to another using the interface command?
answer: The prompt does not change, even though you are in a new interface mode. Be careful not to put the configuration for one interface on a different interface.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# interface serial 0/0/0
answer: Moves to serial interface 0/0/0 configuration mode.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-if)# description Link to ISP
answer: Optional descriptor of the link; it is locally significant.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-if)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
answer: Assigns an address and subnet mask to the interface.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-if)# clock rate 2000000
answer: Assigns a clock rate for the interface. Used only on a serial interface that has a DCE cable plugged into it.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-if)# no shutdown
answer: Turns the interface on.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: When is the clock rate command used on a serial interface?
answer: Only on a serial interface that has a DCE cable plugged into it. There must be a clock rate on every serial link between routers. It does not matter which router has the DCE cable.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Why are serial connections being removed from networks?
answer: Ethernet connections are faster and not reliant on clocking rates. In the book, serial interfaces are used to distinguish WAN connections from LAN connections (Ethernet).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# interface fastethernet 0/0
answer: Moves to Fast Ethernet 0/0 interface configuration mode.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-if)# description Accounting LAN
answer: Optional descriptor of the link; it is locally significant.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-if)# ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
answer: Assigns an address and subnet mask to the Fast Ethernet interface.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/0/0
answer: Moves to gigabitethernet 0/0/0 interface configuration mode.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-if)# ip address 192.168.30.1 255.255.255.0
answer: Assigns an address and subnet mask to the Gigabit Ethernet interface.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
answer: Enables the forwarding of IPv6 unicast datagrams globally on the router.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-if)# ipv6 enable
answer: Automatically configures an IPv6 link-local address on the interface and enables IPv6 processing. The link-local address can only communicate with nodes on the same broadcast segment.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-if)# ipv6 address autoconfig
answer: The router configures itself with a link-local address using stateless autoconfiguration.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001::1/64
answer: Configures a global IPv6 address on the interface and enables IPv6 processing on the interface.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:0:1::/64 eui-64
answer: Configures a global IPv6 address with an interface identifier in the low-order 64 bits of the IPv6 address.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::260:3eff:fe47:1530/64 link-local
answer: Configures a specific link-local IPv6 address on the interface instead of the automatically configured one.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-if)# ipv6 unnumbered type/number
answer: Specifies an unnumbered interface and enables IPv6 processing. The global IPv6 address of the interface specified by type/number is used as the source address.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# banner motd ^ Building Power will be interrupted next Tuesday evening from 8 - 10 PM. ^
answer: Creates a message-of-the-day banner. The delimiter (^) must surround the banner message and can be any character as long as it is not used within the body of the message.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# banner login ^Authorized Personnel Only! Please enter your username and password. ^
answer: Creates a login banner displayed before the username and password login prompts.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: When is the MOTD banner displayed?
answer: On all terminals, before the login prompt and the login banner, via console or Telnet. If connecting using SSH, the MOTD banner appears after the SSH connection.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What commands disable the MOTD and login banners?
answer: no banner motd disables the MOTD banner; no banner login disables the login banner. The MOTD banner displays before the login banner.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# ip host london 172.16.1.3
answer: Assigns a locally significant host name to the IP address, so the host name can be used instead of the IP address when telnetting or pinging.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Why do Router# london, Router# telnet london, and Router# telnet 172.16.1.3 all work?
answer: In user EXEC or privileged EXEC mode, commands that do not match a valid command default to Telnet, so a host name mapping can be used to Telnet to a remote device.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# no ip domain-lookup
answer: Turns off trying to automatically resolve an unrecognized command to a local host name (DNS lookup).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What happens by default when you type a word that is not a command at the EXEC prompt?
answer: The router is set by default to try to resolve any word that is not a command to a Domain Name System (DNS) server at address 255.255.255.255, and unrecognized commands default to Telnet.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What is the syntax variation of no ip domain-lookup in some newer IOS versions?
answer: The command may not have a hyphen: no ip domain lookup.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: If you configure a DNS server with ip name-server but do not configure ip domain-lookup, what happens?
answer: Your DNS server is useless because it will not be used.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# ip name-server
answer: Configures a DNS server on the router.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-line)# transport preferred none
answer: Deactivates the automatic action of telnetting into words that look like host names (your spelling mistakes that do not look like commands).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: On which lines should transport preferred none be applied?
answer: All lines: con 0, aux 0, and vty 0 15.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-line)# logging synchronous
answer: Turns on synchronous logging. Information items sent to the console do not interrupt the command you are typing; the prompt and command line are moved to a new line.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What keyboard shortcut brings a command to the next line if it is interrupted by informational messages?
answer: Ctrl-R (the informational line is not inserted into the middle of the command you are typing).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-line)# exec-timeout 0 0
answer: Sets the limit of idle connection time (minutes seconds), after which the console automatically logs off. A setting of 0 0 means the console never logs off (timeout disabled).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config-line)# exec-timeout 0
answer: Disables the console timeout (using the command without the seconds parameter also works).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What is the default exec-timeout value?
answer: 10 minutes and 0 seconds of idle connection time (exec-timeout 10 0). exec-timeout 0 0 disables the timeout and is considered bad security in the real world.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# copy running-config startup-config
answer: Saves the running configuration to local NVRAM. You will be prompted for a destination filename.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# copy running-config tftp
answer: Saves the running configuration remotely to a TFTP server. You will be prompted to enter the IP address of the TFTP server.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# erase startup-config
answer: Deletes the startup configuration file from NVRAM. You will be prompted to confirm this action. The running configuration is still in dynamic memory; reload the router to clear it.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# write
answer: Saves the running configuration to local NVRAM. You are not prompted for a destination filename.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# write memory
answer: Saves the running configuration to local NVRAM. You are not prompted for a destination filename.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# write erase
answer: Deletes the startup configuration file from NVRAM. You will be prompted to confirm this action.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# write network
answer: Saves the running configuration remotely to a TFTP server. A message shows this command has been replaced with the copy running-config <url> command.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Is the write command still supported on all platforms?
answer: The write command was officially deprecated but still works in many IOS versions. It does not work on all devices and platforms, for example the Nexus platform.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# show ?
answer: Lists all show commands available.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# show arp
answer: Displays the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) table.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# show clock
answer: Displays the time set on the device.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# show controllers serial 0/0/0
answer: Displays statistics for interface hardware, including whether the clock rate is set and whether the cable is DCE, DTE, or not attached.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# show flash
answer: Displays information about flash memory.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# show history
answer: Displays the history of commands used at privileged EXEC level.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# show hosts
answer: Displays the local host-to-IP address cache (the names and addresses of hosts on the network to which you can connect).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# show interface serial 0/0/0
answer: Displays statistics for a specific interface (in this case serial 0/0/0).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# show interfaces
answer: Displays statistics for all interfaces.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# show ip protocols
answer: Displays the parameters and the current state of the active IPv4 routing protocol processes.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# show ipv6 interface brief
answer: Displays a summary of all interfaces, including status and IPv6 address assigned.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# show ipv6 protocols
answer: Displays the parameters and the current state of the active IPv6 routing protocol processes.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# show protocols
answer: Displays the status of configured Layer 3 protocols.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# show running-config
answer: Displays the configuration currently running in RAM.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# show startup-config
answer: Displays the configuration saved in NVRAM.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# show users
answer: Displays all users connected to the device.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router# show version
answer: Displays information about the loaded software version.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Router(config)# do show running-config
answer: Executes the privileged-level show running-config command while in global configuration mode. The router remains in global configuration mode after the command executes.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Which EXEC commands can the do command execute, and which cannot?
answer: The do command can execute show, clear, or debug while in global configuration mode or any configuration submode. You cannot use do to execute the configure terminal command.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Which statement about enable secret and enable password is correct?

enable password is encrypted by default; enable secret is not
Both are encrypted by default
Neither is encrypted

A serial interface that has a DTE cable plugged into it
A Gigabit Ethernet interface

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Which statement about the MOTD banner is correct?

choices.label: It is displayed on all terminals before the login prompt; with SSH it appears after the SSH connection
It appears after the login banner
It appears only when connecting via SSH
It replaces the login banner

question: Which statement about the do command is correct?

choices.label: It executes EXEC commands such as show while in configuration mode
It moves you from global configuration mode to privileged EXEC mode
It can be used to execute configure terminal
It only works in user EXEC mode

explanation: The do command executes EXEC commands (show, clear, debug) while remaining in configuration mode. It cannot execute the configure terminal command.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What is the default exec-timeout value?

choices.label: 10 minutes and 0 seconds
0 minutes and 0 seconds
10 minutes and 10 seconds
5 minutes and 0 seconds

explanation: The default for exec-timeout is 10 minutes and 0 seconds of idle connection time (exec-timeout 10 0).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Which command shows which interfaces are installed on a router?

choices.label: show ip interface brief
show ip route
show running-config
show version

explanation: show ip interface brief displays a summary of all interfaces, including status and IP address assigned, and is used to see which interfaces are installed.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
symptoms: You type show running-config in global configuration mode and get an error.
root_cause: show is an EXEC command, not a global configuration command; not all commands work in all modes.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Confirm the prompt you are in with the prompt indicator.
2. Use the do command, e.g., do show running-config, while in configuration mode.
resolution: Router(config)# do show running-config.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
symptoms: After typing a misspelled command at the EXEC prompt, the router pauses for about a minute before returning an error.
root_cause: The router is set by default to try to resolve any word that is not a command to a DNS server at 255.255.255.255, and unrecognized commands default to Telnet.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Disable domain lookup with no ip domain-lookup.
2. Optionally apply transport preferred none on lines con 0, aux 0, and vty 0 15.
resolution: Router(config)# no ip domain-lookup; Router(config-line)# transport preferred none.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
symptoms: Your command gets interrupted by unsolicited informational console messages while you are typing.
root_cause: Synchronous logging is not enabled, so informational messages insert into the middle of the command you are typing.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Configure logging synchronous on the line.
2. Use the Ctrl-R keyboard shortcut to bring the command to the next line without the message interfering.
resolution: Router(config-line)# logging synchronous.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
symptoms: show controllers serial 0/0/0 shows that the clock rate is not set on a serial link between two routers.
root_cause: The clock rate must be configured on the serial interface with the DCE cable plugged into it; without it the link cannot clock.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Determine which side has the DCE cable using show controllers serial.
2. Configure clock rate on the DCE side.
3. Verify the link is up with show interface serial.
resolution: Router(config-if)# clock rate 2000000 (on the DCE side).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What is the correct order to configure a basic router?
correct_sequence: 1. Enter privileged EXEC mode with enable
2. Enter global configuration mode with configure terminal
3. Set the device name with hostname
4. Configure enable secret and line passwords with login
5. Enter interface mode and assign an IP address
6. Save with copy running-config startup-config
distractor_sequences: 1. hostname 2. enable 3. configure terminal
1. copy running-config startup-config 2. interface fastethernet 0/0 3. ip address
1. login 2. password 3. enable secret 4. line vty 0 4
explanation: You must be in privileged EXEC mode (enable) and then global configuration mode (configure terminal) before configuration commands such as hostname, passwords, and interface addressing work.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What is the correct order to configure a serial interface?
correct_sequence: 1. Router(config)# interface serial 0/0/0
2. Router(config-if)# description Link to ISP
3. Router(config-if)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
4. Router(config-if)# clock rate 2000000 (DCE side)
5. Router(config-if)# no shutdown
distractor_sequences: 1. no shutdown 2. ip address 3. interface serial 0/0/0
1. ip address 2. no shutdown 3. clock rate (on the DTE side)
1. clock rate 2. ip address 3. no shutdown 4. interface serial 0/0/0
explanation: Enter interface mode first, then set the description, IP address, and clock rate (only on the DCE side), and finally enable the interface with no shutdown.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What is the correct order to configure line passwords for remote Telnet access?
correct_sequence: 1. Router(config)# line vty 0 4
2. Router(config-line)# password telnet
3. Router(config-line)# login
distractor_sequences: 1. Router(config-line)# login 2. Router(config-line)# password telnet 3. Router(config)# line vty 0 4
1. Router(config)# enable password 2. Router(config)# line vty 0 4 3. Router(config-line)# login
1. Router(config-line)# password 2. Router(config)# line vty 0 4
explanation: Enter vty line mode, set the password, then enable login for password checking to take effect.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What does the ipv6 enable command do?
answer: Automatically configures an IPv6 link-local address on the interface and enables IPv6 processing. The link-local address can be used only to communicate with nodes on the same broadcast segment.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What does the ipv6 address 2001:db8:0:1::/64 eui-64 command do?
answer: Configures a global IPv6 address with an interface identifier in the low-order 64 bits of the IPv6 address.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What replaces the write network command?
answer: The copy running-config <url> command, as shown in the message when write network is used.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: Which command displays whether the clock rate is set on a serial interface?
answer: show controllers serial 0/0/0, which also shows whether the cable is DCE, DTE, or not attached.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch14: Configuring a Cisco Router
question: What is the delimiting character in a banner command and how is it chosen?
answer: A delimiting character (e.g., ^ or #) must surround the banner message. It can be any character as long as it is not a character used within the body of the message.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What are the two ways to identify where packets should be routed when using the ip route command?
answer: The next-hop address or the exit interface.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: How do you read the static route ip route 172.16.20.0 255.255.255.0 172.16.10.2?
answer: To get to the destination network 172.16.20.0 with subnet mask 255.255.255.0, send all packets to the next-hop address 172.16.10.2.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: How do you read the static route ip route 172.16.20.0 255.255.255.0 serial 0/0/0?
answer: To get to the destination network 172.16.20.0 with subnet mask 255.255.255.0, send all packets out the exit interface serial 0/0/0.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What is a recursive lookup in static routing?
answer: A static route that uses a next-hop address (intermediate address) causes the router to look at the routing table twice: once when the packet first enters the router and a second time to resolve the location of the intermediate address.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: For point-to-point links, what should you always use in static route statements?
answer: An exit interface, for example: ip route 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0 serial 0/0/0.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: For broadcast links such as Ethernet, Fast Ethernet, or Gigabit Ethernet, what should you use in a static route statement?
answer: Both an exit interface and an intermediate address, for example: ip route 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0 fastethernet 0/0 192.138.20.2. This avoids a recursive lookup.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What happens to a static route without the permanent keyword when the interface goes down?
answer: The static route is removed from the routing table along with the directly connected network. If the interface comes back up, the routes are returned.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What does the permanent keyword do in a static route statement?
answer: Keeps the static routes in the routing table even if the interface goes down and the directly connected networks are removed. When the interface comes back up, the routes do not need to be reprocessed.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: How quickly are static routes processed when added or deleted?
answer: In 1 second. Before Cisco IOS Software Release 12.0, this processing time was 5 seconds.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: How often does the routing table process static routes?
answer: The routing table processes static routes every minute to install or remove static routes according to the changing routing table.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What is the default administrative distance of a static route?
answer: 1. The AD rates the trustworthiness of a route.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What is the AD of a directly connected route?
answer: 0 (both IPv4 and IPv6). Only an AD of 0 is better than the default AD of 1 for a static route.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: If your network is using EIGRP and you need a backup route, what AD should the static route have?
answer: An AD greater than 90 (EIGRP internal AD). EIGRP will be used because its AD is lower; if EIGRP goes down, the static route takes over.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What is the AD for unknown or unbelievable routes?
answer: 255 in IPv4 and 254 in IPv6. These routes do not pass traffic.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What is the one exception between IPv4 and IPv6 default ADs?
answer: The AD for unknown or unbelievable routes is 254 in IPv6 instead of 255 in IPv4. All other default ADs are the same.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What is the quad-zero route?
answer: The combination of the 0.0.0.0 network address and the 0.0.0.0 mask used in a default static route statement.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What does the code S represent in the IP routing table?
answer: A static route. A static default route is described as S*; the asterisk indicates the last path option is used when forwarding the packet.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Router(config)# ip route 172.16.20.0 255.255.255.0 172.16.10.2
answer: Configures a static route to destination network 172.16.20.0/24 via next-hop address 172.16.10.2.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Router(config)# ip route 172.16.20.0 255.255.255.0 serial 0/0/0
answer: Configures a static route to destination network 172.16.20.0/24 out the exit interface serial 0/0/0.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Router(config)# ip route 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0 fastethernet 0/0 192.138.20.2
answer: Configures a static route on a broadcast link using both the exit interface (FastEthernet 0/0) and the intermediate address (192.138.20.2) to avoid a recursive lookup.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Router(config)# ip route 172.16.20.0 255.255.255.0 172.16.10.2 permanent
answer: Adds the permanent keyword so the static route stays in the routing table even if the interface goes down.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Router(config)# ip route 172.16.20.0 255.255.255.0 172.16.10.2 200
answer: Assigns an administrative distance of 200 to the static route, creating a floating static route used as a backup.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Router(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 172.16.10.2
answer: Configures a default route: send all packets destined for networks not in the routing table to 172.16.10.2.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Router(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 serial 0/0/0
answer: Configures a default route: send all packets destined for networks not in the routing table out serial 0/0/0.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Austin(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:c18:3::/64 gigabitethernet 0/0
answer: Creates a directly attached IPv6 static route that sends packets out interface gigabitethernet 0/0.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Austin(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:c18:3::/64 gigabitethernet 0/0 2001:db8:c18:2::2
answer: Creates a fully specified IPv6 static route on a broadcast interface. On a broadcast medium such as Ethernet, this is the preferred method for creating static routes.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Austin(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:c18:3::/64 gigabitethernet 0/0 200
answer: Creates an IPv6 static route with an administrative distance of 200 instead of the default AD of 1 (floating static route).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Austin(config)# ipv6 route ::/0 2001:db8:c18:2::2
answer: Creates an IPv6 default route that sends all packets to the next-hop address 2001:db8:c18:2::2.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Austin(config)# ipv6 route ::/0 serial 0/0/0
answer: Creates an IPv6 default route that sends packets out interface serial 0/0/0.
