source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Which statement correctly describes recursive lookups for static routes?

choices.label: A static route using only a next-hop address causes the router to look at the routing table twice
A static route using an exit interface causes the router to look at the routing table twice
Recursive lookups only happen on broadcast links
The permanent keyword causes recursive lookups

explanation: A next-hop (intermediate) address requires the router to resolve the intermediate address, so it looks at the routing table twice.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Which method is preferred for static routes on a point-to-point link?

choices.label: Use the exit interface
Use only the next-hop address
Use the permanent keyword
Use both exit interface and next-hop address

explanation: For point-to-point links, always use an exit interface in static route statements.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Which statement about the permanent keyword is correct?

choices.label: The static route remains in the routing table even if the interface goes down
It removes the route when the interface goes down
It forces the router to do a recursive lookup
It sets the route to a lower administrative distance

explanation: The permanent keyword keeps static routes in the routing table even if the interface goes down, saving reprocessing time when the interface returns.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What is the default administrative distance of a static route?
explanation: By default a static route is assigned an AD of 1; an AD of 0 is assigned to a directly connected route.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Which AD value is assigned to a directly connected route?
explanation: A directly connected route has an AD of 0, meaning it is absolutely trusted.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What is the administrative distance of OSPF?
explanation: OSPF has an AD of 110 (both IPv4 and IPv6).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Which statement about floating static routes is correct?

choices.label: They have an AD higher than the routing protocol and act as a backup route
They always have an AD of 1
They are used instead of the routing protocol when both are up
They are only supported in IPv6

explanation: A floating static route is assigned an AD greater than the routing protocol so it is used as a backup when the routing protocol goes down.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What does S* represent in the routing table?

choices.label: A static default route; the asterisk indicates the last path option is used
A connected route
An OSPF route
A floating static route

explanation: A default route learned by a static route is described as S*; the asterisk indicates the last path option is used when forwarding the packet.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What is the quad-zero route?

choices.label: The 0.0.0.0 network address with the 0.0.0.0 mask
A route with AD 0
A route to 0.0.0.0/32
A fully specified route

explanation: The combination of the 0.0.0.0 network address and the 0.0.0.0 mask is called a quad-zero route (default route).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Which IPv6 static route method is preferred on a broadcast medium such as Ethernet?

choices.label: A fully specified static route (exit interface and next-hop)
A route using only the next-hop address
A route using only the exit interface
A route using the permanent keyword

explanation: On a broadcast medium such as Ethernet, a fully specified static route (gigabitethernet 0/0 plus next-hop) is the preferred method.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
symptoms: A static route configured with only a next-hop address requires extra lookups when forwarding packets.
root_cause: A static route using a next-hop (intermediate) address causes a recursive lookup: the router must look at the routing table twice, once for the destination and once to resolve the intermediate address.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Identify whether the link is point-to-point or broadcast.
2. On point-to-point links, use the exit interface instead.
3. On broadcast links, use both the exit interface and the intermediate address.
resolution: ip route <dest> <mask> serial 0/0/0 for point-to-point, or ip route <dest> <mask> fastethernet 0/0 <next-hop> for broadcast links.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
symptoms: After a serial interface goes down and comes back up, static routes are missing from the routing table for a while.
root_cause: Without the permanent keyword, a downed interface removes the directly connected network and associated static routes; they must be reprocessed and placed back into the table when the interface returns.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify the interface status with show ip interface brief.
2. Check the routing table with show ip route.
3. Add the permanent keyword to the static route statements to keep them installed.
resolution: Router(config)# ip route 172.16.20.0 255.255.255.0 172.16.10.2 permanent.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
symptoms: A static backup route is always preferred over the routing protocol, so failover never happens.
root_cause: The static route has a lower (better) AD than the routing protocol, so it is always used instead of acting as a floating backup.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Check the AD values of the static route and the routing protocol.
2. Verify the routing protocol AD (e.g., EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, RIP 120).
3. Reassign the static route an AD greater than the routing protocol's AD.
resolution: Router(config)# ip route 172.16.20.0 255.255.255.0 172.16.10.2 200 (a value higher than the routing protocol AD).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What is the correct order to configure a static route on a point-to-point link?
correct_sequence: 1. Identify the destination network and subnet mask
2. Choose the exit interface for the point-to-point link
3. Enter Router(config)# ip route 172.16.20.0 255.255.255.0 serial 0/0/0
4. Verify with show ip route or show ip static route
distractor_sequences: 1. Enter ip route with next-hop 2. Verify with show ip route
1. Enter ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 serial 0/0/0 2. Verify with show ipv6 route
1. Enter ip route <dest> <mask> <next-hop> permanent 2. Reload the router
explanation: For point-to-point links always use an exit interface. Configure the static route in global configuration mode, then verify it in the routing table.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What is the correct order to configure a floating static route as a backup to EIGRP?
correct_sequence: 1. Note the AD of the routing protocol (EIGRP internal = 90)
2. Choose an AD greater than 90 for the static route
4. Verify the route appears with show ip route
distractor_sequences: 2. Verify with show ip route
2. Verify with show ipv6 route
explanation: A floating static route must have an AD greater than the routing protocol so it is only used when the routing protocol fails.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: How do you create a static route in IPv6 compared to IPv4?
answer: You use the same format as creating a static route in IPv4, but with the ipv6 route command and IPv6 destination and next-hop addresses.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: How do you create a default route in IPv6 compared to IPv4?
answer: You use the same format as creating a default route in IPv4, but with ipv6 route ::/0 followed by the next-hop address or exit interface.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What does ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 172.16.10.2 mean?
answer: Send all packets destined for networks not in my routing table to 172.16.10.2.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What does ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 serial 0/0/0 mean?
answer: Send all packets destined for networks not in my routing table out my serial 0/0/0 interface.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What does ip classless control?
answer: It enables the router to forward packets to unknown subnets within a known major network toward the best matching route, including the default route. When enabled (the default in modern IOS), a router can use a default route to forward packets to subnets it does not have specific routes for.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What is a fully specified static route?
answer: A static route that includes both the exit interface and the next-hop address, which is the preferred method on broadcast media such as Ethernet.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Router# show ip route ospf
answer: Displays only the OSPF routes in the routing table (useful to compare against static routes).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Which routing protocol has an AD of 120?

choices.label: RIP
OSPF
EIGRP
IS-IS

explanation: RIP has an AD of 120; OSPF is 110, EIGRP internal is 90, and IS-IS is 115.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Which statement about the AD scale is correct?

choices.label: 0 is absolutely trusted and 255 cannot be trusted at all
255 is absolutely trusted and 0 cannot be trusted at all
The scale runs from 1 to 100
Higher AD values mean more trusted routes

explanation: AD is a number from 0 to 255 (254 for IPv6), where 0 is absolutely trusted and 255 (254 for IPv6) cannot be trusted at all.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What is the AD of EIGRP internal routes?
explanation: EIGRP internal routes have an AD of 90; EIGRP external routes have an AD of 170.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: Which command creates a default route sending all unknown traffic to next-hop 172.16.10.2?

choices.label: ip default-network 172.16.10.2

explanation: The quad-zero route ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 <next-hop> sends all packets destined for networks not in the routing table to the next hop.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
symptoms: An IPv6 static route on a broadcast interface works intermittently or packets are not forwarded.
root_cause: The route was created using only an exit interface or only a next-hop on a broadcast medium; on a broadcast medium the preferred method is a fully specified static route with both the exit interface and the next-hop address.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Check the current IPv6 static routes with show ipv6 static.
2. Verify the routing table with show ipv6 route.
3. Recreate the route as a fully specified static route including both the exit interface and the next-hop.
resolution: Austin(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:c18:3::/64 gigabitethernet 0/0 2001:db8:c18:2::2.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What is the correct order to configure a default route on a stub router?
correct_sequence: 1. Confirm the outgoing interface or next-hop for all unknown traffic
2. Enter Router(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 serial 0/0/1
3. Verify the S* default route appears with show ip route
distractor_sequences: 1. Enter ip route 172.16.30.0 255.255.255.0 serial 0/0/1 2. Verify with show ipv6 route
1. Enter ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 permanent 2. Reload the router
1. Enter ipv6 route ::/0 serial 0/0/1 2. Verify with show ip route
explanation: A default route uses the quad-zero network and mask (0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0). On a point-to-point link, use the exit interface. The route shows as S* in the routing table.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch15: Static Routing
question: What is the AD of a static route in IPv6?
answer: 1, the same as IPv4. The only difference between IPv4 and IPv6 default ADs is that unknown/unbelievable is 254 in IPv6 instead of 255.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What is OSPFv2?
answer: The current version of OSPF, developed in the late 1980s, used with the IPv4 protocol stack. In most Cisco documentation, OSPF refers to OSPFv2.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What is OSPFv3?
answer: A new version of OSPF created for IPv6 and other newer technologies. The earliest release of OSPFv3 worked with IPv6 exclusively.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: If you needed to run OSPF for both IPv4 and IPv6 with the earliest OSPFv3 release, what was required?
answer: OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 running concurrently. Newer OSPFv3 updates allow it to handle both IPv4 and IPv6, but that is part of CCNP, not CCNA.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Is multiarea OSPF part of the CCNA 200-301 blueprint?
answer: No. Configuring multiarea OSPF is part of the Implementing Cisco Enterprise Network Core Technologies exam (300-401) and troubleshooting OSPF is part of the 300-410 CCNP concentration exam.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What is the OSPF process ID?
answer: Any positive integer value between 1 and 65,535. It distinguishes one process from another within the device and is not related to the OSPF area.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Does the OSPF process ID need to match between routers for adjacencies to form?
answer: No. The process ID number of one router does not have to match any other router. Unlike EIGRP, matching the number does not ensure that network adjacencies will form.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What does the network command do in OSPF?
answer: OSPF advertises interfaces, not networks. It uses the wildcard mask to determine which interfaces to advertise. The network statement places matching interfaces into an OSPF area.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What does a 0 (zero) in a wildcard mask mean?
answer: Check the corresponding bit in the address for an exact match.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What does a 1 (one) in a wildcard mask mean?
answer: Ignore the corresponding bit in the address — it can be either 1 or 0.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What interfaces does the statement network 172.16.0.0 0.0.255.255 area 0 match?
answer: Any interface with an address of 172.16.x.x (anything between 172.16.0.0 and 172.16.255.255).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What interfaces does the statement network 172.16.8.0 0.0.7.255 area 0 match?
answer: Any interface with an address between 172.16.8.0 and 172.16.15.255 (the third octet ranges from 8 to 15).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What interfaces does the statement network 172.16.10.1 0.0.0.0 area 0 match?
answer: Any interface with an exact address of 172.16.10.1 — the most precise way to place an exact address into the OSPF routing process.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What interfaces does the statement network 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255 area 0 match?
answer: Any interface with any address — every interface runs OSPF and is placed into area 0.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What is a loopback interface and why is it useful for OSPF?
answer: A virtual interface that is always up and up and does not go down unless manually shut down. This makes loopback interfaces great for use as an OSPF router ID.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: In what order does OSPF choose the router ID?
answer: 1. Use the router ID specified in the router-id command. 2. Use the highest IP address of all active loopback interfaces. 3. Use the highest IP address among all active nonloopback interfaces.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: How do you make a manually configured router ID take effect?
answer: You must clear the OSPF routing process with the clear ip ospf process command. On an active process, the new router ID is used at the next reload or manual OSPF process restart.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Is there an IPv6 form of the router ID?
answer: No. All router IDs are 32-bit numbers in the form of an IPv4 address, even if a router is running IPv6 exclusively.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What is the default OSPF interface priority and its range?
answer: The default priority setting is 1. The assigned priority can be between 0 and 255.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What does an OSPF interface priority of 0 mean?
answer: The router is ineligible to become a designated router (DR) or backup designated router (BDR).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: How is the DR/BDR election decided?
answer: The highest priority wins the election and becomes the DR; the second highest priority becomes the BDR. Ties are broken by the highest router ID. A priority of 255 guarantees at least a tie in the election.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What are the default OSPF hello and dead intervals on multiaccess and point-to-point segments?
answer: Hello is 10 seconds and dead is 40 seconds.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What are the default OSPF hello and dead intervals on NBMA segments such as Frame Relay, X.25, and ATM?
answer: Hello is 30 seconds and dead is 120 seconds.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: If you change the hello interval timer, what happens to the dead interval timer?
answer: It is automatically adjusted to four times the new hello interval timer.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What must match between two routers for them to become OSPF neighbors?
answer: The hello and dead interval timers must match.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What does the log-adjacency-changes command do?
answer: Configures the router to send a syslog message when there is a change of state between OSPF neighbors. It is on by default, but only up/down events are reported unless the detail keyword is used.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Does running two different OSPF processes create multiarea OSPF?
answer: No. Running two different OSPF processes merely creates two separate instances of OSPF that do not communicate with each other.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Which command takes precedence: ip ospf process-id area area-number on an interface or the network area command?
answer: The ip ospf process ID area area-number command configured directly on the interface takes precedence over the network area command entered in router configuration mode.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What happens if you assign interfaces to OSPF areas without first using the router ospf command?
answer: The router creates the OSPF process for you, and it shows up in a show running-config output.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router(config)# router ospf 123
answer: Starts OSPF process 123. The process ID is any positive integer between 1 and 65,535 and is not related to the OSPF area.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router(config-router)# network 172.16.10.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
answer: Read: Any interface with an address of 172.16.10.x is to run OSPF and be put into area 0.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router(config-router)# log-adjacency-changes detail
answer: Configures the router to send a syslog message when there is a change of state between OSPF neighbors, with the detail keyword reporting more than just up/down events.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router(config-if)# ip ospf 1 area 51
answer: Places this interface into area 51 of OSPF process 1. Configured directly on the interface, it takes precedence over the network area command.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router(config-if)# ip ospf 1 area 0
answer: Places this interface into area 0 of OSPF process 1.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router(config)# interface loopback0
answer: Creates a virtual interface named Loopback 0 and moves the router to interface configuration mode.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router(config-if)# ip address 192.168.100.1 255.255.255.255
answer: Assigns the IP address to the loopback interface.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router(config-router)# router-id 10.1.1.1
answer: Sets the router ID to 10.1.1.1. If used on an already active OSPF process, the new router ID is used at the next reload or at a manual OSPF process restart.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router(config-router)# no router-id 10.1.1.1
answer: Removes the static router ID from the configuration. On an active process, the old router ID behavior is used at the next reload or manual restart.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router(config-if)# ip ospf priority 50
answer: Changes the OSPF interface priority to 50 (range 0 to 255, default 1).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router(config-if)# ip ospf hello-interval 20
answer: Changes the hello interval timer to 20 seconds. The dead interval is automatically adjusted to four times the hello interval.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router(config-if)# ip ospf dead-interval 80
answer: Changes the dead interval timer to 80 seconds. Hello and dead intervals must match between neighbors.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router# show ip protocol
answer: Displays parameters for all routing protocols running on the router.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router# show ip ospf
answer: Displays basic information about OSPF routing processes.

answer: Displays border and boundary router information.

question: Router# show ip ospf database
answer: Displays the contents of the OSPF database.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router# show ip ospf database summary
answer: Displays a summary of the OSPF database.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router# show ip ospf interface
answer: Displays OSPF information as it relates to all interfaces.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router# show ip ospf interface fastethernet0/0
answer: Displays OSPF information for the specific interface fastethernet0/0.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router# show ip ospf neighbor
answer: Lists all OSPF neighbors and their states.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router# show ip ospf neighbor detail
answer: Displays a detailed list of OSPF neighbors.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router# clear ip route *
answer: Clears the entire routing table, forcing it to rebuild.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router# clear ip route a.b.c.d
answer: Clears a specific route to network a.b.c.d.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router# clear ip ospf counters
answer: Resets OSPF counters.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router# clear ip ospf process
answer: Resets the entire OSPF process, forcing OSPF to re-create neighbors, the database, and the routing table.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router# clear ip ospf 3 process
answer: Resets OSPF process 3, forcing OSPF to re-create neighbors, the database, and the routing table.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router# debug ip ospf events
answer: Displays all OSPF events.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router# debug ip ospf adj
answer: Displays various OSPF states and DR/BDR election between adjacent routers.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router# debug ip ospf packets
answer: Displays OSPF packets.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router# undebug all
answer: Turns off all debug commands.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Router(config-router)# passive-interface gigabitethernet 0/0
answer: Prevents OSPF from sending hello packets on the specified interface so no neighbors are formed there, while the subnet is still advertised in OSPF.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Which statement about the OSPF process ID is correct?

choices.label: It is not related to the OSPF area and does not have to match between routers
It must match on all routers for adjacencies to form
It is the same as the OSPF area number
It must be a number between 0 and 100

explanation: The process ID is any value between 1 and 65,535, distinguishes processes within a device, and does not need to match between routers.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Which statement about OSPF wildcard masks is correct?

choices.label: A 0 means check for an exact match; a 1 means ignore the bit
A 1 means check for an exact match; a 0 means ignore the bit
Wildcard masks are the same as subnet masks
Wildcard masks are not used in OSPF

explanation: A 0 in a wildcard mask checks the corresponding bit for an exact match; a 1 ignores the corresponding bit.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Which network statement places only the interface with the exact address 172.16.10.1 into area 0?
explanation: A wildcard mask of 0.0.0.0 requires an exact match on every bit, so only the address 172.16.10.1 is matched.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Which statement about the OSPF router ID selection order is correct?

choices.label: router-id command, then highest loopback IP, then highest nonloopback IP
highest nonloopback IP, then highest loopback IP, then router-id command
highest MAC address, then router-id command
router-id command, then highest nonloopback IP, then highest loopback IP

explanation: OSPF chooses the router ID in this order: the router-id command, then the highest active loopback IP, then the highest active nonloopback IP.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Which statement about the DR/BDR election is correct?

choices.label: Highest priority becomes DR, second highest becomes BDR, ties broken by highest router ID
Lowest priority becomes DR
The router with the lowest router ID becomes DR
Priority 0 guarantees a router becomes DR

explanation: The highest priority wins the election and becomes DR; the second highest becomes BDR; ties are broken by the highest router ID. Priority 0 makes a router ineligible.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Which statement about OSPF timers is correct?

choices.label: Hello and dead interval timers must match between routers to become neighbors
Only the hello timer must match
Timers never need to match
Only the dead timer must match

explanation: Hello and dead interval timers must match between two routers for those routers to become neighbors.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What is the default OSPF hello interval on a point-to-point segment?

choices.label: 10 seconds
30 seconds
40 seconds
20 seconds

explanation: The default hello timer is 10 seconds on multiaccess and point-to-point segments and 30 seconds on NBMA segments.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What is the default OSPF hello interval on an NBMA segment such as Frame Relay?

choices.label: 30 seconds
10 seconds
40 seconds
120 seconds

explanation: The default hello timer is 30 seconds on NBMA segments such as Frame Relay, X.25, and ATM.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: If you change the OSPF hello interval to 20 seconds, what happens to the dead interval?

choices.label: It is automatically adjusted to 80 seconds
It stays at 40 seconds
It is automatically adjusted to 20 seconds
It must be changed manually to 120 seconds

explanation: If you change the hello interval timer, the dead interval is automatically adjusted to four times the new hello interval (20 x 4 = 80).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What happens if you run two different OSPF processes on the same router?

choices.label: It creates two separate OSPF instances that do not communicate with each other
It automatically creates multiarea OSPF
It doubles the router ID
It is not allowed in Cisco IOS

explanation: Running two different OSPF processes does not create multiarea OSPF; it merely creates two separate instances that do not communicate.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
symptoms: show ip ospf neighbor shows no neighbors, so OSPF adjacencies do not form.
root_cause: Possible causes include mismatched hello/dead timers, interfaces not being advertised (missing or wrong network statement/wildcard mask), or a passive-interface on the link.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify which interfaces are running OSPF with show ip ospf interface.
2. Check that hello and dead timers match on both routers (defaults 10/40; NBMA 30/120).
3. Verify the network statements with show running-config.
4. Check for passive-interface on the link.
5. Use debug ip ospf adj to watch the adjacency process.
resolution: Match timers and correct network statements; remove passive-interface where neighbors are expected.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
symptoms: OSPF neighbors form, but the routing table has no OSPF routes.
root_cause: There are no OSPF routes to install, the OSPF database is empty, or the network statements do not match the interfaces.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Check the routing table with show ip route.
2. Check OSPF routes with show ip route ospf.
3. Verify the OSPF database with show ip ospf database.
4. Confirm network statements are correct in show running-config.
resolution: Correct the network statements and verify with show ip route ospf.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
symptoms: After configuring a new router-id, the router still uses the old router ID.
root_cause: On an already active OSPF process, a manually configured router ID is only used at the next reload or at a manual OSPF process restart.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify the current router ID with show ip ospf.
2. Clear the OSPF process with clear ip ospf process.
3. Re-verify the router ID with show ip ospf.
resolution: Router# clear ip ospf process (or reload the router).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
symptoms: Two routers connected over an NBMA segment such as Frame Relay do not form an adjacency, while the same routers do over a point-to-point link.
root_cause: OSPF default hello/dead timers differ between segment types: 10/40 seconds on multiaccess and point-to-point segments vs 30/120 seconds on NBMA segments.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify the timers on both interfaces with show ip ospf interface.
2. Confirm the segment type (NBMA vs point-to-point).
3. Adjust the timers so they match on both sides.
resolution: Match the hello and dead intervals (e.g., ip ospf hello-interval and ip ospf dead-interval) on both routers.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What is the correct order to configure single-area OSPF on a router?
correct_sequence: 1. Configure interfaces with IP addresses and no shutdown
2. Enter OSPF configuration with Router(config)# router ospf 1
3. Advertise networks with Router(config-router)# network <network> <wildcard> area 0
4. Optionally set the router ID with Router(config-router)# router-id 10.1.1.1
5. Verify with show ip ospf neighbor and show ip route
distractor_sequences: 1. network 172.16.10.0 0.0.0.255 area 0 2. router ospf 1
1. no shutdown 2. router ospf 1 3. ip address 172.16.10.1 255.255.255.0
explanation: Interfaces must have addresses and be enabled before OSPF is started and networks are advertised. Verify adjacency with show ip ospf neighbor.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What is the correct order of OSPF router ID selection?
correct_sequence: 1. Use the router ID specified in the router-id command
2. Use the highest IP address of all active loopback interfaces
3. Use the highest IP address among all active nonloopback interfaces
distractor_sequences: 1. Highest nonloopback IP 2. Highest loopback IP 3. router-id command
1. Highest MAC address 2. router-id command 3. Highest loopback IP
1. Lowest loopback IP 2. router-id command
explanation: OSPF selects the router ID in this exact order: the router-id command, then the highest loopback IP, then the highest nonloopback IP.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What is the correct order of the DR/BDR election process?
correct_sequence: 1. All routers in a segment advertise their OSPF interface priority
2. The highest priority becomes the DR
3. The second highest priority becomes the BDR
4. If priorities tie, the highest router ID wins
distractor_sequences: 1. Lowest priority becomes DR 2. Highest becomes BDR
1. The highest router ID always becomes DR, ignoring priority
2. The lowest router ID becomes BDR
1. Priority 0 becomes the DR 2. The second lowest becomes the BDR
explanation: The highest priority wins the election and becomes DR; the second highest becomes BDR. Ties are broken by the highest router ID. Priority 0 makes a router ineligible.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: Why do loopback interfaces make good OSPF router IDs?
answer: Loopback interfaces are always up and up and do not go down unless manually shut down, providing a stable router ID.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What is the default OSPF dead interval on a multiaccess segment?
answer: 40 seconds (on multiaccess and point-to-point segments; 120 seconds on NBMA segments).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What is the default OSPF dead interval on an NBMA segment?
answer: 120 seconds (on NBMA segments such as Frame Relay, X.25, and ATM).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What is the range of the OSPF process ID?
answer: Any positive integer between 1 and 65,535.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What is the OSPF interface priority range and what does priority 255 guarantee?
answer: The range is 0 to 255. A priority of 255 guarantees at least a tie in the election, assuming another router is also set to 255. Ties are broken by the highest router ID.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch16: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
question: What does the passive-interface command do in OSPF?
answer: It stops OSPF from sending hello packets out the specified interface so no neighbors are formed on it, while the subnet is still advertised in the OSPF domain.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: ip dhcp pool INTERNAL
answer: Creates a DHCP pool named INTERNAL (the name can be anything of your choosing) and enters DHCP pool configuration mode (Router(dhcp-config)#).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: network 172.16.10.0 255.255.255.0
answer: Defines the range of addresses to be leased to DHCP clients (subnet address and netmask).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: default-router 172.16.10.1
answer: Defines the address of the default router for the client. One IP address is required, but you can specify up to eight addresses; they are listed in order of precedence.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: dns-server 172.16.10.10
answer: Defines the address of the DNS server for the client.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: netbios-name-server 172.16.10.10
answer: Defines the address of the NetBIOS name server for the client.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: domain-name fakedomainname.com
answer: Defines the domain name for the client.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: lease 14 12 23
answer: Defines the lease time to be 14 days, 12 hours, 23 minutes.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: lease infinite
answer: Sets the lease time to infinity. The default lease time is 1 day.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: ip dhcp excluded-address 172.16.10.1 172.16.10.10
answer: Specifies the range of addresses (172.16.10.1 to 172.16.10.10) that will not be leased out to clients.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: service dhcp
answer: Enables the DHCP service and relay features on a Cisco IOS router. The DHCP service is on by default.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: no service dhcp
answer: Turns the DHCP service off.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: option 66 ip 10.1.1.250
answer: DHCP option 66 gives the IP address of a single TFTP server to Cisco IP Phones.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: option 150 ip 10.1.1.250 10.1.1.251
answer: DHCP option 150 provides a list of TFTP server IP addresses (here two TFTP servers) to Cisco IP Phones.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: option 3 ip 10.1.1.1
answer: DHCP option 3 sets a default route for Cisco IP Phones.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: ip helper-address 172.16.20.2
answer: Forwards DHCP broadcast messages as unicast messages to this specific address instead of having them be dropped by the router.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: no ip forward-protocol udp 49
answer: Stops the forwarding of broadcast packets to UDP port 49 (the TACACS service).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: ip forward-protocol udp 517
answer: Opens an additional UDP port (517) for broadcast forwarding by the DHCP helper.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: Which UDP ports does ip helper-address forward broadcasts to by default?
answer: Eight ports: TFTP (69), DNS (53), Time service (37), NetBIOS name server (137), NetBIOS datagram server (138), BOOTP client and server (67 and 68), and TACACS (49).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: ip address dhcp
answer: Specifies that the interface acquires an IP address through DHCP (configures the interface as a DHCP client).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: What is the default DHCP lease time?
answer: 1 day (24 hours).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: What is the default state of the DHCP service on a Cisco IOS router?
answer: The DHCP service is on by default in Cisco IOS Software.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: When a Cisco IP Phone starts without preconfigured IP and TFTP addresses, which DHCP options does it request?
answer: Option 150 (a list of TFTP servers) or option 66 (a single TFTP server). Phones may also include option 3, which sets a default route.

answer: Displays a list of all bindings created.

answer: Displays a list of the number of messages sent and received by the DHCP server.

question: clear ip dhcp server statistics
answer: Resets all DHCP server counters to 0.

question: debug ip dhcp server {events | packet | linkage | class}
answer: Displays the DHCP process of addresses being leased and returned.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch17: DHCP
question: clear ip dhcp binding *
answer: Clears all automatic DHCP bindings.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: What is dynamic NAT?
answer: Dynamic NAT maps unregistered (private) IP addresses to registered (public) IP addresses from a pool of registered addresses, one private to one public translation.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: What is PAT (overloading)?
answer: PAT maps multiple unregistered (private) IP addresses to a single registered (public) IP address (many to one) using different port numbers. It is also known as overloading or overload translations.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: What is static NAT?
answer: Static NAT provides a one-to-one permanent mapping between local (private) and global (public) IP addresses.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: ip nat pool scott 64.64.64.65 64.64.64.126 netmask 255.255.255.192
answer: Defines the NAT pool named scott from start address 64.64.64.65 to end address 64.64.64.126 with netmask 255.255.255.192. The private address receives the first available public address in the pool.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: ip nat inside source list 1 pool scott
answer: Creates the dynamic NAT translation: the source of the private addresses is from ACL 1, and the pool of available public addresses is named scott.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: ip nat inside
answer: Defines the interface as the NAT inside interface (the interface containing the private addresses). You can have more than one inside interface on a router.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: ip nat outside
answer: Defines which interface is the outside interface for NAT (the interface leading to the public network).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: ip nat inside source list 1 interface serial 0/0/0 overload
answer: PAT: private addresses from ACL 1 are translated into the public address assigned to serial 0/0/0; the overload keyword states that port numbers are used to handle many translations.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: ip nat inside source list 1 pool scott overload
answer: PAT using the pool scott with the overload keyword so port numbers handle many translations.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: ip nat inside source static 172.16.10.5 64.64.64.65
answer: Permanently translates the inside private address 172.16.10.5 to the public address 64.64.64.65. Use one command per private address to map.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: show ip nat translations
answer: Displays the NAT translation table.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: show ip nat statistics
answer: Displays NAT statistics.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: clear ip nat translation *
answer: Clears the entire translation table before entries time out.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: debug ip nat
answer: Displays information about every packet that is translated. Be careful: the router CPU may not be able to handle the output and the system could hang.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: debug ip nat detailed
answer: Displays greater detail about packets being translated.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: What is the default timeout for a NAT translation entry?
answer: 24 hours.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: What is the theoretical maximum number of translations between internal addresses and a single outside address using PAT?
answer: 65,536, because port numbers are encoded in a 16-bit field (2 to the 16th power = 65,536).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: show access-list
answer: Displays access lists (used to verify which private addresses match the NAT ACL).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: clear ip nat translation inside 1.1.1.1 2.2.2.2 outside 3.3.3.3 4.4.4.4
answer: Clears a specific translation from the table before it times out. Inside: 1.1.1.1=global, 2.2.2.2=local; outside: 3.3.3.3=local, 4.4.4.4=global.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: What routing requirement exists on the ISP router for NAT to work?
answer: The ISP router needs a static route defining a path to the NAT public addresses/networks so packets can travel back to the internal network; advertise the public addresses, not the private ones.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: In dynamic NAT, which public address does a private address receive?
answer: The first available public address in the pool.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Which interfaces are NAT inside interfaces?
answer: The interfaces that contain the private (inside) addresses. More than one inside interface is allowed on a router.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: How many private addresses can a single public IP address handle with PAT?
answer: Thousands of private addresses can be connected using only one real registered public IP address.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: What does a pool of six addresses (64.64.64.70-64.64.64.75) provide for PAT?
answer: A pool of six addresses (and all their ports) available for translation.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: ISP(config)# ip route 64.64.64.64 255.255.255.192 s0/0/0
answer: Informs the ISP router where to send packets with addresses destined for 64.64.64.64 255.255.255.192 (the public NAT range).

question: Company(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.133.219.2

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Which statement correctly describes: dynamic NAT

choices.label: It maps unregistered private addresses to registered public addresses from a pool, one private to one public
It maps many private addresses to one public address using different ports
It provides a one-to-one permanent mapping that never changes
It blocks all traffic from private addresses

explanation: Dynamic NAT maps unregistered (private) IP addresses to registered (public) addresses from a pool; a private address receives the first available public address in the pool.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Which statement correctly describes: PAT (overload)

choices.label: It maps multiple private addresses to a single public address using different port numbers
It maps one private address to one public address from a pool
It provides a permanent one-to-one translation
It does not use the overload keyword

explanation: PAT maps multiple private addresses to a single registered public address using different ports; this is also known as overloading or overload translations.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Which statement correctly describes: static NAT

choices.label: It allows one-to-one mapping between local private and global public addresses permanently
It maps many private addresses to one public address using ports
It assigns the first available public address from a pool
It requires the overload keyword

explanation: Static NAT allows one-to-one mapping between local (private) and global (public) IP addresses, configured with ip nat inside source static.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Which range is an RFC 1918 private Class B range?
explanation: RFC 1918 defines 10.0.0.0/8 (Class A), 172.16.0.0/12 (Class B), and 192.168.0.0/16 (Class C) as private ranges.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Which command configures PAT using the exit interface address?

choices.label: ip nat inside source list 1 interface serial 0/0/0 overload
ip nat inside source list 1 pool scott
ip nat inside source static 172.16.10.5 64.64.64.65

explanation: PAT using the exit interface translates all private addresses into the IP address of the interface (for example the serial link to the ISP) with the overload keyword.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Which statement correctly describes: NAT inside and outside interfaces

choices.label: Inside interfaces contain the private addresses; the outside interface leads to the public network
Inside interfaces lead to the public network; outside interfaces contain private addresses
Both interfaces must contain private addresses
Only one inside interface is ever allowed on a router

explanation: ip nat inside marks interfaces containing private addresses (more than one allowed); ip nat outside marks the interface leading to the public network.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: What is the default timeout for a NAT translation entry?

choices.label: 24 hours
1 hour
10 minutes
7 days

explanation: The default timeout for a translation entry in a NAT table is 24 hours.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: What is the theoretical maximum number of PAT translations to a single outside address?

choices.label: Unlimited

explanation: Port numbers are encoded in a 16-bit field, so 2 to the 16th power equals 65,536 theoretical maximum translations.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Which statement correctly describes: ip nat pool scott

choices.label: It defines the pool name, start address, end address, and subnet mask
It defines the access list for translation
It marks the inside interface
It creates a static mapping

explanation: ip nat pool defines the pool name, the start and end addresses, and the netmask; a private address gets the first available public address in the pool.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Which statement correctly describes: the ISP routing requirement for NAT

choices.label: The ISP router needs a static route to the public NAT addresses so return packets can reach the internal network
The ISP router needs no route for NAT to work
The ISP router must be configured with ip nat inside
The ISP router must run PAT

explanation: Without a static route on the ISP router to the public NAT addresses, packets can leave with a public address but cannot return.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Which statement correctly describes: clear ip nat translation *

choices.label: It clears the entire translation table before entries time out
It clears a single translation from the table
It clears ACL match counters only
It resets NAT statistics to zero

explanation: clear ip nat translation * clears the entire translation table before entries time out; a specific translation is cleared with the inside/outside address pair form.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Which statement correctly describes: debug ip nat

choices.label: It displays info about every translated packet and may hang the router CPU
It displays only the NAT configuration
It clears all NAT translations
It is always safe to run on production routers

explanation: debug ip nat displays information about every packet translated; the router's CPU might not handle the output and could hang the system.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Which ACL statement correctly identifies the private network 172.16.10.0/24 for NAT?

choices.label: access-list 1 permit 172.16.10.0 0.0.0.255
access-list 1 permit 172.16.0.0 0.0.255.255

explanation: NAT ACLs use wildcard masks, so the network 172.16.10.0 with wildcard 0.0.0.255 identifies the /24 subnet; the addresses must be permitted.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Which command translates all private addresses into the single IP address of the exit interface?

choices.label: ip nat inside source list 1 interface serial 0/0/0 overload
ip nat inside source list 1 pool scott
ip nat inside source static 172.16.10.10 64.64.64.67
ip nat outside source list 1 pool scott

explanation: Linking the ACL to the outside interface with the overload keyword translates all permitted private addresses into the exit interface's public address.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: In dynamic NAT, how does a private address receive a public address?

choices.label: It receives the first available public address in the pool
It receives a randomly assigned public address
It always receives the outside interface address
It receives a permanent fixed public address

explanation: In dynamic NAT the private address receives the first available public address in the pool, unlike static NAT which is permanent.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
symptoms: show ip nat translations is empty and inside hosts cannot reach the Internet
root_cause: The ACL used in the NAT command does not permit the private network, or the inside/outside interfaces are not marked, so no translation is created.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify the ACL matches: show access-list (check the increment counter)
2. Confirm ip nat inside and ip nat outside are on the correct interfaces
3. Confirm the pool is defined: show ip nat statistics
4. Verify the translation statement: show running-config | section ip nat
resolution: Company(config)# ip nat inside / Company(config-if)# ip nat inside / ip nat outside

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
symptoms: Hosts can send traffic out to the Internet but replies never return
root_cause: The ISP router does not know where the public NAT addresses exist; there is no static route on the ISP router pointing back to the NAT range.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Ping the public NAT address from the ISP router and verify the routing table
2. Confirm the ISP router has a static route to the NAT public range
3. Add the missing static route

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
symptoms: show ip nat statistics shows no hits and the NAT counters never increment
root_cause: Traffic is not matching the NAT ACL or the inside/outside interface designations are wrong, so packets are not considered for translation.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Run show ip nat statistics and note hits
2. Run show access-list to see whether the ACL is being matched
3. Verify ip nat inside on LAN interfaces and ip nat outside on the WAN interface
4. Use debug ip nat to watch translated packets
resolution: Router# debug ip nat

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
symptoms: Internal users exhaust available translations and new sessions fail to be established
root_cause: Dynamic NAT was configured without overload, so the pool of public addresses runs out instead of sharing addresses by port.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Check show ip nat statistics for pool exhaustion
2. Review the translation statement for the overload keyword
3. Add overload or a larger pool
resolution: Company(config)# ip nat inside source list 1 interface serial 0/0/0 overload

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
symptoms: A statically mapped server does not appear in show ip nat translations
root_cause: The static mapping was not configured, or the inside and outside addresses were entered in the wrong order in ip nat inside source static.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify with show ip nat translations
2. Check running-config for the ip nat inside source static line
3. Re-enter the mapping with the private address first and public address second
resolution: Company(config)# ip nat inside source static 172.16.10.5 64.64.64.65

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
symptoms: The translation table is full of stale entries and new connections are slow
root_cause: Translations only time out after the default 24 hours, so stale entries remain in the table.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. View the table: show ip nat translations
2. Clear stale entries manually
resolution: Router# clear ip nat translation *

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
symptoms: debug ip nat floods the console and the router slows down or appears to hang
root_cause: debug ip nat produces output for every packet translated; under load the CPU cannot keep up.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Stop the debug immediately
2. Use targeted debugging or debug with an ACL to limit output
resolution: Router# no debug ip nat

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
symptoms: show ip nat statistics shows hits but some hosts are never translated
root_cause: The ACL wildcard mask is too restrictive and excludes those hosts from matching.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Run show access-list to see which addresses match
2. Review the wildcard mask
3. Adjust the ACL to cover the private network
resolution: Company(config)# access-list 1 permit 172.16.10.0 0.0.0.255

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
symptoms: clear ip nat translation with inside/outside addresses does not clear the entry
root_cause: The address pair order is wrong; the correct order is inside global, inside local, then outside local, outside global.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify the exact entry in show ip nat translations
2. Match the inside global/local and outside local/global pairs exactly
resolution: Router# clear ip nat translation inside 1.1.1.1 2.2.2.2 outside 3.3.3.3 4.4.4.4

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
symptoms: PAT was configured on a pool but hosts use one public address each and run out
root_cause: The overload keyword was omitted, so the statement behaves as one-to-one dynamic NAT instead of PAT.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Review the translation statement in running-config
2. Add the overload keyword
resolution: Company(config)# ip nat inside source list 1 pool scott overload

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
symptoms: After a reboot all NAT configuration is gone
root_cause: The running configuration was never saved to NVRAM with copy running-config startup-config.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify the NAT statements are absent after reload
2. Recreate or save the configuration
resolution: Company# copy running-config startup-config

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
symptoms: Inside host 172.16.10.10 times out to the Internet while other hosts work
root_cause: A static NAT mapping for that host conflicts with the dynamic pool assignment, so its translations are inconsistent.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Check show ip nat translations for the host
2. Remove the conflicting static mapping
resolution: Company(config)# no ip nat inside source static 172.16.10.10 64.64.64.67

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: What is the correct order to configure dynamic NAT (one private to one public)?
correct_sequence: 1. Add a static route on the ISP router to the public NAT range: ip route 64.64.64.64 255.255.255.192 s0/0/0
2. Define the public address pool: ip nat pool scott 64.64.64.65 64.64.64.126 netmask 255.255.255.192
3. Create an ACL identifying the private addresses: access-list 1 permit 172.16.10.0 0.0.0.255
4. Link the ACL to the pool: ip nat inside source list 1 pool scott
5. Mark the inside interface: interface gigabitethernet 0/0; ip nat inside
6. Mark the outside interface: interface serial 0/0/0; ip nat outside
distractor_sequences: Mark the interfaces before defining the pool and ACL
Create the ACL after linking it to the pool
Define the pool after the translation statement
explanation: Define the ISP return route, the pool, the ACL, the translation statement, then mark inside and outside interfaces.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: What is the correct order to configure PAT using the exit interface?
correct_sequence: 1. Create an ACL for the private network: access-list 1 permit 172.16.10.0 0.0.0.255
2. Link the ACL to the interface with overload: ip nat inside source list 1 interface serial 0/0/0 overload
3. Mark the inside interface: ip nat inside
4. Mark the outside interface: ip nat outside
distractor_sequences: Mark the outside interface before creating the ACL
Use ip nat inside source static instead of the list command
Define a pool of addresses before the ACL
explanation: The ACL is defined first, then linked to the outside interface with overload, then the inside and outside interfaces are marked.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: What is the correct order to configure PAT using a pool of addresses?
correct_sequence: 1. Define the pool (optional): ip nat pool scott 64.64.64.65 64.64.64.70 netmask 255.255.255.192
2. Create the ACL: access-list 1 permit 172.16.10.0 0.0.0.255
3. Link the ACL to the pool with overload: ip nat inside source list 1 pool scott overload
4. Mark the inside and outside interfaces
distractor_sequences: Link the ACL to the pool before defining the pool
Use a static mapping instead of the pool
Mark the inside interface before defining the pool
explanation: The optional pool is defined first, the ACL next, then the translation statement with overload, then the interfaces.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: What is the correct order to verify a NAT configuration?
correct_sequence: 1. show ip nat translations
2. show ip nat statistics
3. show access-list
4. (optional) clear ip nat translation *
distractor_sequences: Clear the table before viewing statistics
Run debug ip nat before viewing the table
Check the ACL before checking the translation table
explanation: Verify the active translations, the statistics, and the ACL matches before clearing any state.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Router# show access-list
answer: Displays access lists (with NAT match counters).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Router# show ip nat translations
answer: Displays the NAT translation table.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Router# show ip nat statistics
answer: Displays NAT statistics.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Router# clear ip nat translation inside 1.1.1.1 2.2.2.2 outside 3.3.3.3 4.4.4.4
answer: Clears a specific translation from the table before it times out. Inside: 1.1.1.1=global, 2.2.2.2=local; outside: 3.3.3.3=local, 4.4.4.4=global.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Router# clear ip nat translation *
answer: Clears the entire translation table before entries time out.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Router# debug ip nat
answer: Displays information about every packet that is translated; heavy output may hang the CPU.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Router# debug ip nat detailed
answer: Displays greater detail about packets being translated.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Company(config)# ip nat inside source list 1 interface serial 0/0/0 overload
answer: PAT: private addresses from ACL 1 translate into the serial 0/0/0 interface address using port overloading.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Company(config)# ip nat inside source list 1 pool scott overload
answer: PAT using pool scott with port overloading.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Company(config)# ip nat inside source static 172.16.10.5 64.64.64.65
answer: Permanently translates inside 172.16.10.5 to public 64.64.64.65.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: ISP(config)# ip route 64.64.64.64 255.255.255.192 s0/0/0
answer: Informs the ISP router where to send packets destined for the NAT public range so replies can return.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Company(config)# access-list 1 permit 172.16.10.0 0.0.0.255
answer: Defines which addresses are permitted to be translated with NAT.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Company(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.133.219.2
answer: Sends all packets not defined in the routing table to the ISP router.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Company(config)# no ip domain-lookup
answer: Turns off DNS resolution to avoid wait time caused by the DNS lookup of spelling errors.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: ISP(config-if)# clock rate 56000
answer: Assigns the clock rate to the DCE cable on this side of the link.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: ISP(config-if)# interface loopback 0
answer: Creates loopback interface 0 and moves to interface configuration mode.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch18: Network Address Translation (NAT)
question: Company(config)# ip nat pool scott 64.64.64.65 64.64.64.70 netmask 255.255.255.192
answer: Defines a pool of six public addresses available for translation.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: ntp server 209.165.200.254
answer: Configures the router to synchronize its clock to the NTP server at 209.165.200.254; this makes the router an NTP client to the external server.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: ntp server 209.165.200.234 prefer
answer: Specifies a preferred NTP server when multiple servers are configured. It is recommended to configure more than one NTP server.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: ntp disable
answer: Disables the NTP server function on a specific interface; the interface still acts as an NTP client. Use it on interfaces connected to external networks.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: ntp master [stratum]
answer: Configures the router to be an NTP master clock to which peers synchronize when no external NTP source is available. Stratum is optional, between 1 and 15; the default is 8.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: What is the default stratum when ntp master is enabled?

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: ntp max-associations 200
answer: Configures the maximum number of NTP peer-and-client associations the router will serve. Range is 0 to 4,294,967,295; default is 100.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: ntp peer 172.16.21.1
answer: Configures an IOS device to synchronize its software clock to a peer at 172.16.21.1 (used in a hierarchical NTP design).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: ntp peer 172.16.21.1 source loopback 0
answer: Synchronizes to the peer using the Loopback 0 interface address as the source IP. A loopback is chosen as the source because it will never go down and ACL statements are easier to write.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: ntp peer 172.16.21.1 source loopback 0 prefer
answer: Makes this peer the preferred peer that provides synchronization.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: ntp peer 172.16.21.1 version 2
answer: Configures the device to synchronize to the peer using NTP version 2. Cisco IOS recognizes three versions of NTP (versions 2 through 4).

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: ntp authentication-key 1 md5 NTPpa55word
answer: Defines an NTP authentication key. 1 is the key number (1 to 4,294,967,295); md5 is the only option available on Cisco devices; NTPpa55word is the password for the key.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: ntp authenticate
answer: Enables NTP authentication.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: ntp trusted-key 1
answer: Defines which keys are valid for NTP authentication. The key number here must match the key number defined in the ntp authentication-key command.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: ntp server 192.168.200.1 key 1
answer: Defines the NTP server at 192.168.200.1 that requires authentication and identifies the peer key number as key 1.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: ntp access-group peer 1
answer: Applies ACL 1. The peer keyword enables the device to receive time requests and NTP control queries and to synchronize itself to servers in the access list.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: ntp access-group serve 1
answer: The serve keyword enables the device to receive time requests and NTP control queries from the servers in the ACL but NOT to synchronize itself to those servers.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: ntp access-group serve-only 1
answer: The serve-only keyword enables the device to receive only time requests from the servers specified in the access list.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: ntp access-group query-only 1
answer: The query-only keyword enables the device to receive only NTP control queries from the servers specified in the access list.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: show ntp associations
answer: Displays the status of NTP associations.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: show ntp associations detail
answer: Displays detailed information about each NTP association.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: show ntp status
answer: Displays the status of NTP, showing whether the router's clock has synchronized with the external NTP server.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: debug ntp adjust
answer: Displays debug output for NTP clock adjustments.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: debug ntp all
answer: Displays all NTP debugging output.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: debug ntp packet
answer: Displays NTP packet debugging; lets you see the time that the peer/server gives you in a received packet.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: debug ntp packet peer a.b.c.d
answer: Displays debugging from the NTP peer at address a.b.c.d.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: calendar set 16:30:00 23 June 2019
answer: Manually sets the system hardware clock using military (24-hour) format. The hardware clock runs continuously even if the router is powered off or rebooted.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: clock calendar-valid
answer: Configures the system as an authoritative time source for the network based on its hardware clock. Use only when a more accurate time source such as NTP is not available.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: clock read-calendar
answer: Manually reads the hardware clock settings into the software clock.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
question: clock set 16:30:00 23 June 2019
answer: Manually sets the system software clock using military (24-hour) format.

source: CCNA Portable Command Guide - Ch19: Configuring Network Time (NTP)
