source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: What is the correct order to secure management access to a switch?
correct_sequence: Assign a device name (hostname)
Secure user EXEC mode access (console)
Secure privileged EXEC mode access (enable secret)
Secure vty access (line vty 0 15)
Encrypt all plaintext passwords (service password-encryption)
Display a login banner (banner motd)
distractor_sequences: Encrypt passwords first, then assign a hostname
Set the banner before assigning a device name
Secure vty before securing the console
explanation: The recommended sequence starts with naming the device, then securing console (user EXEC), privileged EXEC, vty access, encrypting passwords, and finally displaying a login banner.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: What is the correct order to configure the SVI on a switch for remote management?
correct_sequence: Enter global configuration mode (configure terminal)
Enter interface configuration mode for VLAN 1 (interface vlan 1)
Assign the IPv4 address and subnet mask (ip address 192.168.1.20 255.255.255.0)
Enable the virtual interface (no shutdown)
Assign the default gateway (ip default-gateway 192.168.1.1)
distractor_sequences: Enable the interface before assigning the IP address
Set the default gateway before entering interface vlan 1
Assign an IP to a physical switch port
explanation: To remotely manage a Layer 2 switch, configure the SVI (interface vlan 1) with an IP address, enable it with no shutdown, and set a default gateway so it can reach remote networks.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: What is the correct order to capture a configuration to a text file using terminal emulation software?
correct_sequence: Open terminal emulation software (such as PuTTY) connected to the switch
Enable logging in the terminal software and assign a name and file location for the log
Execute the show running-config (or show startup-config) command at the privileged EXEC prompt
Disable logging in the terminal software
distractor_sequences: Disable logging before displaying the configuration
Execute show running-config before enabling logging
Assign a log file name after disabling logging
explanation: Enable logging first so all session output is captured to the file, then display the configuration, then disable logging.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: What is the correct order to restore a saved configuration from a text file to a device?
correct_sequence: Enter global configuration mode on the device
Copy and paste the text file into the terminal window connected to the switch
Verify the text is applied as commands in the CLI, becoming the running configuration
distractor_sequences: Paste the file into user EXEC mode first
Reload the device before pasting
Erase the startup config before pasting
explanation: The text in the file is applied as CLI commands and becomes the running configuration on the device.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: What is the correct order to manually configure an IPv4 address on a Windows host?
correct_sequence: Open Control Panel, then Network Sharing Center, then Change adapter settings and choose the adapter
Right-click and select Properties to display the Ethernet Properties dialog
Highlight Internet Protocol Version 4 (TCP/IPv4) and click Properties
Configure the IPv4 address, subnet mask, and default gateway
Click OK to apply the settings
distractor_sequences: Configure the gateway first, then the IP address
Select Internet Protocol Version 6 before Version 4
Right-click the adapter without opening Properties
explanation: Manual IPv4 configuration on a Windows host is done through the adapter Properties, TCP/IPv4 Properties, then entering the address, mask, and gateway.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: Which statement is true about the running configuration file in a Cisco IOS device?

choices.label: It affects the operation of the device immediately when modified
It is stored in NVRAM
It should be deleted using the erase running-config command
It is automatically saved when the router reboots

explanation: The running-config is stored in RAM and reflects the current configuration; modifying it affects the operation of a Cisco device immediately.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: Which two statements are true regarding user EXEC mode?

choices.label: The device prompt for this mode ends with the > symbol and only some aspects of the configuration can be viewed
All router commands are available and interfaces and routing protocols can be configured
Global configuration mode can be accessed by entering the enable command
It allows execution of any command that changes the configuration

explanation: User EXEC mode has limited capabilities, allowing only basic monitoring commands; its prompt ends with the > symbol.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: Which type of access is secured on a Cisco router or switch with the enable secret command?

choices.label: privileged EXEC
virtual terminal
AUX port
console line

explanation: The enable secret command secures privileged EXEC mode access, which provides complete access to a device.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: What is the default SVI on a Cisco switch?

choices.label: VLAN 1
VLAN 99
VLAN 100
VLAN 999

explanation: Each switch comes with one SVI in the default configuration out of the box; the default SVI is interface VLAN 1.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: Which three naming conventions are part of the hostname guidelines?

choices.label: Fewer than 64 characters, no spaces, and begin with a letter
Written in all lowercase, end with a special character, and begin with a digit
Contain spaces, begin with a special character, and exceed 64 characters
Use only digits, end with a space, and begin with a dash

explanation: Hostname guidelines: start with a letter, include no spaces, end with a letter or digit, use only letters/digits/dashes, and be fewer than 64 characters.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: What is the function of the shell in an OS?

choices.label: It interfaces between the users and the kernel
It interacts with the device hardware
It provides dedicated firewall services
It provides intrusion protection services for the device

explanation: The shell is the user interface that allows users to request specific tasks from the computer, communicating between the user and the kernel.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: Which access method provides out-of-band access and works even if no networking services are configured?

choices.label: console
SSH
Telnet
vty

explanation: The console is a physical management port providing out-of-band access; the device is accessible even if no networking services are configured.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: Which remote access method is insecure because user authentication, passwords, and commands are sent over the network in plaintext?

choices.label: Telnet
SSH
console
AUX port

explanation: Telnet does not provide a secure, encrypted connection; the best practice is to use SSH instead of Telnet.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: Which memory location on a Cisco router or switch loses all content when the device is restarted?

choices.label: RAM
ROM
flash
NVRAM

explanation: RAM is volatile memory and loses all its content when the device is powered off or restarted; it stores the running configuration.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: Which memory location on a Cisco router stores the startup configuration file?

choices.label: NVRAM
RAM
ROM
flash

explanation: The startup configuration file is stored in nonvolatile random-access memory (NVRAM).

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: Why would a technician enter the command copy startup-config running-config?

choices.label: to copy an existing configuration into RAM
to remove all configurations from the switch
to save an active configuration to NVRAM
to make a changed configuration the new startup configuration

explanation: The copy startup-config running-config command copies the saved configuration from NVRAM into RAM (the running configuration).

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: Which functionality is provided by DHCP?

choices.label: automatic assignment of an IP address to each host
remote switch management
translation of IP addresses to domain names
end-to-end connectivity test

explanation: DHCP enables automatic IPv4 address configuration for every end device that is DHCP enabled, assigning the address settings necessary to communicate.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: Which two functions are provided to users by the context-sensitive help feature of the Cisco IOS CLI?

choices.label: Displaying a list of all commands available in the current mode and determining which option, keyword, or argument is available for the entered command
Providing an error message when an incorrect command is submitted and allowing completion with the Tab key
Selecting the best command to accomplish a task
Automatically correcting misspelled commands

explanation: Context-sensitive help (the ? key) answers which commands are available in each mode, which commands start with certain characters, and which arguments and keywords are available.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: A switch with a valid OS has a configuration file in NVRAM with an enable secret password but no line console 0 password. When the switch boots up, which mode will display?

choices.label: user EXEC mode
global configuration mode
setup mode
privileged EXEC mode

explanation: Since no console (user EXEC) password is configured, the console does not require a password, and the device boots into user EXEC mode; privileged EXEC access is protected by the enable secret.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: An administrator just changed the IP address of an interface on an IOS device. What else must be done to apply those changes?

choices.label: Nothing; changes take effect as soon as the command is typed correctly and Enter is pressed
Copy the running configuration to the startup configuration file
Copy the startup configuration to the running configuration
Reload the device and type yes when prompted to save

explanation: Modifying the running configuration affects the operation of a Cisco device immediately; saving to startup-config only preserves changes across reboots.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: Which key combination returns to privileged EXEC mode from any configuration mode?

choices.label: Ctrl+Z
Ctrl+C only when in setup mode
Ctrl+Shift+6
Tab

explanation: Ctrl+Z ends the configuration mode and returns to privileged EXEC mode; it is the same as entering the end command.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: Which statement about abbreviating IOS commands is true?

choices.label: Commands can be shortened to the minimum characters that identify a unique selection; configure can be shortened to conf
All commands can be shortened to their first character
Keywords cannot be shortened
The shortest possible abbreviation is always valid

explanation: For example, configure can be shortened to conf because it is the only command beginning with conf, but con will not work because more than one command begins with con.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: When IOS output produces more text than can be displayed, a --More-- prompt appears. What does pressing the Enter key do?

choices.label: Displays the next line
Displays the next screen
Ends the display and returns to privileged EXEC mode
Refreshes the current screen

explanation: At the --More-- prompt, Enter displays the next line, the Spacebar displays the next screen, and any other key ends the display string.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: What is the purpose of the IP address assigned to the SVI on a Layer 2 switch?

choices.label: To remotely access and manage the switch
To enable the switch to forward frames between ports
To assign the switch a MAC address
To enable VLAN trunking

explanation: A Layer 2 switch does not need an IP address to perform its operations; the IP address on the SVI is used only to remotely access the switch.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: Why are network devices typically accessed through a CLI rather than a GUI?

choices.label: The CLI is less resource intensive and very stable compared to a GUI
GUIs cannot display any output
CLI requires no knowledge of commands
GUIs are not available on network devices

explanation: GUIs may not provide all CLI features and can fail or crash; the CLI is less resource intensive and very stable, so network devices are typically accessed through a CLI.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: Which statement about SSH and Telnet is correct?

choices.label: SSH provides a secure, encrypted connection while Telnet sends data in plaintext
Telnet is more secure than SSH
SSH requires a console connection
Telnet is the recommended method for remote CLI access

explanation: SSH is an in-band, recommended, secure method for remote CLI connection; Telnet is insecure and should only be used in a lab environment.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
question: Which statement about IPv6 addresses is correct?

choices.label: They are 128 bits in length and written as hexadecimal values separated by colons
They are 32 bits in length and written in dotted-decimal notation
They are 64 bits and written in binary
They are case-sensitive and must be uppercase

explanation: An IPv6 address is 128 bits, written as 32 hexadecimal values in groups of four separated by colons, and is not case-sensitive.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
symptoms: After power is lost or the device is restarted, all configuration changes made during the session are gone.
root_cause: The configuration changes were made only to the running-config in RAM, which is volatile and is lost when the device is powered off or restarted.
troubleshooting_steps: Check whether the changes were saved with copy running-config startup-config
Verify the startup-config in NVRAM contains the expected settings using show startup-config
Re-enter the configuration changes if needed
Save the corrected configuration with copy running-config startup-config
resolution: To save changes made to the running configuration, use the copy running-config startup-config privileged EXEC command.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
symptoms: A technician enters the reload command and the device asks whether to save changes; the desired behavior is to discard the changes.
root_cause: IOS detected that the running config has changes that were not saved to the startup configuration.
troubleshooting_steps: When the prompt appears asking whether to save the changes, enter n or no
Wait for the device to reload
Confirm the previous startup configuration is restored
resolution: Answering n or no to the reload prompt discards the unsaved running config changes.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
symptoms: Undesired changes were saved to the startup config and the technician wants to clear all configurations.
root_cause: The startup-config in NVRAM contains the undesired configuration.
troubleshooting_steps: Issue the erase startup-config privileged EXEC command
Press Enter to accept the confirmation prompt
Reload the device to remove the current running config from RAM
Verify the switch loads the default startup config that originally shipped with the device
resolution: The startup config is removed with erase startup-config, then a reload restores the factory default configuration.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
symptoms: Two PCs connected to a configured switch cannot ping each other.
root_cause: One or both hosts are misconfigured: incorrect IPv4 address, subnet mask, or default gateway, or an interface is down.
troubleshooting_steps: Verify each PC's IP configuration using the ipconfig command
Check that IPv4 addresses and subnet masks place both hosts on the same network
Use show ip interface brief to verify the switch interface is up
Ping the gateway and then the other host to isolate the failure point
resolution: Correct the IP addressing on the hosts or enable the appropriate interfaces; ping then verifies end-to-end connectivity.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch2: Basic Switch and End Device Configuration
symptoms: An administrator cannot establish a remote CLI session to a switch using SSH.
root_cause: The switch lacks an active interface with an address (required for in-band SSH), or vty access is not secured/configured.
troubleshooting_steps: Verify the SVI has an IP address and is enabled (no shutdown)
Confirm the switch has a default gateway if connecting across networks
Check that vty lines are configured with a password and login
Verify connectivity with ping before attempting SSH
resolution: Configure the SVI with an IP address, enable it, and secure the vty lines; SSH requires active networking services on the device.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What are the three elements common to all communication methods?
answer: Message source (sender), message destination (receiver), and channel.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is a message source?
answer: People or electronic devices that need to send a message to other individuals or devices.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is a message destination?
answer: The receiver that receives the message and interprets it.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is a channel?
answer: The media that provide the pathway over which the message travels from source to destination.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is a protocol?
answer: A set of agreed-upon rules governing communication; in networks, protocols define common formats and sets of rules for exchanging messages between devices.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What must protocols account for to successfully deliver a message understood by the receiver?
answer: An identified sender and receiver, common language and grammar, speed and timing of delivery, and confirmation or acknowledgment requirements.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What requirements do common computer protocols define for how a message is transmitted?
answer: Message encoding, message formatting and encapsulation, message size, message timing, and message delivery options.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is the role of Internet Protocol (IP)?
answer: IP is responsible for sending a message from the message source to the destination over one or more networks, similar to addressing on an envelope.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: Why is message size an important rule of communication?
answer: Size restrictions on frames require the source host to break a long message into individual pieces that meet minimum and maximum size requirements; the pieces are sent as separate frames and reconstructed at the receiving host.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is an access method?
answer: A message timing element that determines when someone can send a message; for example, a WLAN NIC must determine whether the wireless medium is available before transmitting.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What are the four types of network protocols?
answer: Network communications protocols, network security protocols, routing protocols, and service discovery protocols.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What do network security protocols do?
answer: They secure data to provide authentication, data integrity, and data encryption; examples include SSH, SSL, and TLS.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What do routing protocols do?
answer: They enable routers to exchange route information, compare path information, and select the best path to the destination network; examples include OSPF and BGP.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What do service discovery protocols do?
answer: They are used for the automatic detection of devices or services; examples include DHCP for IP address allocation and DNS for name-to-IP translation.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What are the functions that network protocols provide?
answer: Addressing, reliability, flow control, sequencing, error detection, and an application interface.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does the addressing function of a protocol do?
answer: It identifies the sender and the intended receiver of a message using a defined addressing scheme; examples include Ethernet, IPv4, and IPv6.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does the reliability function of a protocol do?
answer: It provides guaranteed delivery mechanisms in case messages are lost or corrupted in transit; TCP provides guaranteed delivery.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does the sequencing function of a protocol do?
answer: It uniquely labels each transmitted segment of data so the receiving device can reassemble the information correctly if segments are lost, delayed, or received out of order; TCP provides sequencing.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does the error detection function of a protocol do?
answer: It determines whether data became corrupted during transmission; protocols providing error detection include Ethernet, IPv4, IPv6, and TCP.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does the application interface function of a protocol do?
answer: It contains information used for process-to-process communications between network applications, such as HTTP or HTTPS between client and server web processes.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is a protocol suite?
answer: A group of interrelated protocols necessary to perform a communication function; it can be specified by a standards organization or developed by a vendor.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is a protocol stack?
answer: A way of viewing the protocols within a suite in terms of layers, showing how individual protocols are implemented; each higher-level service depends on the functionality defined by the protocols in the lower levels.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is the TCP/IP protocol suite?
answer: The most common and relevant protocol suite used today; an open standard protocol suite maintained by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF).

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What are the OSI protocols?
answer: A family of protocols developed jointly in 1977 by ISO and ITU, which included a seven-layer model called the OSI reference model; today OSI is mainly known for its layered model and its protocols have largely been replaced by TCP/IP.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What was AppleTalk?
answer: A short-lived proprietary protocol suite released by Apple in 1985 for Apple devices; Apple adopted TCP/IP to replace it in 1995.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What was Novell NetWare?
answer: A proprietary protocol suite and network operating system developed by Novell in 1983 using the IPX network protocol; Novell adopted TCP/IP to replace IPX in 1995.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does DNS do?
answer: The Domain Name System translates domain names, such as cisco.com, into IP addresses.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does DHCPv4 do?
answer: A DHCPv4 server dynamically assigns IPv4 addressing information to DHCPv4 clients at startup and allows the addresses to be reused when no longer needed.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does DHCPv6 do?
answer: Similar to DHCPv4; a DHCPv6 server dynamically assigns IPv6 addressing information to DHCPv6 clients at startup.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does SLAAC do?
answer: Stateless address autoconfiguration; it allows a device to obtain its IPv6 addressing information without using a DHCPv6 server.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does SMTP do?
answer: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol; it enables clients to send email to a mail server and enables servers to send email to other servers.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does POP3 do?
answer: Post Office Protocol version 3; it enables clients to retrieve email from a mail server and download the email to the client's local mail application.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does IMAP do?
answer: Internet Message Access Protocol; it enables clients to access email stored on a mail server as well as maintain email on the server.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does FTP do?
answer: File Transfer Protocol; it sets the rules that enable a user on one host to access and transfer files to and from another host over a network. FTP is reliable, connection-oriented, and acknowledged.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does SFTP do?
answer: SSH File Transfer Protocol; as an extension to SSH, it can be used to establish a secure file transfer session in which the file transfer is encrypted.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does TFTP do?
answer: Trivial File Transfer Protocol; a simple, connectionless file transfer protocol with best-effort, unacknowledged file delivery that requires less overhead than FTP.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does HTTP do?
answer: Hypertext Transfer Protocol; a set of rules for exchanging text, graphic images, sound, video, and other multimedia files on the World Wide Web.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does HTTPS do?
answer: HTTP Secure; a secure form of HTTP that encrypts the data exchanged over the World Wide Web.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does TCP do?
answer: Transmission Control Protocol; it enables reliable communication between processes running on separate hosts and provides reliable, acknowledged transmissions that confirm successful delivery.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does UDP do?
answer: User Datagram Protocol; it enables a process running on one host to send packets to a process running on another host but does not confirm successful datagram transmission.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does IPv4 do?
answer: Internet Protocol version 4; it receives message segments from the transport layer, packages messages into packets, and addresses packets for end-to-end delivery over a network using a 32-bit address.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does IPv6 do?
answer: IP version 6; similar to IPv4 but uses a 128-bit address.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does NAT do?
answer: Network Address Translation; it translates IPv4 addresses from a private network into globally unique public IPv4 addresses.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does ICMPv4 do?
answer: Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv4; it provides feedback from a destination host to a source host about errors in packet delivery.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does ICMPv6 Neighbor Discovery (ND) include?
answer: Four protocol messages used for address resolution and duplicate address detection.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does ARP do?
answer: Address Resolution Protocol; it provides dynamic address mapping between an IPv4 address and a hardware address.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does Ethernet define?
answer: The rules for wiring and signaling standards of the network access layer; Ethernet is a LAN technology.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does WLAN define?
answer: Wireless local-area network protocols define the rules for wireless signaling across the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz radio frequencies.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: Why are open standards important?
answer: They encourage interoperability, competition, and innovation, and guarantee that no single company can monopolize the market or have an unfair advantage.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What are standards organizations?
answer: Usually vendor-neutral, nonprofit organizations established to develop and promote the concept of open standards for networking.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does ISOC do?
answer: The Internet Society is responsible for promoting the open development and evolution of internet use throughout the world.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does the IAB do?
answer: The Internet Architecture Board is responsible for the overall management and development of internet standards.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does the IETF do?
answer: The Internet Engineering Task Force develops, updates, and maintains internet and TCP/IP technologies, including the process and documents (RFCs) for developing new protocols and updating existing ones.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does the IRTF focus on?
answer: The Internet Research Task Force is focused on long-term research related to internet and TCP/IP protocols, such as anti-spam, crypto forum, and peer-to-peer research.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does ICANN do?
answer: The Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers coordinates IP address allocation, the management of domain names, and assignment of other information used in TCP/IP protocols.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does IANA do?
answer: The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority is responsible for overseeing and managing IP address allocation, domain name management, and protocol identifiers for ICANN.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is IEEE known for in networking?
answer: The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers creates standards including 802.3 Ethernet and the 802.11 WLAN standard.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is the EIA best known for?
answer: The Electronic Industries Alliance is best known for standards related to electrical wiring, connectors, and the 19-inch racks used to mount networking equipment.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does the TIA do?
answer: The Telecommunications Industry Association is responsible for developing communication standards in areas including radio equipment, cellular towers, VoIP devices, and satellite communications.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does ITU-T define?
answer: The International Telecommunications Union Telecommunication Standardization Sector defines standards for video compression, IPTV, and broadband communications such as DSL.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is an RFC?
answer: A Request for Comments document; authored by networking engineers and sent to other IETF members for comments, defining internet and TCP/IP standards.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is a reference model?
answer: A conceptual framework to help understand and implement the relationships between various protocols.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What are the benefits of using a layered model?
answer: It assists in protocol design, fosters competition so products from different vendors can work together, prevents technology changes in one layer from affecting others, and provides a common language to describe networking functions.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is the OSI reference model?
answer: The Open System Interconnection reference model; a seven-layer model that provides an extensive list of functions and services at each layer, describing what must be done but not prescribing how.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is OSI Layer 7, the application layer?
answer: It contains protocols used for process-to-process communications.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is OSI Layer 6, the presentation layer?
answer: It provides for a common representation of the data transferred between application layer services.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is OSI Layer 5, the session layer?
answer: It provides services to the presentation layer to organize its dialogue and manage data exchange.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is OSI Layer 4, the transport layer?
answer: It defines services to segment, transfer, and reassemble the data for individual communications between end devices.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is OSI Layer 3, the network layer?
answer: It provides services to exchange the individual pieces of data over the network between identified end devices.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is OSI Layer 2, the data link layer?
answer: Its protocols describe methods for exchanging data frames between devices over common media.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is OSI Layer 1, the physical layer?
answer: Its protocols describe the mechanical, electrical, functional, and procedural means to activate, maintain, and deactivate physical connections for bit transmission.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What are the four layers of the TCP/IP model?
answer: Application layer, transport layer, internet layer, and network access layer.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does the TCP/IP application layer do?
answer: It represents data to the user and handles encoding and dialog control.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does the TCP/IP transport layer do?
answer: It supports communication between various devices across diverse networks.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does the TCP/IP internet layer do?
answer: It determines the best path through the network.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What does the TCP/IP network access layer do?
answer: It controls the hardware devices and media that make up the network.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What are the two primary benefits of segmenting messages?
answer: Increased speed (large amounts of data can be sent without tying up a link, allowing multiplexing) and increased efficiency (only a failed segment, not the entire stream, needs to be retransmitted).

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: Which protocol is responsible for sequencing the individual segments of a message?
answer: TCP.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is a PDU?
answer: A protocol data unit; the form that a piece of data takes at any layer. During encapsulation, each layer encapsulates the PDU it receives from the layer above.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is the PDU name for each layer?
answer: Data (application layer), segment (transport layer), packet (network layer), frame (data link layer), and bits (physical layer).

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: If the transport header is TCP, what is the transport layer PDU called?
answer: A segment; if the transport header is UDP, it is a datagram.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: How does the encapsulation process work?
answer: From top to bottom; at each layer the upper-layer information is considered data within the encapsulated protocol. For example, the TCP segment is the data portion of the IP packet.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What are the two types of addresses used to access a local network resource?
answer: Network layer (Layer 3) source and destination addresses, and data link layer (Layer 2) source and destination addresses.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is the role of the network layer addresses?
answer: They deliver an IP packet from the original source to the final destination, which may be on the same network or a remote network.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is the role of the data link layer addresses?
answer: They deliver the data link frame from one network interface card (NIC) to another NIC on the same network.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What are the two parts of an IP address?
answer: The network portion (IPv4) or prefix (IPv6), which indicates the network the address belongs to, and the host portion (IPv4) or interface ID (IPv6), which identifies a specific device on the network.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is a MAC address?
answer: On an Ethernet network, the data link layer addresses are known as Ethernet Media Access Control (MAC) addresses; they are physically embedded on Ethernet NICs.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: Why do data link addresses change at each hop while IP addresses do not?
answer: The IP packet is encapsulated in a new data link frame at each hop; each frame contains the source data link address of the NIC sending it and the destination data link address of the NIC receiving it (next hop router or final destination).

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is Wireshark?
answer: A software protocol analyzer, or packet sniffer application, used for network troubleshooting, analysis, software and protocol development, and education.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What type of communication sends a message to all devices on a local area network?

choices.label: broadcast
multicast
unicast
allcast

explanation: Broadcast transmits information to all end devices; unicast is to a single device and multicast is to one or more.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: In computer communication, what is the purpose of message encoding?

choices.label: to convert information to the appropriate form for transmission
to interpret information
to break large messages into smaller frames
to negotiate correct timing for successful communications

explanation: Encoding is the process of converting information into an acceptable form for transmission; decoding reverses this process to interpret the information.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: Which message delivery option is used when all devices need to receive the same message simultaneously?

choices.label: broadcast
duplex
unicast
multicast

explanation: Broadcast transmits information to all end devices on the network.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: Which type of communication sends a message to a group of host destinations simultaneously?

choices.label: multicast
broadcast
unicast
anycast

explanation: Multicast transmits information to one or more end devices simultaneously.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What process is used to receive transmitted data and convert it into a readable message?

choices.label: decoding
access control
encapsulation
flow control

explanation: Decoding reverses the encoding process to interpret the information received.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What process is used to place one message inside another message for transfer from a source to a destination?

choices.label: encapsulation
access control
decoding
flow control

explanation: Encapsulation is the process of placing one message format inside another, such as a letter inside an envelope.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: Which message timing element determines when a device can send a message?

choices.label: access method
flow control
response timeout
encoding

explanation: The access method determines when someone can send a message, such as a WLAN NIC determining whether the wireless medium is available.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is the purpose of protocols in data communications?

choices.label: providing the rules required for a specific type of communication to occur
specifying the bandwidth of the channel for each type of communication
specifying the device operating systems that will support the communication
dictating the content of a message sent during communication

explanation: Protocols are agreed-upon rules that govern communication; they define common formats and sets of rules for exchanging messages.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: Which two protocols function at the internet layer?

choices.label: ICMP and IP
POP and BOOTP
Ethernet and WLAN
HTTP and FTP

explanation: The internet layer of the TCP/IP suite includes IPv4, IPv6, NAT, and ICMP (ICMPv4/ICMPv6), along with routing protocols such as OSPF, EIGRP, and BGP.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: Which layer of the OSI model defines services to segment and reassemble data for individual communications between end devices?

choices.label: transport
application
presentation
session
network

explanation: The transport layer (Layer 4) defines services to segment, transfer, and reassemble data for individual communications between end devices.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What are two benefits of using a layered network model?

choices.label: It assists in protocol design and prevents technology in one layer from affecting other layers
It speeds up packet delivery and ensures a device at one layer can function at the next higher layer
It prevents designers from creating their own model
It reduces the number of protocols needed

explanation: Layered models assist in protocol design, foster competition, prevent technology changes in one layer from affecting others, and provide a common language.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is the general term used to describe a piece of data at any layer of a networking model?

choices.label: protocol data unit
frame
packet
segment

explanation: The form that a piece of data takes at any layer is called a protocol data unit (PDU); each layer's PDU has a different name such as frame, packet, or segment.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is done to an IP packet before it is transmitted over the physical medium?

choices.label: It is encapsulated in a Layer 2 frame
It is tagged with information guaranteeing reliable delivery
It is segmented into smaller individual pieces
It is encapsulated into a TCP segment

explanation: The IP packet is encapsulated in a data link frame (Layer 2) so it can be transmitted over the physical medium.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: A web client is sending a request for a web page to a web server. From the perspective of the client, what is the correct order of the protocol stack used to prepare the request for transmission?

choices.label: HTTP, TCP, IP, Ethernet
HTTP, IP, TCP, Ethernet
Ethernet, TCP, IP, HTTP
Ethernet, IP, TCP, HTTP

explanation: Encapsulation works from the top down: the application protocol (HTTP) is added first, then TCP, then IP, and finally Ethernet before transmission.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: Which logical address is used for delivery of data to a remote network?

choices.label: destination IP address
destination MAC address
destination port number
source MAC address

explanation: The destination IP address (network layer logical address) delivers the packet to the final destination, which may be on a remote network.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: When the sender and receiver of an IP packet are on different networks, what destination MAC address does the sending device use?

choices.label: The MAC address of the default gateway router
The MAC address of the final destination host
Its own MAC address
The broadcast MAC address

explanation: The Ethernet frame must be sent to the router (default gateway), whose data link address is on the same network as the sender; the router forwards the packet toward the final destination.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: Which statement about the destination MAC address on a single network is correct?

choices.label: It is the MAC address of the receiving device on the same network, so the frame is sent directly
It is always the MAC address of the router
It is never used when hosts are on the same network
It is the same as the destination IP address

explanation: When the sender and receiver are on the same network, the data link frame is sent directly to the receiving device using its MAC address.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: Which protocol is connection-oriented and provides reliable, acknowledged transmissions?

choices.label: TCP
UDP
TFTP
IP

explanation: TCP enables reliable communication and provides reliable, acknowledged transmissions that confirm successful delivery; UDP does not confirm successful datagram transmission.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: Which statement correctly describes the TCP/IP protocol suite?

choices.label: It is an open standard protocol suite maintained by the IETF
It is a proprietary protocol suite owned by Cisco
It consists only of routing protocols
It was developed by ISO and ITU in 1977

explanation: The TCP/IP protocol suite is an open standard protocol suite maintained by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF).

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: Which of the following are standards organizations?

TCP/IP, OSI, and MAC
Ethernet, HTTP, and DNS
REST, TLS, and SSL

explanation: IEEE, IETF, and IANA are standards organizations; TCP/IP, OSI, and MAC are protocols or concepts, not standards bodies.

IEEE
EIA
ITU-T

explanation: The IETF develops, updates, and maintains internet and TCP/IP technologies, including the RFC document process.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: Which OSI model layer maps directly to the TCP/IP internet layer?

choices.label: network layer (Layer 3)
data link layer (Layer 2)
session layer (Layer 5)
physical layer (Layer 1)

explanation: OSI Layer 3, the network layer, maps directly to the TCP/IP internet layer and is used to describe protocols that address and route messages through an internetwork.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: How do the OSI and TCP/IP models differ at the application level?

choices.label: OSI separates the application functions into Layers 5, 6, and 7, while TCP/IP has a single application layer
TCP/IP has seven application layers
OSI has no application layer
The models are identical at every layer

explanation: The TCP/IP application layer includes several protocols; OSI Layers 5, 6, and 7 (session, presentation, application) are used as references for application developers.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: Which PDU name is used at the transport layer when the header is UDP?

choices.label: datagram
segment
packet
frame

explanation: If the transport header is UDP, the PDU is a datagram; if the transport header is TCP, the PDU is a segment.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is the correct order of the TCP/IP encapsulation process when a web server sends a web page to a client?
correct_sequence: The web server prepares the HTML page as data to be sent
The HTTP application protocol header is added to the front of the HTML data
TCP adds header information to the HTTP data to manage the conversation
IP adds source and destination IP addresses, forming an IP packet
Ethernet adds information to both ends of the IP packet, forming a data link frame
The frame is transported as bits through the internetwork
The client de-encapsulates the frame by removing Ethernet, IP, TCP, and HTTP headers
The web page information is passed to the client's web browser
distractor_sequences: Add TCP, then HTTP, then IP, then Ethernet
Add Ethernet, then IP, then TCP, then HTTP data
Remove HTTP first during de-encapsulation
explanation: Encapsulation adds headers top to bottom (HTTP, TCP, IP, Ethernet); de-encapsulation removes them in the opposite order (Ethernet, IP, TCP, HTTP).

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is the correct order of PDUs as data moves down the protocol stack from the application layer to the physical layer?
correct_sequence: Data (application layer)
Segment (transport layer)
Packet (network layer)
Frame (data link layer)
Bits (physical layer)
distractor_sequences: Bits, frame, packet, segment, data
Packet, data, segment, bits, frame
Frame, bits, data, segment, packet
explanation: The PDUs from the application layer down are Data, Segment, Packet, Frame, and Bits.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
question: What is the correct order of the de-encapsulation process at a receiving host?
correct_sequence: The receiving host processes and removes the Ethernet (data link) header
The IP protocol header is processed and removed
The TCP header is processed and removed
The HTTP (application) header is processed and removed
The web page data is passed to the client's web browser
distractor_sequences: Remove HTTP first, then TCP, then IP, then Ethernet
Remove TCP before Ethernet
Pass data to the browser before removing any headers
explanation: De-encapsulation removes protocol headers in the opposite order from how they were added: Ethernet, then IP, then TCP, then HTTP.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
symptoms: A message is not delivered because it does not follow the correct format, similar to a letter with an incorrect destination address on the envelope.
root_cause: The message format or addressing does not follow the required protocol rules; message formats depend on the type of message and the channel used to deliver it.
troubleshooting_steps: Verify the source and destination are identified correctly
Check that the message follows the agreed language, grammar, and format rules
Confirm the channel used matches the message format
Ensure confirmation or acknowledgment requirements are met
resolution: Messages must use a specific format and structure that follows the established rules and protocols to be delivered and understood.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
symptoms: A 100-page message is received with pages out of order, and the receiver cannot reassemble the original message correctly.
root_cause: Each segment of the message can arrive out of order because packets may take different paths; the segments need sequence numbers.
troubleshooting_steps: Verify each segment is uniquely labeled with a sequence number
Use the sequencing information to reassemble the segments in the correct order
Retransmit any segments that are lost or delayed
resolution: TCP is responsible for sequencing the individual segments so the receiving device can reassemble the information correctly.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
symptoms: A link fails during a transmission of a massive data stream and the entire message is lost, requiring full retransmission.
root_cause: The data was sent as one massive, uninterrupted stream rather than being segmented into smaller pieces.
troubleshooting_steps: Segment the data into smaller, more manageable units
Send each segment as a separate packet, possibly over different paths
Retransmit only the segments that failed, not the entire data stream
resolution: Segmentation increases efficiency: if a single segment fails, only that segment needs to be retransmitted rather than the entire data stream.

source: CCNAv7 Intro to Networks - Ch3: Protocols and Models
symptoms: PC1 cannot reach a server on a remote network even though the destination IP address is correct.
root_cause: The Ethernet frame is sent to the wrong destination MAC address or the default gateway is not configured on the host; remote delivery requires the frame to be sent to the default gateway router.
troubleshooting_steps: Verify the destination IP address is on a different network
Confirm the default gateway is configured on the host
Check that the frame is sent to the default gateway's MAC address rather than the remote host's MAC address
Verify the router forwards the packet toward the final destination
resolution: When sender and receiver are on different networks, the data link frame is sent to the default gateway (router), which forwards the IP packet toward the destination; the destination MAC address used is the router's.
