source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
question: Which LSA type exists in all OSPF areas?

choices.label: Router (type 1)
Network (type 2)
Summary (type 3)
AS external (type 5)

explanation: Every OSPF router advertises a type 1 (router) LSA in its area, so a type 1 LSA exists in all OSPF areas.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
question: Which statement is true about an ABR receiving a network (type 2) LSA?

choices.label: The ABR does not forward it to other areas; it uses it to determine the mask when creating type 3 LSAs
The ABR forwards the network LSA to the other connected areas unchanged
The ABR converts it directly into a type 5 external LSA
The ABR discards the network LSA and does not process it

explanation: ABRs do not forward type 1 or type 2 LSAs into other areas. The type 2 LSA is used to determine the network mask of the multi-access network when the ABR creates a type 3 LSA.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
question: When a type 3 LSA is received in a non-backbone area, what does the ABR do?

choices.label: Installs the type 3 LSA for only the area where it was received
Discards the type 3 LSA and does not process it
Advertises the type 3 LSA to the backbone area
Advertises the type 3 LSA to the backbone area and displays an error

explanation: Per the ABR rules, a type 3 LSA received from a non-backbone area only inserts into the LSDB for the source area; ABRs do not create a type 3 LSA for other areas.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
question: What is the LSA age field in the LSDB used for?

choices.label: To age out old LSAs by removing an LSA when it reaches 3600 seconds
For version control to ensure the most recent LSA is present
For troubleshooting to identify exactly when the LSA was advertised
To age out old LSAs by removing an LSA when its age reaches zero

explanation: LSA age increments by 1 every second; when the age reaches 3600 seconds, the LSA is deemed invalid and purged from the LSDB.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
question: Which statement correctly describes a router with interfaces in Area 1 and Area 2?

choices.label: It will NOT be able to inject routes learned from one area into the other area unless it participates in Area 0
It will automatically inject routes learned from one area into the other area
It maintains a single combined LSDB for all areas
It is considered a proper ABR regardless of Area 0 participation

explanation: A router connected to multiple areas maintains a separate LSDB per area and only acts as a proper ABR when it participates in Area 0; otherwise routes are not advertised between areas.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
question: Which statement about an OSPF member router is true?

choices.label: It contains a complete copy of the LSDB only for the areas it participates in
It contains a complete copy of the LSDBs for every area in the routing domain
It never runs the SPF algorithm
It must participate in Area 0 to be a member router

explanation: All routers within the same OSPF area maintain an identical copy of the LSDB for that area; a router with interfaces in multiple areas has multiple LSDBs (one per area), not LSDBs for every area.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
question: Which statement about OSPF path selection is correct?

choices.label: Intra-area routes are preferred over inter-area routes even if the inter-area route has a lower total path metric
OSPF uses the shortest total path metric to identify the best path for every internal OSPF route (intra-area and inter-area)
Inter-area routes are always preferred over intra-area routes
Only the metric is used; path type is never considered

explanation: OSPF path selection prioritizes intra-area routes first, then inter-area routes, then external routes. Intra-area routes are always preferred over inter-area routes, regardless of metric.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
question: How is the process of summarizing internal routes on an OSPF router accomplished?

choices.label: Using the OSPF process configuration command area area-id range network subnet-mask
Using the interface configuration command summary-address network prefix-length
Using the OSPF process configuration command summary-address network prefix-length
Using the interface configuration command area area-id summary-address network subnet-mask

explanation: Inter-area summarization of internal OSPF routes is done with the OSPF process configuration command area area-id range network subnet-mask on the ABR.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
question: True or false: A router with an interface associated with Area 1 and Area 2 will be able to inject routes learned from one area into another area.

choices.label: False
True

explanation: A router connected to multiple areas is not necessarily able to inject routes between them; it must participate in Area 0 to be a proper ABR.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
question: True or false: A member router contains a complete copy of the LSDBs for every area in the routing domain.

choices.label: False
True

explanation: A router contains an identical copy of the LSDB for the areas in which it participates only. If it has interfaces in multiple areas, it has multiple LSDBs, but not LSDBs for areas it does not participate in.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
question: When an ABR receives a type 3 LSA from Area 0, which advertising router does the regenerated type 3 LSA list?

choices.label: The ABR itself, with an additional cost metric
The original advertising router from the backbone
The DR of the destination network
The ASBR that originated the route

explanation: If an ABR receives a type 3 LSA from Area 0, it regenerates a new type 3 LSA for the non-backbone area and lists itself as the advertising router, with the additional cost metric.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
question: What keyword suppresses the creation of type 3 LSAs for a summarized range, filtering the component routes from other areas?

choices.label: not-advertise
summary-only
advertise
discard

explanation: The not-advertise keyword in the area area-id range command prevents creation of any type 3 LSAs for networks in that range, making the component routes visible only within their originating area.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
question: What is the default maximum number of OSPF equal-cost multipath (ECMP) routes?

choices.label: Four
Two
Six
Sixteen

explanation: The default maximum number of ECMP paths is four. The setting can be overwritten with the maximum-paths command under the OSPF process.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
symptoms: Routes from one area are not being advertised into another area even though a router connects both areas.
root_cause: The connecting router does not participate in Area 0, so it is not a proper ABR and does not create type 3 LSAs between areas.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Run show ip ospf interface brief on the connecting router to confirm which areas its interfaces belong to.
2. Verify the router has at least one interface in Area 0.
3. Check show ip route to confirm routes are missing between the areas.
resolution: Add an interface (or network statement) in Area 0 so the router becomes a proper ABR per RFC 3509, allowing type 3 LSAs to be created between areas.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
symptoms: Inter-area traffic is failing or routing oddly in a topology where Area 0 is split by a non-backbone area.
root_cause: Area 0 is not contiguous; inter-area traffic tries to cross a non-backbone area, and type 3 LSAs received from a non-backbone area are only installed in the source area.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Review the area topology and verify every non-backbone area connects directly to Area 0.
2. Check show ip ospf interface brief on all routers for unexpected area assignments.
3. Confirm there is no single point of failure partitioning Area 0.
resolution: Ensure Area 0 is contiguous by providing multiple paths to keep the backbone connected; virtual links or GRE tunnels are other options.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
symptoms: A router is not accepting a newer OSPF route advertisement.
root_cause: The received LSA has a lower sequence number than the one in the LSDB and is deemed old and discarded, or the LSA age has reached 3600 seconds and it is purged.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Use show ip ospf database to inspect LSA age and sequence numbers for the prefix.
2. Compare the sequence number received against the one in the LSDB.
3. Check whether the LSA age has exceeded 1800 seconds, requiring the originator to refresh it.
resolution: Wait for the originating router to refresh the LSA at 30 minutes (age reset to 0), or verify connectivity to the originator so current LSAs are received.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
symptoms: An OSPF summary route is not being advertised into other areas.
root_cause: The area range summarization is misconfigured, placed on the wrong router/area, or the range does not cover the component prefixes.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify the summary configuration with show running-config | section router ospf and confirm the area matches the source area.
2. Confirm the summary is configured on the ABR (not an internal router).
3. Check show ip route ospf to see if the summary and discard route (Null0) were created.
resolution: Correct the area area-id range network subnet-mask command on the correct ABR, and optionally add the cost keyword to statically set the summary metric.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
symptoms: A route is missing from the routing table in one area but the area range command should not have filtered it.
root_cause: An area filter-list prefix or a not-advertise summarization range is unintentionally filtering the type 3 LSA generation on the ABR.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Review the ABR configuration for area area-id filter-list prefix commands and not-advertise ranges.
2. Inspect the prefix list entries and their sequence order for a deny statement or implicit deny.
3. Check show ip ospf database summary on the ABR to confirm whether the type 3 LSA was generated.
resolution: Adjust the prefix list or remove the not-advertise keyword so the intended type 3 LSA is generated for the prefix.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
question: What is the correct order of OSPF path selection priorities?
correct_sequence: 1. Intra-area routes
2. Inter-area routes
3. External routes (additional logic)
distractor_sequences: Inter-area, intra-area, external
External, intra-area, inter-area
Inter-area, external, intra-area
explanation: OSPF always prefers intra-area routes, then inter-area routes, then external routes, regardless of total path metric between the first two types.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
question: What is the correct order of events when a type 3 LSA metric is accumulated across multiple ABRs?
correct_sequence: 1. R2 advertises the network as a type 1 LSA in its area
2. R4 creates a type 3 LSA with the total path metric to the originating router and advertises it into Area 0
3. R5 creates a new type 3 LSA for its non-backbone area using its cost to R4 plus the original type 3 metric
4. R6 calculates its metric to the ABR (R5) plus the type 3 LSA metric
distractor_sequences: Type 3 first, then type 1
R5 creates the LSA before R4
The metric is never accumulated across ABRs
explanation: The type 3 metric starts from the type 1 LSA total path metric, then each downstream ABR adds its own link cost and regenerates the type 3 LSA.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch9: Advanced OSPF
question: What is the correct sequence of LSA age handling in OSPF?
correct_sequence: 1. LSA age is entered into the local LSDB and increments by 1 every second
2. When age exceeds 1800 seconds, the originating router advertises a new LSA with age set to 0
3. Age is incremented with a calculated minimal delay as the LSA is forwarded
4. If the LSA age reaches 3600 seconds, it is purged from the LSDB
distractor_sequences: Purge at 1800 seconds and refresh at 3600
Age decrements over time
Sequence number controls aging and age is never incremented
explanation: LSA age counts up from 0, is refreshed by the originator at 30 minutes (1800 seconds), and any LSA reaching 3600 seconds is purged.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: Which address families does OSPFv3 support?
answer: Both the IPv4 and IPv6 address families.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: Is OSPFv3 backward compatible with OSPFv2?
answer: No. The protocol mechanisms described for OSPFv2 are essentially the same for OSPFv3, but the two versions are not backward compatible.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: Which RFC covers OSPFv3?
answer: RFC 5340, OSPF for IPv6.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What term does OSPFv3 use instead of network, and why?
answer: Link, because the SPF calculations are per link instead of per subnet.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: How is IP prefix information carried in OSPFv3?
answer: It is carried as LSA payload information rather than in the OSPF packet headers, making the protocol essentially address family independent, much like IS-IS.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What network layer does OSPFv3 run directly over?
answer: IPv6. The number of fields in the packet header has been reduced compared to OSPFv2.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: How is the router ID handled in OSPFv3?
answer: The router ID is used to identify neighbors regardless of network type. When configuring OSPFv3 on IOS routers, the ID must always be manually assigned in the routing process. If there are no IPv4 interfaces and no manual RID, the RID is set to 0.0.0.0 and adjacencies cannot form.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: How is neighbor authentication handled in OSPFv3?
answer: Authentication was removed from the OSPF protocol and is now performed through IPsec extension headers in the IPv6 packet.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What addressing is used for OSPFv3 inter-router communication?
answer: IPv6 link-local addressing. Neighbors are not automatically detected over NBMA interfaces; a neighbor must be manually specified using the link-local address.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: Can OSPFv3 form an adjacency between routers that do not share a common subnet?
answer: Yes. IPv6 allows multiple subnets to be assigned to a single interface, and OSPFv3 allows neighbor adjacency to form even if the two routers do not share a common subnet.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What is the instance ID field used for in OSPFv3?
answer: OSPFv3 packets include an instance ID field that may be used to manipulate which routers on a network segment are allowed to form adjacencies (multiple instances).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What is the type 1 router LSA responsible for in OSPFv3?
answer: Only for announcing interface parameters such as the interface type (point-to-point, broadcast, NBMA, point-to-multipoint, and virtual links) and metric (cost).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: Which two new LSA types advertise IP address information independently in OSPFv3?
answer: The intra-area prefix LSA and the link LSA.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: Which LSAs does the OSPFv3 Dijkstra calculation examine to determine the shortest path tree (SPT)?
answer: Only the router and network LSAs.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: Why does OSPFv3 advertise IP prefix information in new LSA types?
answer: To eliminate the need for OSPF to perform full SPF tree calculations every time a new IP address (prefix) is added or changed on an interface. The OSPFv3 LSDB creates a shortest path topology tree based on links instead of networks.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What is the renamed type 3 summary LSA in OSPFv3?
answer: The inter-area prefix LSA.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What is the renamed type 4 ASBR summary LSA in OSPFv3?
answer: The inter-area router LSA.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What IP protocol number do OSPFv3 packets use?
answer: Protocol number 89 in the IPv6 header.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What is the source address used for OSPFv3 packets?
answer: The local interface's IPv6 link-local address.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: How many packet types does OSPFv3 use?
answer: The same five packet types and logic as OSPFv2.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What is the OSPFv3 AllSPFRouters multicast address?
answer: FF02::5. Every router uses it to send OSPF hello messages to routers on the same link, and DR/BDR routers use it to send link-state update and flooding acknowledgment messages to all routers.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What is the OSPFv3 AllDRouters multicast address?
answer: FF02::6. Non-DR/BDR routers send an update or link-state acknowledgment message to the DR and BDR using this address.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What is the prerequisite command for OSPFv3 routing?
answer: ipv6 unicast-routing must be enabled on the router before the OSPFv3 process is configured.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What is the OSPFv3 router ID requirement?
answer: The router ID is a 32-bit value that does not need to match an IPv4 address; it may be any number in IPv4 address format (for example 0.1.2.3), as long as the value is unique within the OSPF domain.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: How is OSPFv3 enabled on an interface?
answer: With the interface command ospfv3 process-id ipv6 area area-id. OSPFv3 does not use the network statement for initializing interfaces.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What are the legacy commands used for OSPFv3 on older IOS versions?
answer: ipv6 router ospf for initialization of the OSPF process and ipv6 ospf process-id area area-id for identification of the interface. These commands are considered legacy and should be migrated.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: How is the address family initialized in OSPFv3?
answer: With the command address-family {ipv6 | ipv4} unicast inside the routing process. The appropriate address family is enabled automatically when OSPFv3 is enabled on an interface.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: Which algorithm does OSPFv3 use for dynamically locating the RID?
answer: The same algorithm as OSPFv2. If there are no IPv4 interfaces available, the RID is set to 0.0.0.0 and does not allow adjacencies to form.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What is the OSPFv3 equivalent of the OSPFv2 command show ip ospf neighbor?
answer: show ospfv3 ipv6 neighbor. OSPFv3 verification commands essentially replace ip ospf with ospfv3 ipv6.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What does show ospfv3 interface display instead of an IP address?
answer: The interface ID value (for example, Interface ID 3) plus link-local address, area, process ID, instance ID, router ID, network type, cost, timers, and DR/BDR state.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What columns does show ospfv3 interface brief display?
answer: Interface, PID (process ID), Area, AF (address family ipv4 or ipv6), Cost, State, and Nbrs F/C (full/configured neighbor count).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What command displays the OSPFv3 routes in the IPv6 routing table, and what do the codes O and OI mean?
answer: show ipv6 route ospf. O indicates intra-area routes and OI indicates inter-area routes. The forwarding address is the link-local address of the neighboring router.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What are the default OSPFv3 hello and dead timers shown in the chapter output?
answer: Hello 10, Dead 40, Wait 40, Retransmit 5 (seconds).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What commands control passive interfaces in OSPFv3?
answer: passive-interface interface-id marks a specific interface passive; passive-interface default makes all interfaces passive; no passive-interface interface-id marks one active. Placing the command under the global process cascades the setting to both address families.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: How do you verify that an OSPFv3 interface is passive?
answer: Use show ospfv3 interface [interface-id] and search for the Passive keyword. The output includes the line No Hellos (Passive interface).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What command summarizes an IPv6 network range in OSPFv3?
answer: area area-id range prefix/prefix-length, which resides under the address family in the OSPFv3 process. Summarization of internal OSPFv3 routes must occur on ABRs and follows the same rules as OSPFv2.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What is a common mistake when summarizing IPv6 addresses?
answer: Confusing hex with decimal. The first and third digits in a hextet should not be confused as decimal values; for example, the hex hextet 2001 represents 32 (20 in hex) and 1, not 20 and 1 in decimal.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What OSPFv3 network types are supported?
answer: The same OSPF network types as OSPFv2. The network type is changed with the interface parameter command ospfv3 network {point-to-point | broadcast}.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What does the interface state P2P indicate in OSPFv3 output?
answer: That the interface has been statically configured as a point-to-point network type (Network Type POINT_TO_POINT).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: Which RFC specifies that OSPFv3 should support multiple address families?
answer: RFC 5838, which specifies setting the instance ID value from the IPv6 reserved range to the IPv4 reserved range (64 to 95) in the link LSAs.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What is required to enable IPv4 support for OSPFv3 on an interface?
answer: 1) Ensure the IPv4 interface has an IPv6 address (global or link-local) configured. 2) Enable the OSPFv3 process for IPv4 on the interface with ospfv3 process-id ipv4 area area-id.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: How does show ospfv3 interface brief behave when both IPv4 and IPv6 are configured on an interface?
answer: An entry appears for each address family, so the same interface is listed with both an ipv4 and an ipv6 row.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: How does show ospfv3 neighbor behave with IPv4 and IPv6?
answer: It displays the neighbors for each address family as separate entities (one section for address-family ipv4 and one for address-family ipv6).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: How are IPv4 routes learned via OSPFv3 displayed in the IPv4 RIB?
answer: The routes are installed in the IPv4 routing table and verified with the command show ip route ospfv3 (or show ip route | begin Gateway).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: router ospfv3 [process-id]
answer: Initializes the OSPFv3 routing process.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: ospfv3 process-id ipv6 area area-id
answer: Enables OSPFv3 on an interface for the IPv6 address family and assigns the interface to an area (interface configuration mode).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: ospfv3 process-id ipv4 area area-id
answer: Enables OSPFv3 on an interface for the IPv4 address family, allowing exchange of IPv4 routes over the OSPFv3 process.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: address-family ipv6 unicast
answer: Initializes the IPv6 address family inside the OSPFv3 routing process (ipv4 unicast initializes the IPv4 address family).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/1
answer: Marks a specific OSPFv3 interface as passive so it does not send hellos or form adjacencies.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: area 0 range 2001:db8:0:0::/65
answer: Summarizes an IPv6 network range on an ABR; configured under the address family in the OSPFv3 process.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: ospfv3 network point-to-point
answer: Changes the OSPFv3 network type of an interface to point-to-point (broadcast is the other option).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: show ospfv3 ipv6 neighbor
answer: Displays the OSPFv3 IPv6 neighbors (neighbor ID, priority, state, dead time, interface ID, and interface).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: show ospfv3 interface [interface-id]
answer: Displays detailed OSPFv3 interface settings including link-local address, interface ID, area, process ID, instance ID, router ID, network type, cost, timers, and DR/BDR state.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: show ospfv3 interface brief
answer: Displays a brief version of OSPFv3 interface settings including process ID, area, address family, interface state, and neighbor count.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: show ipv6 route ospf

question: How many packet types does OSPFv3 use for inter-router communication?

Three
Six
Seven

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What destination address does the OSPFv3 hello packet use?

choices.label: IPv6 address FF02::5 (AllSPFRouters)
IPv6 address FF02::A
IP address 224.0.0.5
MAC address E0:00:00:06:00:AA

explanation: Every OSPFv3 router uses the AllSPFRouters multicast address FF02::5 to send hello messages to routers on the same link.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: How do you enable OSPFv3 on an interface?

choices.label: Use the interface command ospfv3 process-id ipv6 area area-id
Use the command network prefix/prefix-length under the OSPF process
Use the command network interface-id under the OSPF process
Nothing - OSPFv3 is enabled on all IPv6 interfaces when the process is initialized

explanation: OSPFv3 does not use the network statement for initializing interfaces. The interface command ospfv3 process-id ipv6 area area-id enables the protocol and assigns the interface to an area.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: Which statement about forming an OSPFv3 neighborship on a brand-new router is true?

choices.label: It requires a manually assigned router ID in addition to an IPv6 link-local address and OSPFv3 being enabled on the interface
It requires only an IPv6 link-local address and OSPFv3 enabled on the interface
It requires an IPv4 address on the interface
It requires a network statement under the OSPFv3 process

explanation: On IOS routers the OSPFv3 RID must always be manually assigned. If there are no IPv4 interfaces and no manual RID, the RID is set to 0.0.0.0 and adjacencies cannot form.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: True or false: OSPFv3 support for IPv4 networks only requires that an IPv4 address be assigned to the interface and that the OSPFv3 process be initialized for IPv4.

choices.label: False
True

explanation: The IPv4 interface must also have an IPv6 address (global or link-local) configured, then ospfv3 process-id ipv4 area area-id is enabled on the interface.

Inter-area prefix LSA
Link LSA
ASBR summary LSA

explanation: The intra-area prefix LSA and the link LSA advertise IP address information independently, allowing the router LSA to announce only interface parameters.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3

Inter-area prefix LSA
Router LSA
Network LSA

explanation: OSPFv3 renames the ASBR summary LSA (type 4) to inter-area router LSA and the network summary LSA (type 3) to inter-area prefix LSA.

In global configuration mode

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
symptoms: OSPFv3 neighbor adjacencies will not form between routers.
root_cause: The OSPFv3 router ID is not manually assigned, leaving the RID at 0.0.0.0, which does not allow adjacencies to form.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Run show ospfv3 ipv6 neighbor to confirm no neighbors are present.
2. Verify the router ID with show ospfv3 and check for RID 0.0.0.0.
3. Confirm ipv6 unicast-routing is enabled on all routers.
resolution: Assign a unique router-id under each OSPFv3 process using the command router-id router-id.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
symptoms: IPv4 routes are not being exchanged over an OSPFv3 environment that already exchanges IPv6 routes.
root_cause: The ospfv3 process-id ipv4 area area-id command has not been enabled on the interfaces, or the interface lacks an IPv6 address, which is required before enabling IPv4 support.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify an IPv6 address (global or link-local) exists on the IPv4 interfaces.
2. Enable ospfv3 1 ipv4 area area-id on the relevant interfaces.
3. Check show ospfv3 interface brief to confirm both ipv4 and ipv6 address families are listed, then verify routes with show ip route ospfv3.
resolution: Configure ospfv3 process-id ipv4 area area-id on every interface that should exchange IPv4 routes.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
symptoms: An IPv6 summarization is not being advertised into other areas.
root_cause: The area area-id range command is placed under the wrong address family or the summarization is not configured on the ABR.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify the ABR configuration under router ospfv3 and the correct address-family ipv6 unicast.
2. Confirm the summary prefix covers the component routes (mind hex vs decimal hextets).
3. Check show ipv6 route ospf on the remote router for the summary route.
resolution: Place the area area-id range prefix/prefix-length command under the correct address family on the ABR.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
symptoms: A passive interface is still forming adjacencies, or an active interface is not forming adjacencies.
root_cause: The passive-interface command was placed under a single address family instead of the global process, so it did not cascade to both address families.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Check show ospfv3 interface [interface-id] for the Passive keyword.
2. Review the router ospfv3 configuration for the location of the passive-interface command.
3. Confirm whether the command is under the global process or only under an address family.
resolution: Place passive-interface commands under the global OSPFv3 process so the setting cascades to both the IPv4 and IPv6 address families.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
symptoms: An OSPFv3 neighbor over an NBMA interface is not detected.
root_cause: OSPFv3 neighbors are not automatically detected over non-broadcast multiple access (NBMA) interfaces; a neighbor must be manually specified using its link-local address.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Identify the remote router's link-local address on the shared segment.
2. Manually configure the neighbor under the OSPFv3 process.
3. Verify the adjacency with show ospfv3 ipv6 neighbor.
resolution: Manually specify the neighbor using its link-local address because automatic discovery is not available on NBMA interfaces.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What is the correct order of steps to configure OSPFv3 for IPv6?
correct_sequence: 1. Enable ipv6 unicast-routing on the router
2. Initialize the process with router ospfv3 [process-id]
3. Define the router ID with router-id router-id
4. (Optional) Initialize the address family with address-family ipv6 unicast
5. Enable OSPFv3 on each interface with ospfv3 process-id ipv6 area area-id
distractor_sequences: Configure the interface before initializing the process
Use a network statement instead of the interface command
Define the router ID after enabling interfaces
explanation: OSPFv3 configuration follows this sequence: routing must be enabled, the process and RID defined, then the address family initialized (optional) and interfaces enabled individually.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch10: OSPFv3
question: What is the correct order of steps to enable IPv4 support in OSPFv3?
correct_sequence: 1. Ensure the IPv4 interface has an IPv6 address (global or link-local) configured
2. Enable the OSPFv3 process for IPv4 on the interface with ospfv3 process-id ipv4 area area-id
3. Verify the exchange with show ospfv3 interface brief and show ip route ospfv3
distractor_sequences: Enable ipv4 first, then add an IPv6 address
Use the network statement for IPv4 under the OSPFv3 process
Only initialize the IPv4 address family, without enabling interfaces
explanation: IPv4 support requires an IPv6 address on the interface first, then the ospfv3 process-id ipv4 area area-id command enables the IPv4 address family on that interface.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) per RFC 1654?
answer: An Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) standardized routing protocol that provides scalability, flexibility, and network stability. It is the only protocol used to exchange networks on the Internet.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: How does BGP differ from OSPF and IS-IS regarding updates?
answer: BGP does not advertise incremental updates or refresh network advertisements as OSPF and IS-IS do. BGP prefers stability because a link flap could result in route computation for thousands of routes.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is an autonomous system (AS) from BGP's perspective?
answer: A collection of routers under a single organization's control, using one or more IGPs and common metrics to route packets within the AS. An IGP is not required; an AS could use BGP as its only routing protocol.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What was the original ASN size and what RFC expanded it?
answer: ASNs were originally 2 bytes (16-bit range), allowing 65,535 ASNs. RFC 4893 expanded the ASN field to 4 bytes (32-bit range), allowing 4,294,967,295 unique ASNs.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What are the two blocks of private ASNs?
answer: ASNs 64,512 to 65,534 (private in the 16-bit range) and 4,200,000,000 to 4,294,967,294 (private in the extended 32-bit range). They must never be exchanged publicly on the Internet.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: Which RFCs changed the 16-bit private ASN range?
answer: RFC 1930 defined the private ASN range as 64,512 to 65,635, but RFC 6996 changed the 16-bit private ASN range to 64,512 to 65,534. RFC 7300 explains why ASNs 65,535 and 4,294,967,295 should not be used.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: Who is responsible for assigning public ASNs?
answer: The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA), to ensure they are globally unique.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What does IANA require when requesting a public ASN?
answer: Proof of a publicly allocated network range, proof that Internet connectivity is provided through multiple connections, and need for a unique routing policy from providers.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What are the four classifications of BGP path attributes?
answer: Well-known mandatory, well-known discretionary, optional transitive, and optional non-transitive.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What are well-known mandatory path attributes per RFC 4271?
answer: Attributes that must be recognized by all BGP implementations and must be included with every prefix advertisement.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What are well-known discretionary path attributes?
answer: Attributes recognized by all BGP implementations that may or may not be included with a prefix advertisement.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What are optional transitive path attributes?
answer: Attributes that do not have to be recognized by all BGP implementations and stay with the route advertisement from AS to AS.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What are optional non-transitive path attributes?
answer: Attributes that do not have to be recognized by all BGP implementations and cannot be shared from AS to AS.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What type of routing protocol is BGP?
answer: A path vector routing protocol. It does not contain a complete topology of the network as link-state protocols do, and it ensures paths are loop free like distance vector protocols.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is the AS_Path attribute?
answer: A well-known mandatory BGP attribute that includes a complete list of all the ASNs that the prefix advertisement has traversed from its source AS. It is used as a loop-prevention mechanism.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: How does AS_Path prevent routing loops?
answer: If a BGP router receives a prefix advertisement with its AS listed in the AS_Path attribute, it discards the prefix because it thinks the advertisement forms a loop.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What RFC added Multiprotocol BGP (MP-BGP) and what does it add?
answer: RFC 2858 added MP-BGP capability by adding an extension called the address family identifier (AFI).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is an address family and a sub-address family in BGP?
answer: An address family (AFI) correlates to a specific network protocol, such as IPv4 or IPv6. A subsequent address-family identifier (SAFI), such as unicast or multicast, provides additional granularity.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is the Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI)?
answer: The prefix length and the prefix. BGP includes an AFI and SAFI with every route advertisement to differentiate between the AFI/SAFI databases.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: Do different address families maintain separate databases?
answer: Yes. Every address family maintains a separate database and configuration, allowing different routing policies per address family even on the same BGP session.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: How does BGP discover neighbors?
answer: BGP does not use hello packets to discover neighbors, and two BGP neighbors cannot discover each other dynamically like OSPF. BGP neighbors are defined by IP address.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What TCP port does BGP use?
answer: TCP port 179. TCP handles fragmentation, sequencing, and reliability. Recent implementations set the do-not-fragment (DF) bit and rely on path MTU discovery.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: Why can BGP form multi-hop adjacencies while IGPs generally cannot?
answer: IGPs follow the physical topology because their hellos cannot cross network boundaries (single hop only). BGP uses TCP, which is multi-hop capable and can cross network boundaries.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is required for a multi-hop BGP session to establish?
answer: The router must use an underlying route installed in the RIB (static or from any routing protocol) to establish the TCP session with the remote endpoint. A default route is not sufficient.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: How do directly connected BGP neighbors locate each other?
answer: BGP neighbors connected to the same network use the ARP table to locate the IP address of the peer. Multi-hop sessions require routing table information.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is an iBGP session?
answer: A session established with a BGP router in the same AS or in the same BGP confederation. iBGP prefixes are assigned an administrative distance of 200.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is an eBGP session?
answer: A session established with a BGP router in a different AS. eBGP prefixes are assigned an administrative distance of 20.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: Why is a full mesh of iBGP sessions needed inside an AS?
answer: Without iBGP sessions between all routers, intermediate routers would not have the route forwarding information to reach eBGP-learned prefixes, so transit connectivity between autonomous systems would fail.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: Why should BGP tables not be redistributed into an IGP?
answer: Scalability (IGPs cannot handle the 940,000+ Internet prefixes), custom routing (IGPs always use metric, while BGP uses multiple steps and path attributes), and path attributes (IGPs cannot maintain BGP path attributes across the AS).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is the default TTL of eBGP packets, and what is the iBGP TTL?
answer: eBGP packets have a TTL of 1 by default, so multi-hop eBGP sessions drop in transit without modification. iBGP packets use a TTL of 255, allowing multi-hop sessions.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What three behaviors differ on eBGP sessions compared to iBGP?
answer: The advertising router modifies the BGP next-hop address to the IP address sourcing the BGP connection; it prepends its ASN to the AS_Path; and the receiving router verifies the AS_Path does not contain a matching local ASN (loop check).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: How do eBGP and iBGP configurations differ?
answer: The configurations are fundamentally the same except that the ASN in the remote-as statement differs from the ASN defined in the BGP process.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What does an OPEN message contain?
answer: The BGP version number, the ASN of the originating router, the hold time, the BGP identifier, and other optional parameters that establish session capabilities.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: How is the BGP hold time negotiated?
answer: The routers use the smaller hold time value contained in the two routers' OPEN messages. The hold time must be at least 3 seconds, or 0 to disable keepalive messages. Cisco default hold timer is 180 seconds.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is the BGP router ID (RID)?
answer: A 32-bit unique number that identifies the BGP router in the advertised prefixes. It can be used as a loop-prevention mechanism and must be nonzero for routers to become neighbors.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: How often are KEEPALIVE messages exchanged?
answer: Every one-third of the hold timer agreed upon between the two routers. With the Cisco default hold time of 180 seconds, the default keepalive interval is 60 seconds. If hold time is 0, no keepalives are sent.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What does an UPDATE message do?
answer: It advertises feasible routes, withdraws previously advertised routes, or both. It includes advertised prefixes in the NLRI PA and other BGP PAs; withdrawn prefixes are in the WITHDRAWN ROUTES field.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What happens when the BGP hold timer reaches zero?
answer: The BGP session is torn down, routes from that neighbor are removed, and an UPDATE message is sent to other BGP neighbors to withdraw the affected prefixes. An UPDATE can act as a keepalive and resets the hold timer.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: When is a NOTIFICATION message sent?
answer: When an error is detected with the BGP session, such as a hold timer expiring, neighbor capabilities changing, or a BGP session reset being requested. It causes the BGP connection to close.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What are the six BGP FSM states?
answer: Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm, and Established.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What happens in the Idle state?
answer: BGP detects a start event and tries to initiate a TCP connection to the BGP peer while also listening for a new connection from the peer. If BGP returns to Idle a second time, the ConnectRetryTimer is set to 60 seconds, and further failures double it.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What happens in the Connect state?
answer: BGP initiates the TCP connection. If the three-way TCP handshake completes, it resets the ConnectRetryTimer and sends an Open message, then changes to OpenSent. If the timer depletes, it retries in Connect; if TCP fails, it changes to Active.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What happens in the Active state?
answer: BGP starts a new three-way TCP handshake. If a connection is established, an Open message is sent, the hold timer is set to 4 minutes, and the state moves to OpenSent. If the attempt fails, the state moves back to Connect.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is checked when OPEN messages are examined in the OpenSent state?
answer: BGP versions must match; the source IP of the OPEN message must match the configured neighbor; the AS number must match; BGP RIDs must be unique and present; and security parameters (password, TTL) must be set appropriately.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What happens in the OpenConfirm state?
answer: BGP waits for a KEEPALIVE or NOTIFICATION message. Upon receipt of a KEEPALIVE, the state moves to Established. If the hold timer expires or a NOTIFICATION is received, the state moves to Idle.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What happens in the Established state?
answer: The BGP session is established and neighbors exchange routes using UPDATE messages. As UPDATE and KEEPALIVE messages are received, the hold timer is reset. If the hold timer expires, BGP moves the neighbor back to Idle.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What are the components of a basic BGP configuration?
answer: BGP session parameters (ASN of the peer, authentication, keepalive timers), address family initialization, and activating the address family on the BGP peer.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: How is the BGP RID dynamically allocated?
answer: The dynamic RID allocation logic uses the highest IP address of any up loopback interface; if none exists, it uses the highest IP address of any active up interface when the BGP process initializes.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: Why is a static BGP RID a best practice?
answer: To ensure the RID does not change; any IPv4 address can be used, even one not configured on the router. When the router ID changes, all BGP sessions reset and must be reestablished.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What happens when a BGP packet source IP does not match a neighbor table entry?
answer: The packet cannot be associated with a neighbor and is discarded.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What does the command no bgp default ipv4-unicast do?
answer: Disables the automatic activation of the IPv4 address family in IOS XE, making explicit address-family initialization and neighbor activation required.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is the default SAFI for the IPv4 and IPv6 address families on IOS XE?
answer: Unicast, which is optional to specify in the address-family command.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What are the three BGP tables?
answer: Adj-RIB-In (routes in original form before inbound policies; purged after processing to save memory), Loc-RIB (the BGP table with locally originated and received routes after best-path selection), and Adj-RIB-Out (routes after outbound policies).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is the BGP route processing order for received routes?
answer: 1) Store in Adj-RIB-In and apply inbound policy. 2) Update Loc-RIB and clear Adj-RIB-In. 3) Validity check (route valid and next hop resolvable). 4) Identify the BGP best path. 5) Install best path in the RIB, process outbound policy, store in Adj-RIB-Out, and advertise.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is the validity check in BGP route processing?
answer: Verifies that the NLRI is valid and that the next-hop address is resolvable in the RIB. If the check fails, the route remains in the Loc-RIB but is not processed further.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: How many paths does BGP advertise by default?
answer: Only the best path by default, regardless of the number of routes in the Loc-RIB.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What do BGP network statements do?
answer: They do not enable BGP for a specific interface; instead they identify specific network prefixes to be installed into the BGP table (Loc-RIB). BGP searches the RIB for an exact network prefix match.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What BGP path attributes are set for a connected network matched by a network statement?
answer: Next-hop BGP attribute 0.0.0.0, origin attribute i (IGP), and BGP weight 32,768.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What BGP path attributes are set for a static route or routing protocol route matched by a network statement?
answer: Next hop set to the next-hop IP in the RIB, origin set to i (IGP), weight set to 32,768, and MED set to the IGP metric.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is the process for advertising local routes to BGP peers?
answer: 1) Pass a validity check (NLRI valid, next hop resolvable). 2) Process outbound neighbor route policies; non-denied routes are kept in the Adj-RIB-Out. 3) Advertise routes to peers; if the next-hop PA is 0.0.0.0, the next-hop is changed to the IP address of the BGP session.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is the syntax of the BGP network command?
answer: network network mask subnet-mask [route-map route-map-name], residing under the appropriate address family. The optional route-map sets specific BGP PAs when the route installs into the Loc-RIB.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What do the status codes * and > mean in BGP table output?
answer: A valid path is indicated by *; the path selected as the best path is indicated by an angle bracket (>).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What do the origin codes i, e, and ? mean in BGP?
answer: i indicates the route was learned from an IGP (network statement), e indicates EGP, and ? indicates the route was redistributed into BGP (incomplete).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is the Weight column in the BGP table?
answer: A locally significant Cisco-defined attribute used in the BGP best-path algorithm. Routes originated locally show a weight of 32768.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is the LocPrf column in the BGP table?
answer: Local Preference, a well-known discretionary BGP path attribute used in the BGP best-path algorithm for a specific path. Default value is 100.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is the Metric column in the BGP table?

question: What is the Adj-RIB-Out?
answer: A unique table maintained for each BGP peer that enables viewing routes advertised to a specific router. The next-hop reflects the local router and changes as the route advertises to the peer.

question: Is redistributing IGP routes into BGP safe, and is the reverse safe?

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What are the benefits of BGP route summarization (aggregation)?
answer: It conserves router resources, accelerates best-path calculation by reducing table size, and provides stability by hiding route flaps from downstream routers, reducing routing churn.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What are the two techniques for BGP summarization?
answer: Static - create a static route to Null0 for the summary prefix and advertise it with a network statement (the summary is always advertised, even if networks are unavailable). Dynamic - configure an aggregate-address that is created when viable component routes enter the BGP table.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What does the dynamic aggregation technique do for loop prevention?
answer: The originating router sets the next hop to Null0 as a discard route for the aggregated prefix. Because the aggregated prefix is a new route, the summarizing router is the originator.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What does aggregate-address advertise by default?

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is the atomic aggregate attribute?
answer: A BGP attribute that indicates a loss of path information has occurred. When a router summarizes a route, it does not advertise the AS_Path, MED, or BGP communities from before summarization.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What does the as-set keyword do with aggregate-address?
answer: It copies BGP path information from the component routes into the generated summary route. The AS_Path settings are stored in the AS_SET portion of the AS_Path, displayed within brackets, and count as only one hop even if multiple ASNs are listed.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What risk is introduced by using as-set in an aggregate?
answer: If the AS_SET contains an ASN belonging to a receiving router, that router discards the aggregate as a loop because it sees its own ASN in the AS_Path.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
symptoms: A BGP session is stuck in the Idle or Active state and will not establish.
root_cause: TCP connectivity or OPEN validation issues: incorrect neighbor IP, source IP mismatch, AS number mismatch, missing/non-unique BGP RID, or an unavailable route to the peer for multi-hop sessions.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify the neighbor statement matches the actual peer source IP with show bgp ipv4 unicast summary.
2. Confirm connectivity and routing to the peer (ping, show ip route; a default route is not sufficient for multi-hop).
3. Check the BGP RID is statically defined with bgp router-id and unique on both sides.
4. Verify the remote-as matches and that RIDs are nonzero.
resolution: Correct the neighbor configuration, ensure the BGP RID is set, and provide an underlying route in the RIB to the peer address.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
symptoms: A multi-hop eBGP session fails to establish even though the peer is reachable.
root_cause: The default TTL of eBGP packets is 1, so packets drop in transit across multiple hops.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Confirm the peer is more than one hop away.
2. Verify the session state with show bgp ipv4 unicast summary.
3. Configure the eBGP multi-hop TTL on the session.
resolution: Configure the eBGP multi-hop feature (e.g., neighbor ip-address ebgp-multihop) to raise the TTL for the session.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
symptoms: All BGP sessions went down at the same time after a configuration change.
root_cause: The BGP router ID changed; when the router ID changes, all BGP sessions reset and must be reestablished.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Check show bgp ipv4 unicast summary for session state and uptime.
2. Review recent configuration changes with show running-config | section router bgp for the router-id statement.
3. Confirm the static RID is set to prevent future changes.
resolution: Statically configure the BGP RID with bgp router-id router-id and allow sessions to reestablish.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
symptoms: A route is not being advertised even though a network statement exists.
root_cause: BGP requires an exact prefix match in the RIB for the network statement; if the route is missing from the RIB, not activated for the neighbor, or the next hop is not resolvable, the route is not advertised.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify the prefix exists in the RIB with show ip route (exact match required).
2. Check show bgp ipv4 unicast to confirm the prefix is in the Loc-RIB.
3. Verify the address family is activated for the neighbor with show bgp ipv4 unicast summary.
4. Confirm the next hop is resolvable in the RIB.
resolution: Ensure an exact RIB match exists for the network statement, activate the neighbor in the address family, and verify next-hop reachability.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
symptoms: An IPv6 BGP session will not establish on an IPv6-only router.
root_cause: The BGP router ID is not statically defined; routers with only IPv6 addressing must statically define the BGP RID to allow sessions to form.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify the IPv6 address family is initialized and the neighbor activated.
2. Check that a BGP RID is configured with bgp router-id (IPv6-only routers have no IPv4 address for dynamic RID selection).
3. Review show bgp ipv6 unicast summary for the session state.
resolution: Statically define the BGP RID using bgp router-id router-id (an IPv4-format value).

3. Verify the neighbor statement and update the peering configuration.
resolution: Use unique global unicast addressing for BGP peering, or statically assign the link-local address to the interface.

2. (Optional) Statically define the BGP RID with bgp router-id router-id
3. Identify the neighbor and AS with neighbor ip-address remote-as as-number

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is the correct order of the BGP route advertisement process for local routes?
correct_sequence: 1. Pass a validity check (NLRI valid and next hop resolvable in the RIB)
2. Process outbound neighbor route policies and maintain non-denied routes in the Adj-RIB-Out
3. Advertise the routes to BGP peers (changing a next hop of 0.0.0.0 to the BGP session IP)
distractor_sequences: Advertise first, then run the validity check
Skip the outbound policies and advertise everything
Change next hop before the validity check
explanation: Routes pass the validity check, then outbound policies, and only then are advertised to peers with next-hop modification if the next hop was 0.0.0.0.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch11: BGP
question: What is the correct order of BGP route processing for routes received from a peer?
correct_sequence: 1. Store the route in Adj-RIB-In in the original state and apply the inbound route policy
2. Update the Loc-RIB and clear the Adj-RIB-In to save memory
3. Pass the validity check (route valid and next hop resolvable)
4. Identify the BGP best path
5. Install the best path in the RIB, process outbound policy, store in Adj-RIB-Out, and advertise
distractor_sequences: Apply outbound policy before inbound policy
Run the best-path algorithm before the validity check
Install all paths in the RIB, not just the best path
explanation: Received routes flow from Adj-RIB-In through inbound policy into the Loc-RIB, pass validation, best-path selection, then are installed in the RIB and advertised.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch12: Advanced BGP
question: What is BGP's default behavior when advertising routes to the RIB?
answer: BGP advertises only the best path to the RIB, so only one path for a network prefix is used when forwarding traffic to a destination.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch12: Advanced BGP
question: Why might an organization use a different service provider for each circuit?
answer: The choice typically comes down to cost, circuit availability for remote locations, or separation of the control plane. If one SP has problems, traffic can still flow across the other SP.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch12: Advanced BGP
question: What is transit routing in the context of a multihomed enterprise network?
answer: When an enterprise connects to more than one service provider, its AS can become a transit AS, carrying traffic from other ASs across its network (e.g., a user on SP3 routes through the enterprise network to reach a server on SP4).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch12: Advanced BGP
question: How can an enterprise avoid becoming a transit AS on the Internet?
answer: By applying outbound BGP route policies that only allow local BGP routes to be advertised to other autonomous systems (route filtering).

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch12: Advanced BGP
question: What does it mean for a flow between sites to be deterministic?
answer: The path is considered deterministic when the flow between sites is predetermined and predictable (symmetric traffic using the preferred SP in both directions), which simplifies troubleshooting.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch12: Advanced BGP
question: Why should branch routers not act as transit routers in a multihomed environment?
answer: WAN bandwidth may not be sized accordingly. Unplanned transit can oversaturate circuits and make routing unpredictable and nondeterministic, complicating troubleshooting.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch12: Advanced BGP
question: How is transit routing avoided at branch sites in most designs?
answer: By configuring outbound route filtering at each branch site so branches advertise only networks that face the LAN, not what they learn from the WAN. If transit is required, it is restricted to data centers or planned locations.

source: ENCOR 350-401 - Ch12: Advanced BGP
question: Why is transit routing at data centers or planned locations acceptable in enterprise designs?
answer: Because bandwidth can be sized accordingly, proper routing design can accommodate outages, and the routing pattern is bidirectional and predictable.
