source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: Which statement correctly distinguishes ext2, ext3, and ext4?

choices.label: ext2 adds journaling, ext3 is for swap, ext4 is for LVM
ext2 has no journaling, ext3 adds journaling, and ext4 is its successor supporting larger volumes and files
All three are identical except for their maximum file size
ext4 is the oldest and ext2 is the newest

explanation: ext2 (earlier Linux default) has no journaling; ext3 adds journaling for better crash recovery; ext4 is the successor with improvements such as volumes up to 1 exbibyte and file sizes up to 16 tebibytes.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: Which filesystem is the default root filesystem type for RHEL?

choices.label: ext4
btrfs
xfs
ext3

explanation: xfs, the high-performance filesystem originally developed by Silicon Graphics, is the default root filesystem type for RHEL. btrfs is the default on the latest Fedora.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: Which statement correctly describes MBR vs GPT partition size limits?

choices.label: MBR supports up to 9.4 ZB and GPT is limited to 2TB
MBR partitions are limited to 2TB while GPT can create partitions up to 9.4 zettabytes
Both support the same maximum partition size
GPT partitions are limited to 32GB

explanation: The MBR specification limits partitions to 2TB, which drove the need for GUID partition tables that can create partitions up to 9.4 ZB.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: Which tool is used to handle GPT partition tables?

choices.label: fdisk, which fully supports GPT
parted, because the popular fdisk command does not support gpt partitions
mkswap
mkfs

explanation: Because the popular fdisk command does not support gpt partitions, the chapter uses parted to illustrate partitioning with GPT.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: What is a key behavioral difference between parted and fdisk?

choices.label: fdisk saves changes immediately while parted waits for w
parted makes changes immediately, so you cannot just type q to abandon them, whereas fdisk with q exits without saving
Neither lets you abandon changes
both require typing w to write changes

explanation: fdisk lets you type q to exit without saving, but parted applies changes immediately, so a mistake must be corrected before continuing.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: What filesystem does the mkfs command create when no -t option is given?

choices.label: ext4
ext2
xfs
vfat

explanation: By default, mkfs creates an ext2 filesystem. For a journaling filesystem (ext3, ext4, xfs) you must specify the type with -t.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: How are SCSI devices named compared to NVMe devices?

choices.label: SCSI uses sda/sdb, NVMe uses nvme0n1 with namespaces and partitions
Both use the same sd naming
NVMe uses sda/sdb, SCSI uses nvme0n1
SCSI names have no partitions

explanation: SCSI/USB devices use sd? names (sda, sdb) with up to 15 partitions, while NVMe devices use names like /dev/nvme0n1p1 (first partition, first namespace, first NVMe SSD).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: What is the purpose of an extended partition?

choices.label: It is a special swap partition
It is a container for logical partitions so a disk can have more than four total partitions
It speeds up disk I/O
It stores the boot loader only

explanation: Since x86 disks can have at most four primary partitions, one partition must be an extended partition that acts as a container for logical partitions.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: Which pair of commands creates and then enables a swap area?

choices.label: mkfs and mount
mkswap and swapon
swapon and swapoff
mkswap and swapoff

explanation: mkswap formats a partition or file as a swap area, and swapon enables it so the system can use it as swap space.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: Which statement about LVM's ability to shrink filesystems is correct?

choices.label: Shrinking a logical volume requires no unmount and no reboot
Shrinking requires unmounting the logical volume, but no reboot is needed
LVM cannot shrink filesystems at all
Shrinking requires a reboot to take effect

explanation: With LVM it is easier to shrink filesystems, but shrinking does require that you unmount the logical volume; no reboot is needed. Growing can be done while in use.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: Which command creates an LVM physical volume?

choices.label: vgcreate
pvcreate
lvcreate
mkfs

explanation: pvcreate identifies a partition as an LVM physical volume; vgcreate builds a volume group from physical volumes, and lvcreate creates logical volumes from a volume group.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: Which set of names refers to the same LVM logical volume?

choices.label: /dev/vg_abc/lv_root and /dev/mapper/vg_abc-lv_root
/dev/sda1 and /dev/vg_abc/lv_root
/dev/nvme0n1p1 and /dev/mapper/vg_abc-lv_root
/dev/mapper/myvg0 and /dev/myvg0/lv_root

explanation: A logical volume has a device name including the volume group and logical volume name (e.g. /dev/vg_abc/lv_root) and an equivalent /dev/mapper name (vg_abc-lv_root); either can be used.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: Which command is used to detach a filesystem from a mount point?

choices.label: mount
umount
mkfs
df

explanation: umount detaches a filesystem from its mount point; mount connects filesystems, mkfs creates them, and df shows disk usage.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: What does mount -a do at boot?

choices.label: It mounts only removable media
It mounts all filesystems listed in /etc/fstab
It unmounts all filesystems
It checks filesystems for errors

explanation: Linux runs mount -a (mount all filesystems from /etc/fstab) each time you boot, which is how regular partitions get mounted automatically.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: Which statement about umount -l and umount -f is correct?

choices.label: -l forces unmount and -f unmounts lazily
-l is a lazy unmount (happens when no longer busy) and -f forcibly unmounts, e.g. an unavailable NFS filesystem
Both do exactly the same thing
-f is lazy and -l is only for local filesystems

explanation: umount -l performs a lazy unmount that completes once the device is no longer busy; umount -f forcibly unmounts, useful for a remote NFS filesystem whose server went down.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: Which option mounts a disk image file using a loop device?

choices.label: -o ro
-o loop
-t iso
-a

explanation: mount -o loop image.iso /mnt/mydvdimage mounts a disk image file locally so you can view and copy its contents without burning it.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: After writing a partition table with fdisk, how does the kernel learn about the changes without a reboot?

choices.label: Automatically with no further action
By running partprobe /dev/sda
By running mkfs
By editing /etc/fstab

explanation: After a write, the kernel still uses old partitions; run partprobe /dev/sda (or reboot) so the kernel re-reads the partition table. Verify with grep sda /proc/partitions.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: Compare /proc/filesystems and /proc/partitions.

choices.label: /proc/filesystems lists kernel-supported filesystem types and /proc/partitions lists partitions the kernel knows about
Both list the same partitions
/proc/partitions lists filesystem types and /proc/filesystems lists partitions
Neither is related to storage

explanation: cat /proc/filesystems shows filesystem types supported by the kernel, while grep sda /proc/partitions shows the partition devices the kernel currently knows about.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: What is the purpose of using a UUID in the first field of /etc/fstab?

choices.label: It makes the file smaller
It identifies a filesystem uniquely so a device-name change (e.g. a new disk becoming /dev/sda) doesn't break the mount
It is required by the kernel and nothing else can be used
It speeds up mounting

explanation: Device names can change (a newly plugged disk might become /dev/sda), so a UUID uniquely identifies the filesystem regardless of its device name, avoiding mount errors.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: Which fstab field controls the fsck check order?

choices.label: Field 3 (filesystem type)
Field 6 (a number: 1 first, 2 after, 0 don't check)
Field 4 (mount options)
Field 1 (device)

explanation: Field 6 indicates whether and in what order the filesystem is checked with fsck: 1 = check first, 2 = check after those marked 1, 0 = don't check. Field 5 is the dump (backup) flag.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: Which sequence correctly creates a usable LVM logical volume?

choices.label: lvcreate, vgcreate, pvcreate
pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate
vgcreate, lvcreate, pvcreate
mkfs, pvcreate, vgcreate

explanation: LVM is built from the bottom up: create a physical volume (pvcreate), use it to create a volume group (vgcreate), then create a logical volume (lvcreate) from that group.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: Why should you practice partitioning on a USB flash drive rather than your primary hard disk?

choices.label: USB drives are faster
A mistake changing partitions can make your system unbootable, and a bad /etc/fstab entry can hang the system on reboot
Primary disks cannot be partitioned
USB drives support more partition types

explanation: Changing partitioning can make a system unbootable, and a bad /etc/fstab entry can hang the system during reboot, so practice on a USB flash drive you don't mind erasing.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: What is the correct general procedure to add a new storage medium so Linux can use it?
correct_sequence: 1. Install the new hard drive or insert the new USB flash drive
2. Partition the new disk
3. Create the filesystems on the new disk
4. Mount the filesystems
distractor_sequences: 1. Create filesystems, 2. mount, 3. partition
1. Mount, 2. create filesystems, 3. install
explanation: The device is installed first, then partitioned, then filesystems are created on the partitions, and finally mounted so the data becomes accessible.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: What is the correct order to create a single-partition USB disk with parted?
correct_sequence: 1. Plug in the USB drive and find its device name (journalctl -f)
2. Unmount any auto-mounted partitions (umount /dev/sda1)
3. Delete existing partitions with parted (p then rm)
4. Relabel the disk: mklabel gpt
5. Create a partition: mkpart (name, filesystem type, start, end)
6. Print and exit (p, then q)
7. Create a filesystem: mkfs -t xfs /dev/sda1
distractor_sequences: 1. mkfs first, 2. then parted mkpart
1. mklabel, 2. mkfs, 3. mount, 4. umount, 5. delete partitions
explanation: You must identify and unmount the device, delete old partitions, set the label, create a new partition, then format the filesystem before the partition can be used.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: What is the correct order to create and use a new LVM logical volume from scratch?
correct_sequence: 1. Create an LVM-type partition (8e) on the disk
2. Create a physical volume: pvcreate /dev/sda6
3. Create a volume group: vgcreate myvg0 /dev/sda6
4. Create a logical volume: lvcreate -n music -L 1G myvg0
5. Create a filesystem on the logical volume: mkfs -t ext4 /dev/mapper/myvg0-music
6. Make a mount point and mount it: mkdir /mnt/mymusic; mount /dev/mapper/myvg0-music /mnt/mymusic
distractor_sequences: 1. lvcreate, 2. pvcreate, 3. vgcreate
1. mkfs, 2. mount, 3. pvcreate, 4. vgcreate
explanation: LVM is created from the bottom up: partition, then physical volume, then volume group, then logical volume, then filesystem, then mount.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: What is the correct order to grow an LVM logical volume?
correct_sequence: 1. Check available space in the volume group: vgdisplay myvg0
2. Check the current filesystem size: df -h /mnt/mymusic/
3. Expand the logical volume: lvextend -L +1G /dev/mapper/myvg0-music
4. Resize the filesystem to fill it: resize2fs -p /dev/mapper/myvg0-music
5. Verify the new size: df -h /mnt/mymusic/
distractor_sequences: 1. resize2fs, 2. lvextend, 3. vgdisplay
1. Reduce the volume group, 2. then grow the filesystem
explanation: You confirm there is free space in the volume group and record the current size, extend the logical volume, then grow the filesystem to fill it, and verify with df.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: What is the correct order to create and enable a swap file?
correct_sequence: 1. Check current swap: free -m
2. Create a swap file: dd if=/dev/zero of=/var/opt/myswap bs=1M count=1024
3. Restrict permissions: chmod 600 /var/opt/myswap
4. Format it as swap: mkswap /var/opt/myswap
5. Enable it: swapon /var/opt/myswap
6. Verify: free -m
distractor_sequences: 1. swapon, 2. mkswap, 3. dd
1. chmod, 2. free, 3. swapon, 4. dd
explanation: A file is created, restricted to root, formatted with mkswap, and then enabled with swapon so the additional swap is immediately available.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: What is the correct order to view the contents of a downloaded ISO image without burning it?
correct_sequence: 1. Create a mount point: mkdir /mnt/mydvdimage
2. Mount the image with the loop option: mount -o loop whatever-i686-disc1.iso /mnt/mydvdimage
3. cd to the mount point and view/copy the contents
4. Unmount the image: umount /mnt/mydvdimage
distractor_sequences: 1. mount first, 2. mkdir the mount point afterward
1. Copy files, 2. mount, 3. umount, 4. mkdir
explanation: The mount point must exist before mounting, and after browsing the contents you unmount the image with umount.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: What is the correct order to set up multiple partitions with fdisk?
correct_sequence: 1. Overwrite the drive for a fresh MBR: dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/sdX bs=1M count=100
2. Run fdisk /dev/sda and create partitions with n (using sizes like +5G)
3. Where needed, create an extended partition to hold logical partitions
4. Change partition types with t (82 swap, c FAT32, 8e LVM)
5. Check the table with p and write it with w
6. Run partprobe /dev/sda and verify with grep sda /proc/partitions
distractor_sequences: 1. fdisk, 2. partprobe, 3. dd, 4. w
1. Write with w before creating partitions
explanation: A fresh MBR is created, partitions are defined with sizes (remember to include + and M/G), types are set, the table is written, and the kernel is updated with partprobe.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
question: What is the correct order to make a swap area permanent across reboots?
correct_sequence: 1. Format and enable the swap area (mkswap and swapon)
2. Test it is working, e.g. swapon -a
3. Add a line to /etc/fstab (e.g. /var/opt/myswap swap swap defaults 0 0)
4. Verify on next boot it is enabled
distractor_sequences: 1. Edit /etc/fstab before creating the swap
1. Remove the entry, 2. add the entry back permanently
explanation: For permanent swap you must add an /etc/fstab entry; the swap area's device/file, filesystem type 'swap', mount point 'swap', and options defaults 0 0 are listed, and swapon -a enables everything in fstab at boot.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
symptoms: umount fails with the message 'device is busy' when trying to unmount a filesystem.
root_cause: Either an application has a file open on the device or a shell is open with a directory on the device as its current directory, keeping the device busy.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Identify what is holding the device open: lsof /mnt/test or fuser -v /mnt/test
2. Stop the processes using the device
3. Change to a directory outside the device (cd /) if a shell was using it
4. Retry umount /mnt/test
resolution: Stop the processes or leave the directory, then umount succeeds. Alternatively use a lazy unmount (umount -l) so it happens when the device is no longer busy.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
symptoms: After writing a new partition table with fdisk, the new partitions are not visible.
root_cause: The fdisk write message indicates the kernel still uses the old partition table; the new table is used only at the next reboot until the kernel is told to re-read it.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Check the kernel's view: grep sda /proc/partitions
2. Tell the kernel to re-read the partition table: partprobe /dev/sda
3. Re-check grep sda /proc/partitions to confirm the new partitions appear
resolution: Run partprobe /dev/sda (or reboot the computer) so the kernel recognizes the newly written partitions.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
symptoms: After changing disk partitions, the system fails to boot, or hangs on reboot.
root_cause: A partitioning mistake can render the system unbootable, and a bad entry in /etc/fstab can hang the system during reboot.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Refer to Chapter 21 'Troubleshooting Linux' for boot recovery procedures
2. Correct or remove any bad /etc/fstab entries (e.g. from a mount point on a removed device)
3. Repair or reinstall the boot/partition setup as needed
resolution: Fix the partition table or /etc/fstab. Avoid practicing partitioning on the primary hard disk; use a USB flash drive you don't mind erasing.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
symptoms: A USB flash drive providing a swap partition can't be removed safely.
root_cause: The swap area on the device is still enabled and in use, so the device is busy and cannot be removed.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Check swap usage: free -m
2. Disable the swap area: swapoff /dev/sdX (make sure no space is in use)
3. Remove the device safely
resolution: Use swapoff to turn off the swap area so the space can be reclaimed and the USB drive removed safely.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
symptoms: Mounting a Windows disk fails because the filesystem type is not supported or has no driver.
root_cause: NTFS (and sometimes exFAT) require additional kernel drivers that are not installed on every Linux system.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Confirm the filesystem type with blkid
2. Install the needed package, e.g. ntfs-3g on Fedora/Ubuntu (or use VFAT/exFAT where supported)
3. Mount the filesystem again
resolution: Install the appropriate driver/package (such as ntfs-3g) or use a filesystem type the kernel supports (like vfat/exfat), then mount.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
symptoms: A logical volume is full, but the filesystem cannot be grown despite extending the logical volume.
root_cause: Growing a logical volume with lvextend is not enough; the filesystem structure still occupies only the old size until it is resized to fill the logical volume.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Confirm free space in the volume group: vgdisplay myvg0
2. Grow the logical volume: lvextend -L +1G /dev/mapper/myvg0-music
3. Resize the filesystem: resize2fs -p /dev/mapper/myvg0-music
4. Verify the new size: df -h /mnt/mymusic/
resolution: Run resize2fs -p to grow the filesystem to fill the larger logical volume; then the added space becomes available (growing works without unmounting).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
symptoms: A remote NFS or CIFS share listed in /etc/fstab fails to mount at boot.
root_cause: The network may not be up yet when the filesystem is mounted, so network-based mounts fail.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Add the _netdev option to the mount options (Field 4) of the share's /etc/fstab entry
2. (For CIFS) the guest option may also be needed for guest shares
3. Reboot or run mount -a after the network is up
4. Verify with mount
resolution: Add the _netdev option so Linux waits for the network to come up before trying to mount network shares.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
symptoms: An ISO image listed in fstab or mounted manually fails or warns, or mounting an image without preparing fails.
root_cause: A filesystem image needs a loop device; if the mount point does not exist or the -o loop option is missing, the loop mount cannot proceed.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Create the mount point: mkdir /mnt/mydvdimage
2. Mount with the loop option: mount -o loop image.iso /mnt/mydvdimage
3. Browse contents, then unmount with umount /mnt/mydvdimage
resolution: Ensure the mount point exists and use mount -o loop to mount the disk image via a loop device.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch12: Managing Disks and Filesystems
symptoms: A partitioning command affects the wrong disk, risking loss of data.
root_cause: Partitioning (especially dd and fdisk) operates on whatever device name you give; if you identify the wrong disk, you can erase the operating system or valuable data.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Identify the exact device with journalctl -f / parted -l / blkid before acting
2. Verify the correct drive number before any destructive command (dd, mklabel, delete)
3. Unmount any partitions that mounted automatically
4. Test any new filesystem on a disposable USB drive first
resolution: Double-check the device name before destructive operations; practice on a USB flash drive you don't mind erasing to avoid losing data from disks you want to keep.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What is a daemon process?
answer: A process that runs continuously in the background and responds to requests that come to it. Most servers are represented by daemon processes that serve data to remote clients or the local system.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What are the five basic steps for setting up any Linux server?
answer: 1) Install the server, 2) Configure the server, 3) Start the server, 4) Secure the server, 5) Monitor the server.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What are the two major facilities for managing services in Linux?
answer: systemd (used now by RHEL, Ubuntu, and Fedora) and SystemV init scripts (used by RHEL through RHEL 6.x and rarely used anymore).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: Why do daemon processes often run as users and groups other than root (such as httpd running as apache)?
answer: For security: if someone cracks these daemons, they would not have permissions to access files beyond what the services can access.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What is the purpose of files in the /etc/sysconfig directory?
answer: They are daemon configuration files whose job is often just to pass arguments to the server process itself rather than configure the service. For example, options in /etc/sysconfig/rsyslogd are passed to the rsyslogd daemon when it starts.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What is 'security by obscurity' as described in relation to sshd?
answer: Changing the well-known port number a service listens on (for example, moving sshd from TCP port 22 to an unused high port) in the hope that port scanners will be less likely to scan that normally unused port.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What was the xinetd super server and what happened to it?
answer: An older system used to run services on demand rather than continuously. Recent xinetd services in RHEL/Fedora (telnet, tftp) were converted to systemd services; the xinetd package was dropped from Fedora in release 34 but is still available in Ubuntu.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: Which package is used most often to provide print server features on Linux systems?
answer: The Common UNIX Printing Service, the cups package.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: Which package provides the Apache web server in Fedora/RHEL and Ubuntu respectively?
answer: httpd on Fedora/RHEL and apache2 on Ubuntu.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What is the default FTP server used in Fedora and RHEL?
answer: The Very Secure FTP daemon (vsftpd package). Other FTP servers include proftpd and pure-ftpd.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What does the Samba package allow a Linux system to do?
answer: Act as a Windows file and print server (installed with the smb-server group).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What is Network File System (NFS) and which package provides it?
answer: NFS is the standard Linux and UNIX feature for providing shared directories to other systems over a network; the nfs-utils package provides NFS services and related commands.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What is a Mail Transport Agent (MTA) and which MTA is the default in Fedora and RHEL?
answer: An MTA is an email server. Choices include sendmail, postfix (the default in Fedora and RHEL), and exim. Related packages such as dovecot deliver email to clients.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: Which packages provide directory/authentication server services?
answer: Kerberos (krb5-server), LDAP (openldap-servers), and NIS (ypserv), installed with the directory-server group.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What does the Berkeley Internet Name Domain (BIND) service provide?
answer: The software needed to configure a server to resolve hostnames into IP addresses. Optional packages include dnsperf (benchmarking) and nsd (NLnet Labs Name Server Daemon).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: Which packages provide Network Time Protocol (NTP) server service?
answer: ntpd or chronyd, which sync your system clock with clocks from public or private NTP servers.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What SQL database servers are available for Linux and which has supplanted MySQL on many distributions?
answer: PostgreSQL (object-relational) and MySQL; the community-developed branch MariaDB has supplanted MySQL on many Linux distributions.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: How do mail servers (sendmail/postfix) and DNS servers (bind) behave after a default install?
answer: They are installed with default configurations and start on reboot but only listen for requests on localhost, so remote users cannot use them until configured.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What is the main Apache (httpd) configuration file and its configuration directory in Fedora and RHEL?
answer: The main configuration file is /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf and the configuration directory is /etc/httpd/conf.d/ where add-on packages drop .conf files that get included.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: Why is vim recommended over vi for editing configuration files?
answer: vim knows the formats of many configuration files (passwd, httpd.conf, fstab, and others); if you type an invalid term or break the format, the color of the text changes, helping you catch errors.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: Why are RPM packages installed with minimal configuration?
answer: Because RPM packages are designed to be installed unattended, files are placed in set locations and the software starts with limited accessibility; you are expected to configure the software after installation to make the server fully functional.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What is a good password protection technique for SSH servers?
answer: Disallow direct login by root and require every user to log in as a regular user and then use su or sudo to become root. Also use PAM to limit failed login attempts.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What is the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) facility?
answer: A facility used to adjust the number of times someone can have failed login attempts before blocking access, plus other features for locking down authentication to a Linux server.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What does the legacy iptables firewall do?
answer: It tracks and responds to every packet coming from and going to network interfaces, and can drop or reject packets requesting services except those you have enabled, and can allow requests only from certain IP addresses.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: How do firewalld and ufw build on iptables?
answer: firewalld (Fedora/RHEL) lets you organize firewall rules into zones and change rules on the fly; ufw (Ubuntu) provides a simple interface for allowing and denying access to ports on the local system.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What is the major function of SELinux?
answer: To protect the contents of your Linux system from the processes running on it, restricting what files (via file contexts), features (via Booleans), and ports a web, FTP, Samba, or DNS server can access.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What is the rsyslog service?
answer: A service (rsyslogd daemon) that gathers log messages from software on the system and directs them to local log files, devices, or remote logging hosts. By default messages go to files in /var/log.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What does logwatch do?
answer: It runs from a cron job once each night, scans log files, gathers critical information and error conditions, and emails them to an administrator-chosen address.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What does logrotate do?
answer: It backs up log files into compressed archives when the logs reach a certain size or pass a set amount of time since the previous backup.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What is the sar facility and which package enables it?
answer: The System Activity Reporter (sysstat package) watches activities such as memory usage, CPU usage, disk latency, and network activity. By default it launches the sadc program every few minutes to gather data that can be reviewed later.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What is Cockpit and how do you access it?
answer: A web console that lets you watch system activity in real time (CPU, memory and swap, disk I/O, network traffic). Open your browser to https://localhost:9090.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: How do you check whether installed files have been tampered with (signs of crackers)?
answer: Run the rpm -V command, which checks whether commands, document files, or configuration files have been tampered with on the system.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What are the Secure Shell (SSH) tools?
answer: A set of client and server applications for secure communication between clients and servers: ssh, scp, sftp, and related tools. Because communication is encrypted, they replace telnet, rlogin, rsh, and rcp.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: Which packages contain the SSH client and server tools in Fedora/RHEL/Ubuntu?
answer: openssh, openssh-clients, and openssh-server packages. On Ubuntu only openssh-clients is installed by default; install the server with sudo apt-get install openssh-server.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What does the PermitRootLogin setting control in /etc/ssh/sshd_config?
answer: prohibit-password (the default) prevents logging in as root remotely with a password but allows key-based authentication; no stops anyone from remotely logging in as root at all.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: Where is the remote host's public key stored after the first successful SSH connection?
answer: In the client's ~/.ssh/known_hosts file, along with the remote host's IP address. The server's own public and private keys are stored in /etc/ssh.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What encryption does SSH use after you accept a host key?
answer: RSA asymmetric encryption - data exchanged between the client and server can be encrypted and decrypted using the key pair.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What happens if a server's SSH key changes (reinstall or key rotation)?
answer: Attempts to ssh to that system result in a refused connection and dire warnings that you may be under attack. To fix, remove the host's key line from known_hosts and accept the new key.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What is X11 forwarding and how is it enabled?
answer: It lets you run graphical applications from a server securely over an SSH connection using ssh -Y. It requires X11Forwarding yes in /etc/sshd/sshd_config.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What does the sftp command provide?
answer: An interactive FTP-style session over the SSH service. Despite its name it has nothing to do with the FTP protocol and doesn't use FTP servers; it uses an FTP style of interaction between a client and an sshd server.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: How does key-based (passwordless) authentication work?
answer: You create a public/private key pair, guard the private key, and copy the public key to the user account on the remote host. The remote SSH service then compares the two keys and allows access if they match, without asking for a password.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What is the risk of creating a key with no passphrase?
answer: If someone gets hold of your private key, they could act as you in any communication that required that key. A passphrase unlocks the private key even though a password is not needed to authenticate.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: Where must a user's public key be placed to allow key-based authentication?
answer: Copied into the authorized_keys file in the user's .ssh directory on the remote system (done with ssh-copy-id).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What effect does setting PasswordAuthentication no in sshd_config have?
answer: Anyone with a valid key is still accepted, but anyone trying to log in without a key gets Permission denied (publickey,gssapi-keyex,gssapi-with-mic) and cannot even enter a username and password.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What are the shortcomings of scp as a backup tool?
answer: Permissions and date/time stamp attributes are lost; symbolic links are followed rather than copied; and unchanged files are copied again every time because scp cannot tell that a file was already copied.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: Why is rsync a better network backup tool than scp?
answer: rsync can determine that a file has already been copied and not copy it again, preserves symbolic links (with -l) and time stamps (with -a), saving network bandwidth for directories where only a few files change.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What does the --delete option do in rsync?
answer: It deletes files on the destination that no longer exist on the source, making the remote and local directory structures mirror each other exactly.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What are the five main parts of a message in /var/log/messages?
answer: The date and time logged, the name of the computer the message came from, the program or service name, the process number (in square brackets), and the actual text message.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: How are rsyslog rule entries structured in /etc/rsyslog.conf?
answer: Two columns: the left designates what messages are matched (facility.priority, e.g. mail.info) and the right shows where matched messages go (file, device, or @loghost).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What does the @ sign indicate in the destination column of an rsyslog rule?
answer: That the name that follows is the name of a loghost; for example *.* @loghost sends all messages via UDP to the computer named loghost.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What does the minus sign before a log file name (such as -/var/log/maillog) mean in rsyslog?
answer: It means not to sync the log file after each write (which is actually the default).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: Name some rsyslog modules and their purposes.
answer: imjournal gives access to the systemd journal; imuxsock accepts messages from the local system; imklog logs kernel messages; immark provides -- MARK -- messages indicating a service is alive; imudp and imtcp allow accepting remote log messages on port 514.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What is the security benefit of remote logging to a dedicated loghost?
answer: If a system is broken into, the cracker cannot delete or modify log files stored on a separate computer. Running a dedicated loghost makes it nearly impossible for crackers to erase their tracks completely.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: Why use the name 'loghost' as an alias for the remote logging computer?
answer: So that if you need to switch loghost duties to a different machine, you only change the loghost alias instead of re-editing rsyslog.conf on every computer.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: On which standard port does a loghost listen for remote log messages?
answer: UDP port 514, although it can be configured to accept messages on TCP port 514 as well.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What does the RemoteLogs template in rsyslog do?
answer: It defines where remote logs are stored, e.g. $template RemoteLogs,"/var/log/remotelogs/%HOSTNAME%/%PROGRAMNAME%.log" - one directory per host and one file per program.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What does sar -u show?
answer: CPU usage, broken into %user, %nice, %system, %iowait, %steal, and %idle, output every 10 minutes starting at midnight by default.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What does sar -d show?
answer: Disk activity output (tps, rkB/s, wkB/s, and more) in 10-minute intervals starting at midnight.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: How do you run sar live at intervals?
answer: Add counts and time intervals to the command line, e.g. sar -n DEV 5 2 takes network interface samples every 5 seconds, repeated 2 times.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: Where does the sysstat/sar facility store gathered data?
answer: In /var/log/sa/sa?? files, which can be read later with certain options to the sar command.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What do the df options -t, -x, -a, -i, and --block-size do?
answer: -t prints only filesystems of a particular type; -x excludes filesystems of a particular type; -a includes filesystems with no space such as /proc and /dev/pts; -i lists available and used inodes; --block-size=# displays disk space in certain block sizes.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What does the du command do?
answer: Lists all directories below the current directory along with the space consumed by each, and at the end produces total disk space used within that directory structure. Add -h for human-readable and -s for a summary total.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What does the -xdev option of find do?
answer: It prevents filesystems other than the selected filesystem from being searched, cutting out junk from /proc and avoiding large, remotely mounted filesystems.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: How does PXE booting help with automated deployments?
answer: By setting up a PXE server and booting a computer from a PXE-enabled NIC, you can start a full install simply by booting the system; once the install is done, the system reboots to run from the installed system.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: What is the separation of management and worker systems in enterprise computing?
answer: A platform such as Kubernetes or VMware vCenter has management/control-plane nodes that manage the machines (workers/nodes) where workloads run, allowing applications to be deployed on any available worker meeting the application's needs.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: sudo dnf group list --hidden | grep -i server
answer: Lists installed and available server package groups in Fedora/RHEL (mail-server, network-server, smb-server, sql-server, directory-server, dns-server, ftp-server, and so on).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: sudo dnf group install web-server
answer: Installs the web-server group (Apache httpd and required/related packages) on Fedora or RHEL. Add --with-optional to install optional packages for the group.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: dnf group install web-server --with-optional
answer: Installs the web-server group including the optional packages.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: dnf list --installed | grep openssh
answer: Lists the installed openssh packages on Fedora/RHEL (openssh, openssh-clients, openssh-server).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: sudo apt-get install openssh-server
answer: Installs the SSH server package on Ubuntu (only openssh-clients is installed by default).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: sudo systemctl status sshd.service
answer: Checks the status of the SSH server service on RHEL/Fedora (Ubuntu uses ssh.service).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: sudo systemctl start sshd.service
answer: Starts the sshd service on RHEL/Fedora (use ssh.service on Ubuntu).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: sudo systemctl enable sshd.service
answer: Sets the sshd service to start automatically at boot on RHEL/Fedora.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: ssh johndoe@10.140.67.23
answer: Logs in to the account johndoe on the remote system at 10.140.67.23 over an encrypted SSH connection. The first time, you are asked to accept the host's key fingerprint.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: ssh johndoe@10.140.67.23 hostname
answer: Executes the hostname command on the remote system and displays the output (e.g. host01.example.com) on the local screen - remote execution with ssh.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: ssh johndoe@10.140.67.23 "cat myfile"
answer: Runs a remote command with options/arguments; quote the whole remote command line. Relative paths are interpreted relative to the user's home directory.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: ssh -Y johndoe@10.140.67.23 xterm
answer: Uses X11 forwarding to run the xterm graphical application from the remote system, displaying it on the local desktop.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: scp /etc/services johndoe@10.140.67.23:/tmp
answer: Securely copies the local /etc/services file to the /tmp directory on the remote system as user johndoe, with encryption.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: scp -r johndoe@10.140.67.23:/usr/share/man/man1/ /tmp/
answer: Recursively copies an entire directory tree from the remote system to the local /tmp directory using scp with the -r option.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: rsync -avl johndoe@10.140.67.23:/usr/share/man/man1/ /tmp/
answer: Copies files from the remote system with -a (recursive archive), -v (verbose), and -l (copy symbolic links). Only changed files are copied on subsequent runs.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: rsync -avl --delete johndoe@10.140.67.23:/usr/share/man/man1 /tmp
answer: Mirrors the remote directory to local /tmp; the --delete option removes local files that no longer exist on the remote side so the two trees match exactly.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: sftp johndoe@jd.example.com
answer: Starts an interactive FTP-style session over SSH; you can use get and put commands on files over an encrypted and secure connection.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: ssh-keygen
answer: Generates a public/private SSH key pair; by default an ed25519 key saved as ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (private) and ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub (public). rsa and ecdsa keys are also allowed.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub johndoe@10.140.67.23
answer: Copies your public key to the authorized_keys file in johndoe's .ssh directory on the remote system so key-based authentication works for future connections.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: systemctl restart sshd
answer: Restarts the sshd service to apply changes to /etc/ssh/sshd_config.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: journalctl
answer: Displays log messages directly from the systemd journal instead of viewing them from files in the /var/log directory.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: systemctl restart rsyslog
answer: Restarts the rsyslog service so changes to /etc/rsyslog.conf (such as directing logs to a loghost) take effect.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: ss -tupln | grep 514
answer: Shows that the rsyslogd daemon is listening on IPv4 and IPv6 UDP and TCP ports 514 (remote logging). -t TCP, -u UDP, -p process, -l listening, -n numeric.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: dnf install logwatch
answer: Installs the logwatch facility on Fedora or RHEL; once installed, it runs from a cron job and emails a nightly summary of suspicious/critical log messages.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: apt-get install logwatch
answer: Installs the logwatch facility on Ubuntu.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: mail
answer: Displays the root user's mailbox (e.g. /var/spool/mail/root), where daily Logwatch emails appear; type a message number to read it and x to exit.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: systemctl enable sysstat
answer: Enables the sysstat service so system activity data is gathered continuously for later review with sar.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: systemctl start sysstat
answer: Starts the sysstat service so the sadc program begins gathering system activity data.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: sar -u | less
answer: Displays CPU usage from saved system activity data (10-minute intervals starting at midnight), showing %user, %nice, %system, %iowait, %steal, %idle.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: sar -d | less
answer: Displays disk activity output from saved sar data.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: sar -n DEV 5 2
answer: Runs live network device activity reporting: samples taken every 5 seconds, repeated 2 times, showing packets/KB transmitted and received per interface.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: df
answer: Shows the space available in all mounted filesystems in 1KB blocks, including the Filesystem, Used, Available, Use%, and Mounted on columns.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: df -h
answer: Displays filesystem space in a human-readable form using megabytes and gigabytes.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: df -h -x squashfs -x tmpfs -x devtmpfs -x overlay -x efivarfs
answer: Shows disk space excluding temporary/nonpermanent filesystem types, limiting output to filesystems that represent real storage areas.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: df -h -t ext4 -t vfat -t btrfs -t xfs
answer: Shows disk space only for the specified filesystem types.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: du -h /home/jake
answer: Shows the disk space consumed by each directory under /home/jake in human-readable form, with the total on the last line.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: du -s /home/jake
answer: Shows the total disk space used for a directory and its immediate files and subdirectories (summary).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: find ~/Downloads/ -xdev -type f -printf '%s\t%p\n' | sort -rn | head -n 10
answer: Finds all files in ~/Downloads, prints each file's size in bytes and filename, sorts by size descending, and shows the 10 largest files.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: find / -xdev -size +100M -type f -printf '%s\t%p\n' | sort -rn > /tmp/size
answer: Finds all files in the entire filesystem larger than 100MB and saves the list sorted by size to /tmp/size.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: dnf update
answer: Checks for and installs all available package updates on RHEL or Fedora systems.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: sudo apt update; sudo apt dist-upgrade
answer: Updates the package list and performs a full distribution upgrade on Ubuntu systems.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: rpm -V
answer: Verifies RPM packages by checking whether any commands, document files, or configuration files have been tampered with on the system.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch13: Understanding Server Administration
question: ssh joe@localhost
answer: Simulates remote access to the local system (useful when only one Linux system is available); works with any local user account.
