source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Which statement correctly describes the Directory and Location tags in Apache?

choices.label: Directory tags use filesystem paths; Location tags use URIs from the request
Directory tags use URIs; Location tags use filesystem paths
Both use only filesystem paths
Location tags are processed first and can be overridden by Directory

explanation: Directory tags specify a path based on the filesystem location (e.g., <Directory />). Location tags specify the URI used to access a file or directory — the address in the request, not the real location on disk. Location tags are processed last and override Directory and Files blocks.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Which statement correctly describes the Order Deny,Allow setting in Apache?

choices.label: Access is permitted to any host not listed in a Deny directive
Access is denied to any host not allowed in an Allow directive
All hosts are denied regardless of Allow entries
Deny and Allow directives are ignored

explanation: With Order set to Deny,Allow, access is permitted to any host that is not listed in a Deny directive. The setting Allow,Deny does the opposite: it denies access to any host not allowed in an Allow directive.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Which ErrorDocument error code corresponds to 'file not found'?
explanation: ErrorDocument codes include 403 (access denied), 404 (file not found), and 500 (server internal error). 404 means the requested file was not found on the server.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Which statement about Files tags is correct?

choices.label: Files tags can be contained within a Directory block and their settings override Directory block settings
Files tags can only contain Location tags
Files tags are processed before Directory tags are read
Files tags cannot contain regular expressions in any form

explanation: Files tags specify files by name and can be contained within a Directory block to limit them to files under that directory. Settings within a Files block override the ones in Directory blocks. FilesMatch adds regular expression support.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Which statement about DirectoryMatch is correct?

choices.label: It is the same as Directory but can contain regular expressions in the resource specification
It is processed at the same time as Files blocks
It replaces DirectoryIndex
It only applies to virtual hosts

explanation: DirectoryMatch, FilesMatch, and LocationMatch have the same function as Directory, Files, and Location but can contain regular expressions in the resource specification. DirectoryMatch blocks are processed after Directory blocks.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Which statement correctly describes the default DirectoryIndex setting in httpd.conf?

choices.label: If a directory is requested, httpd serves index.html first, then index.php if index.html is absent
httpd always serves index.php first
DirectoryIndex only works for the root of the website
DirectoryIndex lists error pages, not index files

explanation: DirectoryIndex index.html index.php lists files httpd will serve if a directory is requested. If index.html doesn't exist, httpd looks for index.php; if neither is found, the contents of the directory are displayed.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Which statement about name-based virtual hosts and SSL is correct?

choices.label: Each SSL virtual host should have a unique IP address because SSL negotiation happens before HTTP
Multiple SSL virtual hosts can share one IP address without any restrictions
SSL virtual hosts use only port 80
Name-based virtual hosting works perfectly with SSL

explanation: Because SSL negotiation takes place before any HTTP communication, name-based virtual hosting (which occurs at the HTTP layer) does not work easily with SSL. Every SSL virtual host you configure should have a unique IP address.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Which statement correctly describes SSL certificate authentication by a CA?

choices.label: Certificates are digitally signed by a third-party certificate authority that verified the requester's identity
Self-signed certificates are verified by the browser without warning
The client signs the server's certificate
Certificates need no public key to be verified

explanation: Certificates are generally digitally signed by a third-party certificate authority (CA) that has verified the identity of the requester. The CA's certificate is installed and trusted by default in client browsers; the CA charges the server operator for its services.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Which statement about opening Apache firewall ports is correct?

choices.label: HTTP is on TCP port 80 and HTTPS is on TCP port 443
HTTP is on TCP port 443 and HTTPS is on TCP port 80
Both HTTP and HTTPS use UDP
HTTPS uses port 8080 by default

explanation: Standard web service (HTTP) is accessible over TCP port 80; secure web service (HTTPS) is accessible via TCP port 443. Port 443 appears only if you have installed the mod_ssl package.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Which statement correctly describes the Apache graceful restart option?

choices.label: apachectl graceful reloads the configuration without disconnecting active clients
apachectl graceful restarts the entire operating system
apachectl graceful stops Apache permanently
apachectl graceful only checks for syntax errors

explanation: apachectl graceful instructs Apache to reload its configuration without disconnecting any active clients. It automatically tests the configuration before sending the reload signal to Apache.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Where is the mod_ssl configuration file located on Fedora/RHEL?

choices.label: /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf
/etc/ssl/apache.conf
/etc/httpd/ssl/httpd.conf
/var/www/ssl.conf

explanation: The mod_ssl package includes the module mod_ssl.so and a configuration file for SSL hosts at /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf. It defines Listen 443 https and a default VirtualHost block with SSLEngine on.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Which files does the default mod_ssl VirtualHost reference for the certificate and key?

choices.label: SSLCertificateFile /etc/pki/tls/certs/localhost.crt and SSLCertificateKeyFile /etc/pki/tls/private/localhost.key
SSLCertificateFile /etc/httpd/conf/ssl.crt
SSLCertificateFile /var/www/cert.pem
SSLCertificateFile /etc/pki/ca/cert.crt

explanation: When mod_ssl is installed, a self-signed certificate is created at /etc/pki/tls/certs/localhost.crt and the key at /etc/pki/tls/private/localhost.key, and the ssl.conf VirtualHost references them via SSLCertificateFile and SSLCertificateKeyFile. You replace these values when you create your own key and certificate.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Which LogLevel setting is recommended for a typical production server?

choices.label: warn
debug
emerg
info

explanation: On a typical server LogLevel is set to warn. You should not set it to any value lower than crit, and you should avoid leaving it set to debug because that can slow down the server and result in a very large ErrorLog.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Which statement about the Listen directive is correct?

choices.label: It enables you to specify both an IP address and a port to bind to, and multiple Listen statements are allowed
It can only be used once in the configuration file
It cannot use a wildcard for the IP address
It is used only for SSL virtual hosts

explanation: Listen enables you to specify both an IP address and a port. The IP address can be a wildcard and you can have multiple Listen statements. Listen is the most flexible of the three listening directives (BindAddress, Port, Listen) and is the one to use most.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: What does setting SELINUX=permissive in /etc/sysconfig/selinux accomplish?

choices.label: Broken SELinux policies are logged but not prevented
SELinux is turned off entirely
SELinux immediately blocks all httpd access
It only affects the current session

explanation: With SELINUX=permissive, the next time the system reboots it is in permissive mode, meaning broken SELinux policies are logged but not prevented (as they would be in enforcing mode).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: What is the recommended way to manage multiple virtual hosts?

choices.label: Keep each virtual host in a separate file and ensure the primary/default virtual host file is read first
Put all virtual hosts in the main httpd.conf after the Directory blocks
Assign each virtual host its own httpd daemon process manually
Virtual hosts cannot share the same Apache server

explanation: Keeping individual virtual hosts in separate files is convenient, but you should keep your primary virtual host in a file read before the others because the first virtual host receives requests for site names that don't match any configuration. A special default virtual host with an error message is common in commercial web-hosting environments.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Which statement about the squid package in the Web Server group is correct?

choices.label: It provides proxy services for specific protocols such as HTTP
It provides the Apache daemon itself
It generates SSL certificates
It analyzes web server statistics graphically

explanation: squid provides proxy services for specific protocols (such as HTTP). A Squid proxy server typically forwards requests from proxy clients to the Internet or other network providing web content, providing a means of controlling or filtering content.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Address already in use: make_sock could not bind to port 80
symptoms: Apache fails to start and the error log shows '[crit] (98)Address already in use: make_sock: could not bind to port 80'.
root_cause: Something else is bound to port 80, another Apache process is already running, or Apache was told to bind the same IP address and port combination in more than one place (for example, Listen *:80 plus Listen 1.2.3.4:80).
troubleshooting_steps: Run ss -nltp to view the list of programs with TCP ports in the LISTEN state and find what is listening on port 80.
If it is another httpd process, determine whether an old instance is still running and stop it.
If it is a different program, find out why it is running; use the kill command to terminate the process if appropriate.
Check the configuration for duplicate BindAddress, Port, or Listen statements specifying the same IP and port.
resolution: Remove the conflicting service or correct the duplicate Listen/BindAddress/Port configuration so only one listener uses port 80, then restart httpd.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Client denied by server configuration error
symptoms: When requesting a page, the user gets a 'Client denied by server configuration' error.
root_cause: Apache was configured to deny access to the object via Location or Directory sections. Settings applied to a path are also applied to any paths below it.
troubleshooting_steps: Check the configuration files for Location and Directory sections that might affect the file you are trying to access.
Remember that settings applied to a path also apply to paths below it.
To grant access, change permissions only for the more specific path to which you want to allow access.
resolution: Add or adjust an Allow/Require directive in the more specific Directory or Location block so the object is permitted.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: File permissions prevent access error
symptoms: Apache returns a 'File permissions prevent access' error for a requested file even though the file exists.
root_cause: The httpd process runs as the apache user/group and is unable to open the requested file because of missing permissions on the file or on directories above it.
troubleshooting_steps: Check that the apache user has read permission on the file.
Make sure the apache account has execute permission on the directory and every directory above it.
If Apache should generate an index of files, also give read permission on the directory.
resolution: Use chmod (and possibly chown) to grant the apache user/group the needed read and execute permissions on the file and its parent directories.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Directory index forbidden by rule error
symptoms: Accessing a directory shows 'Directory index forbidden by rule'.
root_cause: Apache could not find an index file with a name specified in the DirectoryIndex directive and was configured not to create a list of files in the directory.
troubleshooting_steps: Check whether your index page has one of the names specified in the relevant DirectoryIndex directive.
If you want directory listings, add an Options Indexes line to the appropriate Directory or Location section for that object.
resolution: Rename the index file to match DirectoryIndex, or add 'Options Indexes' to the directory's configuration to allow a generated file list.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Premature end of script headers error
symptoms: A CGI script returns 'Premature end of script headers'.
root_cause: A script is crashing before it finishes. When using suexec or suPHP, this may also be caused by a file ownership or permissions error.
troubleshooting_steps: Check the error log, where the errors that caused the crash may also show up.
Verify file ownership and permissions when using suexec or suPHP.
Check log files in the /var/log/httpd directory.
resolution: Fix the script crash or correct the file ownership/permissions so the script can complete and output proper headers.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: SELinux denies access even though file permissions are open
symptoms: File permissions are open but messages denying permission appear in log files; files are not accessible to httpd.
root_cause: SELinux in enforcing mode is blocking access because file contexts are wrong or a Boolean prevents the feature (for example, serving from a remotely mounted directory, sending an email, or uploading files).
troubleshooting_steps: Temporarily set SELinux to permissive mode with setenforce 0 and try to access the file again.
If the file is now accessible, set SELinux back to enforcing mode with setenforce 1.
Check file contexts and Booleans; file contexts must be correct for httpd to access a file.
Run man httpd_selinux for details about SELinux settings for httpd.
resolution: Set the correct file contexts (e.g., chcon or restorecon) and turn on the required SELinux Booleans, then verify access again.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Configuration passes apachectl configtest but httpd exits after reloading
symptoms: apachectl configtest reports Syntax OK, yet the HTTP daemon exits immediately after reloading its configuration.
root_cause: Some configuration problems pass the syntax tests but cause the daemon to exit, for example SSL configuration errors (missing or malformed key/certificate files).
troubleshooting_steps: Use the tail command to check Apache's error log for useful information (/var/log/httpd/error.log on Fedora/RHEL; otherwise look for the ErrorLog directive).
For SSL errors, make sure all key and certificate files exist and are in the proper format.
Use openssl to examine key and certificate files for validity.
resolution: Fix the reported configuration problem (e.g., correct the SSL key/certificate paths or formats), then restart the httpd service.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: Browser warns that an SSL site's certificate is untrusted
symptoms: When connecting via HTTPS to a site configured with mod_ssl, the browser warns that there is no way to verify the authenticity of the site.
root_cause: A self-signed certificate was installed with mod_ssl. No CA signed it, so there is no way to know who created the certificate you are accepting.
troubleshooting_steps: Click Advanced and then View Certificate to see the certificate details (hostname, issue/expiry dates, organization).
Close the window and select Accept the Risk and Continue to accept the connection.
For public sites, get a certificate validated by a CA; for internal/testing use, create a self-signed certificate with better organization information.
resolution: Accept the self-signed certificate for testing, or replace it with a CA-validated certificate (or a properly filled-out self-signed certificate) via SSLCertificateFile/SSLCertificateKeyFile in ssl.conf.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: File not found error although the file appears to be in the right place
symptoms: Apache returns a file-not-found error for a file you believe is present.
root_cause: Apache may not be looking where you think it is for the file, often because of Alias settings or because you are accessing the wrong virtual host.
troubleshooting_steps: Check the error log; the entire path to the file usually shows up there.
Make sure you are accessing the correct virtual host.
Check for any Alias settings that might be directing your location to an unexpected place.
resolution: Correct the virtual host or Alias configuration so the requested URL maps to the intended file location.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: What is the correct order to generate an SSL key and self-signed certificate for Apache?
correct_sequence: 1. Install the openssl package if needed: dnf install openssl
2. Generate a 2048-bit RSA private key: cd /etc/pki/tls/private; openssl genrsa -out server.key 2048; chmod 600 server.key
3. Generate a self-signed certificate: cd /etc/pki/tls/certs; openssl req -new -x509 -nodes -sha1 -days 365 -key /etc/pki/tls/private/server.key -out server.crt
4. Edit /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf to set SSLCertificateFile and SSLCertificateKeyFile to the new files
5. Restart or reload the httpd server and test from https://localhost
distractor_sequences: 1. Create the CSR first, 2. generate the private key, 3. edit httpd.conf, 4. install mod_ssl
1. Edit ssl.conf, 2. restart httpd, 3. generate the key, 4. create the certificate
1. Install mod_ssl, 2. request a CA-signed certificate, 3. skip generating a key
explanation: The key must be generated before the certificate because the self-signed certificate is created using the key. The certificate must be placed in /etc/pki/tls/certs and referenced by SSLCertificateFile/SSLCertificateKeyFile in ssl.conf, then httpd is reloaded to pick up the changes.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: What is the correct order to add a virtual host to Apache?
correct_sequence: 1. Create a file named /etc/httpd/conf.d/example.org.conf with a <VirtualHost *:80> block including ServerAdmin, ServerName, ServerAlias, DocumentRoot, and DirectoryIndex
2. Create the DocumentRoot directory and add content to it
3. Run apachectl configtest to check the configuration (Syntax OK)
4. Run apachectl graceful to reload the configuration
5. Access the site by its server name (e.g., www.example.org)
distractor_sequences: 1. Restart httpd, 2. create the config file, 3. run configtest
1. Create content, 2. remove httpd.conf, 3. add VirtualHost
1. Run apachectl graceful, 2. edit the file, 3. test the config
explanation: The VirtualHost configuration file must be created first and placed in conf.d so it is included in the main config. apachectl configtest verifies syntax before apachectl graceful reloads without dropping active connections. The first VirtualHost becomes the default for unmatched names.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: What is the correct order to allow users to publish web content from their home directories?
correct_sequence: 1. Create an <IfModule mod_userdir.c> block with UserDir enabled chris and UserDir public_html in httpd.conf
2. Create a <Directory "/home/*/public_html"> block with Options and Require all granted
3. Have users create their own public_html directories: mkdir $HOME/public_html
4. As root, set execute permission so httpd can traverse home directories: chmod +x /home /home/*
5. Set the SELinux Boolean: setsebool -P httpd_enable_homedirs true
6. Restart or reload the httpd service
distractor_sequences: 1. Set SELinux Boolean, 2. create the user's directory, 3. edit httpd.conf
1. Restart httpd, 2. configure mod_userdir, 3. create directories
1. Create public_html, 2. change httpd.conf DocumentRoot, 3. reboot
explanation: mod_userdir configuration must be in place before users can publish; directories must exist with execute permission on /home so httpd can traverse them, and if SELinux is enforcing, the httpd_enable_homedirs Boolean must be on before httpd is restarted.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: What is the correct order to generate a certificate signing request (CSR) and use a CA-signed certificate?
correct_sequence: 1. Create a directory for the CSR: mkdir /etc/pki/tls/ssl.csr; cd /etc/pki/tls/ssl.csr/
2. Generate the CSR: openssl req -new -key ../private/server.key -out server.csr
3. Visit the CA website and paste the contents of server.csr into the request form
4. When the CA sends the certificate, save it in /etc/pki/tls/certs/ (e.g., example.org.crt)
5. Change SSLCertificateFile in ssl.conf (or add a VirtualHost with SSLEngine On) to point to the new certificate
distractor_sequences: 1. Generate the private key after the CSR, 2. submit CSR to CA
1. Save the CA certificate, 2. generate the CSR, 3. create the directory
1. Edit ssl.conf first, 2. generate the key, 3. request the certificate
explanation: A CSR is generated from an existing private key. The CSR is sent to the CA, and the returned certificate is saved in /etc/pki/tls/certs. ssl.conf is then edited so the certificate and key files are referenced, with each SSL host having its own IP address.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: What is the correct order to start and verify an Apache web server on a modern Fedora/RHEL system?
correct_sequence: 1. Install the package: dnf groupinstall "Web Server" (or install httpd-core)
2. Enable the service to start at boot: systemctl enable httpd.service
3. Start the service: systemctl start httpd.service
4. Verify status: systemctl status httpd.service
5. Verify listening ports: ss -tupln | grep httpd
distractor_sequences: 1. Start the service, 2. enable it, 3. install the package
1. Open firewall ports, 2. start the service, 3. install
1. Enable, 2. reboot, 3. start
explanation: The package must be installed first. systemctl enable makes it start at boot and systemctl start launches it immediately; status confirms it is running and ss verifies it is listening on ports 80 (and 443 if mod_ssl is installed).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch17: Configuring a Web Server
question: What is the correct order to test that the default mod_ssl certificate is working from a local browser?
correct_sequence: 1. Install mod_ssl and reload the configuration
2. Open a connection using HTTPS, e.g., https://localhost
3. Note the warning that the authenticity of the site cannot be verified
4. Click Advanced and then View Certificate to inspect the certificate
5. Accept the Risk and Continue, then view the default web page over HTTPS
distractor_sequences: 1. Accept the certificate, 2. install mod_ssl, 3. view the certificate
1. Open the page over HTTP, 2. view certificate, 3. accept risk
1. Generate a CA certificate, 2. test on localhost, 3. install mod_ssl
explanation: mod_ssl must be installed first so a self-signed certificate exists. Because the certificate is self-signed, the browser warns that it is untrusted; you inspect it via View Certificate and then accept the risk to continue, after which HTTPS communication is encrypted.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: How does FTP operate?
answer: FTP operates in a client/server model. An FTP server daemon listens for incoming requests on TCP port 21 from FTP clients. The client presents a login and password; if accepted, the client can interactively traverse the filesystem, list files and directories, and download (and sometimes upload) files.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: Why is FTP insecure?
answer: Everything sent between the FTP client and server is done in clear text, including the authentication process (login and password). Someone sniffing the line between client and server can see the data being transferred. Use SSH commands such as sftp, scp, or rsync for private, encrypted transfers.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What is the anonymous FTP account?
answer: A special, nonauthenticated account used by the FTP server called anonymous. It can be accessed by anyone because it does not require a valid password. An anonymous FTP server is a public FTP server that does not require authentication of a legitimate user account.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What is the difference between active and passive FTP connections?
answer: With an active FTP connection, the server sends data from its TCP port 20 to some random port above 1023 on the client. With a passive FTP connection, the client requests the passive connection and requests a random port from the server. Passive mode requires firewall rules allowing random connections to ports above 1023 on the server.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What are the home directories for the anonymous FTP user?
answer: For Fedora or RHEL, /var/ftp; for Ubuntu and most Debian-based distributions, /srv/ftp. The anonymous user cannot go outside that directory structure. A regular user, such as joe, starts in /home/joe but can change to any part of the filesystem for which he has permission.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What are the basic FTP client commands?
answer: From the interactive FTP prompt you can use pwd (current directory), ls (list contents), cd (change directories), get (download files from the server), and put (upload files to the server). Command-oriented FTP clients such as lftp and ftp run in interactive mode.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What package provides the Very Secure FTP Daemon?
answer: The vsftpd package. It is the FTP server often used with Fedora, Red Hat Enterprise Linux, CentOS, Ubuntu, and other Linux distributions. Setting it up requires only this one package.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What is the main vsftpd configuration file and where is it located?
answer: /etc/vsftpd/vsftpd.conf on RHEL and Fedora; /etc/vsftpd.conf on Ubuntu. The vsftpd daemon reads this file to determine what features the service allows.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What are the ftpusers and user_list files used for?
answer: Files in /etc/vsftpd (Fedora and RHEL, not Ubuntu) that store information about user accounts restricted from accessing the server. They include administrative users such as root, bin, daemon, adm, lp, and others. You can add users you want to deny FTP access.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What do /etc/pam.d/vsftpd and /etc/logrotate.d/vsftpd do?
answer: /etc/pam.d/vsftpd sets how authentication is done to the FTP server. /etc/logrotate.d/vsftpd configures how log files are rotated over time.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What happens when you start vsftpd with default settings?
answer: The vsftpd daemon runs in the background listening on TCP port 21, with data transferred on TCP port 20. Linux user accounts (excluding administrative users) can access the FTP server and the anonymous account can be enabled. The anonymous user has access only to /var/ftp; regular users can access any directory they could reach via a regular login or SSH session.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What are the default upload/download capabilities of a vsftpd server?
answer: By default, the anonymous user can download files from the server but not upload them. A regular user can upload or download files, based on regular Linux permissions. Log messages detailing uploads/downloads are written in /var/log/xferlog in standard xferlog format.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: Why might local user logins fail when SELinux is enforcing?
answer: Although regular Linux user login is enabled by default in Fedora and RHEL, SELinux in enforcing mode prevents logins and file transfers from succeeding. Change an SELinux Boolean to allow regular user logins while keeping SELinux enforcing.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: Which TCP ports must be open for FTP?
answer: TCP port 21 must be open in the firewall to allow new connections to access the FTP service (the control port). Data is transferred on TCP port 20. Passive FTP also requires allowing random connections to ports above 1023 on the server.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: Why is the ESTABLISHED,RELATED line important in iptables rules for FTP?
answer: Without that line, users could connect to SSH (port 22) and FTP (port 21) services but could not communicate after that. A user could get authenticated but not be able to transfer data.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: How do you enable FTP connection tracking on older RHEL systems?
answer: Edit the /etc/sysconfig/iptables-config file so that IPTABLES_MODULES="nf_conntrack_ftp", causing the FTP connection tracking module to be loaded each time the firewall starts.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: How do you open FTP access with firewalld?
answer: In the Firewall Configuration window (firewall-config, from the firewall-config package), select Permanent, then select the ftp check box under the Services tab. This opens TCP port 21 and loads kernel modules needed for passive FTP. Then select Options -> Reload Firewalld to apply permanently.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What SELinux file context is needed for content that FTP clients can download?
answer: public_content_t. Files created in /var/ftp or its subdirectories inherit this context automatically. Be sure to create new content or copy existing content to /var/ftp directories — moving files there may not change the context properly.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What SELinux file context is needed to allow anonymous uploads?
answer: public_content_rw_t must be set on the directory to which anonymous users upload. Other permissions, SELinux Booleans, and vsftpd.conf settings must also be in place for this to work.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: Which SELinux Booleans relate to vsftpd features?
answer: ftpd_anon_write (RHEL 7 or later; allow_ftpd_anon_write on RHEL 6) allows anonymous users to read and write files/directories. allow_ftpd_use_nfs and allow_ftpd_use_cifs allow mounting remote NFS or CIFS (Windows) shared filesystems and sharing them from vsftpd.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What Linux permissions does vsftpd rely on?
answer: For an anonymous user to view or download a file, at least read permission must be open for other (----r--). To access a directory, at least execute permission must be on for other (------x). For regular user accounts, if a user can access a file from the shell, that user can access the same file from an FTP server.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What do the default settings anonymous_enable=NO and local_enable=YES mean?
answer: All local Linux users (those listed in /etc/passwd) are configured to access the server, and the anonymous user is prevented. This is the default vsftpd setup.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: How can you create an FTP-only user account?
answer: Create a user account that has /sbin/nologin as its default shell. For example: bill:x:1000:1000:Bill Jones:/home/bill:/sbin/nologin. Login from a console or via ssh is denied, but as long as bill has a password and local account access is enabled, bill can log in via FTP.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What does userlist_enable=YES do?
answer: It denies access to the FTP server to all accounts listed in /etc/vsftpd/user_list. If changed to NO, the user_list file becomes a list of only those users who do have access to the server. The /etc/vsftpd/ftpusers file always includes users denied access regardless of the setting.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What do the chroot settings do in vsftpd.conf?
answer: chroot_local_user=YES, chroot_list_enable=YES, and chroot_list_file=/etc/vsftpd/chroot_list create a list of local users who, after logging in, are prevented from going outside their home directory structure.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What is required before any form of writing to a vsftpd server is allowed?
answer: write_enable=YES must be set in vsftpd.conf (it is by default). Because of that, if local accounts are enabled, users can log in and immediately upload files to their own home directories. Anonymous users are denied the ability to upload by default.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: How do you allow anonymous uploads to vsftpd?
answer: Set anon_upload_enable=YES to allow anonymous users to upload files and anon_mkdir_write_enable=YES to allow them to create directories. Then create a directory under /var/ftp that is writeable by the ftp user, ftp group, or other (e.g., /var/ftp/uploads owned by ftp:ftp with mode 775).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What does the chown feature of FTP do for anonymous uploads?
answer: With chown_uploads=YES and chown_username=joe, when an anonymous user uploads a file it is immediately assigned ownership of a different user (joe) and the ftp group. Permissions become read/write for the owner and nothing for anyone else (rw-------).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What settings lock down a vsftpd server for anonymous-only Internet downloads?
answer: anonymous_enable=YES, local_enable=NO, write_enable=NO, anon_upload_enable=NO, anon_mkdir_write_enable=NO, and anon_other_write_enable=NO. The sample is at /usr/share/doc/vsftpd/EXAMPLE/INTERNET_SITE/vsftpd.conf (Fedora/RHEL) or /usr/share/doc/vsftpd/examples/INTERNET_SITE (Ubuntu).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What does anon_world_readable_only=YES do?
answer: Ensures that anonymous users can see files where the read permission bit is turned on for other (----r--), but cannot write files. This is used because the vsftpd daemon can read files assigned to the ftp user and group.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What do the pasv_min_port and pasv_max_port settings do?
answer: They restrict the range of ports that can be used with passive FTP (where the server picks a higher-numbered port on which to send data). The Internet-site example restricts the range to between 50000 and 60000.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What do hide_ids=YES and connect_from_port_20=YES do?
answer: hide_ids=YES hides the real permissions set on files, so to the user accessing the FTP site everything appears to be owned by the ftp user. connect_from_port_20=YES gives the vsftpd daemon more permission to send data the way a client might request by allowing PORT-style data communications.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What do xferlog_enable, ls_recurse_enable, and ascii_download_enable do?
answer: xferlog_enable=YES logs all file transfers to /var/log/xferlog. ls_recurse_enable=NO prevents users from recursively listing directory contents (like ls -R), which could drain resources on a large site. ascii_download_enable=NO forces all downloads to be in binary mode, preventing inappropriate ASCII translation of binary files.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What performance settings are in the Internet-site vsftpd.conf?
answer: one_process_model=YES (one process per connection), idle_session_timeout=120 (disconnect idle clients after 2 minutes instead of the default 300 seconds), data_connection_timeout=300 (drop stalled data connections), accept_timeout=60 (time for a PASV connection to be accepted), connect_timeout=60 (time for a PORT-style connection to respond), and anon_max_rate=50000 (limit anonymous transfer rate in bytes per second).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What does the lftp command do?
answer: A command-line FTP client. Used with just the server name it connects as the anonymous user; with -u username it prompts for the user's password. At the lftp prompt you use get and put to download and upload files. The connection is actually made when you type your first command.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What does putting an exclamation mark (!) in front of an lftp command do?
answer: It causes the command to be interpreted by the client system instead of the server. Examples: !pwd shows the current directory on the initiating system (where downloaded files go), !cd changes directories locally, and !ls lists local files.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: What is the gFTP client?
answer: A graphical FTP client that shows both the local (left) and remote (right) sides of an FTP session. To start it, launch it from the applications menu or run gftp & from the shell. It supports bookmarks of FTP site addresses.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: dnf install vsftpd
answer: Installs the vsftpd (Very Secure FTP Daemon) package on Fedora or RHEL.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: sudo apt-get install vsftpd
answer: Installs the vsftpd package on Ubuntu or another Debian-based distribution.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: rpm -qi vsftpd
answer: Gets general information about the vsftpd package (Summary: Very Secure Ftp Daemon, written completely from scratch).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: rpm -qd vsftpd
answer: Lists the documentation files in the vsftpd package, including /usr/share/doc/vsftpd/EXAMPLE directories (INTERNET_SITE, PER_IP_CONFIG, VIRTUAL_HOSTS, VIRTUAL_USERS), the FAQ, and man pages (vsftpd.conf.5.gz, vsftpd.8.gz).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: rpm -qc vsftpd
answer: Lists the configuration files in the vsftpd package: /etc/logrotate.d/vsftpd, /etc/pam.d/vsftpd, /etc/vsftpd/ftpusers, /etc/vsftpd/user_list, and /etc/vsftpd/vsftpd.conf.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: man vsftpd.conf
answer: Reads the manual page about the vsftpd configuration file and its options.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: systemctl status vsftpd.service
answer: Checks whether the vsftpd service is running; shows it is inactive (dead) and disabled by default in Fedora/RHEL.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: systemctl start vsftpd.service
answer: Starts the vsftpd FTP daemon immediately.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: systemctl enable vsftpd.service
answer: Enables the vsftpd service so it starts each time the system boots (creates a symlink in multi-user.target.wants).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: ss -tupln | grep vsftpd
answer: Verifies the vsftpd daemon is listening (LISTEN) on all IP addresses for port 21 (:::21) using the TCP protocol.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: echo "Hello From Your FTP Server" > /tmp/hello.txt
answer: Creates a test file on the server that you can later download via FTP.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: dnf install ftp
answer: Installs the command-line ftp client to test that the vsftpd server is working (curl and wget are also options).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: ftp localhost
answer: Connects to the FTP server on the local host, prompts for a username and password, and opens an interactive ftp prompt where you can use cd, get, put, and exit.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: cat hello.txt
answer: Displays the contents of the downloaded file to confirm the FTP transfer worked (should show 'Hello From Your FTP Server').

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: service iptables restart
answer: Restarts the older iptables firewall service (RHEL 6 and earlier) to apply changes made to /etc/sysconfig/iptables.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: systemctl restart firewalld.service
answer: Restarts the newer firewalld service (RHEL 7 and later) to apply firewall changes.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: firewall-config
answer: Opens the Firewall Configuration window (from the firewall-config package). Select the ftp check box under Services and reload firewalld to open TCP port 21 and load modules for passive FTP.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: getenforce
answer: Shows how SELinux is currently set (e.g., Enforcing, Permissive, or Disabled).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: grep ^SELINUX= /etc/sysconfig/selinux
answer: Shows how SELinux is set when the system comes up (e.g., SELINUX=enforcing).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: semanage fcontext -a -t public_content_t "/var/ftp/pub/stuff(/.*)?"
answer: Adds a file context rule marking /var/ftp/pub/stuff (and everything below) with the public_content_t context so SELinux allows it to be shared read-only via FTP.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: restorecon -F -R -v /var/ftp/pub/stuff
answer: Recursively applies (restores) the correct SELinux file contexts to /var/ftp/pub/stuff and its contents after a semanage fcontext rule is added.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: semanage fcontext -a -t public_content_rw_t "/var/ftp/pub/uploads(/.*)?"
answer: Adds a file context rule marking /var/ftp/pub/uploads with the public_content_rw_t context so SELinux allows uploading of files to that directory.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: setsebool -P ftpd_anon_write on
answer: Turns on the SELinux Boolean permanently (-P) that allows anonymous FTP users to read and write files and directories (ftpd_anon_write on RHEL 7+; allow_ftpd_anon_write on RHEL 6).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: setsebool -P allow_ftpd_use_nfs on
answer: Turns on the SELinux Boolean to allow the vsftpd server to mount remote NFS shared filesystems and share them from the FTP server.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: setsebool -P allow_ftpd_use_cifs on
answer: Turns on the SELinux Boolean to allow the vsftpd server to mount remote CIFS (Windows) shared filesystems and share them from the FTP server.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: mkdir /var/ftp/uploads
answer: Creates the uploads directory under /var/ftp where anonymous users can write.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: chown ftp:ftp /var/ftp/uploads
answer: Sets the owner and group of the uploads directory to the ftp user and group.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: chmod 775 /var/ftp/uploads
answer: Sets permissions so the uploads directory is writeable by owner and group (and readable/listable by others), allowing you to see uploaded files but not change or overwrite them.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: dnf install lftp
answer: Installs the lftp command-line FTP client.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: lftp -u chris localhost
answer: Connects to the FTP server as user chris using lftp, prompting for the Linux user password and opening an lftp prompt for interactive commands.

question: dnf install gftp
answer: Installs the gFTP graphical FTP client.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch18: Configuring an FTP Server
question: gftp &
answer: Starts the gFTP graphical FTP client from the shell in the background.
