source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: What does the Notifications Alert extension do?
answer: Changes the color of the time/date indicator at the top of the desktop if you have unread messages.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: What does the Removable Drive Menu extension do?
answer: Adds a status menu to the top bar to access removable media connected to your computer.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: What happens when you allow extensions at extensions.gnome.org?
answer: You share data with extensions.gnome.org and extensions-next.gnome.org; those sites have access to your browser tabs and display notifications.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: How do you find software in the Fedora Software window?
answer: Search by typing the name into the Find box or select a category; select the spyglass icon in the upper-left corner and type a word associated with the package.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: What is the Add/Remove software tool?
answer: A graphical tool (the Software window) to download and install packages from the Fedora software repository when you have an Internet connection.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: What commands manage software in Fedora and RHEL?
answer: dnf, yum, and rpm commands, used to manage software packages and repositories.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: What happens when Fedora is installed regarding software?
answer: It is automatically configured to connect your system to the huge Fedora software repository available on the Internet.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: Can you clone public Git repositories without an account?
answer: Yes, you can copy (clone) many public Git repositories without an account, but you need an account to submit pull requests or if the repository requires extra permissions.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: Name recommended resources for learning Git.
answer: GitHub Skills (skills.github.com), Git Immersion (gitimmersion.com), and Learn Git Branching (learngitbranching.js.org).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: How do you install Visual Studio Code on Ubuntu?
answer: Open the App Center from the Activities screen, search for Visual Studio Code, click Install (with password if needed), then click Open.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: How do you view a local HTML file in a browser?
answer: Type file:///path/to/file in the browser location box, e.g., file:///home/chris/startbootstrap-grayscale/dist/index.html.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: What keystroke saves changes in Visual Studio Code?
answer: Ctrl+S.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: When are new GNOME workspaces created?
answer: An additional empty workspace is created each time the last empty one is used.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: Why is GNOME called the gold standard of Linux desktops?
answer: It provides a simple, friendly, and uncluttered interface and is the most popular desktop on full-featured Linux distributions.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: How many GNOME shell extensions are available?
answer: More than 100 GNOME shell extensions are available now, and more are being added.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: How can you get GNOME 2 features back in GNOME 3?
answer: Some extensions included with GNOME 3 (but turned off), such as Apps Menu, Places Status Indicator, and Window List, restore GNOME 2 features.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: Where do you get the MATE+Compiz desktop spin?
answer: From fedoraproject.org/spins/mate; download the ISO and run it live or install it.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: What can a Linux developer desktop be used to develop?
answer: Containerized software, software for embedded Linux systems, and artificial intelligence and machine learning software, in an environment essentially the same as where it will run.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: What is the difference between a code editor and an IDE?
answer: Code editors offer features from code highlighting to auto completion to AI integration; complete IDEs offer a more comprehensive set of tools for building, debugging, and deploying software.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: Which correctly describes a window manager vs a desktop environment?

choices.label: A window manager manages windows; a desktop environment adds menus, panels, and an application programming interface
A desktop environment only manages windows
A window manager includes an application API for development
They are the same thing

explanation: A window manager adds the capability to manage windows; a full-blown desktop environment includes a window manager plus menus, panels, and usually an API for applications that work together.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: Which keystroke toggles between the Activities view and active windows in GNOME?

choices.label: The Windows key
Alt+F4
Ctrl+Alt+Delete

explanation: Press the Windows key to toggle between the mini-window (Activities) and active-window views; moving the mouse to the upper-left corner does the same.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: Which is true about running Linux from a live image?

choices.label: Changes you make disappear on reboot unless you save them to disk
Changes are written permanently to the hard drive by default
It runs faster than an installed system
You cannot run any applications

explanation: A live image does all its work in memory; changes disappear on reboot unless saved, and it runs slower than an installed system.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: What is the correct order to open an application from the GNOME Activities screen using the mouse?
correct_sequence: 1. Move the mouse to the upper-left corner (or click the Activities button) to show the Activities screen
2. Click an application icon at the bottom of the screen, or select Show Apps
3. Left-click the application icon to open it in the current workspace
distractor_sequences: 1. Left-click the icon
2. Move to upper-left
3. Select Show Apps
explanation: You toggle to the Activities screen, then either click a dash icon or Show Apps, and left-click the application to launch it.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: What is the correct order to turn on an installed GNOME extension?
correct_sequence: 1. Visit extensions.gnome.org from your browser
2. Select Installed Extensions to see installed extensions
3. Select the ON button next to the extension's name (or open its page and click ON)
distractor_sequences: 1. Select ON
2. Install the OS
3. Visit the site
explanation: You visit the extensions site, look at Installed Extensions, and flip the ON button to enable it; a settings icon next to each extension configures it.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: Which best describes the initial GNOME desktop by design?

choices.label: Very little on it: no bottom task bar, no application icons, just a top bar with Activities, clock, and status icons
A full task bar at the bottom with all apps
Application icons scattered across the screen
A Start menu in the corner

explanation: GNOME deliberately starts with almost nothing: no task bar or app icons; the top bar has the Activities icon, a clock, and status icons, and the Activities screen is where you open apps.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: What runs on the local system in X's client/server model?

choices.label: The X server, providing an interface to the screen, mouse, and keyboard
The X clients only
Both clients and server on remote systems
Nothing; X is not networked

explanation: The X server runs on the local system providing the interface to screen, mouse, and keyboard; X clients can be launched from the local system or from any networked system the X server allows.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: What was LXDE designed to be?
answer: A fast-performing, energy-saving desktop environment, often used on less-expensive devices (such as netbooks) and on live media; default for KNOPPIX.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch2: Creating the Perfect Linux Desktop
question: Can you choose whether a desktop starts at boot?
answer: Yes; after a desktop is installed you can choose whether to start it when the computer boots or start it as needed.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: whoami
answer: Shows your username.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: grep chris /etc/passwd
answer: Shows the definition of the user account chris in the /etc/passwd file; the last field (e.g., /bin/bash) is the default login shell.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: ls /usr/bin | sort -f | less
answer: Lists the contents of /usr/bin, sorts alphabetically regardless of case (sort -f), and pipes to less for paging.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: How do you navigate within the less command?
answer: Press Enter to go a line at a time, press the spacebar to go a page at a time, and press q to quit.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: What do Ctrl+P and Ctrl+N do with command history?
answer: Ctrl+P steps to the previous command and Ctrl+N to the next, the same as the up and down arrow keys.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: What does Ctrl+R do with command history?
answer: Starts a reverse incremental search: as you type a string, a matching command line appears that you can run or edit.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: What do Alt+P and Alt+N do with command history?
answer: Alt+P does a reverse search (type a string and press Enter to see the most recent command containing it); Alt+N does the forward search.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: HISTFILE=/dev/null (in shell config)
answer: Disables storing shell history for the current user, often used for root to prevent activity from being exploited.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: HISTSIZE= (left blank)
answer: Disables history retention by leaving the history size empty; another way to prevent history from being stored.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: PROMPT_COMMAND=date
answer: Runs the date command each time before your shell prompt is displayed, listing the current date/time before the prompt.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: M=/work/time/files/info/memos ; export M
answer: Creates and exports a custom environment variable M storing a long path as a shortcut for your work.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: cd $M
answer: Makes the directory stored in the M variable your current directory.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: $M/hotdog
answer: Runs the program hotdog from the directory stored in the M variable.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: vi $M/bun
answer: Opens the file bun from the directory stored in the M variable in the vi editor.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: help | less
answer: Lists shell built-in commands and pages through the list with less.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: date --help | less
answer: Shows the options and the time format indicators available with the date command.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: man bash
answer: Displays the man page for the bash shell with documentation on its features.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: echo $HOSTTYPE
answer: Prints the value describing the computer architecture, e.g., x86_64 for AMD 64-bit machines or i386 for Intel-compatible PCs.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: echo $OSTYPE
answer: Prints the value identifying the current operating system, such as linux or linux-gnu.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: man 2 mount
answer: Displays the mount man page from section 2 (system calls).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: What does the FCEDIT variable do?
answer: If set, it indicates the text editor used by the fc command to edit history commands; if not set, the vi command is used.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: What are PS2, PS3, and PS4?
answer: Additional prompt variables used when a command requires more input; PS1 is the main shell prompt.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: How many arguments can a command line have?
answer: As many as you want, limited only by the total number of characters allowed on a command line.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: Where is the best place to add aliases?
answer: In the ~/.bashrc file, because it is read at login and each time you open a new Bash shell.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: How do you add system-wide shell settings without editing /etc/profile?
answer: Create an /etc/profile.d/custom.sh file to add system-wide settings, which /etc/profile gathers from the /etc/profile.d directory.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: Which of these is a shell built-in command?

choices.label: cd
date
ls
sort

explanation: cd is a shell built-in (no representation in the filesystem); date, ls, and sort are filesystem commands.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: Which words are shell reserved words?

choices.label: do, while, case, else
date, ls, pwd
alias, history, fc
bash, sh, ksh

explanation: Reserved words are words reserved by the shell for special use, such as do, while, case, and else, used in programming-type functions.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: alias rm='rm -i'
answer: Creates an alias so that each time you type rm it runs with the -i option, prompting before removing each file (often set for the root user).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: alias p='pwd ; ls -CF'
answer: Creates an alias so p prints the current working directory and lists its contents in column form.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: su username
answer: Opens a shell as a new user; exiting that shell returns you to the original shell.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: TMOUT=1800 (in .bashrc)
answer: Sets the idle time before the shell exits to 1800 seconds (30 minutes) as a security feature.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: echo $RANDOM
answer: Generates and prints a random number between 0 and 99999.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: echo $SECONDS
answer: Prints the number of seconds since the time the shell was started.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: echo $SHLVL
answer: Prints the number of shell levels associated with the current session; it is 1 at login and increments each time a new bash command starts.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: wc -w
answer: Runs the word count command counting words (used in arithmetic/command substitution examples).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: echo "There are $(ls | wc -w) files in this directory."
answer: Lists the current directory, counts the words (files) with wc -w, and echoes the number in the sentence.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: ls -l $BASH
answer: Prints a long listing of information about the bash command using the BASH variable's value (/usr/bin/bash).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: Why is the Bash shell important for certification exams?
answer: Bash is the shell you will use with most Linux certification exams.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: man emacs
answer: Displays the man page for the emacs text editor, which bash command-line editing is based on by default.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: If text you type for completion begins with a tilde (~), what does the shell complete?

choices.label: A username (e.g., ~ro expands to ~root)
A variable name
A command in PATH
A history command number

explanation: Text beginning with ~ completes with a username, where ~username indicates that user's home directory.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: Where is the shell history list stored after you exit?

choices.label: In the .bash_history file in your home directory
In /etc/passwd
In /var/log/history
In the kernel memory only

explanation: When you close the shell, the history list is written to the .bash_history file in your home directory, storing up to 1,000 commands by default.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: gunzip < /usr/share/man/man1/grep.1.gz | nroff -c -man | less
answer: Unzips the grep man page, formats it with nroff using the manual macro (-man), and displays it in less.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: What text editors does fc use by default?
answer: Either nano (Ctrl-O saves, Ctrl-X exits) or vi (type :wq to save and exit, or :q! to exit without saving).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: Why might you choose a different shell?
answer: Because you are used to UNIX System V (ksh) or Berkeley UNIX (csh), you need to run scripts made for a particular shell, or you prefer features of one shell over another.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: How can you prevent a shell's history from being stored?
answer: Kill the shell process (e.g., kill -9 1234) rather than exiting it properly, or set HISTFILE to /dev/null or leave HISTSIZE blank.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: What features does Bash incorporate?
answer: Features originally developed for the sh and ksh shells in early UNIX systems, as well as some csh features.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch3: Using the Shell
question: Which command uses a single-letter option and a word option correctly?

choices.label: ls -lat and date --help
ls --lat and date -help
ls -a-t and date help
ls lat and date --h

explanation: Single-letter options are grouped with one hyphen (ls -lat), while word options use a double hyphen (--help).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: ls g*t
answer: Matches files beginning with g and ending in t (e.g., grapefruit).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: ls *e*
answer: Matches any file that contains e in the name (e.g., apple, grape, grapefruit, watermelon).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: ls *n*
answer: Matches any file that contains n in the name (e.g., banana, watermelon).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: ls g???e*
answer: Matches any file beginning with g with e as its fifth character (e.g., grape, grapefruit).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: ls [abw]*
answer: Matches any file beginning with a, b, or w (e.g., apple, banana, watermelon).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: ls [agw]*[ne]
answer: Matches any file beginning with a, g, or w that also ends with n or e.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: ls [a-g]*
answer: Matches any filename beginning with a letter from a through g (e.g., apple, banana, grape, grapefruit).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: What does the 'total' line in an ls -l listing show?
answer: The total amount of disk space used by the files in the list (e.g., 158 kilobytes).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: What does the 4096-byte size of a directory represent?
answer: The size of the file containing information about the directory, not the size of files contained in it; it can grow above 4096 for directories with lots of files.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: Why might the date column in an ls -l listing vary?
answer: It can vary based on the distribution and the language setting (LANG variable), e.g., 'May 12' vs '2025-05-12'.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: What are hidden dot files typically used for?
answer: Configuration files (like .bash files) or directories (.kde) that need to be in your home directory but don't need to be seen in daily work.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: Who owns /home?
answer: The /home directory is owned by root; the user's subdirectories are owned by the user.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: What is the user private group scheme?
answer: Assigning a new user to a group of the same name by default (as done in Ubuntu, Fedora, RHEL, and most other systems).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: What does a capital S or T in permission bits mean?
answer: The set GID or sticky bit permission was set, but for some reason the execute bit was not also turned on.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: What is an example of a set UID program?
answer: The mount command has permissions -rwsr-xr-x, which allows any user to run mount to list mounted filesystems, though mounting still needs root.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: ls -l /usr/bin | grep rws
answer: Lists files in /usr/bin that have set UID/GID permissions (containing 'rws' in the permission string).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: What does 'rm *' remove?
answer: Removes all files in the current directory, but not directories and not files that start with a dot.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: Why are cp and mv usually aliased with -i?
answer: To prompt before overwriting existing files and prevent inadvertent data loss.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: alias mv
answer: Shows the alias for mv; on many systems it is 'alias mv="mv -i"'

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: /bin/ed /etc/resolv.conf <<resendit (with thetext block)
answer: Uses a here document with the ed text editor to add commands (a, w, q) and an IP address to edit /etc/resolv.conf from within a script.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: What is in /misc?
answer: A directory sometimes used to automount filesystems upon request.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: What is in /sys?
answer: Parameters for such things as tuning block storage and managing cgroups.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: Why were file permissions designed in Linux?
answer: To keep users from accessing other users' private files and to protect important system files, which is why you often get 'Permission denied'.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: Do three-character file suffixes have required meaning in Linux?
answer: No; suffixes like .txt are useful for identifying file type, but DOS extensions like .com, .exe, and .bat don't signify an executable (permission flags do).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: touch apple banana grape grapefruit watermelon
answer: Creates multiple empty files (or updates modification dates on existing ones).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: ln -s apple pointer_to_apple
answer: Creates a symbolic link named pointer_to_apple pointing to the file apple.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: mkdir Stuff
answer: Creates a directory named Stuff, which appears with its own permissions in an ls -l listing.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: How does ls --color=auto display different file types?
answer: Directories appear blue, symbolic links red, executable files green, and other regular files in the default Terminal color.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: Which command removes an empty directory?

choices.label: rmdir
rm
mv
chmod

explanation: rmdir removes a directory only if it is empty; to remove a non-empty directory you use rm -r (or rm -rf).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: With umask 002, what permissions result for a new directory and file?

choices.label: Directory 775 (rwxrwxr-x), file 644 (rw-rw-r--)
Directory 777, file 666
Directory 755, file 644
Directory 700, file 600

explanation: umask 002 masks the fully opened directory (777) to 775 and the file (666) to 644; execute is off by default for regular files.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: Which option shows hidden (dot) files with ls?

choices.label: -a
-F
-t
-S

explanation: The -a (all) option shows files beginning with a dot, which are hidden by default.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: What is the correct order to create a nested directory path and files?
correct_sequence: 1. Use mkdir -p to create the multi-layer path (e.g., mkdir -p $HOME/projects/houses/doors)
2. Use touch to create files (e.g., touch house1 house2)
3. Verify with ls or ls -l
distractor_sequences: 1. touch files
2. mkdir -p
3. list
explanation: Create the directory structure first with mkdir -p (which makes all layers at once), then create the empty files, then verify.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: What is the correct order to copy a directory tree while preserving timestamps and permissions?
correct_sequence: 1. Create a destination directory if needed
2. Use cp with the -a (archive) flag to copy recursively, e.g., cp -ra source dest
3. Verify the copy with ls -l to confirm timestamps/permissions are kept
distractor_sequences: 1. Use cp -r
2. Use plain cp
3. Verify
explanation: The -a (archive) option maintains the original date/time stamps and permissions, whereas plain recursive (-r) uses current timestamps and umask permissions.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: chmod 755 scriptx.sh
answer: Makes scriptx.sh executable with rwxr-xr-x permissions, so it runs as a command.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: Why does a symbolic link show a small size (e.g., 5) in an ls -l listing?
answer: A symbolic link's size reflects the length of the target pathname it points to (e.g., 'apple' is 5 characters).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: touch scriptx.sh apple
answer: Creates two empty files, scriptx.sh and apple, in the current directory.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: What are the root user's default file and directory permissions?
answer: Root gets files with rw-r--r-- and directories with rwxr-xr-x.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: What is the difference between the set UID bit and the sticky bit?
answer: Set UID (s in owner execute position) makes a program run with the file owner's privileges; the sticky bit (t on a directory) lets the owner allow others to add files but prevents them from deleting each other's files.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: touch {John,Bill,Sally}-{Breakfast,Lunch,Dinner}
answer: Uses brace expansion with two sets to create files combining each name with each meal (John-Breakfast, Bill-Lunch, etc.).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: How can you easily delete files created with brace expansion if you made a mistake?
answer: Recall the command and change touch to rm, e.g., rm {John,Bill,Sally}-{Breakfast,Lunch,Dinner}.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: What does the archive (-a) option to cp preserve?
answer: The original date/time stamps and permissions of files being copied.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch4: Moving Around the Filesystem
question: What does the d at the start of a directory entry indicate?
answer: That the entry is a directory; regular files begin with a dash (-), and directories (.) and (..) represent the current and parent directories.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is the sequence of events for a Linux system installed on a PC to boot up?
answer: Turn on power; start hardware from BIOS/UEFI firmware; find and start the boot loader; choose an operating system from the boot loader; start the kernel and initial RAM disk; start the initialization process (init, upstart, or systemd); start all services associated with the runlevel or default target.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is UEFI and how does it relate to BIOS?
answer: UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) is a newer type of firmware that has replaced BIOS (Basic Input Output System) on almost all computers. The two are mutually exclusive.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is the UEFI secure boot feature?
answer: A feature that ensures only operating systems whose components have been signed can be used during the boot process. Secure boot can be disabled to allow nonsigned operating systems; Ubuntu supported it first in 12.04.2 and RHEL 7 and later support it.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: Which distributions adopted systemd and when?
answer: systemd was adopted in Fedora 15 and RHEL 7, and it replaced Upstart in Debian and Ubuntu 15.04. It is now the primary initialization system for most Linux systems.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is the first running process (PID 1) on a systemd-enabled RHEL/Fedora system, and how does it appear on Ubuntu?
answer: On RHEL and Fedora the first process is the systemd daemon. On Ubuntu it appears as /sbin/init, which is actually a symbolic link to the systemd daemon.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What command manages systemd journal (log) messages?
answer: journalctl.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How do systemd targets align with System V runlevels?
answer: graphical.target aligns with runlevel 5, while multi-user.target is essentially runlevel 3. There are many more targets than runlevels, allowing finer-grained management of units. systemd also supports System V init scripts and commands such as chkconfig and service.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is dependency-based startup in systemd?
answer: Any service in the default target that has had its dependencies met can start, so a single stalled service does not make other, independent services wait. This can speed up the boot process.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How does systemd use cgroups to control resource usage?
answer: systemd uses cgroups to limit how much memory, CPU, or other resources an entire service can consume, so a runaway process or a service that spins off too many child processes cannot exceed its allowed resources.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is the Setup utility in UEFI?
answer: A screen reached by interrupting the boot process (often F1, F2, or F12) that lets you change hardware settings, enable or disable hardware components/features, and see an overview of hardware (system type, processors, memory, 32/64-bit, devices in slots).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is the boot order and why would you change it?
answer: The order in which devices (CD/DVD, hard disk, USB drive, network interface card) are checked for a boot loader. Changing it lets you boot from a selected device, e.g., a USB drive to enter rescue mode or installation media for a fresh install.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is PXE boot?
answer: A feature of many modern NICs that allows them to boot from servers found on the network. If the NIC does not appear as a bootable device, you may need to enable the feature in the firmware.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What virtualization support must a CPU include to run a Linux virtual host?
answer: Intel Virtual Technology or AMD Secure Virtual Machine (SVM) support. Even if the CPU has it, it may be disabled in the firmware, so enable the Virtualization setting (often under Performance) in Setup.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: Which boot loader is used with most modern Linux systems including RHEL, Fedora, and Ubuntu?
answer: GRUB 2 (referred to as GRUB 2, distinct from the legacy GRUB).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How do you interrupt the GRUB 2 boot prompt?
answer: Just after the BIOS screen, press any key (such as the up arrow) to see the kernel menu items. The default is the latest kernel; you can pick a different entry if the current kernel is broken, or to run a rescue kernel.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How do you add arguments to a kernel at the GRUB prompt?
answer: Highlight the kernel entry, type e to see the boot commands, move to the end of the line beginning with linux, add the arguments, then press Ctrl+X to boot.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What kernel argument disables SELinux at boot if it makes the system unusable?
answer: selinux=0 added to the end of the line beginning with linux at the GRUB prompt.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is SMT and how can it be turned off at boot?
answer: Simultaneous Multithreading lets a single CPU core execute multiple threads; to fix some microprocessor flaws, pass the smt=1 or nosmt argument on the kernel command line.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is the kernel ring buffer?
answer: A buffer that stores kernel boot messages, throwing out older messages after the buffer is full. Its messages can be captured with the dmesg command.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How can you capture kernel messages to a file for later examination?
answer: Use dmesg > /tmp/kernel_msg.txt, then view with less /tmp/kernel_msg.txt. Messages appear as components (CPU, memory, network cards, drives) are detected.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How do you view kernel messages stored in the systemd journal?
answer: Run journalctl -k to see kernel messages from boot time to the present.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is /etc/systemd/system/default.target?
answer: A file (a symbolic link to a file in /usr/lib/systemd/system) that systemd keys off to determine what to start. For a server it links to multi-user.target; for a desktop it links to graphical.target.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How does systemd determine what to start compared with System V init?
answer: System V init runs service scripts in alphanumeric order, while systemd works backward from the default.target to discover required units (e.g., graphical.target requires multi-user.target, which requires basic.target and display-manager.service).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/?
answer: A directory containing symbolic links to services that start with the multi-user.target, added when a service's package is installed or when enabled with systemctl enable.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How can you tell from systemctl output that a unit failed to start?
answer: Run systemctl and look for a unit with LOAD/ACTIVE/SUB of loaded failed failed (e.g., httpd.service), then investigate with journalctl -u for that service.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is systemd-analyze used for?
answer: It analyzes the systemd startup process: systemd-analyze time shows how long each phase (firmware, loader, kernel, userspace) took, and systemd-analyze plot creates an SVG graphic of each startup component.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is dnf and how do yum and apt relate to it?
answer: dnf is the package management facility for RPM packages on Fedora and RHEL; yum is aliased to dnf and works on older and newer systems. apt manages DEB packages on Ubuntu.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is the meaning of apt-get update versus apt-get upgrade in Ubuntu?
answer: apt-get update downloads the latest packaging metadata (package names, versions) to the local system; apt-get upgrade upgrades installed packages that have new versions available, based on the latest downloaded metadata.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How does dnf/yum update differ from apt-get update/upgrade?
answer: Every dnf or yum command downloads the latest metadata about packages for the current release; dnf update then gets the latest packages for that release. To move to the next release you must run dnf system-upgrade.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is the dnf-plugin-system-upgrade plugin for?
answer: It enables upgrading to the next Fedora/RHEL version using dnf system-upgrade download --releasever=NN and dnf system-upgrade reboot.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is the cron facility?
answer: A facility that runs commands at predetermined times and intervals, configured via /etc/crontab (system-wide, for root) or per-user crontab files.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What are the fields in an /etc/crontab entry?
answer: Five time fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week), a user field, and a seventh field with the command line. User crontab files exclude the user field. Ranges/lists and */* skip values are allowed.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How are network interfaces named by default in Ubuntu, RHEL, and Fedora?
answer: Based on physical connection, e.g., enp11s0 means wired Ethernet (en) on PCI board 11, slot 0; wireless starts with wl (e.g., wlp0s20f3). This makes NIC names predictable across reboots instead of eth0/eth1.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is ethtool -p used for?
answer: Given an interface name (ethtool -p eth0), it makes the associated NIC blink so you can identify which physical card matches the interface; Ctrl+C stops the blinking.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is the default gateway (router)?
answer: The address to which all communication not addressed to the local network is sent, shown as the default line in ip route show (e.g., default via 192.168.1.1 dev wlp0s20f3).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What does a 'Destination Host Unreachable' ping message indicate?
answer: The router is either turned off or, for a wired network, not physically connected to you (e.g., the router is not connected to the switch you share).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What does mtr provide that traceroute does not?
answer: mtr queries the route to a host continuously so you can watch the performance of each leg of the journey over time, instead of a single snapshot. Install with dnf install mtr.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: Where do DNS server names and addresses end up on a Linux system?
answer: In /etc/resolv.conf, set manually or picked up from a DHCP server, e.g., 'search example.com' and 'nameserver 192.168.0.254' entries. /etc/hosts is searched first, then the name servers in resolv.conf in order.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: If you can reach hosts by IP but not by name, what is the likely problem?
answer: A hostname-resolution (DNS) problem. Ping each name server IP to check reachability, then test each server with host or dig to see if it can resolve names.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is nmap and how is it used in troubleshooting?
answer: nmap scans for open ports and services on a host. On your own system it is legitimate (e.g., nmap 192.168.0.119 shows 22/tcp ssh, 80/tcp http, 443/tcp https); using it on another system looks like an intrusion attempt.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What do nmap port states open, closed, and filtered mean?
answer: Open means a service is listening; closed means the service (e.g., httpd) either is not running or is not listening on that port; filtered usually means the firewall is blocking packets to that port.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What does the ss command do?
answer: A general-purpose tool for checking network services. ss -tupln lists all processes listening for TCP (t) and UDP (u) services with PIDs (p) and port numbers (n); filter with grep, e.g., ss -tupln | grep httpd.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How can httpd be told which ports/addresses to listen on?
answer: Edit /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf with Listen directives, e.g., Listen 80 (all addresses) or Listen 192.168.0.100:80 (a specific address).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is swap space?
answer: A way of extending RAM: a place (usually on hard disk, but not a regular Linux filesystem) for temporary data that does not fit in RAM but is expected to be needed by the CPU at some point.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How does RAM compare with disk storage?
answer: RAM is nearer the processor, faster, has less capacity, is more expensive per GB, and is temporary (data is lost when the computer is turned off).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What performance effects does swapping have?
answer: Swapping out (moving data from RAM to swap) and swapping in (returning it to RAM) each cause a performance hit because writing/reading disk is much slower than RAM. If RAM runs out, swapping slows the system, but processes stay active and do not lose data.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is an out-of-memory (OOM) condition and what does the kernel do?
answer: When both RAM and swap are full and no data can be discarded or written to disk, the system reaches an OOM condition; the kernel OOM killer kicks in and begins killing processes one by one to regain memory.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is swappiness?
answer: Settings that relate to how aggressively a system swaps. More aggressive swapping can improve performance in some cases (e.g., swapping out a long-minimized document frees RAM for active applications).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: In top output, what do VIRT, RES, SHR, and %MEM mean?
answer: VIRT is memory promised (allocated) to an application (can exceed total RAM); RES is non-swappable memory actually being used; SHR is memory potentially shareable with other apps (e.g., libraries); %MEM is the percentage of total memory consumed.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How do you sort top by memory usage?
answer: Run top and type a capital M; top sorts on the RES column.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is a memory leak?
answer: A process that continuously asks for and uses more memory without giving any back. In top its VIRT grows and, more importantly, its RES memory continues to grow.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How do you kill a process from within top?
answer: Type k in the top window, enter the PID of the process, then choose signal 15 or 9 to send.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How do you drop inactive page caches to free memory temporarily?
answer: As root, run echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches. Some pages are written to disk and others are discarded because they are stored permanently and can be retrieved from disk when needed.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What are Alt+SysRq keystrokes and when are they used?
answer: Keystrokes the kernel processes ahead of other requests, so they work on an otherwise unresponsive system (e.g., to kill an out-of-memory process). They require /proc/sys/kernel/sysrq set to 1 and must be run from a text-based interface (e.g., Ctrl+Alt+F2).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What do Alt+SysRq+f, Alt+SysRq+e, Alt+SysRq+t, and Alt+SysRq+b do?
answer: Alt+SysRq+f kills the process with the highest OOM score; Alt+SysRq+e terminates all processes except init; Alt+SysRq+t dumps a list of all current tasks; Alt+SysRq+b reboots the system.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How do you enable Alt+SysRq keystrokes?
answer: Set /proc/sys/kernel/sysrq to 1, easily done by adding 'kernel.sysrq = 1' to /etc/sysctl.conf.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is rescue mode and when would you use it?
answer: When a Linux system becomes unbootable, you bypass the hard-disk Linux and boot a rescue medium (bootable USB drive or boot CD/DVD), which then tries to mount filesystems from your installed system so you can repair problems.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: Under what directory does rescue mode mount the installed Linux filesystems?
answer: /mnt/sysimage. You can run ls /mnt/sysimage to check that files from the hard disk are present.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What does chroot /mnt/sysimage do in rescue mode?
answer: It makes /mnt/sysimage become the root of the filesystem (/), so it looks like the filesystem installed on your hard disk, enabling you to run repair commands against your installed system.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What can you do in rescue mode to repair an unbootable system?
answer: Fix /etc/fstab entries and run mount -a; reinstall missing components (e.g., reinstall util-linux to restore the mount command); and run fsck to check and fix corrupt filesystems.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is the fsck command?
answer: The filesystem check command; it checks a disk partition for corruption and attempts to correct any problems it encounters.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: Why might you reinstall the util-linux package during rescue mode?
answer: If a critical command such as /bin/mount was deleted, the system would have no command to mount filesystems; reinstalling util-linux replaces the missing mount command.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: dmesg > /tmp/kernel_msg.txt
answer: Captures kernel ring buffer messages into a file so they can be examined later or sent to someone for debugging.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: journalctl -k
answer: Shows kernel messages from boot time to the present, pulled from the systemd journal.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: journalctl -u httpd.service
answer: Shows log/error messages systemd recorded for the httpd service, useful when a service fails to start.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: systemctl
answer: Lists every unit file systemd tried to start, showing LOAD, ACTIVE, and SUB state (e.g., loaded failed failed) so you can spot failed services.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: systemd-analyze time
answer: Shows how long each phase of the startup process (firmware, loader, kernel, userspace) took and when the default target was reached.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: systemd-analyze plot > /tmp/systemd-plot.svg
answer: Creates an SVG graphic of each component of the startup process, which you can open with an image viewer such as eog.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: systemctl start httpd
answer: Starts the httpd service after its configuration has been corrected.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: dnf upgrade --refresh -y
answer: Upgrades to the latest software for your current release, refreshing package metadata and answering yes to prompts.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: dnf install dnf-plugin-system-upgrade -y
answer: Installs the plugin needed to release a Fedora/RHEL system to the next version.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: dnf system-upgrade download --releasever=41
answer: Downloads the packages needed to upgrade to the new release (version 41).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: dnf system-upgrade reboot
answer: Reboots the system to begin the actual upgrade process to the new release.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: dnf system-upgrade clean
answer: Removes cached metadata and transactions after the system comes back up from the upgrade.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: dnf -y --exclude=somepackage update
answer: Updates all packages needing an upgrade except the one named somepackage, useful when a package is broken and holding up the update.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: ethtool -p eth0
answer: Blinks the NIC associated with interface eth0 so you can identify the physical card behind the computer (Ctrl+C stops blinking).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: ping -c 2 192.168.1.1
answer: Sends 2 ICMP echo requests to the router to confirm you can reach your default gateway.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: ping -c 2 8.8.8.8
answer: Pings the Google public DNS server to test connectivity beyond your router and help isolate a hostname-resolution problem.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: traceroute www.google.com
answer: Shows each hop taken en route to the remote host, along with the time taken for each hop.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: mtr
answer: Watches the route taken to a host continuously so you can observe the performance of each leg over time.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: host www.google.com 192.168.0.254
answer: Tests whether the DNS server at 192.168.0.254 can resolve www.google.com into an IP address.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: dig @192.168.0.254 www.google.com
answer: Queries the specified DNS server for the address (A record) of www.google.com to verify the DNS server works.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: nmap 192.168.0.119
answer: Scans the host for open ports and running services (e.g., 21/tcp ftp, 22/tcp ssh, 80/tcp http, 443/tcp https) to check what is exposed.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: top (then type M)
answer: Displays live process activity; typing a capital M sorts the list by memory usage (on the RES column) to find memory-hungry processes.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches
answer: Drops inactive page caches to free memory immediately; some pages are written to disk and others are discarded.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: chroot /mnt/sysimage
answer: Makes /mnt/sysimage the root of the filesystem so it looks like the installed hard-disk system, enabling you to run repair commands.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: fsck
answer: Checks a filesystem for corruption and attempts to correct any problems found.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between systemd targets and System V runlevels?

choices.label: graphical.target aligns with runlevel 5 and multi-user.target with runlevel 3
graphical.target aligns with runlevel 3 and multi-user.target with runlevel 5
Targets and runlevels are identical and interchangeable without mapping
systemd only supports runlevels and does not use targets

explanation: graphical.target aligns with runlevel 5, while multi-user.target is essentially runlevel 3, though there are far more targets than runlevels.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: Which statement correctly describes UEFI versus BIOS?

choices.label: UEFI is a newer firmware that has replaced BIOS on almost all computers, and the two are mutually exclusive
BIOS and UEFI normally run together at the same time
BIOS is a feature that runs inside UEFI to provide secure boot
UEFI only works with signed operating systems and cannot be disabled

explanation: UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) has replaced BIOS on almost all computers, and the two are mutually exclusive. UEFI supports secure boot, which can be disabled for unsigned operating systems.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: Which command captures and views kernel ring buffer messages?

choices.label: dmesg
systemctl
nmap
fsck

explanation: dmesg captures and displays the kernel ring buffer messages. On systemd systems, journalctl -k can also be used.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: Which correctly describes apt-get update in Ubuntu compared with dnf update?

choices.label: apt-get update only downloads packaging metadata, while dnf downloads metadata automatically on every command
Both apt-get update and dnf update install new versions of packages
apt-get update upgrades the entire system to the next release
Only apt-get update requires a separate upgrade step to install packages

explanation: apt-get update downloads latest packaging metadata; apt-get upgrade then installs packages. dnf/yum download latest metadata with every command, and dnf system-upgrade moves to the next release.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: In top output, which column shows non-swappable memory actually being used and is the sort column when you press M?

choices.label: RES
VIRT
SHR
%CPU

explanation: RES shows non-swappable memory actually being used, and top sorts on RES when you sort by memory with M. VIRT is memory promised to the application, SHR is shareable memory.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What happens when RAM and swap are both full and no data can be discarded or written to disk?

choices.label: The kernel OOM killer begins killing processes one by one to regain memory
The system reboots automatically to prevent data loss
All processes continue running with no performance impact
The kernel immediately shuts down swap permanently

explanation: When neither RAM nor swap can hold more data, the OOM killer kicks in and kills processes one by one until the kernel has enough memory to function.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: Which statement correctly describes the ss command?

choices.label: It checks network services and listeners; ss -tupln lists processes listening for TCP/UDP with port numbers
It is only used for scanning another host's open ports like a cracker tool
It displays the routing table and default gateway
It verifies DNS name-to-address resolution

explanation: ss is a general-purpose tool for checking network services and listeners. ss -tupln | grep httpd verifies a service is listening on its ports.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: If nmap reports port 80 as 'closed', what does that indicate?

choices.label: The httpd service is either not running or not listening on that port
The firewall is blocking packets to that port
The network interface is down
The DNS server is unreachable

explanation: A filtered state usually means the firewall blocks the port; a closed state means the httpd service is not running or not listening on that port. Open means a service is listening.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is the purpose of chroot /mnt/sysimage in rescue mode?

choices.label: It makes the installed hard-disk filesystem the root so you can run repair commands
It permanently deletes the rescue medium's filesystem
It mounts the rescue medium's root as a secondary filesystem
It converts /mnt/sysimage back into a swap area

explanation: chroot /mnt/sysimage makes the mounted installed filesystem the root (/), so it looks like the filesystem on the hard disk for repair work.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is the correct order of events for a Linux system to boot up?
correct_sequence: 1. Turn on the power
2. Start the hardware from BIOS or UEFI firmware
3. Find the location of the boot loader and start it
4. Start the kernel and initial RAM disk for the selected OS
5. Start the initialization process (init, upstart, or systemd)
6. Start all services associated with the selected runlevel or default target
distractor_sequences: 1. Start the kernel, 2. Start firmware, 3. Start the boot loader, 4. Start the init process
1. Initialize init, 2. Start firmware, 3. Start the boot loader, 4. Start the kernel
explanation: Boot proceeds from power-on and firmware, to boot loader, to kernel and initramfs, to the init system, to services started for the default target or runlevel.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is the correct order to upgrade a Fedora/RHEL system to a new release?
correct_sequence: 1. dnf upgrade --refresh -y
2. dnf install dnf-plugin-system-upgrade -y
3. dnf system-upgrade download --releasever=41
4. dnf system-upgrade reboot
5. dnf system-upgrade clean
distractor_sequences: 1. dnf system-upgrade reboot, 2. dnf system-upgrade download, 3. dnf upgrade
1. dnf system-upgrade clean before downloading the new release
explanation: First update the current release, install the plugin, download the upgrade for the new release, reboot to upgrade, then clean cached metadata and transactions.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is the correct order to interrupt GRUB 2 and modify the boot process?
correct_sequence: 1. Press any key (such as the up arrow) just after the BIOS screen
2. Highlight the desired kernel entry with arrow keys
3. Type e to edit the commands that start the system
4. Add kernel arguments to the end of the line beginning with linux
5. Press Ctrl+X to boot with the added arguments
distractor_sequences: 1. Type e first, then press any key, then boot with argument flags
2. Reboot and immediately press Ctrl+X before selecting a kernel
explanation: Interrupt GRUB, select a kernel, edit with e, append kernel arguments such as selinux=0 or nosmt, then boot with Ctrl+X.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What is the correct order to enter rescue mode from a RHEL installation DVD/USB?
correct_sequence: 1. Burn the install image to USB, CD, or DVD
2. Insert the medium into the broken system and reboot
3. Press the boot-device function key at the BIOS screen and select the drive
4. Choose Troubleshooting (or Rescue Mode) and Rescue a Red Hat Enterprise Linux system
5. Select Continue to mount the installed filesystems under /mnt/sysimage
6. chroot /mnt/sysimage and begin repairs
distractor_sequences: 1. Boot the broken hard disk normally, then select Rescue
2. Mount under /mnt/sysimage before booting the rescue medium
explanation: Boot from the rescue medium, select the troubleshooting/Rescue menu option, let the filesystems mount under /mnt/sysimage, then chroot to repair.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
symptoms: A newly installed kernel is broken, or third-party (video/wireless) drivers no longer work after a kernel update, so the graphical login or network fails.
root_cause: Third-party kernel driver packages only work with specific kernel versions; installing a later kernel breaks them.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Reboot and interrupt GRUB by pressing any key just after the BIOS screen
2. Highlight the previous, still-working kernel entry and press Enter to boot it
resolution: Boot the older (still working) kernel to get the system up while you obtain a driver rebuilt for the current kernel (e.g., from rpmfusion.org) or download drivers from the manufacturer.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
symptoms: dnf install reports that dependent packages needed for the installation are not available.
root_cause: Dependency inconsistencies, more common with short release cycles and larger/third-party repositories that cannot control their dependencies.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Use recent, well-tested main repositories for your distribution
2. Update the system regularly (e.g., dnf update)
3. Use third-party apps/repos only when necessary; look in main repos first
resolution: Stick to stable repositories, update regularly, avoid unnecessary third-party repos, and reinstall/upgrade packages; exclude failing packages with dnf -y --exclude=somepackage update if needed.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
symptoms: You open a web browser but cannot reach any websites; you suspect you are not connected to the network.
root_cause: Could be a down network interface, a broken route/gateway, or a hostname-resolution (DNS) problem.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Run ip addr show to see if the interface is up and has an inet address
2. Run ip route show to check the default gateway
3. ping -c 2 the gateway, then ping -c 2 8.8.8.8; if these work, test name resolution with host or dig
resolution: Fix the interface (plug in cable, enable in firmware) or routing, or correct your DNS servers in resolv.conf/DHCP.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
symptoms: You can reach remote hosts by IP address (ping 8.8.8.8 works) but not by hostname.
root_cause: Name-to-address resolution is failing, typically a DNS server that is unreachable, down, or misconfigured.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Check the DNS servers in /etc/resolv.conf
2. ping -c 2 each nameserver IP to see if it is reachable
3. Use host or dig with each nameserver to see if it can resolve a hostname
resolution: Correct your DNS server IP addresses or fix the resolver configuration (e.g., via DHCP/NetworkManager); check /var/log/messages or journalctl for assigned DNS servers.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
symptoms: Clients cannot reach your Apache web server even though networking is otherwise fine.
root_cause: The service may not be running, not listening on the expected ports, blocked by a firewall, or restricted in its config.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. From the server run systemctl status httpd.service to confirm it is running
2. Run ss -tupln | grep httpd to verify it is listening on ports 80/443
3. From a client run nmap your_server_ip to see if ports 80/443 are open, closed, or filtered
4. Check /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf for Listen directives and allowed/denied host settings
resolution: Start/fix the service, correct Listen directives, adjust firewall rules to allow the ports, and correct access controls in httpd.conf.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
symptoms: ip addr show reports eth0 state DOWN, or no interface appears at all, and there is no connectivity.
root_cause: Interface is down, cable unplugged or in the wrong port, NIC not fully seated, or NIC disabled in firmware; on laptops a physical wireless switch may be off.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Check physical connections and plug the cable into the correct NIC (use ethtool -p eth0 to identify it)
2. Verify the NIC is not disabled in the BIOS/firmware
3. On a laptop, check for a tiny wireless on/off switch
resolution: Connect/seat the cable properly, reseat or enable the NIC in firmware, and flip the laptop wireless switch on.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
symptoms: The system slows down to nearly unusable and applications begin to crash; the MiB Mem free space is near zero and swap usage keeps growing.
root_cause: The system is running out of memory, likely due to an errant process or a memory leak, leading to heavy swapping or an OOM condition.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Run top and type M to sort processes by memory usage
2. Look for a process whose VIRT and especially RES memory keeps growing (memory leak)
3. Kill the errant process with k in top (send signal 15 or 9)
resolution: Kill the runaway/leaking process; if the system is unresponsive use Alt+SysRq+f (with kernel.sysrq=1) to kill the highest-OOM process; consider adding capacity.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
symptoms: A service (e.g., httpd) shows as failed in systemctl output.
root_cause: The service failed to start, for example due to an error in its configuration such as a misconfigured httpd.conf.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Run systemctl to identify the failed unit (httpd.service loaded failed failed)
2. Run journalctl -u httpd.service to see error messages
3. Correct the configuration error (e.g., fix an unclosed <Directory> directive)
resolution: Fix the reported configuration/syntax error, then start the service with systemctl start httpd.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
symptoms: A bootable device (e.g., a USB drive for rescue or a NIC for PXE) does not appear in the boot order menu.
root_cause: The device is disabled in the firmware, or its boot feature (such as PXE) is not enabled.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Go into the UEFI Setup utility (often F1, F2, or F12)
2. Enable the device or turn on the boot/PXE feature
3. Return to the boot order and select the device
resolution: Enable the device or feature in the Setup screen so it appears in and can be selected from the boot order.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
symptoms: The system fails to boot because filesystems cannot be mounted, possibly due to an error in /etc/fstab.
root_cause: Invalid fstab entries such as wrong device names or a mount point directory that does not exist.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Boot into rescue mode and chroot /mnt/sysimage
2. Edit /etc/fstab to correct bad entries
3. Run mount -a to verify all filesystems mount
resolution: Correct the fstab entries, then use mount -a; reboot to finish.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
symptoms: A service hangs or the boot process seems to stall; you want to find where the delay occurs.
root_cause: Some service or phase of startup is taking an unusually long time.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Run systemd-analyze time to see how long each phase took
2. Run systemd-analyze plot > /tmp/systemd-plot.svg and open it with eog to find services with long dark-red start bars or white (failed) bars
3. Use journalctl -u for the offending service to debug
resolution: Fix or disable the stalling service based on the analysis; restart the system to verify.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: In top output, what do the MiB Mem and MiB Swap lines tell you?
answer: MiB Mem shows total, free, used, and buff/cache RAM (e.g., 7717.2 total, 4830.8 used); MiB Swap shows total, free, and used swap (e.g., 844.5 used). Used swap with near-zero free RAM indicates an out-of-memory trend.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How can you watch memory usage live in a web browser?
answer: If Cockpit is installed and enabled, open Cockpit and select Overview, then View Metrics And History from the Usage box to watch memory and swap usage over time.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What signs in top indicate the system is reaching an out-of-memory state?
answer: Free space on the MiB Mem line near zero; used space on the MiB Swap line nonzero and growing with a slowdown; a process whose VIRT (and especially RES) memory keeps growing indicates a memory leak; if swap runs out the kernel kills processes.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: Why can the VIRT column total exceed the amount of RAM on the system?
answer: Because VIRT shows only the amount of memory promised (allocated) to the application, which can exceed total RAM. RES shows the non-swappable memory actually being used.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What should you check if the ip command shows no network interface at all?
answer: Check that the hardware isn't disabled: for a wired NIC the card may not be fully seated in its slot or may be disabled in the BIOS; on a laptop check for the tiny switch that disables the NIC.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How do you isolate a connectivity problem when you cannot reach any websites?
answer: Check ip addr show for interface status, ip route show for the default route, ping -c 2 the router, then ping -c 2 8.8.8.8. If those succeed, test hostname resolution with host or dig; use traceroute or mtr for slow connections.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What does it mean if nmap shows port 80 as filtered rather than open or closed?
answer: Filtered usually means the firewall is blocking packets to that port; you need to check your firewall configuration to allow access to ports 80/443. Open means a service is listening; closed means the service is not running or not listening.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How can a server's hostname become resolvable so any client on the Internet can reach it?
answer: Lock the system down to a particular public IP address and register that address with a public DNS server, typically using a domain registrar such as networksolutions.com.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What does 'ss -tupln | grep httpd' output indicate when it shows tcp 0 0 :::80 :::* LISTEN?
answer: It shows the httpd process (PID) is listening on port 80 for all interfaces (:::80). If it only listened on the local interface the entry would be 127.0.0.1:80. Listening on selected interfaces is controlled with Listen directives in httpd.conf.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How can you find the DNS server IP addresses that were actually assigned to your system?
answer: Search /var/log/messages or the output of journalctl for your DNS servers' IP addresses; with NetworkManager connecting via DHCP you should see name server lines with the IP addresses being assigned.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: How often does Fedora stop supplying updated packages for a release, and what does that mean for upgrades?
answer: Fedora stops supplying updated packages 13 months after a version is released. You should upgrade to a new release about once a year or face possible dependency and security problems.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: Where can you get rebuilt third-party kernel drivers for video/wireless cards after a kernel update?
answer: Sites such as rpmfusion.org build third-party, non-open-source driver packages and upgrade those drivers when a new kernel is available; alternatively download Linux drivers from the manufacturer (e.g., Nvidia) or build from source.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What should you do with the output of a cron job command?
answer: Direct the output to a file or pipe it to a command that can deal with it (e.g., dnf -y update >> /tmp/cron.txt). If you don't, any output is sent to the user that created the cron job.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What are the valid ways to specify times in crontab fields?
answer: A single number, a list of numbers (1,5,17), a range (1-3), or skip values (*/3 = every three hours). Days of the week and months can be entered as numbers or words.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What types of units can systemd manage besides services?
answer: systemd can start, stop, and manage unit files representing devices, automounts, paths, sockets, swap areas, timers, and more, in addition to services.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: Why might you select an older kernel from the GRUB menu?
answer: If the current kernel is broken, or if third-party kernel drivers (video/wireless) no longer work after a kernel update, you can boot a previous kernel that you know is working while you obtain a permanent fix.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: What should you look for in kernel boot messages?
answer: Drivers that fail to load or messages showing hardware features failing to be enabled (e.g., a TV tuner card set to the wrong tuner type). Options passed to a driver can try different settings until a working one is found.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch21: Troubleshooting Linux
question: top (then type k, enter a PID, choose 15 or 9)
answer: From the top window, typing k lets you kill a process by PID; choose signal 15 (graceful) or 9 (forced) to terminate it.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch22: Configuring an Artificial Intelligence Chatbot
question: What is the general difference between a large language model (LLM) and a small language model (SLM) in terms of parameters?
answer: SLMs generally have between 1 billion and 7 billion parameters, while LLMs can have more than 30 billion parameters (some over 70 billion). Fewer parameters means SLMs cannot do problem solving that is as deep or complex as LLMs.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch22: Configuring an Artificial Intelligence Chatbot
question: How do LLMs and SLMs differ in resource requirements?
answer: SLMs can run on less powerful and less expensive hardware, e.g., with 4-8 GB of memory, and some SLMs can run on CPUs. LLMs may need 40 GB or more of memory and often require GPUs to run effectively.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch22: Configuring an Artificial Intelligence Chatbot
question: How do task requirements differ between LLMs and SLMs?
answer: SLMs are good at simple tasks needing to be done quickly without much complexity. LLMs have much broader knowledge and can work on tasks with multiple complex steps, producing better output such as in-depth reports or creative writing.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch22: Configuring an Artificial Intelligence Chatbot
question: Why might SLM answers be less informed or more biased than LLM answers?
answer: SLMs work from a smaller knowledge base, so answers may be less informed and even factually incorrect, and unless very carefully curated an SLM is much more likely to have biased results because small amounts of biased or false data have a greater effect.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch22: Configuring an Artificial Intelligence Chatbot
question: When is an SLM a good choice over an LLM?
answer: When you have limited compute resources or money; when the task is simple with well-defined boundaries; when speed of response matters; when privacy requires not uploading your data to outside servers; and when you need to run disconnected (e.g., edge devices).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch22: Configuring an Artificial Intelligence Chatbot
question: What is Phi-3 and how did it perform in the chapter?
answer: A family of models from Microsoft available in mini, small, and medium versions. It easily wrote shell scripts but tends to give long-winded answers; phi3:mini is the only version that ran well on the author's moderate (8 GB) hardware.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch22: Configuring an Artificial Intelligence Chatbot
question: What is Llama 3.1?
answer: An open source language model developed by Meta, one of the first reduced-size LLMs to run well on limited hardware. The llama3.1:8b version performed well on the author's moderate hardware.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch22: Configuring an Artificial Intelligence Chatbot
question: What is Mistral and what makes it distinctive?
answer: A language model developed by the French start-up Mistral AI, trained in English, French, Spanish, German, and Italian, so it can handle multilingual queries (e.g., translation).

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch22: Configuring an Artificial Intelligence Chatbot
question: What is Ollama?
answer: A tool designed to run AI language models on your local computer. After installation it runs as a systemd service and exposes an API at 127.0.0.1:11434.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch22: Configuring an Artificial Intelligence Chatbot
question: What memory (RAM) is needed to run different model sizes in Ollama?
answer: 13B models need at least 32 GB of RAM, 7B models need at least 16 GB, and 3B models need at least 8 GB.

source: Linux Bible 11th Ed - Ch22: Configuring an Artificial Intelligence Chatbot
question: What CPU and GPU requirements are recommended for Ollama?
answer: CPUs: eight cores recommended (four will work with smaller SLMs); choose CPUs with AVX-512 or AVX support for parallel processing.
