question: Which command is the only one required to enable IP multicast routing support?

choices.label: ip pim dense-mode
ip multicast-routing
ip igmp version 2
ip pim rp-address

explanation: ip multicast-routing enables the support of all IP multicast routing functions; the others are optional or protocol-specific.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: What happens to LAN interfaces when ip multicast-routing is enabled?

choices.label: They must have IGMP configured manually
IGMPv2 is automatically enabled on them
IGMPv1 is automatically enabled on them
IGMP is disabled on them

explanation: When IP multicast routing is enabled, IGMPv2 is automatically enabled on LAN interfaces.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the default for ip igmp query-timeout?

choices.label: 10 seconds
60 seconds
2 times the query interval (120 seconds)
3 times the query interval

explanation: The default querier timeout is 2 times the query interval, i.e., 120 seconds with the default 60-second interval.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: When two equal-cost paths exist to a source, which neighbor does PIM choose as the RPF?

choices.label: The neighbor with the lower IP address
The first neighbor in the routing table
The neighbor with the numerically higher IP address
The neighbor with the higher metric

explanation: PIM breaks the tie by choosing the interface to the neighbor with the numerically higher IP address as the RPF interface.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: Which statement about the IGMP querier and PIM DR on a multiaccess subnet is TRUE?

choices.label: The same router must be both querier and DR
The lowest IP address wins the querier; the highest IP address wins the DR
The highest IP address wins the querier; the lowest wins the DR
The DR is always the IGMP querier

explanation: The router with the lowest IP address becomes the IGMPv2 querier and the highest becomes the PIM DR.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: When AD and metric to a source are equal on two routers sharing a subnet, which router becomes the PIM forwarder?

choices.label: The router with the lower IP address
The router with the higher IP address
The IGMP querier
The router with the higher metric

explanation: If both administrative distances and metrics are equal, the router with the highest IP address is the forwarder.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: When does a Cisco PIM-SM router switch from the RPT to the SPT by default?

choices.label: After traffic exceeds 100 kbps
After the first multicast packet is received
After 10 seconds of traffic
Only when statically configured

explanation: By default, after the first multicast packet is received, a PIM-SM router with an attached member switches to the SPT.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: Why can a PIM router not forward a group's packets out the group's RPF interface?

choices.label: RPF requires a single incoming interface
It is the multicast version of the split-horizon rule - packets are not forwarded out the interface they arrived on
The RPF interface is always pruned
The RP forbids it

explanation: A PIM router cannot forward a group's packets out that group's RPF interface - a multicast version of split horizon.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: What is a disadvantage of static RP configuration compared to Auto-RP?

choices.label: It requires more bandwidth
Changing the RP requires manual reconfiguration of all PIM routers, and failover to an alternate RP is difficult
It cannot support multiple groups
It only works with PIM-DM

explanation: Static RP requires manual reconfiguration on all PIM routers to change or fail over the RP; Auto-RP automates discovery.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: What happens if PIM is not configured on a mapping agent's loopback interface?

choices.label: The router refuses the command and the mapping agent does not work
The command is accepted but the interface is ignored and the mapping agent does not work
The mapping agent works but uses a physical interface address
The router automatically enables PIM on the loopback

explanation: The command is accepted with a Non PIM interface warning but the interface is ignored, so the mapping agent does not work.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: How does the Auto-RP mapping agent select the RP for a group range?

choices.label: The C-RP with the lowest address
The C-RP with the highest address
A hash of the group address
The first C-RP to announce

explanation: The mapping agent chooses the RP for a group based on the highest RP address.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: How long does a mapping agent wait to declare an Auto-RP dead after its last announcement?

choices.label: 60 seconds
120 seconds
180 seconds (3 times the announcement interval)
300 seconds

explanation: If no RP-Announce is heard within 180 seconds (3 times the 60-second interval), the RP is declared dead.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: Who selects the RP when using the bootstrap protocol?

choices.label: The mapping agent
The BSR
Each PIMv2 router, using a hash algorithm that all routers compute identically
The C-RP with the highest address

explanation: Unlike Auto-RP, the BSR does not select RPs; each PIMv2 router selects the RP itself with the same hash algorithm.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: With equal priorities, which C-RP is elected the RP under bootstrap versus Auto-RP?

choices.label: Bootstrap picks the lowest address; Auto-RP picks the highest
Both pick the highest address
Both pick the lowest address
Bootstrap picks the highest; Auto-RP picks the lowest

explanation: Bootstrap elects the lowest RP address; Auto-RP selects the highest RP address.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: What does a BSR hash-mask length of 26 mean?

choices.label: 26 consecutive group addresses per range
64 consecutive group addresses per range
2^26 ranges
The mask length has no effect

explanation: A 26-bit mask leaves 6 variable bits, bundling 64 consecutive group addresses per range.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: Why can multicast traffic not be load-balanced directly over parallel equal-cost physical links?

choices.label: Unicast routing does not support it
RPF requires a single incoming interface, so traffic arriving on the non-RPF link is dropped
Multicast packets cannot be load balanced
The RP forbids it

explanation: RPF requires all traffic to arrive on the same upstream interface, so traffic on the non-RPF link is dropped.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the purpose of a static mroute?

choices.label: It forwards unicast traffic to a next hop
It statically configures the RPF interface for a source, overriding the unicast routing table; it is not used for forwarding
It blocks multicast from a source
It changes the metric of a multicast route

explanation: Static mroutes override dynamic entries to set the RPF interface, but are not used for forwarding.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: Why does RPF succeed for packets arriving on a GRE tunnel from either physical path?

choices.label: The tunnel sets a special flag
All packets appear to arrive on the same interface (TU0) from the same upstream neighbor
RPF is disabled on tunnels
The unicast table is updated automatically

explanation: At the virtual tunnel interface the encapsulation is removed, so packets appear to arrive on the same interface from the same upstream neighbor.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: When are mstat's per-hop delay times valid?

choices.label: Always
Only when routers' clocks are synchronized
Only for the first hop
Only for dense mode

explanation: Delay times between routers are valid only if the routers' clocks are synchronized.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: What does a negative lost-packet count like -3/85 in mstat indicate?

choices.label: A rounding error
A packet gain, which may signify a loop
A clock synchronization problem
Normal operation

explanation: Negative packet loss represents a packet gain - extra packets received - which may signify a loop.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: What group address does mtrace use by default when none is specified?

choices.label: 224.2.0.1 (MBone audio)

explanation: When no group is specified, mtrace uses the MBone audio group address 224.2.0.1.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the correct order of the Auto-RP discovery process?
correct_sequence: A C-RP sends RP-Announce messages to 224.0.1.39 every 60 seconds
The mapping agent receives the announcements
The mapping agent selects the RP (highest address wins)
The mapping agent sends RP-Discovery messages to 224.0.1.40 every 60 seconds
Routers in the domain learn the group-to-RP mappings
distractor_sequences: The mapping agent advertises RPs before receiving announcements
Routers select the RP themselves without the mapping agent
explanation: C-RPs announce to 224.0.1.39; the mapping agent selects the RP and advertises mappings to 224.0.1.40.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the correct order of the Auto-RP RP failover process?
correct_sequence: The active RP stops sending RP-Announce messages
The mapping agent waits 180 seconds without hearing an announcement
The mapping agent declares the RP dead
The mapping agent selects the next-highest qualifying C-RP
The mapping agent advertises the new RP to the domain
distractor_sequences: The mapping agent immediately switches to a new RP on the first missed announcement
The C-RP selects a new RP itself
explanation: The mapping agent waits 3 announcement intervals, then promotes the next-highest C-RP and advertises it.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the correct order of the bootstrap RP discovery process?
correct_sequence: C-BSRs send Bootstrap messages to 224.0.0.13 with address and priority
The BSR is elected (highest priority, then highest address)
C-RPs unicast Candidate-RP-Advertisement messages to the BSR
The BSR collects the C-RPs into an RP-Set in its Bootstrap messages
Each PIMv2 router selects the RP using the hash algorithm
distractor_sequences: C-RPs multicast their advertisements to the whole domain
The BSR selects the RP for all routers
explanation: The BSR floods the RP-Set; each router computes the RP itself with the hash algorithm.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the correct order of the PIM forwarder failover process?
correct_sequence: The forwarder (DR) fails
The backup router stops hearing PIM Hellos within the holdtime
The backup router declares the neighbor dead
It assumes the DR/forwarder role
It sends PIM Graft messages to its neighbors to reattach the interface
distractor_sequences: The backup immediately sends Grafts without waiting for the holdtime
The IGMP querier handles the failover instead
explanation: After the holdtime expires with no hellos, the neighbor is declared dead and the backup takes over and sends Grafts.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the correct order of a PIM-SM router switching from the RPT to the SPT?
correct_sequence: A member joins the group and the DR joins the RPT toward the RP
The first multicast packet is received by the last hop router
The last hop router sends a Join toward the source to build the SPT
Traffic begins arriving on the SPT
The router prunes the RPT branch toward the RP
distractor_sequences: The router prunes the RPT before joining the source
The RP initiates the SPT switch
explanation: The last hop router joins the source first, then prunes the RPT once SPT traffic flows.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the correct order to configure multicast load sharing over parallel paths?
correct_sequence: Configure a GRE tunnel between the routers' loopback interfaces
Give the tunnel an IP address and enable PIM on it
Put the tunnel in OSPF passive-interface mode so only multicast crosses it
Add a static mroute (ip mroute) so the tunnel becomes the RPF interface
Disable fast switching (no ip route-cache) for per-packet load balancing
distractor_sequences: Load balance directly over the physical links without a tunnel
Configure the static mroute before building the tunnel
explanation: The tunnel unifies the RPF interface; the static mroute overrides the unicast table; fast switching is disabled for per-packet balancing.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: debug ip mpacket shows 'not RPF interface' for packets arriving on the tunnel interface. What is the cause and fix?
symptoms: debug ip mpacket shows 'IP: s=10.1.1.88 (Tunnel0) d=228.13.20.216 len 569, not RPF interface' on the receiving router.
root_cause: The unicast routing table still shows a physical interface (Stetson or Fedora) as the next hop to the source, so packets arriving on the tunnel fail the RPF check.
troubleshooting_steps: Run show ip route 10.1.1.88 to confirm the unicast next hop is a physical interface
Run show ip mroute to inspect the RPF neighbor
Confirm the tunnel is built between loopbacks and PIM is enabled on it
resolution: Add a static mroute: ip mroute 10.1.1.88 255.255.255.255 Tunnel0, so the tunnel becomes the RPF interface.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: Multicast is forwarded by one router on a multiaccess subnet but the IGMP querier is a different router. Is this a problem?
symptoms: show ip igmp interface shows the IGMP querier as one router while show ip mroute shows a different router forwarding the group.
root_cause: This is normal: the querier is the lowest IP address and the forwarder is chosen by lowest AD/metric/highest IP; they need not be the same router.
troubleshooting_steps: Verify the querier has the lowest IP address on the subnet
Verify the forwarder wins the AD/metric/IP tiebreak
Confirm the forwarder hears the member's IGMP Membership Reports
resolution: No action required unless forwarding or membership fails.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: A router has two equal-cost paths to a source. Which interface does PIM pick as RPF, and why might traffic from the other path be dropped?
symptoms: Multicast traffic arriving on one of two equal-cost links is dropped; the other is forwarded.
root_cause: PIM picks the interface to the neighbor with the numerically higher IP address as the RPF interface; traffic on the other path fails the RPF check and is dropped because RPF requires a single incoming interface.
troubleshooting_steps: Run show ip route <source> to confirm two equal-cost paths
Run show ip mroute to see which interface is the RPF interface
Run debug ip mpacket to confirm the drops
resolution: Accept the single-path behavior, or use a tunnel plus static mroute to load balance.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: PIM-SM has stopped working domain-wide. The single Auto-RP mapping agent has failed. Why is this catastrophic?
symptoms: PIM-SM fails domain-wide; routers lose all group-to-RP mappings.
root_cause: With a single mapping agent, no RP-Discovery messages are sent when it fails, so no RPs are advertised to the domain and PIM-SM fails.
troubleshooting_steps: Check the mapping agent's reachability
Run show ip pim rp mapping to see if mappings expire
Configure redundancy
resolution: Make C-RPs also mapping agents (or add multiple mapping agents) so another can advertise RPs if one fails.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: After configuring ip pim send-rp-discovery Loopback0 scope 5, the router reports 'Non PIM interface ignored in accepted command' and the mapping agent does not work. What is wrong?
symptoms: The router accepts the send-rp-discovery command but shows 'Non PIM interface ignored in accepted command'; the mapping agent does not work.
root_cause: PIM-SM is not configured on the loopback interface, so the specified interface is ignored.
troubleshooting_steps: Configure ip pim sparse-mode on Loopback0
Re-enter ip pim send-rp-discovery Loopback0 scope 5
Verify with show running-config that the interface is accepted
resolution: Enable PIM-SM on the loopback interface first, then reconfigure the mapping agent.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: You want Stetson to be the BSR but Fedora is winning the election. Both have default priority and hash-mask. What change makes Stetson the BSR?
symptoms: show ip pim bsr-router shows Fedora as the BSR though Stetson is preferred.
root_cause: With equal priority (0) and hash-mask length, the higher BSR address (Fedora, 10.224.1.2) wins the election.
troubleshooting_steps: Run show ip pim bsr-router to confirm the active BSR
Give Stetson a higher priority
resolution: Configure Stetson with ip pim bsr-candidate Loopback0 0 100 so it wins the election and Fedora becomes backup.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: Routers in a pure PIM-SM domain cannot learn the RP because they cannot join the Auto-RP groups. What is the fix?
symptoms: Routers never learn RP mappings in a PIM-SM domain; Auto-RP messages cannot be received.
root_cause: In sparse mode, routers must join a group to receive it, but they cannot join 224.0.1.39/224.0.1.40 because they do not yet know an RP - a Catch-22.
troubleshooting_steps: Confirm interfaces are in pure sparse mode
Configure interfaces as sparse-dense mode
resolution: Use ip pim sparse-dense-mode; the Auto-RP groups then operate in dense mode and are flooded even before an RP is known.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: PIM-DM is configured but no multicast traffic is being forwarded. What fundamental requirement may be missing?
symptoms: PIM-DM is enabled on interfaces but multicast traffic is not forwarded.
root_cause: No unicast routing protocol is running, so PIM has no mechanism to determine the RPF interface and the RPF check cannot succeed.
troubleshooting_steps: Run show ip route to confirm a unicast routing protocol is active
Run show ip pim neighbor to check PIM adjacencies
Verify ip multicast-routing is enabled
resolution: Enable a unicast routing protocol (e.g., OSPF) so PIM can determine RPF paths.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: Why can failing to enable PIM on every interface cause inadvertent RPF failures?
symptoms: Multicast works on some paths but fails intermittently on others; RPF failures are hard to explain.
root_cause: If a multicast packet arrives on an interface where PIM is disabled, the RPF check may fail because that interface is not a PIM neighbor interface.
troubleshooting_steps: Audit all interfaces for ip pim configuration
Run show ip pim neighbor to see which adjacencies exist
Compare the RPF interface against PIM-enabled interfaces
resolution: Enable PIM on every interface (or at least all that face PIM neighbors) to avoid RPF failures.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: How do you verify which RP a specific group will use before that group is active on a router?
symptoms: Need to determine the RP for a group address that is not yet active on the router.
root_cause: The basic show ip pim rp only shows active groups; the mapping for an inactive group must be queried explicitly.
troubleshooting_steps: Run show ip pim rp-hash 235.1.2.3
Compare the result to the configured access list constraints
resolution: Use show ip pim rp-hash <group> to see which RP the group will map to.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: After ip pim spt-threshold infinity is configured on a router whose RPF interface equals the RPT path, its (*, G) entry shows a pruned flag and forwarding stops. What is happening?
symptoms: After enabling ip pim spt-threshold infinity, the router's (*, G) entry is pruned and it stops forwarding the group.
root_cause: The router's RPF interface is the same interface the RPT arrives on, and a PIM router cannot forward a group's packets out its RPF interface (multicast split-horizon rule).
troubleshooting_steps: Run show ip mroute to observe the (*, G) flags and interfaces
Check the RPF interface against the incoming RPT interface
Understand that forwarding duties pass to the upstream router
resolution: This is expected behavior; the upstream router (e.g., Porkpie) forwards the group while the RPT-only router is pruned.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: mstat shows one packet lost on the hop between two routers. Does this indicate a problem?
symptoms: mstat reports a small packet loss on one hop.
root_cause: A single lost packet may or may not indicate a problem; it must be observed over multiple runs to determine if loss is consistent.
troubleshooting_steps: Run mstat several times for the same (S, G)
Check whether the packet loss is consistent
If consistent, use debugging to investigate the hop
resolution: Investigate with debugging only if the packet loss is consistent across iterations.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch6: Configuring and Troubleshooting IP Multicast Routing
question: mstat output shows nonsensical per-hop delay times but valid packet rates. What is the likely cause?
symptoms: mstat shows nonsensical per-hop delay times while packet rates and trace information are valid.
root_cause: The routers' clocks are not synchronized; delay times are valid only when clocks are synchronized, though packet rates remain valid.
troubleshooting_steps: Verify router clock synchronization (NTP)
Compare trace information and packet rates, which remain valid
Synchronize clocks to make delay times meaningful
resolution: Synchronize the routers' clocks (e.g., with NTP) so per-hop delay statistics are valid.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: TTL scoping
answer: A method of limiting multicast packet scope in which the TTL value of multicast packets is set so packets travel only a certain distance before the TTL is decremented to 0 and the packet is discarded. Granularity can be added by setting boundaries on interfaces with the ip multicast ttl-threshold command, which drops all packets with a TTL equal to or below the configured value.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Administrative scoping
answer: A method of limiting multicast scope in which the multicast group address range 224.0.0.0-239.255.255.255 is partitioned so certain ranges are assigned certain scopes, and domain boundaries are created by filtering on these address ranges. Defined in RFC 2365 and implemented with the ip multicast boundary command referencing an access list.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What happens when an interface is configured with ip multicast ttl-threshold 5?
answer: Only packets with TTL values greater than 5 are forwarded out of the interface. Any packets with TTL values of 5 or below are dropped.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: MBone TTL threshold value for a host
answer: TTL 0 restricts a multicast packet to the same host.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: MBone TTL threshold value for a subnet
answer: TTL 1 restricts a multicast packet to the same subnet.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: MBone TTL threshold value for a site
answer: TTL 15 restricts a multicast packet to the same site.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: MBone TTL threshold value for a region
answer: TTL 63 restricts a multicast packet to the same region.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: MBone TTL thresholds for worldwide reachability
answer: TTL 127 permits worldwide reachability; TTL 191 permits worldwide reachability with limited bandwidth; TTL 255 is unrestricted.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: RFC 2365
answer: The RFC that specifies administrative scoping of IP multicast, partitioning the multicast address space into scope ranges such as link-local (224.0.0.0/24), global (224.0.1.0-238.255.255.255), and organization-local (239.192.0.0/14).

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Link-local scope multicast range
answer: 224.0.0.0/24. Multicast packets in this range (IGMP 224.0.0.1/2, OSPF 224.0.0.5/6, EIGRP 224.0.0.10, PIM 224.0.0.13) are never forwarded by a router and are restricted to the data link on which they were originated.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Organization-local scope range per RFC 2365
answer: 239.192.0.0/14. Multicast packets destined to this range are blocked at an administrative boundary configured to deny organization-local scope.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What does adding the ip multicast boundary command to an interface do?
answer: It creates an administrative boundary. The command references an IP access list that specifies the group address range to be permitted or denied at that interface.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: How do you connect two PIM domains separated by a unicast-only IP domain?
answer: Create a GRE tunnel between the two border routers that can carry the PIM traffic. PIM is configured on the tunnel interface (not on the physical interface), OSPF runs passively on the tunnel to prevent unicast traffic crossing it, and static multicast routes (mroutes) reference the tunnel as the upstream interface to prevent RPF failures.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Why are static multicast routes (ip mroute) needed when tunneling multicast across a unicast-only domain?
answer: Without them, RPF checks would use the OSPF routes and determine the upstream interface to be the routers' Ethernet interfaces rather than the tunnel, so all multicast packets arriving on the tunnel would fail the RPF check. The static mroute references all possible source addresses from the opposite domain and shows their upstream interface as the tunnel.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: How does a Cisco router detect and enable DVMRP on a PIM-configured interface?
answer: When an interface is configured to run PIM, the router listens for DVMRP Probe messages. When Probes are heard, Cisco IOS Software automatically enables DVMRP on the interface; no special configuration is required. PIM routes are advertised to the DVMRP neighbor in DVMRP Report messages.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Why do Cisco routers listen for DVMRP Probe messages but never originate them?
answer: Because if a Cisco router generated a Probe on a multiaccess network with other Cisco routers, the neighboring Cisco routers would mistakenly record the originator as a DVMRP router rather than a PIM router. Cisco routers therefore listen for Probes to discover DVMRP neighbors but do not send Probes.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: How does Cisco IOS Software handle DVMRP Prune messages on multiaccess versus point-to-point interfaces?
answer: Cisco routers do not maintain DVMRP neighbor state, so to prevent one downstream neighbor's Prune from pruning traffic needed by another, Cisco routers ignore DVMRP Prune messages received on multiaccess interfaces. On point-to-point interfaces Prunes are received and processed normally, because there can be only one downstream neighbor. Cisco routers send Prune messages normally on both types of interfaces.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the solution to DVMRP routers not being able to prune a Cisco router on a multiaccess network?
answer: Create tunnels to each of the DVMRP routers using tunnel mode dvmrp. Cisco IOS Software then sees the DVMRP neighbors as connected via point-to-point links rather than a multiaccess link, and the Cisco router accepts Prunes.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What does the show ip dvmrp route command display?
answer: DVMRP-specific route information learned from DVMRP neighbors, kept in a separate DVMRP routing table. It shows the metric and TTL, the next-hop neighbor, the interface, the mrouted version, and flags (GPM). PIM on the Cisco router still makes the multicast forwarding decisions.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What is a PIM Multicast Border Router (PMBR)?
answer: A router at the edge of a PIM domain that builds special branches to all RPs in the domain, represented by (*,*,RP) entries, where the two wildcard components represent all source and group addresses that map to that RP. RPs forward all source traffic to the PMBR, which forwards it into the neighboring domain. PMBRs were proposed mainly to connect PIM-SM domains to DVMRP domains; Cisco IOS Software does not support them because of the poor scalability of the flood-and-prune approach.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: The two issues that must be addressed when routing between PIM-SM domains
answer: 1) When a source is in one domain and group members are in other domains, RPF procedures must remain valid. 2) To preserve autonomy, a domain cannot rely on an RP in another domain.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Why can't unicast BGP routes alone be used for multicast RPF checks across AS boundaries?
answer: Multicast traffic may need to use different links than unicast traffic (traffic engineering). If a multicast packet arrives on link A, and BGP indicates the unicast route to the source is via link B, the RPF check fails. Static mroutes are impractical on a large scale, so BGP must be extended to indicate whether an advertised prefix is for unicast routing, multicast RPF checks, or both.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What is MBGP and what RFC defines it?
answer: Multiprotocol BGP (MBGP) is BGP extended with multiprotocol support, described in RFC 2283. The extensions allow BGP to carry reachability information for protocols such as IPv6 and IPX, and the widespread application is to advertise multicast sources. The 'M' in MBGP represents 'multiprotocol', not 'multicast'.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: The two new BGP attributes defined by RFC 2283
answer: Multiprotocol Reachable NLRI (MP_REACH_NLRI, type 14), which advertises feasible routes, and Multiprotocol Unreachable NLRI (MP_UNREACH_NLRI, type 15), which withdraws feasible routes. Both are optional, nontransitive attributes.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What does 'optional, nontransitive' mean for MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI?
answer: BGP speakers are not required to support the attributes, and BGP speakers that do not support them do not pass them to their peers.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: When MBGP is used for IP multicast, what does the NLRI always contain?
answer: The NLRI is always an IPv4 prefix describing one or more multicast sources. PIM routers do not use this information for packet forwarding but only for determining the RPF interface toward a particular source.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the Address Family Identifier (AFI) value for IPv4 in MBGP?
answer: 1. The AFI for IPv4 is always set to 1 for IP multicast. The Address Family Information consists of an AFI and a Subsequent AFI (Sub-AFI).

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: MBGP Sub-AFI value 1
answer: Sub-AFI 1 indicates the NLRI carries unicast route information only.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: MBGP Sub-AFI value 2
answer: Sub-AFI 2 indicates the NLRI carries multicast RPF information only.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: MBGP Sub-AFI value 3
answer: Sub-AFI 3 indicates the prefix can be used for both unicast routing information and multicast RPF information. A prefix configured under both BGP and MBGP is advertised with Sub-AFI 3.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Does MBGP affect the forwarding of multicast traffic?
answer: No. MBGP just allows the dissemination of RPF information across AS boundaries. Further configuration is needed to force multicast traffic over a multicast-only link; MBGP itself does not affect multicast packet forwarding.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the purpose of MSDP?
answer: Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP) allows RPs to discover multicast sources in other PIM domains. RPs exchange source information with RPs in other domains so group members do not have to be directly dependent on another domain's RP.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What transport protocol and port does MSDP use?
answer: MSDP uses TCP, port 639, for its peering connections. As with BGP, using point-to-point TCP peering means each peer must be explicitly configured.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What does an MSDP Source Active (SA) message contain?
answer: 1) The address of the multicast source, 2) the group address to which the source is sending, and 3) the IP address of the originating RP.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What is peer RPF flooding in MSDP?
answer: To prevent SA looping, an RP that receives an SA consults the BGP next-hop database to determine the next hop toward the SA's originator; if both MBGP and unicast BGP are configured, MBGP is checked first, then unicast BGP. That next-hop neighbor is the RPF peer for the originator, and SAs received from the originator on any interface other than the interface to the RPF peer are dropped. Because of this mechanism, BGP or MBGP must be running in conjunction with MSDP.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: How often does the originating RP send periodic SAs for an active (S,G)?
answer: Every 60 seconds, for as long as the source is sending packets to the group.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the trade-off of caching MSDP SAs?
answer: Caching SAs lets an RP join the source tree as soon as a host requests a join (reducing join latency), but consumes memory caching SA messages that may or may not be needed. In a very large MSDP mesh with many SAs, memory consumption can be significant. By default Cisco IOS Software does not cache SAs.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What are MSDP SA Request and SA Response messages used for?
answer: They reduce join latency without turning on SA caching. When a host requests a join to a group, the RP sends an SA Request to its caching peer(s). If a peer has cached source information for the group, it sends it to the requesting RP in an SA Response message. The requesting RP uses the information but does not forward it to other peers. A noncaching RP that receives an SA Request returns an error message.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: How are MSDP peers established on TCP port 639?
answer: The router with the higher IP address listens on TCP port 639, and the router with the lower IP address attempts an active connect to port 639.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the MSDP Keepalive timer and who tracks it?
answer: The active side (the peer with the lower IP address) of an MSDP connection tracks the passive side with a 75-second Keepalive timer. If no MSDP message is received from the passive side before the timer expires, the active peer resets the TCP connection. If the passive peer has no other messages to send, it sends a Keepalive message to prevent the reset.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: The five MSDP message types
answer: 1 Source Active, 2 Source Active Request, 3 Source Active Response, 4 Keepalive, 5 Notification. MSDP messages use a TLV (Type/Length/Value) format.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Fields of the MSDP Source Active TLV
answer: Entry Count (number of (S,G) entries advertised), RP Address (originating RP), Reserved (all zeroes), Sprefix Length (always 32), Group Address, and Source Address. Multiple (S,G) entries can be advertised by a single SA.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the length field of the MSDP Notification TLV?
answer: Length = x + 5, where x is the length of the data field and 5 is the first 5 octets. The Notification contains an O bit (open bit): if cleared (MC - must close), the connection must be closed upon receipt; for CC (can close), the O bit might be cleared.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: MSDP error code for 'Hold timer expired'
answer: Error code 4, subcode 0, with the O bit in MC (must close) state.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: MSDP error subcode 'Does not cache SA'
answer: This is under error code 2 (SA Request error), subcode 1, with the O bit in MC state. It is returned by a noncaching peer that receives an SA Request.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What does the command address-family ipv4 multicast do?
answer: It enables MBGP. It implicitly enables the address-family ipv4 unicast command, which is applied to the unicast BGP configuration even though it is never displayed in the configuration. The multicast keyword sets the MBGP attributes' Sub-AFI to multicast.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Why is the no bgp default ipv4-unicast command used in MBGP configurations?
answer: When address-family ipv4 multicast is invoked, address-family ipv4 unicast is invoked automatically and implicitly. On links where unicast BGP traffic is unwanted, no bgp default ipv4-unicast prevents this automatic behavior, and the neighbor activate command explicitly enables unicast BGP only on the desired links.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: When is the connect-source option used with ip msdp peer?
answer: For MSDP peering to an address that is not part of a directly connected subnet. By default the source address of the TCP packets carrying the MSDP session is the address of the originating physical interface; connect-source changes the default source address (e.g., to a loopback for resiliency, similar to IBGP peering).

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What options exist for filtering at an MSDP router?
answer: 1) Control the local sources allowed to register with the RP, 2) control the SA messages the RP sends to and receives from its MSDP peers, and 3) control the SA Request messages the RP sends to and receives from its peers. Other options are descriptions for each peer and configurable TTL values for MSDP messages.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What does ip msdp redistribute reference an access list for?
answer: To filter the SA messages originated by the local router. Any source can still register with the RP (within PIM-SM configuration limits), but only the sources permitted by the access list are advertised in SA messages.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What does ip msdp sa-filter out apply to?
answer: All SA messages being forwarded to an MSDP peer, whether locally originated or received from another MSDP peer. Incoming SA messages can be filtered with ip msdp sa-filter in. Route maps and AS path access lists can be used in place of or in addition to access lists.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What is an MSDP mesh group?
answer: A set of fully meshed MSDP peers in which no transiting of SA messages takes place. When an RP receives an SA from a peer, it does not forward the message to any other peer. Mesh groups prevent the peer RPF flooding failures and MSDP notification messages caused when SA messages are flooded among fully meshed peers.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Why can an MSDP mesh group be given an arbitrary name?
answer: So that one RP can belong to more than one mesh group, if necessary. The members of the mesh group are specified with the ip msdp mesh-group command.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What is Anycast RP?
answer: A method of allowing the mapping of a single group to multiple RPs. The RPs are distributed throughout the domain and all use the same RP address, creating a 'virtual RP'. MSDP is fundamental to the creation of a virtual RP. Anycasting generically means packets can be sent to a single address and one of several devices can respond to it.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: The problems PIM-SM's single group-to-RP mapping presents in large domains
answer: 1) Possible traffic bottlenecks, 2) lack of scalable register decapsulation (when using shared trees), 3) slow failover when an active RP fails, 4) possible suboptimal forwarding of multicast packets, and 5) dependence on remote RPs.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: How does Anycast RP provide fast failover?
answer: The unicast routing protocol of each anycast RP advertises the common RP address, so a DR sees a single RP with several routes to it and chooses the shortest (nearest) route. If the anycast RP fails, the unicast protocol announces the route as unfeasible, the DR chooses the next-best route to the next-nearest anycast RP, and RP failover is linked to and almost as fast as unicast reconvergence time.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What does ip msdp originator-id do and why is it needed in Anycast RP?
answer: It changes the default RP address used in MSDP messages. Because all anycast RPs announce the same RP address, MSDP must be configured to use a unique address in its SA messages (e.g., each router's unique Loopback0 address) so MSDP peering sessions have unique endpoints.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Why must the OSPF and BGP router IDs be explicitly configured in an Anycast RP design?
answer: OSPF and BGP use the highest IP address configured on any loopback as the router ID. If the virtual RP address on Loopback5 is numerically higher than Loopback0, every router would use the same router ID, causing thrashing of the OSPF databases as each router's LSAs try to override the others. Forcing each router to use its unique LO0 address with router-id avoids this.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What does ip msdp default-peer do?
answer: It disables the MSDP dependency on the BGP next-hop database for peer RPF checks. MSDP just accepts all SA messages from default peers. It is useful when an AS is a stub or nontransit AS that does not run BGP to its transit AS.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: How does a stub AS with two default MSDP peers choose among them?
answer: SA messages cannot be accepted from both default peers because there is no RPF check mechanism. The active default peer is the first peer in the configuration; SAs are not accepted from the second peer unless the first fails. The underlying assumption is that both default peers are sending the same SA messages.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: How can an RP accept SA messages from multiple default MSDP peers while preventing loops?
answer: Use BGP-style prefix lists. The RP accepts SA messages from all of its default peers, but only for source prefixes allowed by each peer's associated prefix list. The underlying assumption is that each AS uses distinct prefixes, so loop avoidance is ensured.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: ip multicast boundary 10
answer: Designates an interface as a multicast boundary for administrative scoping. References access list 10, which specifies the group address ranges to be permitted or denied at the interface.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: ip multicast ttl-threshold 5
answer: Designates an interface as a multicast boundary for TTL scoping. Only multicast packets with TTL values greater than 5 are forwarded out of the interface; packets with TTL 5 or below are dropped.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: tunnel mode dvmrp
answer: Sets the tunnel encapsulation mode to DVMRP (instead of the default GRE). Used to create point-to-point connections to DVMRP routers across a multiaccess network so that DVMRP pruning works correctly.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: debug ip dvmrp detail
answer: Enables detailed DVMRP debugging, showing events such as received Probe messages on interfaces and aging of DVMRP routes.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: show ip dvmrp route
answer: Displays the DVMRP-specific routing table, including the metric/TTL, next-hop neighbor, interface, mrouted version, and flags (GPM) for routes learned from DVMRP neighbors.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: neighbor 192.168.254.2 next-hop-self
answer: Sets the next-hop-self attribute for the MBGP neighbor, used for IBGP neighbors just as it is with unicast BGP. MBGP IBGP configurations such as next-hop-self and update-source are used the same way as with BGP.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: show ip bgp ipv4 unicast
answer: Displays BGP table entries whose Sub-AFI matches the unicast keyword, i.e., unicast-only prefixes. The output is the same as the output of show ip bgp.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: show ip bgp ipv4 multicast
answer: Displays BGP table entries whose Sub-AFI matches the multicast keyword, i.e., prefixes advertised for multicast RPF information. A prefix configured as both unicast and multicast appears in both displays.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: show ip rpf 172.16.227.1
answer: Performs an RPF lookup for the address and displays the RPF interface, RPF neighbor, the matching route/mask, and the RPF type (e.g., mbgp). The same address can reference a different next hop than a normal IP route lookup.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: ip msdp peer 192.168.254.1 connect-source Loopback0
answer: Designates a router as an MSDP peer. The connect-source option specifies that the TCP session source address is the address of Loopback0, used for peering to addresses not part of a directly connected subnet.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: ip msdp cache-sa-state list 101
answer: Enables SA caching. The optional access list specifies which (S,G) pairs to cache, helping alleviate memory stress in large MSDP meshes.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: ip msdp sa-request 192.168.254.1
answer: Enables an RP to send MSDP SA Request messages to the designated caching peer, reducing join latency. The command can be used multiple times to specify multiple caching peers.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: ip msdp description 192.168.254.1 Rodan in AS 100
answer: Adds descriptive text to an MSDP peer configuration. The description always appears directly after the ip msdp peer command for a specific peer and is useful when there are large numbers of MSDP peers.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: ip msdp sa-filter out 192.168.254.1 list 101
answer: Enables a filter for outgoing MSDP SA messages to the specified peer. Applies to all SA messages forwarded to the peer, whether locally originated or received from another MSDP peer.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: ip msdp sa-filter in 192.168.1.9 list 101
answer: Enables a filter for incoming MSDP SA messages from the specified peer. The router accepts SA messages from the peer only if the (S,G) pair is permitted by the referenced access list.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: ip msdp filter-sa-request 192.168.254.1 list 1
answer: Enables a filter for outgoing SA Request messages to the specified peer. The filter references an access list that allows only the specified group prefixes to be requested from that peer.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: ip msdp redistribute list 102
answer: Enables a filter for MSDP SA messages originated by the local router, referencing an access list that permits the specified source prefixes and group address prefixes to be advertised in SA messages.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: ip msdp ttl-threshold 192.168.254.1 5
answer: Sets a TTL value for MSDP messages originated by the local router and sent to the specified peer. Messages whose TTL falls below the threshold are not forwarded.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: ip msdp mesh-group Boogeymen 10.100.1.3
answer: Designates a peer to be a member of a mesh group. SA messages from a mesh group member are not forwarded to other mesh group members, preventing SA flooding among fully meshed peers.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: ip msdp originator-id Loopback0
answer: Changes the default RP address used in MSDP messages. In Anycast RP designs it forces MSDP to use the router's unique Loopback0 address in SA messages instead of the shared virtual RP address.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: ip msdp default-peer 192.168.1.1 prefix-list AS1
answer: Specifies an MSDP peer from which SA messages are accepted without performing an RPF check. The optional prefix-list restricts which source prefixes are accepted from each default peer, allowing acceptance from multiple peers while providing loop avoidance.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: show ip msdp peer
answer: Displays detailed information about MSDP peers, including connection state, resets, connection source, uptime, messages sent/received, SA filtering configuration, SA-Request status, and peer TTL threshold.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: show ip msdp sa-cache
answer: Displays information about SA state cached in the local router, i.e., the (S,G) pairs and originating RPs learned from cached SA messages.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: show ip msdp summary
answer: Displays summary information about MSDP peers.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Which statement correctly describes TTL scoping versus administrative scoping?

choices.label: Administrative scoping filters on multicast group address ranges, giving more flexibility than TTL scoping, which applies a boundary to all multicast packets
TTL scoping filters on group address ranges, while administrative scoping applies an absolute TTL boundary to all packets
Both methods filter exclusively on the multicast source address
Administrative scoping requires configuration of TTL thresholds on every interface

explanation: TTL scoping applies a TTL boundary at an interface to all multicast packets and lacks flexibility. Administrative scoping partitions the group address range (RFC 2365) and filters on address ranges, so some packets can be blocked while others are forwarded.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Which statement correctly describes the MBGP Sub-AFI values?

choices.label: Sub-AFI 1 = unicast only, 2 = multicast RPF only, 3 = both unicast and multicast RPF
Sub-AFI 1 = multicast only, 2 = unicast only, 3 = both
Sub-AFI 1 = both, 2 = unicast only, 3 = multicast only
Sub-AFI values are irrelevant to IP multicast; only the AFI matters

explanation: Table 7-3 defines Sub-AFI 1 as unicast route information only, 2 as multicast RPF information only, and 3 as a prefix usable for both unicast routing and multicast RPF information.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Which statement correctly describes the MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI attributes?

choices.label: Both are optional, nontransitive; MP_REACH_NLRI advertises feasible routes and MP_UNREACH_NLRI withdraws routes
Both are optional, transitive; MP_REACH_NLRI withdraws routes and MP_UNREACH_NLRI advertises routes
They are mandatory BGP attributes that all BGP speakers must support
MP_REACH_NLRI has type 15 and MP_UNREACH_NLRI has type 14

explanation: RFC 2283 defines MP_REACH_NLRI (type 14) to advertise feasible routes and MP_UNREACH_NLRI (type 15) to withdraw feasible routes. Both are optional, nontransitive, so unsupporting speakers do not pass them to peers.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: In what order does an MSDP RP consult its databases when determining the RPF peer toward an SA originator?

choices.label: MBGP is checked first, then unicast BGP
Unicast BGP is checked first, then MBGP
Only the IGP routing table is consulted
MSDP keeps its own RIB independent of BGP

explanation: If both MBGP and unicast BGP are configured, MBGP is checked first, and then unicast BGP, to determine the next-hop neighbor that is the RPF peer for the SA's originator.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: How does Cisco IOS Software handle DVMRP Prune messages?

choices.label: Prunes are ignored on multiaccess interfaces and processed normally on point-to-point interfaces
Prunes are processed normally on all interfaces
Prunes are ignored on all interfaces
Prunes are ignored on point-to-point interfaces and processed on multiaccess interfaces

explanation: Cisco routers do not maintain DVMRP neighbor state. To avoid one downstream neighbor's Prune pruning traffic needed by another, Cisco routers ignore Prunes received on multiaccess interfaces and process them normally on point-to-point interfaces, where only one downstream neighbor can exist.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Which statement correctly describes MSDP session establishment on TCP port 639?

choices.label: The router with the higher IP address listens and the router with the lower IP address actively connects
The router with the lower IP address listens and the higher connects
Both routers actively connect to each other simultaneously
The RP always listens and the source DR always connects

explanation: When two routers are configured as MSDP peers, the router with the higher IP address listens on TCP port 639, and the router with the lower IP address attempts an active connect to port 639.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the default SA caching behavior of Cisco IOS Software, and what reduces join latency without caching?

choices.label: SA caching is off by default; SA Request/SA Response messages reduce join latency without caching
SA caching is on by default; SA Request messages disable it
SA caching is off by default; the only way to reduce latency is to enable caching
SA caching is always on and cannot be configured

explanation: By default, Cisco IOS Software does not cache SAs; caching is enabled with ip msdp cache-sa-state. If a peer caches SAs, the RP can reduce join latency by sending SA Request messages and receiving SA Response messages from the caching peer.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Which statement correctly describes the configuration of Anycast RP with MSDP?

choices.label: The virtual RP address is announced by all RPs, and ip msdp originator-id gives MSDP a unique per-router address
Each anycast RP uses a distinct RP address and MSDP redistributes between them
The virtual RP address is also used as the MSDP session endpoint on every router
Anycast RP requires DVMRP tunnels between the RPs

explanation: All anycast RPs announce the same virtual RP address, so MSDP must be configured with ip msdp originator-id to use a unique address (e.g., each router's Loopback0) in SA messages so peering endpoints are unique.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Which statement correctly describes the PIM Multicast Border Router (PMBR) concept?

choices.label: The PMBR builds (*,*,RP) branches to all RPs in the domain and was proposed mainly to connect PIM-SM to DVMRP domains; Cisco IOS Software does not support it
The PMBR is a Cisco IOS Software feature used at NAP peering points
The PMBR builds one shared tree to a single RP using (S,G) state
The PMBR replaces MSDP entirely for inter-AS multicast

explanation: A PMBR resides at the edge of a PIM domain and builds (*,*,RP) branches to all RPs; RPs forward all source traffic to the PMBR along these branches. Because of the poor scalability of this flood-and-prune approach, Cisco IOS Software does not support PMBRs.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Which statement correctly describes MSDP default peers in a transit AS?

choices.label: Prefix lists let an RP accept SA messages from multiple default peers while providing loop avoidance
An RP can accept SAs from only a single default peer under any circumstances
Default peers bypass the need for prefix filtering entirely
Default peers require a full BGP mesh in the transit AS

explanation: An RP in a transit AS with multiple default peers uses BGP-style prefix lists per peer: it accepts SA messages from all default peers but only for source prefixes allowed by each peer's associated prefix list, assuming distinct prefixes per AS for loop avoidance.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the correct order of MSDP operations after a PIM DR registers a source with its RP?
correct_sequence: 1. The RP sends a Source Active (SA) message to all of its MSDP peers
2. Each peer floods the SA to its own peers downstream from the originator
3. Each receiving RP checks the BGP next-hop database to determine the RPF peer for the originator and drops SAs received from other interfaces
4. An RP that has group members sends an (S,G) join toward the source, building a source-tree branch across AS boundaries
5. Multicast packets arriving at the RP are forwarded down its own shared tree to members
distractor_sequences: 1. SA is sent to members' DRs directly, 2. DR sends an (S,G) join, 3. RP caches the SA
1. RP sends an (S,G) join toward the source, 2. source registers with the RP, 3. SA is flooded
explanation: When a PIM DR registers a source, the RP sends SA messages to all MSDP peers, which flood them using peer RPF flooding. RPs with members join the source tree, after which multicast packets flow down the RP's shared tree to members.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the correct order of configuration steps to build an Anycast RP design?
correct_sequence: 1. Configure a unique Loopback0 address on each router for MSDP peering endpoints
2. Configure a shared virtual RP address on Loopback5 of every router with PIM enabled
3. Announce the virtual RP address with ip pim send-rp-announce / send-rp-discovery
4. Configure full-mesh MSDP peering between the unique loopback addresses with ip msdp peer connect-source Loopback0
5. Configure ip msdp mesh-group and ip msdp originator-id Loopback0
6. Force unique OSPF and BGP router IDs with the router-id statement
distractor_sequences: 1. Configure MSDP peering on the shared virtual RP address, 2. Announce unique RP addresses, 3. Disable MSDP
1. Configure BGP only, 2. Skip MSDP, 3. Use the virtual address as the MSDP source
explanation: Anycast RP requires unique MSDP endpoints (LO0) with a shared virtual RP address (LO5), mesh groups, originator-id to make SA messages unique, and explicit router IDs to avoid OSPF/BGP database thrashing caused by duplicate router IDs.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What is the correct order of configuration to tunnel multicast between two PIM domains across a unicast-only domain?
correct_sequence: 1. Create a tunnel interface with ip unnumbered referencing the Ethernet interface
2. Configure ip pim sparse-dense-mode on the tunnel interface
3. Set tunnel source and tunnel destination to the physical addresses at each end
4. Run OSPF passively on the tunnel so no unicast traffic traverses it
5. Add static mroutes referencing the tunnel as the upstream interface for sources in the opposite domain
distractor_sequences: 1. Enable PIM on the physical interface, 2. Remove the tunnel, 3. Use static unicast routes
1. Configure DVMRP tunnels, 2. Disable PIM, 3. Rely on OSPF for RPF
explanation: The GRE tunnel carries PIM traffic while OSPF runs passively on TU0 to avoid unicast transit, and static mroutes prevent RPF failures by making the tunnel the upstream interface for remote sources.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What does the debug output 'IP: s=192.168.14.35 d=228.13.20.216, mrouting disabled' indicate?
symptoms: debug ip mpacket shows multicast packets arriving on an interface with the message 'mrouting disabled' for every packet
root_cause: IP multicast routing is not enabled on the router, so incoming multicast packets are not being processed or forwarded.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Issue the global command ip multicast-routing to enable multicast routing on the router
2. Verify PIM is configured on the incoming interface (ip pim sparse-dense-mode or similar)
3. Re-run debug ip mpacket and confirm the packets are now forwarded
resolution: Enable IP multicast routing globally and configure PIM on the required interfaces.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: What does the debug output 'not RPF interface' indicate?
symptoms: debug ip mpacket shows multicast packets arriving on an interface flagged 'not RPF interface'; packets are being dropped rather than forwarded
root_cause: The interface on which the multicast packet arrives is not the RPF interface for the source as determined by the unicast routing table, so the packet fails the Reverse Path Forwarding check and is dropped. This commonly occurs when a multicast packet arrives via a tunnel or a different path than the unicast route to the source.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Use show ip rpf <source> to determine the correct RPF interface and neighbor for the source
2. Compare the RPF interface with the interface on which packets are arriving
3. If packets legitimately arrive via a different interface (e.g., a tunnel), add a static mroute (ip mroute) pointing at the correct upstream interface
4. Verify MBGP or unicast BGP routes are providing the correct RPF path when inter-AS
resolution: Add a static multicast route or correct the unicast/MBGP routing so the RPF interface matches the arrival interface.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Why are unwanted multicast packets being forwarded into a DVMRP domain across a multiaccess link?
symptoms: DVMRP routers downstream of a Cisco router cannot prune unwanted multicast traffic across a shared multiaccess network; the Cisco router keeps forwarding
root_cause: Cisco routers do not maintain DVMRP neighbor state, so they ignore DVMRP Prune messages received on multiaccess interfaces to prevent one neighbor's Prune from affecting another. Without neighbor state, DVMRP routers on a multiaccess link cannot prune themselves.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Confirm the DVMRP neighbors are connected over a multiaccess interface
2. Create tunnels to each DVMRP router and configure tunnel mode dvmrp so the neighbors appear on point-to-point links
3. Verify PIM is configured on the tunnels but not on the physical multiaccess interface
4. Confirm DVMRP Prunes are now accepted and traffic is pruned
resolution: Use dvmrp-mode tunnels to make each DVMRP neighbor appear as a point-to-point neighbor, so Prunes are processed normally.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Why are large numbers of MSDP peer RPF flooding failures and notifications occurring between fully meshed RPs?
symptoms: MSDP peers in the same AS exchange many peer RPF flooding failures and MSDP notification messages
root_cause: Every RP has an MSDP connection to every other RP in a full mesh, so each SA generated by one router is flooded by all the others, causing SAs to arrive on non-RPF interfaces and triggering peer RPF flooding failures. No flooding is actually needed because every RP receives a copy directly from the originator.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Verify the MSDP peering topology with show ip msdp peer and show ip msdp summary
2. Confirm each RP is peered to every other RP in the domain (full mesh)
3. Configure an MSDP mesh group on each router listing all other RPs with ip msdp mesh-group
4. Verify SAs are no longer transitively forwarded between mesh group members
resolution: Place all RPs in an MSDP mesh group so SA messages received from a mesh group member are not forwarded to other members.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch7: Large-Scale IP Multicast Routing
question: Why are the OSPF databases thrashing in an Anycast RP design?
symptoms: OSPF LSAs flap as each router's link state advertisements try to override other routers' LSAs; neighbor relationships are unstable
root_cause: The shared virtual RP address on Loopback5 is numerically higher than Loopback0 on each router, so OSPF and BGP each select 10.100.254.1 as their router ID on every router, producing duplicate router IDs.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Check the OSPF and BGP router IDs with show ip ospf and show ip bgp
2. Confirm every router is using the same router ID derived from the highest loopback
3. Configure the router-id statement under router ospf and router bgp to force each router to use its unique Loopback0 address
4. Clear OSPF and BGP processes and verify adjacencies stabilize
resolution: Explicitly configure unique router-id values (e.g., each router's LO0 address) under OSPF and BGP.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: The three design goals of IPv6
answer: Improve scalability, ease configuration, and maintain/improve security. IPv6 draws from the lessons learned with IPv4 but is not designed to solve the Internet routing table size explosion; strict allocation rules and hierarchy for aggregation can contain table size.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: How many bits is an IPv6 address?
answer: 128 bits. This allows roughly 340,282,366,920,938,463,463,374,607,431,768,211,456 nodes (about 3.4 x 10^27 addresses per person if the world population is 10 billion).

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: What IPv4 techniques prolonged address depletion and why does IPv6 still matter?
answer: NAT allowed enterprises to use private addresses hidden from the public Internet, and CIDR added hierarchy by aggregating addresses. However, many addresses cannot be aggregated (pre-CIDR addresses, some multihomed connections), NAT is not always easy to implement or maintain, some applications do not work through NAT, and future Internet appliances may require globally routable addresses.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: How is an IPv6 address written in text?
answer: As eight 16-bit pieces separated by colons, each piece represented by four hexadecimal digits, e.g., FEDC:BA98:7654:3210:FEDC:BA98:7654:3210.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: What is the rule for removing leading zeros in an IPv6 address?
answer: In any 16-bit field, you can remove leading zeros, but at least one digit must be present in every field. Multiple contiguous fields of all zeros can be replaced with a double colon (::), which can be used only once per address.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: Why can the :: notation be used only once in an IPv6 address?
answer: Because multiple ::s would make the address ambiguous - the number of zero fields it represents would be unclear. For example, 1080::3245::200c:417A does not provide sufficient information about the correct position of 3245.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: The mixed IPv6/IPv4 text representation
answer: X:X:X:X:X:X:d.d.d.d, where X represents the hexadecimal IPv6 fields and d.d.d.d denotes the last 32 bits of the address in dotted-decimal notation, e.g., ::13.1.68.3. It provides a method for IPv6 and IPv4 nodes to coexist on the same network.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: IPv6 address prefix notation
answer: IPv6-address/prefix-length, where IPv6-address is any valid address and prefix-length is the number of contiguous bits comprising the prefix, e.g., 200F::AB00:0:0:0:0/56. As with host addresses, the double colon is used only once.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: What is the format prefix (FP)?
answer: The variable-length field of high-order bits in an IPv6 address that defines the address type. Only about 15 percent of the address space is currently allocated. Some space is reserved (for future NSAP and IPX routing and special addresses such as loopback and unspecified), and much is initially unassigned.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: Aggregatable global unicast addresses
answer: IPv6 addresses analogous to globally routable IPv4 addresses, defined by format prefix 001 (1/8 of the address space). They are assigned in blocks to Internet providers and exchanges and define multiple levels of hierarchy and aggregation. This is the largest assigned address space.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: How can you tell a multicast address from a unicast address in IPv6?
answer: Multicast addresses always begin with 0xFF. An address beginning with anything else is a unicast address.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: The IPv6 address types defined by their first digits
answer: 00 - unspecified, loopback, IPv4-compatible; 2/3 - aggregatable global unicast; FE8 - link-local; FEC - site-local; FF - multicast.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: The fields of the aggregatable global unicast address format
answer: FP (format prefix, 3 bits = 001), TLA ID (top-level aggregation identifier, 13 bits), RES (reserved, 8 bits), NLA ID (next-level aggregation identifier, 24 bits), SLA ID (site-level aggregation identifier, 16 bits), and Interface ID (64 bits). The network portion is the first 64 bits; the node portion is the last 64 bits. The FP, TLA, RES, and NLA fields comprise the public topology; SLA is the site topology; Interface ID is the interface topology.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: Top-Level Aggregation Identifier (TLA ID)
answer: The top levels in the IPv6 routing hierarchy; the TLA ID field is 13 bits. Routers in the default-free zone must have a routing entry for every TLA ID. If more TLAs are needed, another FP can be assigned or the TLA field can expand to the right into the reserved field. IANA initially allocated TLA 0x0001, subdivided into sub-TLAs for the RIRs.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: Reserved field (RES) in the aggregatable global address
answer: Not currently used (all bits set to zero), except in the case of TLA 0x0001. Future use could include growth of the TLA ID and NLA ID.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: Next-Level Aggregation Identifier (NLA ID)
answer: Used by an organization allocated a TLA ID to create address hierarchy and identify sites. An organization given a TLA has 24 bits, and one given a sub-TLA has 13 bits of NLA. The minimum size of address space an NLA registry can assign is a prefix of 48 bits (/48), giving the customer at least 16 bits of SLA.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: Site-Level Aggregation Identifier (SLA ID)
answer: Used by a site to create as many levels of hierarchy as appropriate within its 16-bit SLA field, from a flat numbering scheme to further subdivision into subnets.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: Interface Identifier in IPv6 addresses
answer: The 64-bit interface identifier, unique to the link, used to identify interfaces on a specific link. All addresses with high-order bits between 001 and 111 (excluding multicast) must have interface IDs in EUI-64 format.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: How is an EUI-64 interface ID derived from a MAC address?
answer: FFFE is inserted between the company ID (OUI) and the node ID of the 48-bit MAC address, and the universal/local (U/L) bit is set to 1 to indicate global value. For example, MAC 0000:0C0A:2C51 becomes EUI-64 0200:0CFF:FE0A:2C51.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: The IPv6 unspecified address
answer: All zeros, 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:0 (::). It represents the absence of an address, must never be assigned to any node, and must never be used as a destination address. One use is as the source address of an initializing host before it has been assigned a valid address.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: The IPv6 loopback address
answer: 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1 (::1), analogous to the IPv4 loopback address 127.0.0.1. A node uses it to send IP packets to itself; it can never be assigned to any physical interface and traffic destined to it must never leave the sending node.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses
answer: Special-format IPv6 unicast addresses with the IPv4 address embedded in the low-order 32 bits and all other bits zero, formatted as ::d.d.d.d. They are used by dual-stack nodes that support automatic tunneling.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: Link-local addresses
answer: Addresses meaningful only to nodes on a single link, defined by FP 1111111010 (FE80::/10) followed by 54 zeros and the interface ID. They contain no TLA, NLA, or SLA information. Routers must not forward packets with either source or destination link-local addresses beyond the link. Every node assigns every active IPv6 interface a link-local address. Examples: FE80::5ABC:01FF:FE01:1111, FE80::200:CFF:FE0A:2C51.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: Site-local addresses
answer: Addresses meaningful only to nodes within a site, defined by FP 1111111011 (FEC0::/10) followed by 38 zeros, a 16-bit subnet field, and the 64-bit interface ID. They are not globally unique, are used like private IPv4 addresses, and must not be propagated beyond the site boundaries. It is recommended to use site-local addresses, not global aggregatable addresses, on router interfaces. Examples: FEC0::1:5ABC:1FF:FE01:1111.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: IPv6 anycast addresses
answer: Addresses assigned to multiple interfaces, usually on different nodes, with the same IP address; traffic is routed to the nearest node. Anycast addresses have the same format as unicast addresses - no special FP defines them - and are taken from the Interface ID field. Because they are syntactically indistinguishable from unicast addresses, an interface must be explicitly configured to recognize its address as anycast.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: The Subnet-Router anycast address
answer: A pre-defined anycast address that all router interfaces connected to a link must be assigned. It is a unicast address with an all-zero interface identifier, e.g., FEC0:0:0:A:: on a router interface assigned unicast address FEC0:0:0:A:200:CFF:FE0A:2C51.

source: Routing TCP/IP Vol II - Ch8: IP Version 6
question: Reserved subnet anycast addresses
answer: Anycast addresses available on every IPv6 subnet regardless of the type or format of the prefix, taken completely from the Interface ID field. The top 128 interface IDs are reserved for anycast allocation, and the last 7 bits identify the specific anycast address.
