answer: Is that really a .doc, or a .exe with .doc embedded in the name—human interface danger.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: X11 window manager
answer: The window manager has special properties (open/close/resize windows) but is still an ordinary application making network requests.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: X11 xdm root
answer: xdm (X Display Manager) typically runs as root and has had security problems (CERT VB-95:08); limit access via xauth/xhost.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: Small services trusted
answer: Because they're simple and small, believed to be safe—often left on in hosts and even routers—risky assumption.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: Echo broadcast storm
answer: Locate two echo servers, send packet with spoofed return to the other—they echo back and forth for days.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: UDP small service info leak
answer: Any TCP service can leak TCP sequence number state—information useful for IP spoofing attacks.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: Small Services list
answer: chargen, daytime, discard, echo, time—typically processed by inetd on UNIX systems.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: cgi-bin contamination
answer: Anything in the FTP/Web area is potentially contaminated, including /s binaries—guard execute bits carefully.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: FTP third-party transfer
answer: PASV feature intended for third-party transfers: one FTP client talks to two servers simultaneously.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: NFS mount daemon
answer: In older implementations, the mount daemon checks client hostname and requested file system against admin-supplied list; verifies read-only vs read-write.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: NFS mount-based control inadequacy
answer: Any client retaining a root file handle has permanent access—no enforceable renegotion requirement.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: NFS UID mapping
answer: NFS relies on numeric UID/GID consistent across served machines—not a scalable solution; some impls provide a map function.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: NFS file lock state
answer: Some operations (locks) require server-retained state via RPC auxiliary processes; these need not be consistent for auth.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: X11 auth host-based granularity
answer: Host-based auth allows all users from an authorized machine to connect—no per-user restriction.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: X11 xauth
answer: xauth command manages magic cookies for X11 access control.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: X11 xhost
answer: xhost command controls host-based X11 access.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: Small services TCP leak
answer: TCP versions can leak TCP sequence number state—useful for IP spoofing; small unaudited TCP service makes experiments easy.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: SNMP read-only default
answer: Many community strings (especially 'public') grant only read access, but can still leak sensitive data.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: NTP radio clock indoor issue
answer: GPS/satellite signals don't penetrate well to most machine rooms—creating wiring issues for indoor NTP masters.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: NTP i-node tamper
answer: Hackers temporarily change system clock to match tampered timestamps; NTP complains to logs when unsettled.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: r-command password alternative
answer: The usual alternative to rlogin is telnet plus cleartext password—perils of cleartext outweigh r-command risks in many cases.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: SSH host-based auth
answer: SSH can replace host and password authentication with RSA/DSC-keyed challenge/response.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: SSH protocol 1 issues
answer: Protocol 1 had a number of problems; IETF is standardizing version 2. Protocol 2 is preferred.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: Sendmail non-root front end
answer: Simple SMTP front ends that don't run as root implement a reliable subset of SMTP commands (Carson 1993, Avolio and Ranum 1994).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: Sendmail port 25 via inetd
answer: Sendmail binds to port 25; easiest accomplished by running via inetd so sendmail itself need not issue the bind call.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: Sendmail spool permissions
answer: Sendmail needs write permission on its spool directory (typically /var/spool/mqueue) and read on /dev/kmem for load average.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: FTP control vs data
answer: Control channel carries commands/responses; data channel carries file transfers and directory listings.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: FTP new channel per file
answer: Despite spec suggesting one channel for all transfers, real-world implementations open a new channel per file.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: TFTP boot targets
answer: Used to boot routers, diskless workstations, and X11 terminals.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: TFTP restricted directories
answer: Properly configured daemon restricts to one or two directories, e.g. /usr/local/boot and X11 font library.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: IM file send feature
answer: Client software usually has feature to send files—another attack surface.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: IM security bugs
answer: Security bugs have appeared in number of IM clients; locally run servers have better security model.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: SIP ASCII format
answer: SIP messages are ASCII, resembling HTTP, and use MIME/S/MIME for data transport.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: H.323 ASN.1
answer: H.323 uses ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One) for call signaling messages that firewalls must parse.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: RPC over UDP reliability
answer: UDP RPC must worry about lost messages, duplicates, out-of-order messages.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: RPC sequence number
answer: The header includes a sequence number used to match queries with replies.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: RPC program/procedure
answer: Header includes program number (identifies service), procedure number (entry point), and version numbers.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: NIS key database
answer: NIS distributes public and private key databases used for Secure RPC; private keys encrypted with login passwords.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: NIS password file
answer: NIS distributes the password file; an intruder obtaining it has a precious asset.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: NFS random port services
answer: With the notable exception of NFS, RPC servers use dynamic ports—not fixed—registered via rpchind/portmapper.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: NFS unprivileged ports
answer: Many NFS-related RPC services live on ports >1024, making per-port firewalling insufficient.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: X11 local tunnel
answer: With ssh, set up TCP socket forwarded to X11 bound to 127.0.0.1 with local random key—should be safe.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: X11 keyboard grab
answer: An app can grab sole control of keyboard when reading passwords—few users use this; another mechanism polls keyboard status.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: Samba SMB ports
answer: Ports 135-139 and sometimes 445; nbaudit scans for active ports and extracts system/file info.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: WWW client threat
answer: Unlike most protocols, the Web is a threat to clients as well as servers—firewall should block both client and server Web access.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: Proxy server Web threat
answer: The most dangerous 'Web servers' aren't Web servers—they're proxy servers that let blocked clients reach the Web.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: CGI interpreter presence
answer: Powerful interpreters (Perl, shell) must reside in the network service area to run CGI scripts—large attack surface.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: NNTP gateway compromise
answer: If gateway receives news and passes via NNTP, a hole in NNTP exposes inside news machine if gateway is taken over.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: MBone channel registration
answer: Anyone can register new sessions on arbitrary ports above 3456—a hacker can attack any UDP service needing one packet.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch3: A Security Review of Protocols Upper Layers
question: X11 TCP default
answer: X11 listens on TCP by default; should be disabled (local access only) and tunneled via ssh.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch4: The Web
question: Is HTTP stateless?
answer: Yes, HTTP is stateless; each request involves a separate TCP connection.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch4: The Web
question: What is the most important HTTP method for retrieving documents?
answer: GET.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch4: The Web
question: Which HTTP methods can upload data to a server?
answer: POST and PUT.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch4: The Web
question: The HTTP method that is 'charming' but rarely used?
answer: DELETE.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch4: The Web
question: What does the User-Agent header inform the server of?
answer: The browser and operating system you are running, and hence what bugs your system has.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch4: The Web
question: What does the Referer header contain?
answer: The URL that has a link to this page (the page you came from).

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch4: The Web
question: What is the purpose of the Accept header?
answer: Declares which data formats the client accepts.

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch4: The Web

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Password guessing attack
answer: An attack that attempts to log in using known or assumed usernames and likely guesses at passwords, succeeding when sites use predictable account-password pairs like field-service/guest

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Shadow password file
answer: A UNIX security feature that conceals hashed passwords from even legitimate users by storing them in a separate, access-restricted file

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Security by obscurity
answer: A weak security approach relying solely on the secrecy of implementation details (like a password file's name) with no other defensive layers

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Stack-smashing
answer: A buffer overflow technique that overwrites the return address in a function's stack frame, as exploited by the Internet Worm via the gets() call

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Orange Book
answer: The U.S. DoD Rainbow Series document describing security levels from D (least secure) through A1, focused on process and assurance for 1970s time-sharing mainframes

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: B3 rating
answer: An Orange Book security level requiring the TCB to use a complete, conceptually simple protection mechanism with layering, abstraction, and data hiding

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Common Criteria
answer: An international ISO-adopted standard for evaluating IT security, evolved from the UK Confidence Levels, Canadian CTC, and draft Federal Criteria

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Address-based authentication
answer: An authentication mechanism relying on the source IP address of a connection, which fails if the source machine is not trustworthy (e.g. a compromised PC)

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Source-address spoofing
answer: Forging the source IP address in a packet, possible because of insufficient randomness in TCP initial sequence number generation

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Authentication race attack
answer: An attack on some one-time password schemes using multiple connections to race the legitimate user in submitting the final password digit

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Challenge/response authentication
answer: An authentication method issuing a unique challenge per connection, completely frustrating race attacks because each requires a different response

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Information leakage
answer: When protocols reveal information about systems, users, or data that can aid attackers, such as the finger protocol exposing user details

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Monoculture
answer: A population where all members run identical software (like the Internet's shared TCP/IP stack), making common-mode attacks highly effective

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Exponential attack
answer: An attack using self-replicating programs: worms travel by themselves, viruses attach to other programs; both multiply quickly across networks

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Botnet
answer: A network of compromised bot/zombie machines controlled by an attacker via a master program, used for DDoS, scanning, and other nefarious purposes

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Zombie
answer: A compromised host that is part of a botnet, bound to a port and waiting for instructions from a master program to participate in DDoS floods

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Backscatter
answer: Return packets sent by attacked hosts back to spoofed IP addresses, observable through a packet telescope on an announced but unused network

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: SYN flood attack
answer: A DoS attack sending repeated TCP SYN packets to fill a server's half-open connection table, denying new legitimate connections

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Half-open connection
answer: A TCP connection state (received SYN but not completed handshake) whose kernel table SYN floods exhaust, dropping all further connection attempts

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Pushback
answer: A congestion-control approach where routers identify and drop traffic aggregates causing congestion, propagating drop requests back toward the source

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Packet telescope
answer: Infrastructure on an announced-but-unused network that monitors backscatter traffic to measure the global rate and targets of DoS attacks

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Bloom filter
answer: A space-efficient probabilistic data structure (Bloom, 1970) used to test set membership, e.g. filtering packets from unannounced IP network blocks

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Port scanning
answer: A reconnaissance technique sweeping port numbers to discover hidden services and hosts, which firewalls must block

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Address space scan
answer: Probing IP ranges and port numbers to build a target list, revealing vulnerable or hidden hosts

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Active attack
answer: In cryptographic literature, an attack where the intruder can modify, introduce, or delete messages in the communication stream

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Passive attack
answer: In cryptographic literature, an attack where the adversary can only eavesdrop on network communication to learn confidential information

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Mail-spoofing
answer: A social engineering technique using forged email appearing from a system administrator, asking users to run a 'test program' that prompts for passwords

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: OTP race
answer: An attack on single-use one-time password schemes where the attacker wins a race to submit the final password digit before the legitimate user

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: TCP/IP monoculture
answer: The Internet's reliance on a shared TCP/IP implementation across most hosts, so one discovered bug affects millions of machines

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Finger protocol
answer: A service (query 'finger <username>') revealing user details such as login status, real name, and last login, aiding social engineering and password guessing

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Gets function
answer: A C library function reading input without a bounded length argument, causing buffer overflows when input exceeds the fixed buffer (used by the Internet Worm)

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Password entropy
answer: The effective information content of a password in bits; 8-letter English-word passwords yield ~19 bits, far below the 56-bit DES key size

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Low TTL attack packets
answer: Attack packets with an unusually low initial Time-To-Live field, revealing the attacker's random number generator signature

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Router traceback
answer: The technique of tracing attack packets back through ISP routers hop-by-hop, typically requiring ISP cooperation and sometimes court orders

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: ISP ingress filters
answer: Edge router ACLs that verify a customer's incoming packets have a source address matching the nets announced for that customer, blocking spoofed traffic

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: DNS information leakage
answer: The DNS's wealth of organizational details and target lists that attackers gather data from, hard to control but best limited to gateway machines

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: TCP sequence number attack
answer: A spoofing attack exploiting insufficient randomness in TCP's initial sequence number generation, allowing source-address impersonation

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Human-propagated virus
answer: A message (often an urban legend) forwarded by people to friends with harmful removal advice, sometimes damaging systems of less knowledgeable users

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Virus scanner limitations
answer: Scanners must constantly update and now emulate code to detect viral behavior, as viruses hide better than static signature matching allows

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Targets of opportunity
answer: How viruses and worms infect any susceptible system encountered rather than targeting specific individuals or organizations

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: ICMP subnet mask reset
answer: An attack sending bogus ICMP messages that reset a host's subnet mask, questioning why hosts accept unsolicited configuration changes

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Routing protocol manipulation
answer: Playing games with routing protocols to deny a host communication with peers, not to penetrate but to disrupt service

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: DoS cost
answer: The assessable business loss when a public service is rendered unavailable, helping justify investment in mitigation

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Link-level flood threshold
answer: Less than 200 KB/second can flood a T1 link, making single-host link attacks feasible when the attacker's link is faster

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Cooperative flooding
answer: Multiple attackers each sending low-rate traffic whose combined sum exceeds the receiver's link capacity, as in DDoS attacks

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Anomaly detection products
answer: Commercial products that detect statistical anomalies in packet characteristics (random source IPs, low TTL) to drop attack traffic

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Shunning
answer: The practice of denying all access to someone, used by sites to cut off an entire offending university's access after too many compromised hosts

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: MIT shunning incident
answer: An event where so many hackers used MIT hosts that many sites refused to accept packets from the entire MIT network

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Legal spam recourse
answer: Court cases like CompuServe v. Cyber Promotions that bar spammers from ISP subscribers, requiring court-ordered ISP cooperation

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: International traceback
answer: The difficulty that international boundaries add to obtaining court orders for ISP cooperation when tracing spoofed attack sources

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Traceroute low TTL
answer: The observation that legitimate traceroutes also produce low TTL values, raising the question of whether to block those packets

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Zombie program binding
answer: The step in a DDoS attack where installed zombie code binds to a port and waits for instructions from the master program

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Master program
answer: A component the attacker installs somewhere on the Internet that holds the list of all zombie locations and relays target instructions

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Encrypted botnet C2
answer: The technique where master-to-bot communication is encrypted to avoid detection, used by advanced tools like Stacheldraht

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: IRC botnet control
answer: A communication method where botnets use IRC channels as command and control, leveraging existing mass-communication infrastructure

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Peer-to-peer botnet
answer: A decentralized botnet (like Slapper) where slave nodes form a P2P network to ease the master's communication burden

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Worm backdoor takeover
answer: Behavior of some worms that search for previously installed back doors and take over another attacker's existing bots

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Distributed vulnerability scanning
answer: Botnet activity using hundreds of compromised machines to probe for vulnerabilities instead of the attacker's own machine

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Distributed password cracking
answer: Speculated use of botnets for password-cracking or distributed cryptanalysis across a large population of compromised hosts

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Booby-trapped bot-builder
answer: A Trojan that tricks a person into thinking they are building their own botnet, when in fact their bots and machine join someone else's net

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Orange Book monoculture criticism
answer: The critique that the Orange Book assumed 1970s mainframes and did not address networking, viruses, or modern host environments

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Shadow file vulnerability
answer: Even with shadow files, if keys are derived from weak user passwords, dictionary attacks can still succeed (as shown by Kerberos experiments)

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: One-time password scheme
answer: An authentication using OTPs (e.g. S/key, described in Section 7.4) as an alternative to passwords, though susceptible to race attacks without challenge/response

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Password file theft services
answer: FTP, TFTP, mail, NIS, rsh, finger, uucp, and X11 were exploited to snatch password files from systems

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Shadow/adjunct file recommendation
answer: The strong recommendation to conceal hashed passwords from users via a shadow or adjunct password file when the system provides it

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Token-based authentication
answer: The best alternative to passwords, using hardware tokens or one-time passwords to eliminate static password vulnerabilities

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Guessable passphrase weakness
answer: A warning that one-time password schemes and tokens are still vulnerable if users choose guessable passphrases

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Password file concealment
answer: The vital step of keeping the password file out of enemy hands when users cannot be prevented from choosing bad passwords

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Information theory of passwords
answer: Using Shannon's information theory to measure password entropy in bits; English names give ~7.8 bits, phrases ~1.2-1.5 bits/letter

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: DOS attack obviousness
answer: DOS attacks are obvious and not subtle—easy to detect that a service is attacked, though the source may be hard to trace

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Attacker position requirement
answer: The attacker must be positioned on the network between communicating victims so they can see packets going by for an active attack

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: TCP stack complexity
answer: A typical TCP/IP implementation involves tens of thousands of lines of C code running in privileged space, making all bugs hard to debug

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Server code paranoia
answer: The first rule of writing network servers: be very paranoid, check all input, guard fixed-size buffers, prepare for memory exhaustion

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Input grammar definition
answer: The need for a precisely defined input syntax, achievable with compiler-writing tools (yacc/lex), so input can be checked for correctness

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Least privilege daemons
answer: The principle that network daemons should have no more power than they need; very few need to run as superuser, especially on firewalls

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Privileged front-end design
answer: A design where a small privileged program processes only USER/PASS commands, sets up environment, drops privileges, then execs the protocol handler

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Efficiency vs correctness
answer: The warning not to sacrifice verifiable correctness for efficiency—intrusion cleanup and outages cost more than extra hardware

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Protocol assumption failure
answer: Holes arise in cryptographic protocols often because of different assumptions made by the designers, not just simple mistakes

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: SSH authorized_keys trust
answer: The authorized_keys file in ~/.ssh/ lets a user with the private key log in without a password, but trust is granted per key

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: WEP design flaw
answer: The 802.11 WEP design problems demonstrate that security is hard to get right and engineers should consult cryptographers

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Cryptography amateurism
answer: The principle that cryptographic security is a specialized discipline not well suited to amateurs designing their own schemes

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Backscatter measurement
answer: Using unused network announcements (like AT&T's net 12.0.0.0/8) to catch random return packets and observe global DoS attack rates

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Moore et al. backscatter
answer: Research (Moore et al., 2001) that monitored backscatter to gain a global picture of DoS attack targets and prevalence rates

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Small telescope sampling
answer: Even small announced networks like a /28 (16 hosts) can get a representative sample of backscatter traffic for analysis

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Attackers avoiding telescopes
answer: Attackers may avoid return addresses from monitored networks, creating an arms race with distributed packet telescopes

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Court-ordered ISP cooperation
answer: Most ISPs will cooperate in traceback when served with a court order, though international boundaries complicate this

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Router config DoS command
answer: A hypothetical router command to stop forwarding packets that could itself become a DoS vector, requiring cryptographic signatures or rate limits

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Regular-user filtering
answer: Building a filter from monthly logs of legitimate users' addresses and ports to reject non-friend packets during an attack

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Filter tradeoffs
answer: Filters need not be perfect; sometimes letting 80% of users in rather than 0% during an attack is an acceptable business decision

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Capacity as primary remedy
answer: Increasing target CPU speed, memory, and link capacity is often the most effective but also the most expensive DoS mitigation

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: DoS after encryption
answer: Even after networks are encrypted, keys distributed, servers bug-free, hosts secure, and users authenticated, DoS attacks remain possible

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Kerberos password derivation
answer: Experiments with Kerberos show cryptography may not help if keys are derived from user-supplied passwords (Wu, 1999)

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: finger command info
answer: finger happily supplies personal information (room number, phone, hobbies) to callers, aiding password-cracking dictionaries

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Password reuse danger
answer: Because users reuse passwords, attackers who steal one password file try the cracked passwords on other machines

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Anonymous FTP exposure
answer: A defensive concern requiring that a genuine /etc/passwd file not be placed in the anonymous FTP area

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Password file logging
answer: A log of login failure usernames will invariably contain some passwords, so logs must be checked and protected

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Login attempt limits
answer: Few systems resist inside attacks; users should not get infinite login attempts and failures should be logged and reported

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Worm spread timeframe
answer: Worms can spread around the world within hours and potentially in a few minutes

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Melissa worm impact
answer: The Melissa worm clogged Microsoft-based e-mail in some companies for five days

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: IBM Christmas Card virus
answer: A 1987 bisync network virus that clogged IBM's internal network, one of the earliest large-scale incidents

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Windows monoculture
answer: Microsoft Windows systems have traditionally hosted the vast majority of viruses, though this is changing for Linux too

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Virus propagation methods
answer: Viruses and worms spread via popular monoculture, network access, Web pages, and e-mail

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Virus scanner arms race
answer: There is a constant arms race between virus writers and detection software companies as viruses get more sophisticated

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Virus hiding techniques
answer: Modern viruses become fantastically effective at hiding presence and activities, forcing emulation-based scanner detection

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Approved program execution
answer: It would be ideal to execute only approved, unmodified programs, though this is tied up with copyright protection politics

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: ICMP Destination Unreachable attack
answer: Bogus ICMP Destination Unreachable messages can disrupt host communications

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Attacker packet randomness
answer: Attack packets typically have spoofed random return IP addresses and lack the characteristics of normal, predictable traffic

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Bitmap network filter
answer: A 224-entry bitmap (or Bloom filter) of unassigned/unannounced networks can filter packets appearing to come from those nets

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Multicast net disabling
answer: Turning off all multicast networks is recommended to reduce the attack surface for spoofed addresses

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: BGP4 announced network filtering
answer: Using BGP4's list of announced networks to discard packets appearing to come from unannounced/never-external networks

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Random ping filtering
answer: Randomly pinging a small portion of incoming flow and rejecting packets from unresponsive nets is a possible but risky filtering technique

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Log-based user filtering
answer: Scanning logs to collect IP addresses and ports of regular users to build a friend-only filter that rejects non-friends

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Shunning technique
answer: Deny access entirely to someone, similar to how religious groups like the Amish enforce rules

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Panix attack mitigation
answer: Early on, the predictable TCP sequence number made filtering easy; attackers switched to random numbers, starting the arms race

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Router debugging impact
answer: Cisco IP DEBUG can match and print packets on busy routers but may hang the router under heavy load

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: ISP disconnection test
answer: An ISP can disconnect a major feed for a few seconds to see if the packet flow stops at the target, physically narrowing the source

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Route announcement hijack risk
answer: A cooperative ISP announcing a route to the attacked network can short-circuit packets but may itself become a DoS vector if misconfigured

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Cryptographic router command
answer: A router command to stop forwarding could need a cryptographic signature, or be rate-limited to one per few minutes, to prevent abuse

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Traffic aggregate identification
answer: Pushback routers identify aggregates of traffic responsible for congestion and drop them preferentially

source: Firewalls & Internet Security - Ch5: Classes of Attacks
question: Aggressive DoS future
answer: Well-prepared dissidents will orchestrate well-publicized attacks on popular targets like governments and companies for years to come
